Held, yes [Paras 34, 38 and 51] [In favour of revenue]

Section 45, read with  Section 2(47), of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Capital gains - Chargeable as - Whether reduction of share capital resulting in release of assets would attract capital gains in hands of shareholders - Held, yes - Whether, therefore, surplus resulting from surrender of shares in a company was liable to be taxed as capital gain in hands of assessee - Held, yes

Section 2(22) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 2(6A)(a) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Deemed dividend -  Assessment year 1956-57 - Whether expression "income" in entry 54 of List I of Seventh Schedule to Government of India Act, 1935, and corresponding entry 82 of List I of the Seventh Schedule to Constitution of India, shall be widely and liberally construed so as to enable a legislature to provide by law for prevention of evasion of income-tax but there must be a reasonable nexus between item taxed and legislative field delineated - Held, yes - Whether as section 2(6A)(d) of 1922 Act embodies a law to prevent evasion of tax, it falls within ken of entry 54 of List I of Schedule VII to Government of India Act, 1935 - Held, yes - Whether if accumulated profits were distributed, it would satisfy not only definition of 'dividend' in section 2(6A)(d) of 1922 Act but also would bix year in which it would be deemed to be income - Held, yes - Whether dividends may be paid or credited to different shareholders during different accounting years; and shareholders may be assessed in respect of the said payments in different years even so, payments are referable only to declaration of dividends out of profits of a particular year - Held, yes - Assessee company by sanction of High Court reduced its capital from Rs. 50 lakhs to Rs. 15 lakhs and got requisite certificate from Registrar of companies - Noties were issued to shareholders inviting applications for refund and after receipt of applications amounts payable to shareholders were debited in accounts and refunds were actually granted during accounting year 1955, i.e., between 1-12-1954, and 30-11-1955 - Whether amounts were distributed only during accounting year, when amounts were both debited and paid and, therefore, dividends were distributed to shareholders during accounting year, i.e., 1954-55 - Held, yes

Section 115-O, read with  section 246A of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Tax on distributed profits of certain distributed companies - Appellable orders (Scope of) - Assessee sought for an approval of scheme under sections 391 to 393 of Companies Act, 1956, involving purchase of shares from its shareholders - Scheme was approved by Court - In pursuance to same, assessee bought back shares from its shareholders and, accordingly, it was treated as capital gains - Respondent passed impugned order inter alia holding that transactions made in pursuant to buy back arrangement effected as a consequence to approval of Scheme required to be taxed under section 115-O on premise that it would constitute dividend and not capital gain - Against said order, assessee filed writ petition - Single Judge held that there was no merit in assessee's contention that shares purchased pursuant to order of Company Court would be a capital gain and not to be treated as dividend - He, however, dismissed assessee's petition with a liberty to them to file an appeal under section 246A in view of fact that assessee had already deposited a part of amount demanded - Whether, on facts, Single Judge was not right in going to merit while granting liberty to file an appeal - Held, yes - Whether, therefore, findings rendered by Single Judge on nature of transaction and scope under section 115-O were to be set aside - Held, yes - Whether, however, impugned order passed by Single Judge to extent that an appeal could be entertained and decided on merit was justified and, thus, same did not require any interference - Held, yes [Paras 10.4, 11 and 13][Partly in favour of assessee]INCOME TAX: Where there was dispute relating to taxability of transaction of buy back of shares from shareholders by assessee-company in terms of section 115-O, Single Judge while directing assessee to file an appeal before Commissioner (Appeals) under section 246A, was not justified in entering into merits of case so far as taxability under section 115-O was concerned

Section 45, read with section 2(47) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Capital gains - Chargeability of - When a company reduces its share capital by paying off a part of paid up capital in exercise of powers under section 100(1)(c) of the companies act, does it result in extinguishment of right of shareholders to the extent of reduction of face value of shares - Held, yes - Whether any profits or gains arising from such extinguishment are chargeable to income-tax under section 45 - held, yes

Section 271(1)(c) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Penalty - For concealment of income - Assessment year 1974-75 - Assessee-company, with permission of Calcutta High Court, in accordance with provisions of the Companies Act, reduced its share capital by cancelling specified number of fully paid-up equity shares - Assessing Officer was of view that reduction of share capital did not represent a loss incurred by assessee and, therefore, taxed that amount, which was upheld by Tribunal - Assessing Officer also levied penalty under section 271(1)(c) - Whether, on facts, Assessing Officer was justified - Held, no

Section 2(47), read with section 45, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Transfer - Whether reduction of share capital by company paying a part of capital by reducing face value of its share would result in extinguishment of proportionate right in shares held by shareholder so that amount paid by company to shareholder on reduction of share capital would be exigible to capital gains tax in hands of shareholder - Held, yes

Section 256, read with section 28(i) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Reference - Question, of law - Assessee-company held 25,000 shares of face value of Rs. 10 each in company H - Share capital of H was reduced as a result of an order of High Court to 20,000 shares - Revenue authorities including Tribunal disallowed assessee's claim for short-term capital loss of Rs. 5 lakhs - On assessee's application under section 256(1) Tribunal referred to High Court question as to whether assessee was entitled to claim a short-term capital loss of Rs. 5 lakhs on reduction of capital of H sanctioned by High Court - On application under section 256(2) assessee sought to raise certain other questions - Whether question referred by Tribunal was wide enough to cover entire controversy being raised by assessee - Held, on facts, yes

Section 2(22)(e) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deemed dividend - Whether in view of facts stated under head ‘Revision - Of orders prejudicial to interests of revenue’ and as well as facts that there was no reduction of share capital of H and that there was no distribution of shares by parent company, it could be said that case of assessee did not come within ambit of section 2(22) - Held, yes

Section 2(22) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 2(6A) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922], read with section 78 of the Companies Act, 1956 - Deemed dividend - Assessment year 1954-55 - Assessee-company held preference shares in 'R' company which had in year 1945 issued share at a premium and kept share premiums so received under head 'capital reserve' - Out of said capital reserve, 'R' company paid a sum as dividend to assessee - For relevant assessment year, ITO taxed said sum in hands of assessee as dividend with section 2(6A) of 1922 Act - Tribunal as well as High Court upheld ITO's order - Whether if a distribution of accumulated profits, whether capitalised or not, entails release by company to its shareholder of all or any part of its assets, it is dividend - Held, yes - Whether since it could not be said that premiums received by 'R' company were not profits within Regulation 97 of Table A of 1913 Act, ITO, therefore, rightly taxed sum received by assessee as dividend - Held, yes

Section 230 of the Companies Act, 2013 - Compromise and arrangement - A composite scheme of arrangement between petitioner companies was approved by NCLT - Income tax department opposed said scheme on ground that conversion of preference shares into loan would substantially reduce profitability of demerged company, which would act as a tool to avoid and evade taxes - NCLAT by impugned order held that without going to record and without placing any evidence to substantiate allegation by appearing before Tribunal, it was not open to Income-tax department to hold that overall scheme of arrangement was giving undue favour to shareholders of company and resulted into tax avoidance and approval by NCLT to such scheme was not to be interfered with - On appeal before Supreme Court, Joint Commissioner of Income-tax submitted that impugned orders and/or sanction of Scheme might come in way of Department while framing assessment and to that extent, interest of revenue would be affected - However, NCLT as well as NCLAT had already clarified that IT department would be entitled to take out appropriate proceedings for recovery of any tax statutorily due from transferor or transferee company or any other person who was liable for payment of such tax due - Whether therefore, impugned judgment and orders passed by NCLAT as well as NCLT approving scheme could not have been interfered with - Held, yes [Paras 5, 6 and 7]

Section 2(47),  read with section 45, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Transfer - Whether reduction of share capital by company paying a part of capital by reducing face value of its share would result in extinguishment of proportionate right in shares held by shareholder so that amount paid by company to shareholder on reduction of share capital would be exigible to capital gains tax in hands of shareholder - Held, yes

Section 2(45), read with section 56 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 (Corresponding to section 2(15), read with section 12 of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922) read with section 55 of the Super-tax Act, 1920 - Income, profits or gains - Meaning of - Company ‘D’ in which assessee-company was one of shareholders, by special resolution, decided to distribute its accumulated profits in form of additional shares to shareholders - Thus, existing capital of company ‘D’ was increased by creation of new shares which ranked pari passu in all respects with existing ordinary shares of company - Whether, on facts, assessee-company was liable to pay super-tax on value of shares newly issued by ‘D’ company - Held, no

Section 115QA of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Tax on distributed income to shareholders (General) - Assessment year 2017-18 - Whether prior to 1-6-2016 if company purchases its own shares in accordance with provisions of section 77A of Companies Act, such domestic companies were required to pay tax under section 115QA and after 1-6-2016 if company purchases its own shares in accordance with any of provisions of any law relating to companies, buyback tax liability would arise in hands of company - Held, yes - Assessee-company paid consideration for purchase of its own shares from its shareholders in accordance with scheme sanctioned by High Court - Such capital reduction of assessee had been completed on 31-5-2016 - Assessing Officer held that said payment would attract provisions of section 115QA and, accordingly, levied tax under section 115QA and treated assessee as assessee-in-default under section 115QC - Whether since assessee had carried out capital reduction under provisions of sections 100-104 of Companies Act, 1956 and same had been completed on 31-5-2016, capital reduction carried out by assessee would not be covered in definition of buyback as per Explanation (i) to section 115QA and tax on distributed income to shareholders was not payable by assessee-company - Held, yes [Paras 17 to 20 and 22] [In favour of assessee]

Section 115QA of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Tax on distributed income to shareholders (General) - Assessment year 2017-18 - Whether prior to 1-6-2016 if company purchases its own shares in accordance with provisions of section 77A of Companies Act, such domestic companies were required to pay tax under section 115QA and after 1-6-2016 if company purchases its own shares in accordance with any of provisions of any law relating to companies, buyback tax liability would arise in hands of company - Held, yes - Assessee-company paid consideration for purchase of its own shares from its shareholders in accordance with scheme sanctioned by High Court - Such capital reduction of assessee had been completed on 31-5-2016 - Assessing Officer held that said payment would attract provisions of section 115QA and, accordingly, levied tax under section 115QA and treated assessee as assessee-in-default under section 115QC - Whether since assessee had carried out capital reduction under provisions of sections 100-104 of Companies Act, 1956 and same had been completed on 31-5-2016, capital reduction carried out by assessee would not be covered in definition of buyback as per Explanation (i) to section 115QA and tax on distributed income to shareholders was not payable by assessee-company - Held, yes [Paras 17 to 20 and 22] [In favour of assessee]INCOME TAX : Where assessee-company paid consideration for purchase of its own shares from its shareholders in accordance with scheme sanctioned by High Court, since assessee had carried out capital reduction under provisions of sections 100-104 of Companies Act, 1956 and same had been completed on 31-5-2016 i.e. prior to 1-6-2016, capital reduction carried out by assessee would not be covered in definition of buyback as per explanation (i) to section 115QA and tax on distributed income to shareholders was not payable by assessee-company

Section 230 of the Companies Act, 2013 - Compromise and arrangement - A composite scheme of arrangement between petitioner companies was approved by NCLT - Income tax department opposed said scheme on ground that conversion of preference shares into loan would substantially reduce profitability of demerged company, which would act as a tool to avoid and evade taxes - NCLAT by impugned order held that without going to record and without placing any evidence to substantiate allegation by appearing before Tribunal, it was not open to Income-tax department to hold that overall scheme of arrangement was giving undue favour to shareholders of company and resulted into tax avoidance and approval by NCLT to such scheme was not to be interfered with - On appeal before Supreme Court, Joint Commissioner of Income-tax submitted that impugned orders and/or sanction of Scheme might come in way of Department while framing assessment and to that extent, interest of revenue would be affected - However, NCLT as well as NCLAT had already clarified that IT department would be entitled to take out appropriate proceedings for recovery of any tax statutorily due from transferor or transferee company or any other person who was liable for payment of such tax due - Whether therefore, impugned judgment and orders passed by NCLAT as well as NCLT approving scheme could not have been interfered with - Held, yes [Paras 5, 6 and 7]COMPANY LAW : Where IT department opposed composite scheme of arrangement of petitioner companies on ground that scheme was a tool to avoid and evade taxes, NCLT as well as NCLAT having clarified that IT department was entitled to take out appropriate proceedings for recovery of any tax statutorily due from transferor or transferee company or any other person who was liable for payment of such tax due, impugned judgment and orders passed by NCLAT as well as NCLT approving scheme could not have been interfered with

Section 66, read with section 421 of the Companies Act, 2013 - Share capital - Reduction of - Respondent company listed at Regional Stock Exchange was in process of exit in terms of SEBI's exit circular dated 30-5-2012 - In pursuance to said circular, Board of Directors of respondent company decided to pay off capital of non-promoter shareholders of company by providing exit to them - Subsequently, they filed an application under section 66(1) praying for reduction of share capital - Regional Director of Ministry of Corporate Affairs filed an affidavit to Tribunal with an observation that outgoing shareholders should have been paid as per NAV valuation only and not as per valuation, as arrived at by DCF method; that valuation of shares had not been done in consultation with designated stock exchange and that votes of public shareholders and promoters had not been counted separately which would have shown defeat of resolution passed on proposed reduction of shares capital - It was alleged that since Regional Director had not filed said affidavit within statutory time, Tribunal did not consider same while passing impugned order - Whether where affidavit by an important authority like Regional Director had been filed, public interest required to consider it and not ignore it on technicalities - Held, yes - Whether Tribunal should have given an opportunity to parties to make their submissions on said affidavit - Held, yes [Para 46]CL: Where in exit process of non-promoter shareholders, in respect of being of capital, Regional Director of Ministry of Corporate Affairs had belatedly filed affidavit raising objection about valuation of shares and validity of resolution passed on proposed reduction, it was to be considered in public interest

Section  115QA,  read with sections  56  and  36(1)(iii), of the Income-tax Act, 1961, and rule  11UA  of the Income-tax Rules, 1962 - Tax on distributed income in case of buy-back of shares (Illustrations) - Assessment year  2017-18  - Assessee-company bought back its equity shares pursuant to a High Court approved Scheme of Arrangement and no tax was paid under section 115QA - Case was selected for scrutiny and a survey under section 133A was conducted - Assessing Officer issued show-cause notices on (i) levy under section 115QA, (ii) addition under section 56(2)(viia), and (iii) disallowance of proportionate interest under section 36(1)(iii) - Assessing Officer held that buy-back attracted section 115QA notwithstanding recourse to a court-sanctioned scheme, computed distributed income and levied additional tax; he also made additions under section 56(2)(viia) and section 36(1)(iii) -  Commissioner(Appeals) sustained levy under section 115QA while deleting addition under section 56(2)(viia) and disallowance under section 36(1)(iii)  - It was observed that authorities below had not properly appreciated detailed NAV workings under rule 11UA, financial extracts showing availability of interest-free funds, judicial precedents cited before it, workings relating to section 77A ceiling on buy-back, and factual distinction between a court-approved scheme and a buy-back under section 77A - Whether, therefore, order of Commissioner(Appeals) was to be set aside and matter remitted to Assessing Officer for framing assessment de novo - Held, yes [Paras 29 and 30] [Matter remanded]

Section 2(47) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Transfer - Whether transaction of reduction of share capital by company and prorata distribution of amount/assets to shareholders amount to 'transfer' within meaning of section 2(47) - Held, yes

Section 2(22)  of the Income-tax Act, 1961  [Corresponding to section 2(6A) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Deemed dividend - On distribution of assets of certain company including house and buildings amongst shareholders on 19-4-1947, profit balance including depreciation reserve shown in balance-sheet as on 31-3-1947 was held by income-tax authority to be distributed as accumulated profits within meaning of section 2(6A)  - Company’s balance sheet showed that it had created a depreciation found, which meant that year by year a portion of profit had been set apart to agument that fund - This found was created out of capital - Whether, in view of above, Tribunal was not justified in excluding depreciation reserve in determining profits of company to be treated as having been distributed as dividend under section 2(6A) as a result of transfer of assets - Held, yes

Section 2(22)  of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 2(6A) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Deemed dividend - Assessment year 1941-42 - Assessee was a shareholder of a company - He filed return of his income which included a sum said to be dividend received from company - ITO discovered that said sum had not been paid to assessee in cash but represented nominal value of certain bonus shares allotted to him - Company had, of course, paid income - tax on said amount at a higher rate - Consequently, assessee sought to recover difference between amount of tax company had paid and what he would have paid if tax had been levied according to rate appropriate to his income - Revenue authorities rejected assessee’s claim - Whether since bonus shares received by shareholders including assessee represented capitalisation of profits by company, in such circumstances, there had been no release of assets of company to shareholders - Held, yes - Whether, therefore, bonus shares received by assessee would not represent his dividend income, and, consequently, authorities below rightly rejected assessee’s claim - Held, yes

Section 45 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Capital gains - Chargeable as - Assessment year 1997-98 - Assessee-company started a Panasonic Division in collaboration with a foreign company M in 1993 for manufacture of colour television sets - During relevant accounting year, assessee decided to spin off aforesaid Division to company M - Under scheme of arrangement as approved by High Court, shareholders of assessee were entitled to claim from company M, two equity shares of Rs. 10 each credited as fully paid - Accordingly, out of total consideration of Rs. 50.12 crores, assessee received sale consideration of Rs. 32.48 crores and Rs. 17.64 crores was value of shares allotted to shareholders of assessee - Whether once scheme of arrangement was approved by High Court, it acquired statutory recognition - Held, yes - Whether amount given to shareholders of assessee was diversion of amount at source and it could not be said to be  an application of income in hands of assessee and, thus, it would be outside scope of computation of capital gains - Held, yes

II. Section 2(22) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deemed dividend (Sub-clause (d)) - Assessment years 2009-10 and 2010-11 - Assessee had issued 0.5 per cent redeemable non-cumulative preference shares to its AE, APFI - During relevant assessment year, assessee redeemed some of preference shares at a premium based on valuation done by expert valuer by adopting Net Asset Value (NAV) method - Assessing Officer computed value of preference shares and made addition on account of difference between actual premium and premium as computed by Assessing Officer - Assessing Officer stated that as per India-Singapore DTAA, capital gain arising to resident of Singapore from alienation of shares in Indian company would be taxable only in Singapore and, therefore, proceeded to make addition under section 93 - On appeal, Commissioner (Appeals) held that addition made by Assessing Officer under section 93 could not survive - However, Commissioner (Appeals) retained addition by stating that excess premium paid by assessee on redemption of preference shares would constitute deemed dividend under section 2(22) - Whether sub-clause (d) of section 2(22) is applicable when there is any distribution by company to its shareholders on reduction of its capital and in order to attract clause (d), payment should be by way of advance or loan to a shareholder, being a person who is beneficial owner of shares - Held, yes - Whether since in given case, payment made by assessee towards premium on redemption of preference shares was neither towards reduction of share capital nor towards advance or loan, excess premium paid to AE on redemption of preference shares could not be taxed under section 2(22)(d) - Held, yes [Para 24] [In favour of assessee]

Part II of the Schedule to the Finance Act, 1956, read with section 104 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 23A of the Income-tax Act, 1922] - Rates of super-tax - Assessment year 1956-57 - Whether merely because an amount is deemed to have been notionally distributed, it could not be said that such amount is, therefore, incapable of being subsequently distributed as dividend - Held, yes - Whether fiction created by section 23A of 1922 Act which is intended for taxing income in hands of shareholders cannot be extended when taxing income of a company - Held, yes - Assessee company distributed by way of dividends during relevant accounting year amounts that exceeded six per cent of its paid up capital - Amount distributed was made up of profits of earlier years in respect of which provisions of section 23A of 1922 Act were applied - Whether merely because distribution had taken place out of profits of previous years, it could not be said that distribution had not been made during relevant accounting year 1955 in which said amounts had been distributed - Held, yes - Whether distribution in question fell within meaning of clause I(b) of second proviso to paragraph D of Part II of Schedule to Finance Act, 1956 and, therefore, ITO was justified in reducing rebate allowable to assessee-company under clause (ii) of proviso 1 to paragraph D thereof - Held, yes - Whether distribution of dividend in accounting year 1955 was also not saved by orders of ITO under section 23A of 1922 Act in respect of profits of earlier years - Held, yes

Section 230 of the Companies Act, 2013 - Compromise and arrangement -  A composite scheme of arrangement between petitioner companies was approved by NCLT - Income tax department opposed said scheme on ground that conversion of preference shares into loan would substantially reduce profitability of demerged company which would act as a tool to avoid and evade taxes - Whether without going to record and without placing any evidence to substantiate allegation by appearing before Tribunal, it was not open to Income-tax department to hold that composite scheme of arrangement amongst petitioner companies and their respective shareholders and creditors was giving undue favour to shareholders of company and also overall scheme of arrangement resulted into tax avoidance - Held, yes - Whether since in view of decision of Supreme Court in Department of Income-tax v. Vodafone Essar Gujarat Ltd. [2016] 66 taxmann.com 374 liberty was given to Income-tax department to take out appropriate proceedings for recovery of any tax statutorily due from transferor or transferee company or any other person who was liable for payment of such tax due, scheme of arrangement as approved by NCLT was not to be interferred with - Held, yes [Paras 36, 39 and 40]COMPANY LAW : Where IT department opposed composite scheme of arrangement of petitioner companies on ground that scheme was a tool to avoid and evade taxes, approval by NCLT to such scheme was not interferred with as IT department was entitled to take out appropriate proceedings for recovery of any tax statutorily due from transferor or transferee company or any other person who was liable for payment of such tax due

II Section 56 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Income from other sources - Chargeable as (Buyback of shares) - Assessment year 2011-12 - During relevant assessment year, assessee-company bought its own share from its parent company - Market value, applying rule 11UA of such shares purchased was found to be Rs. 115.59 whereas assessee-company purchased it for Rs. 89 per share - Assessing Officer invoked provisions of section 56(2)(viia) and treated difference in price as deemed income under head 'Other Sources' - Whether provisions of section 56(2)(viia), can be invoked only where assessee receives a property for an inadequate consideration - Held, yes - Whether since in instant case, assessee-company only brought back its own shares from its shareholder and there was reduction of share capital by such buyback hence, this would not tantamount to purchase or acquire of any property as envisaged under section 56(2)(viia) - Held, yes - Whether therefore, arguments made by revenue i.e., assessee had earned hidden asset, could not be agreed with as on issue of buyback of shares, assessee had not acquired any share of any other company which would become property of recipient company and it would be reduction in capital and nothing more - Held, yes [Para 9.1] [In favour of assessee]

Section 66 of the Companies Act, 2013/Section 100 of the Companies Act, 1956 - Share capital - Reduction of - Whether before a Court can decline sanction to a scheme of reduction on account of a valuation, an objector to scheme must first show that valuation is ex-facie unreasonable - Held, yes - Whether sanctioning Court has no power or jurisdiction to exercise any appellate functions over scheme; it is not a valuer and it does not have necessary skills or expertise - Held, yes - Whether Court cannot substitute its own opinion for that of shareholders, its jurisdiction is peripheral and supervisory, not appellate - Held, yes - Whether it is impossible to say which of several available valuation models are 'best' or most appropriate - Held, yes - Whether no valuation is to be disregarded merely because it has used one or other of various methods; it must be shown that chosen method of valuation is such as has resulted in an artificially depressed or contrived valuation well below what a fair-minded person may consider reasonable - Held, yes - Whether where in proposed scheme of reduction of share capital of Cadbury India valuation of shares was done by Court appointed valuer and was accepted by overwhelming majority including a bulk of non-promoter minority, scheme was to be sanctioned - Held, yes [Paras 7.1.5, 7.1.7, 7.1.9, 7.1.11  8.1]CL: To disregard a method of valuation of shares in scheme of reduction, it must be shown that chosen method of valuation is such as has resulted in an artificially depressed or contrived valuation well below what a fair-minded person may consider reasonable

Section 46, read with section 158BB, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Capital gains - Distribution of assets by companies in liquidation - Block period from 1-4-1989 to 8-12-1999 - ‘S’ Group was engaged in business of manufacturing aluminium, copper telephone cables, etc. - Two main companies of ‘S’ Group were SIIL and MALCO - Assessee-company was one of three investment companies which were holding shares in SIIL and MALCO - Shares of SIIL and MALCO were held by assessee as investments till 31-3-1991 - However, with effect from 1-4-1991, holding in said two companies were converted into stock-in-trade but again on 31-3-1998, said shares were converted into investments - Said aspects were duly disclosed by assessee in return of income filed for assessment year 1998-99 and accepted by department - Subsequently, in April, 1999 assessee-company was liquidated and shares of SIIL and MALCO held by assessee were transmitted to TSHL, a Mauritian Company - Thereafter, a search was carried out at various offices and factories of ‘S’ group of companies and also at residences of key individuals of group including assessee - On basis of documents seized,  Assessing Officer concluded that conversion of stock-in-trade into investment was a well-planned and a calculated mode to avoid payment of tax which assessee would otherwise had to pay on liquidation - He, therefore, levied tax under section 46(2) and made certain addition to income of assessee - On appeal, Commissioner (Appeals) held that in course of regular assessment proceedings, Assessing Officer had himself accepted conversion and he could not change his stand in block assessment proceedings - He, therefore, held that said shares were truly investment and not stock-in-
 trade and, hence, assessee was not required to pay tax under section 46(2), thereby deleting said addition - Whether Commissioner (Appeals) was fully justified in deleting said addition - Held, yes

Section 45 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Capital gains - Chargeable as - Assessment year 1997-98 - Assessee-company started a Panasonic Division in 
 collaboration with a foreign company M in 1993 for manufacture of colour television sets - During relevant accounting year, assessee decided to spin off aforesaid Division to company M - Under scheme of arrangement as approved by High Court, shareholders of assessee were entitled to claim from company M, two equity shares of Rs. 10 each credited as fully paid - Accordingly, out of total consideration of Rs. 50.12 crores, assessee received sale consideration of Rs. 32.48 crores and Rs. 17.64 crores was value of shares allotted to shareholders of assessee - Whether once scheme of arrangement was approved by High Court, it acquired statutory recognition - Held, yes - Whether amount given to shareholders of assessee was diversion of amount at source and it could not be said to be an application of income in hands of assessee and, thus, it would be outside scope of computation of capital gains - Held, yes

Section 66 of the Companies Act, 2013 - Share capital - Reduction of - Applicant, a public company was registered in Regional Stock Exchange (RSE) - As per instructions of SEBI on Exit Circulars, Board of Directors of respondent-company decided to pay off capital of non-promoter shareholders by providing an exit to them - Company filed a petition seeking confirmation of reduction of share capital - One 'D', being a shareholder, along with four other objected to said scheme of reduction - They alleged that net asset value and discounted cash flow methods had not been employed to arrive value of shares; votes of public shareholders and promoters had not been counted separately which would have shown defeat of resolution passed on proposed reduction; valuation of shares had not been done in consultation with designated stock exchange - Whether discounted free cash flow method was one of recognized fair value method which was in consonance with International Financial Reporting Standards which Ministry of Corporate Affairs also acknowledged, thus, any method of fair valuation could be used as long as there was no inherent defect in mode of valuation - Held, yes - Whether section 66 does not make any distinction between number of public and promoter shareholders who have cast their votes for and against resolution - Held, yes - Whether on different dates three letters had been sent to NSE but, company had not received any objections from NSE to methodology of exit opportunity given by company - Held, yes - Whether thus, proposed reduction of share capital was not contrary to any regulations - Held, yes - Whether therefore, objections raised by objectors was to be rejected - Held, yes - Whether prayers sought for, was to be confirmed - Held, yes [Para 22]CL: Section 66 does not make any distinction between number of public and promoter shareholders who have cast their votes for and against resolution

Section 48 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Capital gains - Computation of - Assessment year 1971-72 - Assessee was a shareholder of company - Company effected reduction of paid-up capital and as a result assessee was entitled to Rs. 1,06,650 - Company paid Rs. 60,683 in cash and in lieu of Rs. 45,967 properties of company valued at book value was given to assessee - Market value of properties was Rs. 5,29,754 - Assessee sold one of property whose market value was Rs. 75,000 - Whether value of asset shown at the time of its transfer to present assessee should be the proper value for purpose of determining capital gains tax and not market value of said asset - Held, yes - Whether there would be no justification for holding any other value except one which has been shown in resolution of company transferring property as value of acquisition of asset - Held, yes

Section 48 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Capital gains - Computation of - Assessment year 1971-72 - Assessee was a shareholder of company - Company effected reduction of paid-up capital and as a result assessee was entitled to Rs. 106,650 - Company paid Rs. 60,683 in cash and in lieu of Rs. 45,967 properties of company valued at book value was given to assessee - Market value of properties was Rs. 5,29,754 - Assessee sold one of property whose market value was Rs. 75,000 - Whether value of asset shown at the time of its transfer to present assessee should be the proper value for purpose of determining capital gains tax and not market value of said asset - Held, yes -Whether there would be no justification for holding any other value except one which has been shown in resolution of company transferring property as value of acquisition of asset - Held, yes

Section 66, read with sections 397 and 398 of the Companies Act, 2013 - Share capital - Reduction of - Original petitioner held shares in applicant company and filed a petition under sections 397 and 398 against applicant company alleging oppression and mismanagement in company - NCLT directed applicant company to purchase shares held by original petitioner at determined value with 9 per cent interest per annum - Later, both original petitioner and the company appealed to NCLAT, which directed company to purchase shares and lowered interest rate - In meantime, original petitioner passed away and his legal heirs were substituted - R1, son of original petitioner, filed a probate suit on basis of will executed by original petitioner in favour of R1, which was granted in his favor, leading to transmission of shares to them - Applicant company then agreed to a settlement with R1, where they would pay Rs. 4.27 crores to R1 for reduction and cancellation of shares and payment would extinguish all disputes and claims against company and its directors - Whether since, Company Law Board (CLB) order did not provide for reduction of share capital and did not find case of oppression and mismanagement, NCLT could not order for reduction of share capital - Held, yes - Whether if applicant Company wanted to have reduction of share capital, then notice to other shareholders, creditors, Central Government (RD/ RoC) and such other authorities, as may have been required keeping in view facts and circumstances, should have been issued with a prayer to CLB originally and not at this stage and, that too on basis of settlement agreement at behest of shareholder, who had been allowed to have exit route from applicant company by his shareholding - Held, yes - Whether, therefore, application was to be dismissed - Held, yes [Paras 13 and 14]

Section 19, read with section 18, of the Sick Industrial Companies (Special Provisions) Act, 1985 - Rehabilitation by giving financial assistance - Plaintiff company was declared sick by BIFR and accordingly, scheme was sanctioned for its revival, which was subsequently approved by AAIFR - In process of revival, AAIFR also allowed reduction of share capital of plaintiff company by 99 per cent - Subsequently, plaintiff received a letter from defendant, wife of one of its shareholders, informing death of her husband with a request to transfer his standing shares to defendant and further requested to issue duplicate share certificate - Plaintiff forwarded duplicate certificates recording name of defendant as shareholder of 50 shares of face value of Re.1 each in lieu of 500 shares held by defendant's deceased husband - Defendant refused to accept said certificates and demanded that 500 shares of face value of Rs. 10 should be issued and thereafter, filed a complaint before SEBI alleging fraud by plaintiff - This prompted plaintiff to file instant suit for a declaration that paid up share capital of company stood reduced by order of AAIFR and, thus, defendant was entitled only to reduced number of shares - A consequential relief of permanent injunction restraining defendant from claiming any share in excess of 50 shares had also been sought for - It was noted that under provisions of Specific Relief Act, 1963, declaration is ordinarily granted in respect of crystallized rights - Whether since in instant case rehabilitation scheme, which permitted reduction of share capital was in operation at time when suit was instituted and had not been successfully implemented, right as to reduction of share capital in favour of plaintiff had not been crystallized and, thus, plaintiff's right to claim a declaration that defendant was entitled only to reduced number of shares could not be granted - Held, yes - Whether consequential injunction could not also be granted in facts of case - Held, yes - Whether instant suit was accordingly dismissed - Held, yes [Paras 21 and 22]FEMA, BANKING  INSURANCE : Where AAIFR allowed scheme for revival of plaintiff company and said scheme was in operation, reduction of share capital allowed under said scheme, would crystallize only on scheme being successfully worked out and, thus, plaintiff's right to claim a declaration that shareholder was entitled only to reduced number of shares could not be granted

Section 48 of the Income-tax Act, 1961, read with sections 18, 17 and 22A, of the Sick Industrial Companies (Special Provisions) Act, 1985 - Capital gains - Computation of (Shares) - BIFR declared assessee-company as a sick industrial company within meaning of section 3(1)(o) and appointed Central Bank of India as operating agency to prepare a rehabilitation package for company - Draft rehabilitation scheme was approved by BIFR - Said scheme had set out reliefs and concessions to be provided by Income Tax Department (ITD) - Assessee inter alia, sought an additional relief from ITD in respect of sale of shares, which were gifted by promoters of company as a part of their promoters' contribution, which had resulted in capital gains, chargeable to income tax - Said request was opposed by ITD on ground that it had granted all reliefs and concession as envisaged in scheme - However, BIFR had modified said scheme, requiring ITD to consider grant of further additional concession - High Court noted that obligation to extend further concessions could not be imposed on Central Government without its consent and that since ITD had not consented for extending any further concession , order requiring ITD to consider grant of further concessions, could not be interpreted as making it obligatory on ITD to grant such concessions and further, BIFR's order did not indicate that it had examined transactions, which had led to capital gains arising in hands of company or context in which additional concessions were sought - High Court held that ITD was not required to grant any further concession contrary to IT Act, to company and, thus, impugned order could not be sustained and was to be set aside - Whether SLP was to be granted against order of High Court - Held, yes [Para 2] [In favour of assessee]INCOME TAX/COMPANY LAW : SLP granted against order of High Court that BIFR cannot sanction any modification to scheme requiring income-tax department to give further tax concessions without department consenting to grant such additional concessions

Section 101 of the Companies Act, 1956 - Reduction of share capital - Application to Tribunal for confirming order, objections by creditors, and settlement of list of objecting creditors Principles to be observed in reduction of share capital Khattar Electrical Engg. & General Supply Co. Ltd., In re [1938] 8 Comp. Cas. 314 (Peshawar) The authorities lay down the following principles : (i) That a company has the power to reduce its capital, much more so if the power is conferred by the articles of association; (ii) Subject to confirmation by the Court which is the safeguard of the minority, the question of reducing capital is a domestic one for the decision of the majority; (iii) The company is to determine the extent, the mode and incidence of the reduction; (iv) The company may reduce the share capital of all its shareholders pro rata or may reduce the shares of any individual shareholder or any class of shareholders wholly or in part; (v) That the Court has to see that interests of the minority have been protected and no unfairness has been shown to it; and (vi) That in doing so the Court should keep in view the consideration that the decision has been arrived at by businessmen who are fully cognizant of their necessities and are the best custodians of their interests, and should therefore be slow to interfere. The assets of the company were found to be overvalued with the result that heavy depreciation was charged thereon leaving no surplus to be declared as dividend. It was suggested that by reducing the value of assets with consequent reduction of capital the amount of depreciation would be reduced, enabling dividend to be declared. The shareholding of one particular shareholder was reduced more than the reduction effected in the shareholding of other members on the ground that he owed substantial money to the company which he had taken as loan and was unable to pay and there was very little likelihood of such a large amount being realised from his assets. The amount becoming due to him by way of reduction of share capital was thus proposed to be adjusted against his loan. Held that the reduction was to be approved.

Section 2(22)  of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 2(6A) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Deemed dividend - Assessment year 1950-51 - Whether accumulated profits referred to in sub-clause (c) of section 2(6A) of 1922 Act are profits made by company before it went into liquidation, and as that expression stands it can only mean accumulated profits which have not been capitalized  because, once accumulated profits are capitalized in ordinary law they would cease to be profits which are capable of being distributed as dividend - Held, yes - Assessee was a shareholder of a company - By a resolution dated 5-12-1946, company converted partly paid up shares into fully paid up shares by transferring certain amount out of its undistributed profits - Company went into liquidation on 5-1-1949 - Assessee received a dividend from liquidator in year of account, and Taxing Department held that said dividend was covered by definition of “dividend” in section 2(6A)(c) of 1922 Act, and, therefore, liable to tax - Whether sum in question ceased to be accumulated profits when it was transferred to capital account, and same constituted capital of company and was no longer profits which was capable of being distributed as dividends - Held, yes

Section 220 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Collection and recovery of tax - When tax payable and when assessee deemed in default (Stay) - Assessment year 2017-18 - Assessee paid consideration to buy back its own shares and claimed that consideration paid would be taxable as capital gains under section 46A in hands of shareholders - Assessing Officer communicated on 22-3-2018, that assessee was required to pay DDT under section 115-O as consideration was paid out of reserves/accumulated profits – On 3-4-2018, Commissioner (Appeals) passed an interim order on basis of which assessee paid a sum of Rs. 495 crores in cash and made a fixed deposit of Rs. 2806 crores by way of security - It was noted that money held by revenue by way of TDS and interim order of Commissioner (Appeals) was more than 20 per cent of disputed demand - Furthermore, said amount was lying with revenue for more than four years without any utilisation - Whether since said issue was already decided by Supreme Court where it was held that communication by Assessing Officer was to be treated as show cause notice and not demand, and amount deposited by assessee as per interim order was subject to decision of concerned authority, Commissioner (Appeals) was directed to pass appropriate order with respect to stay of demand and lift lien with regard to balance deposits of assessee in excess of 20 per cent of disputed demand - Held, yes [Para 20] [In favour of assessee]INCOME TAX : Where on basis of interim order of Commissioner (Appeals), assessee paid certain sum in cash and made a fixed deposit by way of security, since said sum along with TDS amount held by revenue amounted to more than 20 per cent of disputed demand which was lying with revenue for more than four years without any utilisation, Commissioner (Appeals) was directed to pass appropriate order with respect to stay of demand and lift lien with regard to balance deposits of assessee

Section 2(22), read with section 2(24) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 2(6A), read with section 2(6C) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Deemed dividend - Assessment year 1952-53 - Excess of compensation over cost received by certain mills on acquisition by Government of Land and Building owned by it which was initially transferred to capital reserve accounts was distributed to shareholders including assessees - Amount so received on distribution was treated as ‘dividend’ within meaning of section 2(6A) and brought to tax in assessee’s hands - Whether though compulsory acquisition by Government may not constitute sale, it would still be ‘transfer’ and profit obtained by transferor on such transfer would be capital gains - Held, yes - Whether distribution by mills entailed release of part of its assets and, thus, fell within terms of section 2(6A)(a), and it could not be regarded as ‘dividend’, as profit which mills made on account of sale of land and building was capital gain arising after 31-3-1948 and, therefore, excluded from expression ‘accumulated profits’ for purpose of clause (6A) and thus from category of ‘dividend’, mentioned in sub-clause (a) of said clause (6A) - Held, yes - Whether in view of above, amount received by assessees was not taxable as dividends - Held, yes

Section 2(22)(d) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deemed dividend - Assessment year 1974-75 - Whether entire amount received by shareholder on purchase by company of shares pursuant to scheme of reduction of capital would constitute divided under section 2(22) without deducting face value of shares - Held, yes

facts.text:
The assessee was shareholder of a company ‘R’ which had substantial reserve, passed a resolution for capitalising the sum standing to the credit of the reserve funds and the capitalized fund was to be distributed amongst the members of the company ‘R’ in effect as bonus shares. On the next day the company ‘R’ resolved to purchase shares in the company ‘A’ out of its capitalized reserve. Later on the company ‘R’ resolved to reduce its capital by returning to the shareholders the shares in the company ‘A’ and this resolution was confirmed by an order of the District Court. As a result of this resolution, certain shares in the Company A were allotted to the assessee. The view which the ITO took was that the whole transaction by the company ‘R’ for the increase and subsequent decrease of its capital and purchase and distribution of company ‘A’ shares was illusory, and that accordingly he could treat the company ‘A’ shares allotted to the assessee as never having become capital, but as their representing profits of the company ’R’. Both the Assistant Commissioner and commissioner agreed with the decision of the ITO

On reference:

The assessee was a shareholder of the company, ‘AIPL’. During the previous year relevant to the assessment year under consideration, AIPL had effected reduction of its share capital from Rs. 100 per equity share to Rs. 45 per equity share. Before this reduction of capital, there had been two amalgamations where other companies of the same group, including some wholly-owned subsidiaries of AIPL, had amalgamated with AIPL. On account of amalgamation, equity shares of AIPL were issued in exchange of shares of subsidiaries and, thus, surplus was capitalised. Further, the subsidiaries held shares of each other which were cancelled on amalgamation and the surplus arising in the process was christened as capital reserve account No. 1. Next, excess of distribution over the book value of the shares of certain wholly-owned subsidiaries was received from liquidators of those subsidiaries which was entered in the books as capital reserve account No. 2. During the assessment proceedings, the Assessing Officer held that the capitalised part of the share capital of AIPL and the above said two reserve accounts were accumulated profit within the meaning of section 2(22)(d). He worked out accumulated profit of AIPL by further including proportionate current year profit of the company, provision for taxation included in debit balance of P&L Account and existing tax liability raised by the income-tax authorities but disputed by the company and not provided in books. The Assessing Officer, accordingly, concluded that the payment of Rs. 55 per share was out of accumulated profits and taxed the amount of distribution as deemed dividend. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) worked out the accumulated profits at a negative figure and, hence, held that distribution made by the company to its shareholders on reduction of share capital did not attract provisions of section 2(22)(d). He further held that since the company had not received any amount in excess of what was paid for acquiring the share, no capital gains tax was leviable in the matter.

On appeal by the revenue :

The assessee-company reduced its share capital and, in consequence, it became liable to pay a sum of Rs. 2,01,500 to the shareholders. To discharge that liability, the assessee-company distributed to the shareholders certain shares held by it in two companies. At the time of distribution of these shares, the assessee revalued those shares and the difference between the book value of the said shares and their market value was Rs. 56,181 as per the assessee's own balance sheet. This amount was shown as capital reserve arising on revaluation of investment at market value. Treating the difference between the market value of the shares and their book value as capital gains, the Commissioner directed the ITO under section 263 to bring to tax such difference to capital gains. On appeal, the Tribunal held that there was no transfer of shares from the assessee-company to its shareholders and as such there was no liability to pay capital gains tax on the part of the assessee.

On reference, the assessee contended that there was only transfer of shares at the book value and there was no question of those shares being transferred at the market value and only if the shares had been transferred at the market value, the question of capital gains arising out of the transfer will arise.

On the orders of the High Court as a consequence of the take-over by the State of the assessee’s business of generation and supply of electricity, the share capital of the assessee-company was substantially reduced, and the company distributed the amounts in cash to its shareholders in consequence of such reduction. The ITO having found accumulated profits, regarded the distribution as dividend to the extent of the accumulated profits. He, concluded that since no part of these profits were allowed to have arisen before 1-4-1933, the company would be deemed to have declared dividend in the assessment year 1957-58 under section 2(6A)(d). Tax was calculated accordingly. On appeal, the two contentions namely, (a) that the definition in clause (d) of section 2(6A) means a distribution out of the accumulated profits and not any distribution on the reduction of its capital; and (b) that the distribution in clause (c) of the second proviso to paragraph ‘D’ of the Finance (No. 2) Act, 1957, means actual distribution and did not include notional distribution, were dismissed by the AAC as without merit. On second appeal, the Tribunal observed that section 2(6A)(d) is general and applied to any distribution by the company on the reduction of its capital to the extent to which the company possessed accumulated profits and it did not matter whether the reduction of capital was bona fide or with a view to avoidance of super-tax by the shareholder. However, it opined that the rebate allowable to the assessee could not be withdrawn under the terms of the second proviso to Para D of the 1957 Act, and that the assessee being a company in which public are not substantially interested the rebate admissible was 20 per cent as mentioned in clause (iii) of the first proviso, and there was no question of any further withdrawal of the rebate.

On reference :

The share capital of assessee-company was reduced from Rs. 50 lakhs to Rs. 15 lakhs which was sanctioned by High Court, and on 4-11-1954, the Registrar of Joint Stock Companies issued a certificate under section 61(4) of the Indian Companies Act, 1913. On 5-11-1954, the company issued notice to the shareholders inviting applications for the refund of the share capital so reduced and the necessary funds were distributed between 1-12-1954 and 30-11-1955. The assessment year in this case was 1956-57 and the accounting year ended on 30-11-1955. All the shares of this company were fully paid. According to the findings of the Income-tax Officer the accumulated profits of the assessee at the time of reduction of capital to Rs. 15 lakhs were Rs. 8,42,337 in the form of different reserves. The ITO also held that the assessee had actually distributed dividends of Rs. 1,06,250. The ITO required the assessee to explain why the distribution on the reduction of its share capital to the extent to which the company possessed accumulated profits to be not treated as distribution on account of dividend in accordance with section 2(6A)(d). As regards the item of 'reserve for taxation', the ITO held that the whole amount should be treated as a reserve within the meaning of the proviso to section 23A(1), but the AAC took the view that only the difference between the amount set apart to provide for taxation less the actual tax payable would be the amount which could be said to be the 'reserve'. As soon as the resolution was passed capitalising the reserves, such reserves became capital and could not afterwards be dealt with by the company as income; and subsequently, when the capital was reduced, - which was in the next year, - and part of the proceeds of the capitalised reserves was handed back to the shareholders, that part could only be handed back in the form in which it existed, namely, capital. Per Rangnekar, J. [Concurrent view]

It is perfectly competent to a joint stock company to convert its surplus profits into capital and give the benefit of such conversion to the shareholders in any manner, either by the issue of new shares as bonus shares or by the issue of debentures, or in cash there was no evidence before the Income-tax authorities that the various transactions, which resulted in the transfer of shares in the company A, to the assessee, were illusory. A company, however, is incapable of having any intention. The intention must be of the share-holders, who are the masters of the Company. But assuming that the motive of the Managing Agents of the Company and of the shareholders was to escape super-tax,-and that seemed to be the ground on which the opinion of the Income-tax authorities was based -, the consideration of such a question was entirely irrelevant and immaterial in construing the legal effect of the transfer of undivided profits to the shareholders by way of capital.

Regarding the provision for taxation included in debit balance of P&L account and existing tax liability raised by the IT authorities but disputed by the assessee and not provided in the books, the accumulated profits are to be construed as commercial profits for the purposes of section 2(22). In the absence of specific reserves for taxation created by the company those liabilities might have to be met from the general reserves. In such circumstances to take the figure of general reserve from the balance sheet for ascertaining the accumulated profits would not be a correct procedure for the quantum of the general reserves would not represent the accumulated profits. Having regard to the aforesaid reasons, deduction was liable to be made for ascertaining accumulated profits.

However, the accumulated profit worked out in this way being a negative figure, it could not be said that the company possessed accumulated profits and, hence, provisions of section 2(22) were not applicable.

As regards the issue of levy of capital gains, the Commissioner (Appeals) had held against levy of capital gains without discussing facts and issues involved and without indicating reasons in support of his finding in the impugned order.

The basic issue for the purposes of levy of capital gains is whether reduction of share capital by a company results in extinguishment of rights in shares held by shareholders covered by the expression ‘transfer’ as defined in section 2(47). When a company reduces its share capital by paying off a part of the capital thereby reducing the face value of the shares, the share remains but the right of the shareholder to dividend of his share capital and the right to share is extinguished proportionately to the extent of reduction in capital. In the instant case, the Assessing Officer had no occasion to consider the issue of levy of capital gains under section 45 as a result of reduction of share capital since he came to the conclusion that accumulated profits possessed by the company exceeded the distribution made to the shareholders on reduction of share capital. While reversing the conclusion of the Assessing Officer and deleting the addition on account of dividend under section 2(22)(a) the Commissioner (Appeals) did not apply his mind to the issue of levy of capital gains under section 45, particularly since the distribution made by the company on reduction of share capital had been treated as transfer by the Supreme Court in the various decisions. In the circumstances the issue of levy of capital gains was set aside to the file of the Assessing Officer with the direction that the issue of levy of capital gains might be re-examined by him.

By using the expression 'whether capitalised or not', the legislative intent clearly is that the profits which are deemed to be dividend would be those which were capable of being accumulated and which would also be capable of being capitalised. This would clearly exclude return of a part of the capital by the company from section 2(22), as the same cannot be regarded as profits capable of being capitalised, the return being of the capital itself. Thus, the amount distributed by a company on reduction of its share capital has two components-distribution attributable to accumulated profits and distribution attributable to capital (except capitalised profits). Therefore, in the instant case, to the extent of the accumulated profits in the hands of the company, whether such accumulated profits were capitalised or not, the return to the shareholder on the reduction of his share capital was a return of such accumulated profits. This part would be taxable as dividend. The balance could be subject to tax as capital gains, if they accrued.

The assessee in the instant case had been paid not merely cash but had also been given a property for the reduction in the value of his shares from Rs.1,000 to Rs.210. Out of the total amounts so received including the value of the property so received, the portion attributable to accumulative profits would have to be deleted. Only the balance amount could be treated as a capital receipt. Thereafter looking to the cost of acquisition of that portion of the share which had been diminished, capital gains would have to be determined. The Tribunal, while computing capital gains, would have to decide how this property should be valued for the purpose of deciding what the assessee had received on reduction in the value of his shares and whether any capital gains had accrued to the assessee or not. This question was not considered by the Tribunal because the Tribunal came to the conclusion that there being no transfer of any capital asset, the question of capital gains did not arise. But the question would now have to be considered and decided by the Tribunal when the matter goes back before it for the determination of capital gains, if any.

It is a well settled rule of construction that entries in the legislative lists cannot be read in a narrow or restricted sense: they should be construed most liberally and in their widest amplitude. The Supreme Court in a number of decisions held that the expression 'income' in entry 54 of List I of the Seventh Schedule to the Government of India Act, 1935, and the corresponding entry 82 of List I of the Seventh Schedule to the Constitution of India, shall be widely and liberally construed so as to enable a legislature to provide by law for the prevention of evasion of income-tax.

While an entry delineating a legislative field must be widely and liberally construed, there must be a reasonable nexus between the item taxed and the field so delineated. The section 2(6A)(d) of the 1922 Act, deals with the distribution by a company on the reduction of its capital to the extent to which the company possesses accumulated profits. Accumulated profits of a company may be utilised in the following 3 ways: (1) for increasing the capital stock; (2) for distributing the same among the shareholders by way of dividends; and (3) for reducing the capital. Ordinarily, a company reduces the capital when there is loss or depreciation of assets; in that event there is no question of distribution of profits to the shareholders but the shares are only devaluated. But a company may, on the pretext of reducing its capital, utilise its accumulated profits to pay back to the shareholders the whole or part of the paid up amounts on the shares. A shareholder though in form gets back the whole or a part of the capital contributed by him, in effect he gets a share of the accumulated profits which, if a straightforward course was followed, he should have received as dividend. This is a division of profits under the guise of division of capital; a distribution of profits under the colour of reduction of capital. If this was permitted, there would be evasion of super-tax, the extent of the evasion depending upon the prevalence of the evil. The legislature, presumably in the interest of the exchequer, enlarged the definition of 'dividend' to catch the said payments within the net of taxation. By doing so, it is really taxing the profits in the hands of the shareholders, though they are receiving the said profits under the cloak of capital.

Under company law the question of reducing capital is a domestic one for the decision of the majority of shareholders. The court comes into the picture only to see that the reduction is fair and equitable and that the interests of the minority and the creditors do not suffer. It may not also be concerned with the motive of the general body in resolving to reduce the capital; but the income-tax law is concerned with tax evasion. Tax can be evaded by breaking the law, or avoided in terms of the law. When there is a factual avoidance of tax, in terms of law, the legislature steps into amend the income-tax law so that it can catch such an income within the net of taxation. There is, therefore, no inconsistency between a receipt being a capital one under the company law, and by fiction being treated as taxable income under the Income-tax Act.

Therefore, as section 2(6A)(d) of the 1922 Act, embodies a law to prevent evasion of tax, it falls within the ken of entry 54 of List I of Schedule VII to the Government of India Act, 1935.

'Dividend', which was distributed was not that which one ordinarily understand by that expression, but dividend by definition. Under section 2(6A)(d) of the 1922 Act it is one of the ingredients of the definition that it shall have been distributed by a company on reduction of the capital to the extent to which the company possesses accumulated profits. Under section 16(2) of the 1922 Act such a dividend shall be deemed to be an income of the previous year in which it is paid, credited or distributed. Unless such a distribution as is mentioned in clause (d) of section 2(6A) of the 1922 Act had taken place, it would not be a dividend. If it was not so distributed, section 16(2) of the 1922 Act would not be attracted. To put it in other words, if the accumulated profits were distributed, it would satisfy not only the definition of 'dividend' in clause (d) but also would fix the year in which it would be deemed to be income. What then is the meaning of the expression 'distribution'? The dictionary meaning of the expression 'distribution' is 'to give each a share, to give to several persons'. The expression 'distribution' connotes something actual and not notional. It can be physical; it can also be constructive. One may distribute amounts between different shareholders either by crediting the amount due to each one of them in their respective accounts or by actually paying to each one of them the amount due to him.
