Javeri v. K.K. Sen3, the validity of section 12(1B) of the 1922 Act, was questioned. Section 12(1B) provided that a loan made to a shareholder by private-controlled company is taxable as dividend. It was recognized that merely because the loan is taxed as a dividend in the hands of a shareholder, the loan may not cease to be a loan, and that it would be open to the company to recover the loan by resorting to law. The petitioner’s argument was that what is not income is being taxed as ‘income’ and, therefore, it is beyond the legislative competence of the Parliament. (The impugned provision was introduced by the Finance Act, 1955.) The argument was rejected in the following words :

“In dealing with this point, it is necessary to consider what exactly is the connotation of the word ‘income’ used in the relevant entry. It is hardly necessary to emphasize that the entries in the Lists cannot be read in a narrow or restricted sense, and as observed by Gwyer, CJ. in the United Provinces v. Atiqa Begum1, each general word should be held to extend to all ancillary or subsidiary matters which can fairly and reasonably be said to be comprehended in it. What the entries in the Lists purport to do is to confer legislative powers on the respective Legislatures in respect of areas or fields covered by the said entries; and it is an elementary rule of construction that the widest possible construction must be put upon their words. This doctrine does not, however, mean that Parliament can choose to tax as income an item which in no rational sense can be regarded as a citizen’s income. The item taxed should rationally be capable of being considered as the income of a citizen. But in considering the question as to whether a particular item in the hands of a citizen can be regarded as his income or not, it would be inappropriate to apply the tests traditionally prescribed by the Income-tax Act as such...” (p. 1379)

The Court reaffirmed the principles enunciated in Navinchandra Mafatlal’s case (supra), Baldeo Singh’s case (supra) and Balaji’s case (supra).

It is equally relevant to notice that in Baldeo Singh’s case (supra), the validity of section 23A of the 1922 Act was questioned. Section 23A provided that where the ITO is satisfied that in respect of any previous year the profits and gains distributed as dividend by any company within twelve months immediately following the expiry of that previous year are less than 60 per cent of the total income of the company of that previous year [as reduced by the amounts specified in clauses (a), (b) and (c) of sub-section (1)], the ITO shall, unless he is satisfied that having regard to losses incurred by the company in earlier years, or to the smallness of the profits made in the previous year, the payment of a dividend, or a larger dividend than that declared, would be unreasonable, make an order in writing that the company shall, apart from the sum determined as payable by it on the basis of the assessment under section 23 of the 1922 Act, be liable to pay super-tax at the rate specified by sub-section (1) of section 23A. This section was enacted to prevent avoidance of super-tax by shareholders of a company in which the public are not substantially interested. The assessee’s argument was that since the company and shareholders are distinct entities, taxing the shareholders on dividends not distributed by the company, and not received by them, cannot be justified as a tax on income received by shareholders. This argument was repelled on the ground that the obvious intention of section 23A was to prevent evasion of tax, and that Entry 54 in List I of the Seventh Schedule should be read not only as authorising the imposition of a tax, but also as authorising an enactment which prevents the tax imposed being evaded. It was also observed that section 23A dealt with a situation where shareholders did not deliberately distribute the accumulated profits as dividend among themselves and, therefore, provided that these accumulated profits will be deemed to have been distributed to shareholders and tax levied on that basis.

Section 46 deals with capital gains on distribution of assets by companies on liquidation. Section 46(1) provides that notwithstanding anything contained in section 45, where the assets of a company are distributed to its shareholders on its liquidation, such distribution shall not be regarded as a transfer by the company for the purposes of section 45. 6.2 Buy-back of shares will be taxable as capital gains [Section 69 of ITA 2025 (corresponding to Section 46A of ITA 1961)]

The Finance Act, 2026 has made several amendments to the provisions of the ITA 2025 regarding the taxation of buy-back of shares. Under the amended provisions, the sum paid by a domestic company to the shareholders under a buyback shall be treated as capital gains in the hands of the shareholders.

6.2-1 Introduction

Corporate action to buyback shares can serve multiple strategic purposes. Primarily, it's used to increase earnings per share by reducing the number of outstanding shares, often leading to a higher stock price. Additionally, buybacks are a method to return excess cash to shareholders, an alternative to dividend payouts. Companies might also repurchase shares if they believe their stock is undervalued, signalling confidence in the future. Moreover, buybacks can deter hostile takeovers by increasing the company's ownership percentage.

Section 68 of the Companies Act, 2013 gives the company the power to purchase its own securities. It defines a buyback as the purchase of its own shares or other specified securities (i.e., Employee Stock Options or Sweat Equity) by the Company itself.

6.2-2 History of tax on buyback of shares as per the ITA 1961

Before the assessment year 2000-01, the Income Tax Act did not include a special provision for taxing share buybacks. There were two views on the buyback of shares: either it could attract dividend distribution tax, or shareholders would be liable to pay tax on any gains.

To set the controversy at rest, the Finance Act, 1999 inserted section 46A with effect from assessment year 2000-01, which stated that shareholders would be charged to tax on the capital gains arising from the buyback of shares. A corresponding amendment was also made to section 2(22) by inserting clause (iv), which provides that a payment for the purchase of shares does not constitute a dividend. Therefore, the consideration received by a shareholder on the buyback of shares by the company in accordance with section 77A of the Companies Act, 19561 (corresponding to Section 68 of the Companies Act, 2013) was not treated as a dividend. The same was taxed under Section 46A of the Act as capital gains.

Subsequently, the unlisted companies, as part of the tax avoidance scheme, were found resorting to buyback of shares instead of payment of dividends in order to avoid payment of tax by way of DDT, particularly where the capital gains arising to the shareholders were either not chargeable to tax or were taxable at a lower rate under respective Double Taxation Avoidance Agreements. In A Mauritius, In re [2012] 20 taxmann.com 52, the AAR held that only a genuine buyback is excluded from the definition of 'dividend' under section 2(22)(iv) and exempt from DDT under section 115-O. A colourable buyback will attract DDT. In that case, the buyback was held to be a colourable device for tax avoidance, as dividends were distributed in the guise of a buyback to avoid DDT.

Taking a cue from the above decision of the AAR, the Finance Act, 2013 inserted a new Chapter XII-DA, 'Special Provisions relating to tax on distributed income of domestic company for buyback of shares,' consisting of sections 115QA to 115QC, with effect from 1-6-2013. The Finance (No. 2) Act, 2019 extended the levy of tax on the buy-back of shares listed on a recognised stock exchange on or after 5 July 2019 by amending section 115QA.

In November 2022, the Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI) released a consultation paper on a review of the SEBI (Buyback of Securities) Regulations, 2018, proposing various changes to existing buyback norms. One of the proposed changes is to shift the tax burden of buybacks from the company to the shareholders. This proposal was based on the fact that promoters tendered more shares than their pre-buyback holdings, resulting in the company paying taxes not only on shares tendered by the promoters but also on the additional shares tendered by them. These taxes were paid from the company's reserves on behalf of the existing shareholders and promoters at the expense of continuing shareholders. Therefore, it was suggested that the tax burden on buybacks should be shifted to shareholders, as it is with dividend distributions.

6.15-5Eg LOANS AND ADVANCES TO REGISTERED SHAREHOLDERS - Loan or advance allowed to a shareholder is dividend. The shareholder should be a registered shareholder. When, suppose an advance or loan is given to a Hindu undivided family, whose karta is the registered shareholder of the advancing or lending company, the amount, thus, advanced or loaned cannot be taken to be deemed dividend, because the karta is the registered owner, though the beneficial ownership vests with the Hindu undivided family and it is not the registered owner who is getting advance or loan.3

The Finance Act, 1987, however, amended the section by virtue of which, advance or loan to such person as Hindu undivided family would be deemed dividend, if the advance or loan is made after 31-5-1987.

6.15-5Eh LOAN AND ADVANCE - Payment of loan is taken as dividend irrespective of the fact that such loan is temporary for a few days.4 The fiction comes into operation at the time of payment of advance or loan to shareholder. The tax is attracted to the amount, thus, paid to the extent of accumulated profits. Even if the loan or advance is subsequently repaid or adjusted so that no amount is outstanding at the end of the year, it would still be assessed as deemed dividend.5

In Dictionary for Accountants, ‘advance’ has been defined as payment of cash or the transfer of goods for which accounting must be entered by the recipient at some later date.6 Section 2(22)(e) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 makes it clear that any payment by any company of any sum representing a part of the assets by way of advance would come within the mischief of the said section. The Calcutta High Court in M.D. Jindal v. CIT7 held that value of the goods supplied by the company to the assessee and his wife could be treated as dividend.

6.15-5Ei INTEREST - Income as interest is also taxable under the residuary head. It means income from debt-claims. Debt is a property. It is a chose-in-action and is heritable and assignable and it is treated as property under the transfer of Property Act which calls it ‘actionable claim’. Chose-in-action arising out of contract has two aspects (i) as property, and (ii) as involving a contractual obligation for performance. The property aspect is relevant for purposes of assignment, administration, and taxation and like; the contractual aspect, for performance. The debt being intangible, cannot have location unless except notionally and in order to give it notional position, rules have to be framed along arbitrary lines. In the case of a debt due to a foreigner, the proper law of the contract is to be applied, i.e., the law of the country in which, elements of the contract are most densely grouped and with which factually, the contract is most closely connected.1

HEADNOTE: Section 5 of the Income tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 4 of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Income - Accrual of - Assessment year 1935-36 company ‘R’ had accumulated substantial reserve and resolved to capitalize it - It was also decided that capitalized fund would later on be distributed amongst shareholders as bonus share - Company ‘R’ purchased share of company ‘A’ - Later on; it resolved to reduce its capital by returning to shareholder share in company ‘A’, which was confirmed by District Court - Revenue held that whole transaction was illusory and share of company ‘A’ allotted to assessee shareholders had never become capital and it would represent profits of company ‘R’ which would be taxable in hands of assessee - Whether department was competent to go behind order of court confirming reduction of capital and to hold that what was sought to be released and reduced of its share capital was release of profits - Held, No - Whether value of shares of company ‘A’ received by assessee was not liable to be included in his income - Held, yes

FACT: The assessee was shareholder of a company ‘R’ which had substantial reserve, passed a resolution for capitalising the sum standing to the credit of the reserve funds and the capitalized fund was to be distributed amongst the members of the company ‘R’ in effect as bonus shares. On the next day the company ‘R’ resolved to purchase shares in the company ‘A’ out of its capitalized reserve. Later on the company ‘R’ resolved to reduce its capital by returning to the shareholders the shares in the company ‘A’ and this resolution was confirmed by an order of the District Court. As a result of this resolution, certain shares in the Company A were allotted to the assessee. The view which the ITO took was that the whole transaction by the company ‘R’ for the increase and subsequent decrease of its capital and purchase and distribution of company ‘A’ shares was illusory, and that accordingly he could treat the company ‘A’ shares allotted to the assessee as never having become capital, but as their representing profits of the company ’R’. Both the Assistant Commissioner and commissioner agreed with the decision of the ITO

On reference:

HELD: As soon as the resolution was passed capitalising the reserves, such reserves became capital and could not afterwards be dealt with by the company as income; and subsequently, when the capital was reduced, - which was in the next year, - and part of the proceeds of the capitalised reserves was handed back to the shareholders, that part could only be handed back in the form in which it existed, namely, capital. The ITO, when he said that the whole transaction was illusory, apparently meant that the real motive of the directors in putting forward those various resolutions, and of the shareholders in passing them, was not to increase the capital for any commercial purposes of the Company, but to increase the capital in order that the subsequent distribution among the shareholders of the reserve funds might be in the form of capital and not of income; but the High Court could not go into the question of what was at the back of the mind of the directors or the shareholders.

It was not competent to the Income-tax authorities to go behind the order confirming the reduction of capital made by the District Court and to hold that what was sought to be released and reduced by the Resolution passed by the Company ‘R’ for reduction of its Share Capital was release of profits and not Share Capital.

Therefore, the value of shares of the Company ‘A’ received by the assessee was not liable to be included in the assessee’s income.

Per Rangnekar, J. [Concurrent view]

It is perfectly competent to a joint stock company to convert its surplus profits into capital and give the benefit of such conversion to the shareholders in any manner, either by the issue of new shares as bonus shares or by the issue of debentures, or in cash there was no evidence before the Income-tax authorities that the various transactions, which resulted in the transfer of shares in the company A, to the assessee, were illusory. A company, however, is incapable of having any intention. The intention must be of the share-holders, who are the masters of the Company. But assuming that the motive of the Managing Agents of the Company and of the shareholders was to escape super-tax,-and that seemed to be the ground on which the opinion of the Income-tax authorities was based -, the consideration of such a question was entirely irrelevant and immaterial in construing the legal effect of the transfer of undivided profits to the shareholders by way of capital.

Note : The case was decided in favour of the assessee.

Coltman and Hathising for the Applicant.

Regarding capital reserve account No. 2, a part of the said reserve had been admitted by the assessee before the Commissioner (Appeals) as forming part of the accumulated profits and, therefore, no grievance whatsoever could be raised in second appeal. The current profits had been excluded from the computation of accumulated profits by the Commissioner (Appeals) without discussing the issue. In the 1961 Act definition of ‘dividend’ contained under section 2(22) is materially different from the definition contained under section 2(6A) of the 1922 Act due to the presence of Explanation 2 which enacts that the expression ‘accumulated profits’ in sub-clauses (a), (b), (d ) and (e) shall include all profits of the company upto the date of distribution or payment. Therefore current profits had been rightly included by the Assessing Officer.

Regarding the provision for taxation included in debit balance of P&L account and existing tax liability raised by the IT authorities but disputed by the assessee and not provided in the books, the accumulated profits are to be construed as commercial profits for the purposes of section 2(22). Since tax liabilities had been created by the I.T. authorities and assessment orders as well as demand notices in support of the said liabilities had been produced during the assessment proceedings, such liabilities were to be taken note of, even if not provided in the books for ascertaining the accumulated profits. In the absence of specific reserves for taxation created by the company those liabilities might have to be met from the general reserves. In such circumstances to take the figure of general reserve from the balance sheet for ascertaining the accumulated profits would not be a correct procedure for the quantum of the general reserves would not represent the accumulated profits. Having regard to the aforesaid reasons, deduction was liable to be made for ascertaining accumulated profits.

However, the accumulated profit worked out in this way being a negative figure, it could not be said that the company possessed accumulated profits and, hence, provisions of section 2(22) were not applicable.

As regards the issue of levy of capital gains, the Commissioner (Appeals) had held against levy of capital gains without discussing facts and issues involved and without indicating reasons in support of his finding in the impugned order.

The basic issue for the purposes of levy of capital gains is whether reduction of share capital by a company results in extinguishment of rights in shares held by shareholders covered by the expression ‘transfer’ as defined in section 2(47). When a company reduces its share capital by paying off a part of the capital thereby reducing the face value of the shares, the share remains but the right of the shareholder to dividend of his share capital and the right to share is extinguished proportionately to the extent of reduction in capital. In the instant case, the Assessing Officer had no occasion to consider the issue of levy of capital gains under section 45 as a result of reduction of share capital since he came to the conclusion that accumulated profits possessed by the company exceeded the distribution made to the shareholders on reduction of share capital. While reversing the conclusion of the Assessing Officer and deleting the addition on account of dividend under section 2(22)(a) the Commissioner (Appeals) did not apply his mind to the issue of levy of capital gains under section 45, particularly since the distribution made by the company on reduction of share capital had been treated as transfer by the Supreme Court in the various decisions. In the circumstances the issue of levy of capital gains was set aside to the file of the Assessing Officer with the direction that the issue of levy of capital gains might be re-examined by him.

On appeal by the revenue : HELD: Section 2(22) deals with various types of cases and creates a fiction by which certain amounts, which are actually not distributed as dividends, are also brought within the net of dividend. It is a cardinal rule of interpretation that such a deeming section must receive a strict interpretation. The object and purpose of introducing the legal fiction in the statute is to frustrate any attempt by a company to avoid dividend tax by distributing the profits of the company to its shareholders under the guise of loan, reduction of capital, etc.

Insofar as profits of capital nature are concerned arising from the sale of capital assets, such profits are to be excluded for the purpose of ascertaining the accumulated profits under section 2(22) unless such capital profits have been subjected to capital gains under section 45.

In a nutshell, it may be said that no part of any capital profits, except capital gains as assessable under section 12(b) of the 1922 Act as well as under section 45 of the 1961 Act, of a company can ordinarily be included in "accumulated profits" for the purpose of determination of dividend under section 2(22). In view of specific provision in the constitution of AIPL capital profits of the company could not be distributed and, therefore, such profit, unless charged to capital gains tax, would not form part of "accumulated profits".

So far as the contention of the Department that AIPL and various allied companies of the Group had carried out series of amalgamations as a tax planning device was concerned, the same could not be accepted. There was substantial merit in the contention of the assessee that various amalgamations and mergers had been duly approved by the High Court and after such amalgamations had been sanctioned as made in conformity with the requirements under the Companies Act, no such allegation of tax planning or tax evasion could be levelled by the revenue against the assessee. While according sanction the High Court had duly considered that the scheme of amalgamation was in public interest which essentially implied that the amalgamation was not motivated by consideration of capital gains tax. It was not the business of the company (AIPL) to take over the assets and liabilities of the amalgamating companies and make a profit by realising the assets and paying off the liabilities. Amalgamation cannot be treated as a part of the business activity. No profit could accrue at the time of taking over of the assets and liabilities of the amalgamating companies. Any surplus arising on account of amalgamation would not be taxable as a revenue income. The process of merger or amalgamation could not be described as a purchase and in any case no profit could arise by this process alone.

The legal propositions governing the operation of section 2(22)(d) may be summarised as under :

1.Section 2(22) introduces legal fiction and would necessarily receive strict interpretation.

2.The expression "accumulated profits" used in the section would be construed as commercial profits computed in accordance with principles of commercial accounting. These profits are not to be treated as equivalent to assessable income.

3.Capital gains chargeable under section 45 would be includible as part of the accumulated profits

4.If there is a provision in the constitution of the company against distribution of dividend out of capital profits, such profits would not form part of accumulated profits unless charged to capital gains tax.

5.Surplus arisen on the amalgamation of companies would not result in revenue gain since amalgamation even if treated as an activity of purchase would not result in profit to the amalgamated company.

6.Since amalgamating company is a separate entity, profits in its balance sheet, after amalgamation, cannot be treated as accumulated profits of the amalgamated company.

Therefore, the surplus realised by the amalgamating company and capitalised by the issue of paid-up capital would not be covered under the expression ‘accumulated profits or capitalised profits’ for the purpose of section 2(22)(d).

Strictly construed, ‘accumulated profits’, whether capitalised or not, held by the amalgamating companies, which were separate independent entitles, could not by any stretch of imagination be treated as accumulated profits or capitalised profits of amalgamated company, i.e., AIPL after the amalgamation.

As regards the surplus in capital reserve account No. 1, the same was merely a paper surplus and could not be treated as revenue gain or liable to capital gains tax. In view of the basic principles governing the surplus realisation on amalgamation/merger, the Commissioner (Appeals) rightly excluded the said reserve from the purview of the accumulated profits under section 2(22)(d).

Regarding capital reserve account No. 2, a part of the said reserve had been admitted by the assessee before the Commissioner (Appeals) as forming part of the accumulated profits and, therefore, no grievance whatsoever could be raised in second appeal.

On appeal : HELD: It is a well settled rule of construction that entries in the legislative lists cannot be read in a narrow or restricted sense: they should be construed most liberally and in their widest amplitude. The Supreme Court in a number of decisions held that the expression 'income' in entry 54 of List I of the Seventh Schedule to the Government of India Act, 1935, and the corresponding entry 82 of List I of the Seventh Schedule to the Constitution of India, shall be widely and liberally construed so as to enable a legislature to provide by law for the prevention of evasion of income-tax.

While an entry delineating a legislative field must be widely and liberally construed, there must be a reasonable nexus between the item taxed and the field so delineated. The section 2(6A)(d) of the 1922 Act, deals with the distribution by a company on the reduction of its capital to the extent to which the company possesses accumulated profits. Accumulated profits of a company may be utilised in the following 3 ways: (1) for increasing the capital stock; (2) for distributing the same among the shareholders by way of dividends; and (3) for reducing the capital. Ordinarily, a company reduces the capital when there is loss or depreciation of assets; in that event there is no question of distribution of profits to the shareholders but the shares are only devaluated. But a company may, on the pretext of reducing its capital, utilise its accumulated profits to pay back to the shareholders the whole or part of the paid up amounts on the shares. A shareholder though in form gets back the whole or a part of the capital contributed by him, in effect he gets a share of the accumulated profits which, if a straightforward course was followed, he should have received as dividend. This is a division of profits under the guise of division of capital; a distribution of profits under the colour of reduction of capital. If this was permitted, there would be evasion of super-tax, the extent of the evasion depending upon the prevalence of the evil. The legislature, presumably in the interest of the exchequer, enlarged the definition of 'dividend' to catch the said payments within the net of taxation. By doing so, it is really taxing the profits in the hands of the shareholders, though they are receiving the said profits under the cloak of capital.

Under company law the question of reducing capital is a domestic one for the decision of the majority of shareholders. The court comes into the picture only to see that the reduction is fair and equitable and that the interests of the minority and the creditors do not suffer. It may not also be concerned with the motive of the general body in resolving to reduce the capital; but the income-tax law is concerned with tax evasion. Tax can be evaded by breaking the law, or avoided in terms of the law. When there is a factual avoidance of tax, in terms of law, the legislature steps into amend the income-tax law so that it can catch such an income within the net of taxation. There is, therefore, no inconsistency between a receipt being a capital one under the company law, and by fiction being treated as taxable income under the Income-tax Act.

Therefore, as section 2(6A)(d) of the 1922 Act, embodies a law to prevent evasion of tax, it falls within the ken of entry 54 of List I of Schedule VII to the Government of India Act, 1935.

By using the expression 'whether capitalised or not', the legislative intent clearly is that the profits which are deemed to be dividend would be those which were capable of being accumulated and which would also be capable of being capitalised. This would clearly exclude return of a part of the capital by the company from section 2(22), as the same cannot be regarded as profits capable of being capitalised, the return being of the capital itself. Therefore, in the instant case, to the extent of the accumulated profits in the hands of the company, whether such accumulated profits were capitalised or not, the return to the shareholder on the reduction of his share capital was a return of such accumulated profits. This part would be taxable as dividend. The balance could be subject to tax as capital gains, if they accrued.

The assessee in the instant case had been paid not merely cash but had also been given a property for the reduction in the value of his shares from Rs.1,000 to Rs.210. Out of the total amounts so received including the value of the property so received, the portion attributable to accumulative profits would have to be deleted. Only the balance amount could be treated as a capital receipt. Thereafter looking to the cost of acquisition of that portion of the share which had been diminished, capital gains would have to be determined. The Tribunal, while computing capital gains, would have to decide how this property should be valued for the purpose of deciding what the assessee had received on reduction in the value of his shares and whether any capital gains had accrued to the assessee or not. This question was not considered by the Tribunal because the Tribunal came to the conclusion that there being no transfer of any capital asset, the question of capital gains did not arise. But the question would now have to be considered and decided by the Tribunal when the matter goes back before it for the determination of capital gains, if any.

HEADNOTE: Section 45 of the income-tax act, 1961-Capital gains-Chargeable as-Consequent on reduction of share capital effected by assessee-company, company became liable to pay a sum to the shareholders-To discharge its liability, assessee distributed to shareholders shares held by it and at the time of their distribution to shareholders, it revalued them at market price and credited the difference between book value and market value in capital reserve account-Whether difference between book value of shares and the market value at which they were transferred to shareholders was capital gains chargeable to tax as there was transfer of these shares from company to shareholders-Held, on facts, yes

FACT: The assessee-company reduced its share capital and, in consequence, it became liable to pay a sum of Rs. 2,01,500 to the shareholders. To discharge that liability, the assessee-company distributed to the shareholders certain shares held by it in two companies. At the time of distribution of these shares, the assessee revalued those shares and the difference between the book value of the said shares and their market value was Rs. 56,181 as per the assessee's own balance sheet. This amount was shown as capital reserve arising on revaluation of investment at market value. Treating the difference between the market value of the shares and their book value as capital gains, the Commissioner directed the ITO under section 263 to bring to tax such difference to capital gains. On appeal, the Tribunal held that there was no transfer of shares from the assessee-company to its shareholders and as such there was no liability to pay capital gains tax on the part of the assessee.

On reference, the assessee contended that there was only transfer of shares at the book value and there was no question of those shares being transferred at the market value and only if the shares had been transferred at the market value, the question of capital gains arising out of the transfer will arise.

HELD: Any transaction under which the ownership or right to a property is transferred from one person to another for consideration, the transaction can only be taken to be a transfer by way of a sale. The so-called distribution by the assessee-company of its shares to the shareholders to discharge its liability of Rs. 2,01,500 arising out of the reduction in share capital, clearly amounted to a transfer. The Tribunal was not right in holding that there was no transfer involved in the distribution of shares by the assessee-company to the shareholders. There was no merit in the assessee's contention that there was transfer of shares from the company to its shareholders at the book value and the shareholders were willing to accept shares of the book value of Rs. 1,47,100 as against the amount of Rs. 2,01,281 ( Rs. 219 having been paid in cash) due to them. Two factors were present in this case which militated against the said contention, one was that there was no material on record to show that the shareholders agreed to take shares of the book value of Rs. 1,47,100 as against the— sum of Rs. 2,01,281 and to forego the difference. The other factor was that the assessee itself had revalued the shares before actual transfer of the shares to the shareholders and as per the revaluation, the shares transferred were said to be of the market value of Rs. 2,01,281. In fact, the assessee in its balance sheet as on 31-12-1973 had shown the difference between the book value of the shares and their market value at Rs. 54,181 and it had shown this amount under the head 'Capital gains'. Thus, the assessee's own records made it clear that the assessee, before it effected the transfer of shares to the shareholders, took the market value of the shares into account and transferred the shares whose market value was Rs. 2,01,281 to the shareholders but whose book value was Rs. 1,47,100.

Thus, it was clear that by transfer of shares by the company to its shareholders, the assessee had realised a sum of Rs. 54,161 over and above the book value and this had rightly been treated as capital gains arising out of the transfer of shares.

No doubt, a fiction should not be extended beyond its limits though it must be given its full effect. Section 2(22)(e) does not in terms provide that what has been deemed as dividend should be deemed to have come from accumulated profits. But in section 2(22)(e) there is an indication that the deemed dividend is not unconnected with the accumulated profits. In fact, there is a clear provision that the deeming provision will attach only to that part of the amount paid which is represented by the accumulated profits of the company. When this provision is read with the language of the section which provides for deduction of tax on such dividend and also read with the statutory restriction of payment of dividend out of the capital assets, it is reasonable to come to the conclusion that a dividend would and should come out of the accumulated profits. There may be other objects also in such reduction of capital. Perhaps it is to minimise the possibility of such distribution of amounts that the deeming provision in section 2(22)(d ) had been introduced by the statute by insisting that on such assets being distributed, tax should be paid deeming such assets as dividends issued by the company. A shareholder can transfer a share. He can also surrender the share to the company and when surrendering the share, there may be relinquishment of the share. There can also be cancellation of the shares. Apart from that, there can be no transactions vis-a-vis the company and the shareholders as regards the shares held by a shareholder. The shares as such are held by the shareholders and the only provision in the Companies Act which would have any representations between the company and the shareholder would be in the circumstances of surrender and cancellation of shares. There had been no surrender or cancellation of shares in the company. It could not be said that there had been any exchange on reduction of the shares or any part of the value of the shares. The shareholder had not transferred anything to the company. Therefore, section 45 was not attracted. All the rights of the shareholder as a shareholder in the company still remained. He continued to hold the same number of shares. Whether, on liquidation, he would get the amount which he would have received had a liquidation taken place at the time of the reduction of capital could not touch the question as to whether by the reduction of capital there had been any extinguishment. It was conceivable that he would receive less in the event of the winding up of the company after reduction of capital in view of the fact that there had been distribution of assets. But on the possibility of the company not prospering and not augmenting its assets, it is not possible to come to any conclusion that there had been any extinguishment of the rights of the shareholder. The shareholder's right to receive the assets of the company, can arise only in the event of winding up of the company and on liquidation taking effect. That event not having taken place, it could not postulate any extinguishment. Therefore, the Tribunal was right in holding that no capital gain was assessable in the hands of the assessee as there was no extinguishments of any right of the assessee and consequently there was no transfer within the meaning of section 2(47) by the assessee of any capital assets for the relevant assessment year.

The term 'dividend' has been defined under section 2(22)(a) and as per said definition, any distribution by a company to its shareholders to the extent of accumulated profits, whether capitalized or not, such distribution entails the release by the company to its shareholders of all or any part of the assets of the company. The definition is an inclusive definition and it goes beyond the conventional or traditional meaning associated with dividend. The definition is broad and covers a wide variety of payments made by a company. In fact, section 2(22)(e) even includes a loan given by a company to its shareholder, subject to certain conditions, within the ambit of dividend. Therefore, the object of such an expansive definition seems to be ensure that the taxpayer do not camouflage payments out of accumulates profits to its shareholders through different channels in order to avoid payment of tax. Section 2(22)(a) covers any distribution by a company of accumulated profits which entails the release by the company to its shareholders of all or any of the assets of the company. Section 2(22)(d) covers distribution made to the shareholders by a company on the reduction of its share capital to the extent the company possess accumulated profits. Two essential pre-requisites must be satisfied in order to come within the ambit of section 2(22)(d) i.e., there must be a distribution to the shareholders on the reduction of the capital and further, it must be to the extent that the company possess accumulated profits. In the instant case, which is evident from the audited financial statement that the share capital has been reduced by around Rs. 9.4 Crs. which is equivalent to 54.70 per cent of the total paid up share capital. Further, Clause 7 of the scheme makes it clear that the distribution of money will be out of the general reserves and accumulated credit balance in the profit and loss account. Thus, both conditions are satisfied to treat the transaction within the ambit of section 2(22)(d). [Para 34]

On appeal to the Supreme Court : HELD: A dividend under section 205 of the Companies Act, 1956 can be paid only out of the profits of a company, whether for that year or out of the profits of the company for any previous financial years as set out in that section and in the manner set out in that section. Therefore, under section 2(22) when any payment by a company is treated as a deemed dividend, the section has provided that it should be treated as payment out of the accumulated profits of the company, whether capitalised or not. In fact, under section 194 an obligation is cast upon the principal officer of the company to deduct from the payment so made under section 2(22)(e) income-tax at the rates in force. Section 194 clearly treats such payment as dividend. Therefore, when a loan by a company to a shareholder in the manner set out in section 2(22)(e) is treated as a deemed dividend, it is to be treated as payment out of the accumulated profits of the company. Any legal fiction will, therefore, have to be carried to its logical conclusion. If the payment under section 2(22)(e) is treated as a deemed dividend and is required to be so treated to the extent that the company possesses accumulated profits, the logical conclusion is that this payment must be considered as adjusted against the company's accumulated profits to the extent that it is treated as deemed dividend while calculating accumulated profits of the company. Whenever accumulated profits of the company are required to be determined, such an adjustment will have to be made.

The High Court was, therefore, right in coming to the conclusion that when section 2(22)(e) is read with the language of section 194 which provides for deduction of tax on such 'dividend', as also the statutory restriction under the Companies Act on payment of dividend out of any capital assets, it would be reasonable to come to the conclusion that the sum advanced to the shareholders must be taken to have come out of the accumulated profits. It must, therefore, be treated as dividend for all purposes and would go to reduce the accumulated profits of the company, whether capitalised or not, whenever such accumulated profits are required to be determined.

As held by the Supreme Court in Kartikeya Sarabhai v. CIT [1997] 228 ITR 163/94 Taxman 164, relinquishment of the asset or extinguishment of any right in it, which may not amount to a sale, can also be considered as a transfer. Any profit or gain which arises from the transfer of a capital asset is liable to be taxed under section 45. As a result of a reduction in the face value of the share, the share capital is reduced, the right of the shareholder to the dividend and his right to share in the distribution of net assets upon liquidation, are extinguished proportionately to the extent of reduction in the capital. Even though the shareholder remains a shareholder, his right as a holder of those shares stands reduced with the reduction in the share capital. Therefore, this extinguishment of right is transfer. The amount received by the assessee for such reduction is liable to capital gains under section 45. In view of this judgment, the property and money received by the assessee from the company on the reduction in the face value of his shares is a capital receipt subject to section 45.

Under section 2(22)(d) any distribution to its shareholders by a company on the reduction of its capital is deemed to be a distribution of dividend to the extent that the company possesses accumulated profits, whether such profits have been capitalised or not. Therefore, any distribution which is made by a company on a reduction of its share capital which can be correlated with the company's accumulated profits (whether capitalised or not), will be dividend in the hands of the assessee. Therefore, it will have to be treated as income of the assessee and taxed accordingly.

It is only when any distribution is made which is over and above the accumulated profits of the company (capitalised or otherwise) that the question of a capital receipt in the hands of a shareholder arises. The original cost to that shareholder of the acquisition of that right in the share which stands extinguished as a result of reduction in the share capital will have to be deducted from the capital receipt so determined. Only when the capital receipt is in excess of the original cost of the acquisition of that interest which stands extinguished, will any capital gains arise. By using the expression 'whether capitalised or not', the legislative intent clearly is that the profits which are deemed to be dividend would be those which were capable of being accumulated and which would also be capable of being capitalised. This would clearly exclude return of a part of the capital by the company from section 2(22), as the same cannot be regarded as profits capable of being capitalised, the return being of the capital itself.

On reference : HELD: As regards vires of section 2(6A)(d ) it was contended that a legislation under entry 54 of the Federal Legislative List-I of the Seventh Schedule of the Government of India Act, 1935 must confined itself to taxes on ‘income’ and section 2(6A)(d) in so far as it makes ‘capital’ taxable is ultra vires the Central Legislative. It is a well-settled principle that entries in legislative lists are given a broad and comprehensive interpretation; the cardinal rule of construction being, that words should be read in their natural and grammatical meaning subject to the rider that in construing the words in a constitutional enactment conferring legislative power the most liberal construction should be put upon the words so that the same may have effect in their widest amplitude. Moreover, the various entries in the Lists are not powers of legislation but fields of legislation. Thus, the legislative field is extensive and the items of legislation include not merely the main purposes but also all ancillary and subsidiary matters which can fairly and reasonably be said to fall within the scope of a particular entry.

According to section 2(6A)(d ) any distribution on the reduction of capital becomes dividend to the extent to which the company possessed accumulated profits. The effect of section 2(6A)(d) was that distribution by a company on the reduction of its capital to the extent of the amount which the company possessed as accumulated profits was being treated as dividend. The capital character of the distribution which was in excess of the accumulated profits was not being distributed and to that extent that sum was not being treated as dividend under section 2(6A)(d ). In the instant case, the company, on the reduction of its capital from Rs. 25 lakhs to Rs. 15 lakhs, had to distribute a sum of Rs. 10 lakhs. Out of this Rs. 10 lakhs, law treats the distribution of Rs. 4,69,244 as of accumulated profits and, therefore, as "dividend". The company could not by styling the entire amount for distribution as capital evade its liability to be taxed on Rs. 4,69,244, which, being accumulated profits, fell within the definition of "dividend". The amendment to section 2(6A) had succeeded in according the likehood of evasion by a company, by transferring its profits to the capital and then by reducing the capital proportionately and thereby distributing profits under the label of ‘capital reduction’ this is authority for the proportion that competent to legislate regard income-tax would include the power to legislate in order to check evasion [vide K.M.S. Lakshmana Aiyer v. Addl. ITO [1960] 40 ITR 469, 478 and S. Kumaraswami v. ITO [1961] 43 ITR 423, 426]. In view of the above the impugned provision of section 2(6A)(d) was within the legislative competence of the Central Legislature and was within the ambit of entry No. 54 of List I of the said Seventh Schedule not only in form but also in substance.

Dissenting view as per Bachawat J.

The distribution contemplated by section 2(6A)(d) is a distribution by a company 'on the reduction of its capital'. The word 'on' has no fixed meaning, but in the context of the sub-section, it must be given the meaning 'at the time of', as 'on entering', 'on the 1st of the month'. The distribution contemplated by the sub-section is, therefore, distribution at the time of the reduction of its capital, that is to say, when the resolution for reduction of its capital under section 55(1)(c) of the Indian Companies Act, 1913, takes effect. As soon as the resolution for reduction of capital and consequential refund of the surplus capital to the shareholders takes effect, the capital stands reduced, the surplus ceases to be capital and stands allotted to the shareholders, each shareholder obtains a vested right to the refund of his share of the surplus, and a liability arises on the part of the company to make the refund. This liability arises as soon as the reduction of capital takes effect, and it matters not that the company has not made the necessary book entries showing the reduction of capital and the transfer of the surplus to the account of the shareholders. The word 'distribution' has several dictionary meanings. In the context of section 2(6A)(d), of the 1922 Act it means allotment or apportionment of the surplus amongst the shareholders; this allotment takes place and each shareholder gets a vested right to his portion of the surplus as soon as the capital stands reduced.

A close scrutiny of section 2(6A)(d) of the 1922 Act reveals that (a) the distribution takes place on a single date and (b) the expression 'accumulated profits' means profits accumulated up to the date of the distribution. These two basic ideas which are implicit in section 2(6A)(d) of the 1922 Act are forcibly brought out in the Explanation to the corresponding section 2(22) of the Income-tax Act, 1961. Thus the entire distribution of the surplus amongst the shareholders takes place on a single date. Now if the distribution is to have certain single date, that date can only be the date when the reduction of capital becomes effective. The payments to the shareholders either actual or notional by credit entries in the books of account are made subsequently. The payments need not be made on one date; they may be and often are made on several dates. The successive payments cannot be the distribution contemplated by section 2(6A)(d) of the 1922 Act. The accumulated profits are to be ascertained on the date of the distribution. But the accumulated profits must be ascertained on the date of the reduction of capital. Thus the two events, namely, the distribution and the reduction of capital must synchronise, and the accumulated profits must also be ascertained at the same point of time. The synchronisation is also obvious on a plain reading of the abridged text 'any distribution on the reduction of capital to the extent of accumulated profits'.

that it can catch such an income within the net of taxation. There is, therefore, no inconsistency between a receipt being a capital one under the company law, and by fiction being treated as taxable income under the Income-tax Act.

Therefore, as section 2(6A)(d) of the 1922 Act, embodies a law to prevent evasion of tax, it falls within the ken of entry 54 of List I of Schedule VII to the Government of India Act, 1935. 'Dividend', which was distributed was not that which one ordinarily understand by that expression, but dividend by definition. Under section 2(6A)(d) of the 1922 Act it is one of the ingredients of the definition that it shall have been distributed by a company on reduction of the capital to the extent to which the company possesses accumulated profits. Under section 16(2) of the 1922 Act such a dividend shall be deemed to be an income of the previous year in which it is paid, credited or distributed. Unless such a distribution as is mentioned in clause (d) of section 2(6A) of the 1922 Act had taken place, it would not be a dividend. If it was not so distributed, section 16(2) of the 1922 Act would not be attracted. To put it in other words, if the accumulated profits were distributed, it would satisfy not only the definition of 'dividend' in clause (d) but also would fix the year in which it would be deemed to be income. What then is the meaning of the expression 'distribution'? The dictionary meaning of the expression 'distribution' is 'to give each a share, to give to several persons'. The expression 'distribution' connotes something actual and not notional. It can be physical; it can also be constructive. One may distribute amounts between different shareholders either by crediting the amount due to each one of them in their respective accounts or by actually paying to each one of them the amount due to him.

Distribution is a culmination of a process. Firstly, there will be a resolution by the general body of a company for reduction of capital by distribution of the accumulated profits amongst the shareholders; secondly, the company will file an application in the court for an order confirming the reduction of capital; thirdly, after it is confirmed, it will be registered by the Registrar of Joint Stock Companies; fourthly, after the registration the company issues notices to the shareholders inviting applications for refund of the share capital; and fifthly, on receiving the applications the company will distribute the said profits either by crediting the proportionate share capital to each of the shareholders in their respective accounts or by paying the said amounts in cash. Out of the said 5 steps, the first 4 are only necessary preliminary steps which entitle the company to distribute the accumulated profits. Credits or payments are related to the said declaration: that is to say, distribution is from and out of the accumulated profits resolved to be distributed by the company. In this view, the accumulated profits to be distributed are fixed by the resolution and the figure does not change with the date of payment or credit. Indeed, a similar process is to be followed in the case of declaration of ordinary dividends; firstly, there will be a resolution by the general body of the company declaring the dividends; secondly, thereafter the amounts payable to each of the shareholders are distributed by appropriate credits or payments. Dividends may be paid or credited to different shareholders during different accounting years; and the shareholders may be assessed in respect of the said payments in different years. Even so, the payments are referable only to the declaration of the dividends out of the profits of a particular year.

The Supreme Court had in the various decisions held that the year of credit or payment to a shareholder was crucial for the purpose of assessment and not the day of the declaration.

The appellant-company set up a claim for a rebate on the super-tax under clause (ii) of the first proviso to paragraph D of Part II of the first Schedule to the Finance Act, 1956. The assessee claimed that as the dividends were not distributed in the accounting year, there could not be any reduction of the rebates under clause (i)(b) of the said proviso. If, as had been held, the distribution was made during the year ending 30-11-1955, i.e., the accounting year when the amounts were paid, the revenue would be entitled to reduce the rebate by the amount computed at the prescribed rates on the amount of dividends. Some complication may arise only if we accept the argument that the date of payment fixes the date for ascertaining the quantum of accumulated profits. But the court had rejected that contention. In this view, the claim of reduction of rebate on super-tax provided by the First Schedule to the Finance Act, 1956, can be worked out without any confusion or complication. It was therefore, held that the dividends must be deemed to have been paid or distributed in the year when it was actually, whether physically or constructively, paid to the different shareholders, that is to say, when the amount was credited to the separate accounts of the shareholders or paid to them.

FACT: On the orders of the High Court as a consequence of the take-over by the State of the assessee’s business of generation and supply of electricity, the share capital of the assessee-company was substantially reduced, and the company distributed the amounts in cash to its shareholders in consequence of such reduction. The ITO having found accumulated profits, regarded the distribution as dividend to the extent of the accumulated profits. He, concluded that since no part of these profits were allowed to have arisen before 1-4-1933, the company would be deemed to have declared dividend in the assessment year 1957-58 under section 2(6A)(d). Tax was calculated accordingly. On appeal, the two contentions namely, (a) that the definition in clause (d) of section 2(6A) means a distribution out of the accumulated profits and not any distribution on the reduction of its capital; and (b) that the distribution in clause (c) of the second proviso to paragraph ‘D’ of the Finance (No. 2) Act, 1957, means actual distribution and did not include notional distribution, were dismissed by the AAC as without merit. On second appeal, the Tribunal observed that section 2(6A)(d) is general and applied to any distribution by the company on the reduction of its capital to the extent to which the company possessed accumulated profits and it did not matter whether the reduction of capital was bona fide or with a view to avoidance of super-tax by the shareholder. However, it opined that the rebate allowable to the assessee could not be withdrawn under the terms of the second proviso to Para D of the 1957 Act, and that the assessee being a company in which public are not substantially interested the rebate admissible was 20 per cent as mentioned in clause (iii) of the first proviso, and there was no question of any further withdrawal of the rebate.

FACT: The assessee held 70 shares of Rs. 1,000 each in a company. During the relevant accounting period, the said company passed a resolution to reduce its capital as a result of which the face value of the shares in the company was reduced from Rs. 1,000 each to Rs. 210 each. As a result of this reduction, there was a pro-rata distribution of some properties of the company and payment of money to the shareholders including the assessee. Before the Tribunal the questions for consideration were as to whether advances given by the company to its shareholders should be deducted from the accumulated profits of the company at the time of the company's reductions of share capital and whether any capital gain accrued to the assessee out of the property/amounts received by him on reduction of his share capital in the said company. The Tribunal held that the sum advanced to the shareholders being the deemed dividend should be deducted from the accumulated profits in the hands of the company and that no capital gains accrued to the assessee as there was no extinguishment of any right of the assessee. On reference, the High Court upheld the order of the Tribunal.

The Tribunal, therefore, held that it could not be said that anything was given to the shareholders without adequate consideration, and, there was, therefore, no gift within the meaning of section 4(a) or otherwise.

On reference: HELD: The opening words of section 2 viz., 'unless the context otherwise requires', permit the court to take into consideration the basic principle regulating the reduction of the share capital of a company, and does not compel the court to apply the definition of 'transfer property' in clause (xxiv ) of section 2 to a case to which, having regard to those basic principles, it cannot apply. It is true that a company is, in law, a separate legal entity from its shareholders, but when the assets of the company are distributed amongst its shareholders, either on a reduction of capital or in the course of the winding-up of that company, new rights are not created so as to amount to a transfer of property, an ingredient which is implicit in the very concept of transfer. Therefore, when property is received by shareholders in the course of reduction of the share capital of a company in which they are shareholders, such a transaction does not amount to a transfer of property and cannot, therefore, fall within the ambit of section 4(a ). The transfer of the shares was for adequate consideration, having regard to the market value of the shares as on 10-1-1958, and section 4(a) would, therefore, in any event, not be attracted. The Tribunal rightly took the view that the market value of the said shares as on the 20-3-1958 had no relevance for the purpose of considering the liability to gift-tax under section 4(a ) in the instant case. In that connection, there are three possible dates which need consideration, and the question is, whether regard must be had to the market value of the shares as on 10-1-1958, which was the date of the special resolution passed by the company; or as on 21-2-1958, which was the date of the High Court's order confirming that special resolution; or as on 20-3-1958, which was the date on which the share certificates were actually handed over by the company to the shareholders, presumably, along with the transfer forms. The statutory provisions under the Companies Act, 1956 relating to reduction of capital clearly show that what is effective for the purpose thereof is the special resolution itself, and that what the court does is merely to confirm that resolution with or without modifications, or to refuse to confirm the same. If the resolution is confirmed by the court, whether it be confirmed, with or without any modification, it is the resolution which takes effect for the purpose of reducing the share capital of the company, and that is clear, particularly from the language of sub-section (2) of section 103 of the 1956 Act, read along with sub-section (1) of section 102 thereof. It may, in this connection, be pointed out that the language of section 102(1) clearly shows that even when the court makes a variation in regard to the terms and conditions relating to the reduction of share capital, what it does is to confirm the resolution, subject to the alterations which it makes. The legislature has, perhaps, advisedly not used language to the effect that the court may confirm or vary the terms and conditions of the special resolution, but has couched sub-section (1) of section 102 of the 1956 Act in language which makes it quite clear that the court, unless it decides not to confirm the reduction of share capital, must confirm the resolution whereby that reduction is effected, whether such confirmation be on the same terms and conditions on with such modifications as the court considers necessary. In this connection, it is pertinent to note the difference in the language which the legislature has used in the same Act in connection with the confirmation of alternations in the memorandum of association. In that case also, the company has to pass a special resolution which has to come up before the court for confirmation.

, looking again at the provisos, there was no justification for coming to the conclusion, which the Tribunal did, in saying that clause (ii) of the proviso applied only to an Indian company but clause (iii) applied only to foreign companies which had not provided for declaration of dividends in Indian and to Indian companies in which public were not substantially interested. Therefore, that the distinction between foreign and Indian companies intended to be drawn by the Tribunal was not justified on a reading of these provisos. Thirdly, proviso (i)( a) makes it clear that the rebate shall be allowed in the case of a company which satisfies the condition that it must have ‘made the prescribed arrangements for the declaration and payment within India of the dividends payable out of such profits and for the deduction of the super-tax from the dividends in accordance with section 18(3D) of the Income-tax Act’. The words ‘prescribed arrangements’ could only mean arrangements prescribed either by the Act or the rules made thereunder or by the Companies Act or the rules made thereunder or under the articles of the company. Such prescribed arrangements for the declaration and payment of dividends could not mean notional or deemed dividends such as were contemplated in section 23A section 18(3D) is not also concerned with deemed or notional dividends but with deducting super-tax on the amount of the dividend as increased in accordance with section 16(2). The two parts of proviso (i)(a ) are clearly separate, namely, the part that makes for ‘prescribed arrangements for the declaration and payment of dividends payable out of such profits’ on the one hand and the part ‘for the deduction of super-tax on dividends in accordance with the provision of section 18(3D) of the Income-tax Act’. The first part cannot include deemed or notional dividends at all. As the language clearly says, it means dividend which has been declared and paid by the prescribed arrangements. The second part under section 18(3D) may include consideration of deemed dividend as the section itself provides. In order to succeed, therefore, the revenue had to establish in the instant case that the dividend taken to be dividend in this case was a dividend according to prescribed arrangements within the meaning of proviso (i)(a ) of Paragraph D of the Finance Act. On the facts the revenue could not do this in the instant case. Therefore, the contention of the revenue to come within clause (a) of proviso (i) could not succeed. No doubt, the ITO, had tried to describe as accumulated profit a certain figure, manifestly under a misconception because he tried to include contingency reserve, accumulated balance under the profit and loss account and provision for income-tax which could by no means be considered as accumulated profits of the company. Even profits from the sale of machinery could not be said to be accumulated profits without something more and mere appreciation of the original value of the machinery will not bring it within the expression ‘accumulated profits of the company’. Accumulation of profits is a deliberate act and implies a conscious volition to accumulate the profits. It is well known that reduction of share capital can be effected in company law by various methods, particularly classified as (i) with sanction of the court, and (ii) without such sanction. Forfeiture or surrender of shares of cancellation of unissued shares are examples of reduction of share capital for which sanction of the court is not necessary. In other cases, where the company wants to reduce its share capital, it can do so after obtaining sanction of the court. Section 2(6A) did not expressly mention or even impliedly include the concept of deemed dividend. The express section dealing with deemed dividend, and specially with super-tax on such deemed dividend, is section 23A. Explanation (ii ) of Paragraph D of Part II of the Finance (No. 2) Act, 1957, expressly says that the expression ‘dividend’ shall be deemed to include any distribution included in the expression ‘dividend’ as defined in clause (6A) of section 2. In the instant case, the reduction of share capital had not produced or had not been shown to have produced on any evidence an income by way of ‘dividend’ as contended by the revenue, according to the extended connotation of the word ‘dividend’. Before the Tribunal came to any finding of following rebate on super-tax, it had to be satisfied that the super tax was leviable on the total income of the company under Paragraph D of the Finance (No. 2) Act, 1957, because it was only in that event that the question of rebates on that super tax could arise. This primary condition, had not been satisfied in the instant case and, therefore, the Tribunal was not right in holding that any rebate of super-tax was allowable in the sense that no super-tax itself was leviable on the reduction of share capital which occurred in the facts and circumstances of the case. As the first condition had not been satisfied the consequential question of allowing rebate on super tax really did not arise. Further, this reduction of share capital had not produced an income on which a super-tax could be attached nor was it a dividend within the meaning of the Act or Paragraph D of the Finance (No. 2) Act, 1957. Further there was no evidence to hold that this reduction of share capital in the particular case meant any return of ‘accumulated profits’

The amalgamation order passed by the High Court is a judicial order and has statutory force and in case, the department had any objection, then same should have been given before the High Court for which sufficient time was allowed. Now, the department cannot clamour that such an amalgamation have been used by the assessee as a tool for tax evasion or as colourable device. [Para 15] Here in this case, by transferring the excess fair market value of the assets/shares to capital reserve could not be treated as a tax evasion practice. The difference between the fair market value of assets and liabilities taken over as per the book values, which has resulted in 'capital reserve', was recorded in the books. As per said scheme itself, such capital reserve was prohibited for any purpose by the transferee company, thus, such a creation of capital reserve cannot be questioned by the Assessing Officer or Commissioner (Appeals) or perceive it as any kind of tax evasion practice. Here in this case, the assets transferred to the assessee company from transferor companies pursuant to scheme of amalgamation, included 1,06,39,926 shares of IHFL. The fair market value of the said shares on the date of amalgamation was Rs. 456.47 per share which aggregated to Rs. 485.68 crores. Post amalgamation, the assessee company had sold 20,42,053 shares of IHFL out of 1,06,39,926 shares acquired on amalgamation, which was sold for consideration of Rs.453.88 per share resulting into a short term capital loss of Rs. 52.69 lakhs. Said loss has been included in the profit and loss account. The Assessing Officer has alleged that this reserve which has been created is on account of revaluation of assets and since during the relevant previous year such revalued assets has been disposed of and such amount which is standing as reserve was not credited in the profit and loss account. [Para 16]

Such a premise of the Assessing Officer cannot be approved for the reason that; firstly, this reserve has not been created on revaluation of asset albeit same has been acquired through amalgamation and the shares have been valued as per the purchase method for a certain price. Secondly, it is not revaluation of any asset held by the assessee, because no such reserve has been created by the assessee on revaluation of shares and revaluation of assets takes place only when the assessee decides to revalue the asset existing in the balance sheet. Lastly, in this case all the assets belonged to amalgamating companies, that is, the shares of IHFL originally belonged to PREPL and PPPL and appeared in their balance sheet; and these assets entered in the books of assessee by virtue of amalgamation valued on fair market value as mandated by the order of High Court. Thus, it would be wrong to say that there was any kind of revaluation of assets. Therefore, there could not be any question of invoking clause (j) of Explanation to section 115JB for calculation of book profit under section 115JB. Here in this case, nowhere it has been disputed that the profit and loss account has not been prepared in compliance of requirement of Part-I and Part-II of the Companies Act, 2013 and as per accounting standard. The profit and loss account has been approved by the statutory auditors and also laid before the Members in the AGM, which is sacrosanct for computing the book profit under section 115JB. Thus, once the accounts have been prepared in accordance with the Companies Act duly certified by statutory auditors and approved by Company AGM, then same cannot be disturbed. Here the Assessing Officer cannot tinker with such profit and loss account or treat the part of capital reserve by holding that it should have been routed through regular profit and loss account. [Para 17]

Thus, in this case the provisions of clause (j) of Explanation 1 to section 115JB would not be applicable at all as, there is no disposal of asset from the amount standing in revaluation reserve relating to revalued asset as per the reasoning given above; and accordingly, the addition made by the Assessing Officer and sustained by the Commissioner (Appeals) is directed to be deleted. [Para 19]
