On second appeal: HELD: The sole issue involved in this case is, whether the addition can be made in the book profit under section 115JB on account of shares sold by the assessee, which was held as 'capital reserve', which the Assessing Officer and Commissioner (Appeals) have treated on account of amount standing in revalued reserve relating to revaluation of assets in terms of clause (j) of Explanation 1 of section 115JB. Two subsidiary companies of the assessee, PREPL and PPPL were amalgamated with the assessee company being holding company, vide judgment and order of High court, wherein the Court has sanctioned the scheme of amalgamation. First of all it would be quite pertinent to note the relevant clauses of scheme of amalgamation which are important for the purpose of adjudication of present controversy. The relevant clauses dealing with accounting standard and purchase method adopted for valuing the assets and liabilities at a fair market value and how any excess on such transfer of assets and liabilities has to be treated as part of the capital reserve, which reads as that on the scheme becoming effective and with effect from the appointed date, transferee company shall account for amalgamation of transferor company no. 1 and transferor company no. 2 in its books of account as per the 'purchase Method' specified under the Accounting Standard 14 - 'Accounting for Amalgamation'. All the assets and liabilities of transferor company No. 1 and transferor company No. 2 shall be transferred to and vested in transferee company pursuant to this scheme and shall be recorded at their respective fair values. Any excess arising on transfer of assets and liabilities of transferor company no. 1 and transferor company no. 2 would be considered to form part of the "capital reserve" of transferee company. Such capital reserve shall be a reserve which arises pursuant to this scheme and shall not be, for any purpose, be considered to be a reserve created by transferee company. Any deficit shall be considered to form part of goodwill. [Para 13]

Aforesaid scheme thus clearly provides that, firstly, the 'purchase method' as prescribed in AS-14 was adopted stating that the transferee company shall account for amalgamation of transferor companies in its books of account; secondly, all assets and liabilities of the transferor companies shall be transferred and would be recorded in the respective fair values; and lastly, any excess arising on transfer of assets and liabilities of the transferor companies would be considered to form part of the "capital reserves" of the transferee company and such capital reserve shall not be for any purpose be considered to be a reserve created by the transferee company. Ergo, and if there is an excess on account of valuation on purchase method determining the fair market value was to form part of the capital reserve and no other mandate was given to the transferee company. The shares of IHFL was held by the amalgamating companies which has been transferred to the assessee-company and thus, it was akin to acquisition of an asset which as per the mandate of amalgamation scheme has to be treated as part of the capital reserve. Now, this scheme has been duly approved by High Court. In the conclusion of the said order, Court has specifically observed that any person interested shall be at liberty to apply to the court in the above matter for any directions that may be necessary. The said order of High Court sanctioning the entire amalgamation scheme had become final. It is further seen that vide General Circular No. 1 of 2014 issued by Ministry of Corporate Affairs to all Regional Directions and Registrars of Companies and all stake holders and notices were issued to all the concerned parties including the Income Tax Department. [Para 14]

Thereafter, High Court had also issued notices to the Income Tax Department through Assessing Officer which was received in the office of the Assessing Officer. The Assessing Officer/ Department nowhere had objected to said Scheme at any point of time, neither in pursuance of circular issued by Ministry of Corporate Affairs nor when the notice was issued by the High Court. Thus, scheme of amalgamation sanction by High court had become final. Such an order has a binding effect upon all. Once the amalgamation scheme has been approved and sanctioned by the Court, it has a statutory force and is binding on the company and all the stake holders.Thus, when amalgamation scheme has been approved by the Court, it is not open for the Assessing Officer and Commissioner (Appeals) to hold that amalgamation has been used by the assessee-company as a tool for tax evasion. The amalgamation order passed by the High Court is a judicial order and has statutory force and in case, the department had any objection, then same should have been given before the High Court for which sufficient time was allowed. Now, the department cannot clamour that such an amalgamation have been used by the assessee as a tool for tax evasion or as colourable device. [Para 15]

HEADNOTE: Section 2(22)(d) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deemed dividend - Assessee held shares in banking company, which was nationalised under the banking companies (Acquisition and Transfer of Undertakings) Act, 1970 - Company continued its business after nationalisation and offered option to shareholders to sell their shares to company itself - Assessee exercised such option - Reduction in share capital was also confirmed by High Court - Whether excess over original cost of shares received by assessee was distribution of accumulated profits by company and was hence taxable as deemed dividend - Held, no

FACT: The assessee, a sitting judge of the Delhi High Court, held shares in Punjab National Bank Ltd. The Bank was nationalised in 1969 under the Banking Companies (Acquisition and Transfer of Undertakings) Act, 1970 and received compensation of Rs. 10.20 crores as against its share capital of Rs. 2 crores. The bank, however, continued business even after nationalisation, and decided to purchase the shares from shareholders, if they so desired, so as the reduce its capital. The assessee exercised this option, and received in 1974 Rs. 6,400 from the Bank for his shares originally costing Rs. 2,910. The reduction in share capital was also approved by the High Court in January 1974. The AAC held that the surplus received by the assessee was a deemed dividend under section 2(22)(d) being a distribution made by the company out of accumulated profit.

On second appeal :

HELD: In accordance with the decision of the Supreme Court in Punjab Distilling Industries Ltd. v. CIT [1965] 57 ITR 1, the availability of accumulated profits had to be determined on the date on which reduction in capital took place, viz., 31-1-1974 in this case. The available balance sheet as on 31-12-1974 showed that the payment of purchase price of shares was made out of general reserves which had an opening balance of Rs. 7.38 crores. This amount included Rs. 8.20 crores, being the compensation money in excess of capital originally received. Proceeding on the basis that this amount of Rs. 8.20 crores did not include any element of capital gains, if this amount was excluded, there would be no accumulated profits from which the purchase price could have been paid. Even assuming that there was an element of capital gain, the payment could not be regarded as ‘distribution to shareholders’ since payments were made only to those who exercised the option and not to all the shareholders. If any distribution of accumulated profits was to be considered as deemed dividend under section 2(22)(d), the distribution should be to all the shareholders of the company. Either way, the AAC was not right in treating the amount as deemed dividend. It represented capital gains and being less than Rs. 5,000 was ab initio not liable to tax.

The Assessing Officer called for the details and placed on record the transfer, amalgamation and the approval of the Bombay High Court and finally accepted the assessee’s computation as regards the capital gains. This was not a case where the Assessing Officer had not made any enquiry and had reached at a wrong conclusion without fully dealing with all the required details. It was on record that the assessee in the course of its business of investment in shares and securities of other body corporate had subscribed and paid application money to various companies in the group between June 1997 to December 1999 for allotment of shares at par and there was a scheme of arrangement/re-organization under section 391/394 of the Companies Act. The Bombay High Court approved the scheme of reduction of the share capital as well as the amalgamation of the companies of different dates. The Board of Directors of all these companies had followed all the prescribed procedures under section 101(2) of the Companies Act to effect the reduction of share capital and the assessee had done nothing but saw the reduction of investments as a result of the scheme of arrangement as approved by the Bombay High Court. It could not be said that the entire reduction and subsequent amalgamation of the companies was done for dubious purpose of saving income-tax on possible capital gain arising on the sale of some other investments. The theory of the Commissioner could not be accepted that the entire arrangement was fraudulent scheme arranged just to avoid the payment of capital gains tax. The legal effect of the reduction of the share capital on the arrangement had resulted in satisfying the definition of the word ‘transfer’ in section 2(47) and the Assessing Officer had only given effect to the legal consequences of extinguishment of right in the investments made by the assessee. Therefore, it could not be said that the view taken by the Assessing Officer was one of the impossible views. He had taken one of the possible views considering the facts of the case and the ratio laid down by the Supreme Court in its decisions which had been elaborately discussed by the Assessing Officer. The Commissioner wanted to take a different view on the basis of the same decision which might perhaps be a view favourable to the interest of the revenue. But that did not render the order of the Assessing Officer as erroneous. The Assessing Officer had only followed what, according to him, was the correct legal consequence of the decisions of the Apex Court. In such a situation, it could not be said that the order of the Assessing Officer was erroneous. It was, therefore, to be held that the order passed by the Commissioner under section 263 was the result of a change of opinion and all that the Commissioner acting under section 263 wanted was the substitution of his own opinion for that of the Assessing Officer which was clearly impermissible within the scope of section 263. [Para 11]

Accordingly, the order of the Commissioner under section 263 was vacated.

If the second condition had not been introduced, bonus shares issued credited as fully paid up would have been liable to be regarded as "dividend" within section 2(6A)(a) but the legislature obviously did not want to tax such bonus shares as dividend and it, therefore, introduced the second condition in section 2(6A)(a) of the 1922 Act. When accumulated profits are capitalized and redeemable preference shares are issued as bonus shares credited as fully paid-up, the capitalized accumulated profits are converted into preference share capital. The balance-sheet thereafter shows the profit and loss account or reserves at a reduced figure and the issued capital at a correspondingly increased figure, the only effect being that one item on the liabilities side of the balance-sheet becomes replaced in whole or part by another item, namely, preference share capital, while the assets side of the balance-sheet remains unaffected. Now it is a fundamental principle of company law that the capital of a company must be maintained intact, for the company being a mere abstraction of law distinct from its members and the liability of the members being limited, it is the capital of the company which provides a minimum safeguard to third parties dealing with the company and the law, therefore, requires that no part of the capital shall be returned to the shareholders except under certain circumstances and by following a certain procedure requiring the scrutiny of the Court and, it is only if the Court sanctions, that there can be repayment to the shareholders in reduction of the capital. But notwithstanding this fundamental principle of maintenance of capital, redeemable preference shares can be repaid in accordance with the terms of issue otherwise than on a formal reduction of capital approved by the Court. The preference share capital collected from the holders of redeemable preference shares or credited as fully paid up out of capitalised accumulated profits can be returned to the shareholders without going through the procedure of reduction of capital, though such return of preference share capital would amount to reduction of capital. This would appear to constitute a departure from the fundamental principle of maintenance of capital, but if one look at section 105B of the Indian Companies Act, 1913, which was the section which governed redemption at the time when the redeemable preference shares in the present case were redeemed, it is found that the purity of this principle is not only not violated but is, on the contrary, preserved in effect, if not in name, by the stringent provisions contained in the section. Redeemable preference shares, according to these provisions, can be repaid out of profits or out of the proceeds of a fresh issue of shares made for the purpose of redemption or out of sale proceeds of any property of the company. If they are redeemed out of the proceeds of a fresh issue, the capital raised on that issue will obviously replace the capital redeemed and, consequently, the capital of the company will be maintained at the original yardstick. If on the other hand they are redeemed out of profits or out of sale proceeds of any property of the company, then out of profits an amount equivalent to the nominal amount of the shares redeemed is required to be transferred to a reserve fund to be called "The capital redemption reserve fund" which is to be treated as equivalent to paid up capital. Hence, although the redeemable preference shares disappear on redemption, the capital which they represent is retained for accounting purposes and there is no reduction of the capital yardstick. This analysis of the mechanics of redemption clearly shows that when redeemable preference shares are redeemed, the preference share capital is returned to the shareholders and since such return of the preference share capital would deplete the capital of the company and consequently affect the sanctity of the principle of maintenance of capital which is regarded as a principle of paramount importance, the law requires that the preference share capital so returned should be replaced by other capital either provided by a fresh issue of shares made for the purpose of redemption or transferred out of the profits of the company in case redemption is made out of profits or out of sale proceeds of any property of the company. It is undoubtedly true that redemption cannot be made except out of profits of the company or out of proceeds of a fresh issue of shares made for the purpose of redemption or out of sale proceeds of any property of the company, but these merely indicate the sources of the moneys which may be utilised for the purpose of returning the preference share capital to the shareholders. The only inhibition is that if a company wants to return the preference share capital to the shareholders the company must do so out of moneys earned by the company as profits or derived by the company from a fresh issue of shares or obtained by the company by selling any property belonging to it and if there are no such moneys, the company cannot return the preference share capital to its shareholders. But what is returned to the shareholders on redemption, what is distributed amongst them, is the preference share capital and not the profits of the company, or proceeds of the fresh issue of shares made for the purpose of redemption or sale proceeds of the property belonging to the company which merely provide the moneys for return of the preference share capital.

HEADNOTE: Section 2(22) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 2(6A)(a) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Deemed dividend -  Assessment year 1956-57 - Whether expression "income" in entry 54 of List I of Seventh Schedule to Government of India Act, 1935, and corresponding entry 82 of List I of the Seventh Schedule to Constitution of India, shall be widely and liberally construed so as to enable a legislature to provide by law for prevention of evasion of income-tax but there must be a reasonable nexus between item taxed and legislative field delineated - Held, yes - Whether as section 2(6A)(d) of 1922 Act embodies a law to prevent evasion of tax, it falls within ken of entry 54 of List I of Schedule VII to Government of India Act, 1935 - Held, yes - Whether if accumulated profits were distributed, it would satisfy not only definition of 'dividend' in section 2(6A)(d) of 1922 Act but also would bix year in which it would be deemed to be income - Held, yes - Whether dividends may be paid or credited to different shareholders during different accounting years; and shareholders may be assessed in respect of the said payments in different years even so, payments are referable only to declaration of dividends out of profits of a particular year - Held, yes - Assessee company by sanction of High Court reduced its capital from Rs. 50 lakhs to Rs. 15 lakhs and got requisite certificate from Registrar of companies - Noties were issued to shareholders inviting applications for refund and after receipt of applications amounts payable to shareholders were debited in accounts and refunds were actually granted during accounting year 1955, i.e., between 1-12-1954, and 30-11-1955 - Whether amounts were distributed only during accounting year, when amounts were both debited and paid and, therefore, dividends were distributed to shareholders during accounting year, i.e., 1954-55 - Held, yes

FACT: The assessee, a public limited company, was incorporated with a share capital of Rs. 50 lakhs. Got a sanction from the High Court for the reduction of the capital from Rs. 50 lakhs to Rs. 15 lakhs. The Registrar of Companies granted the requisite certificate under section 61(4) of the Indian Companies Act. The appellant issued notices to the shareholders inviting applications for the refund of share capital so reduced. On the receipt of the applications, appropriate debit entries were made in the accounts of the shareholders and the amounts were actually paid to them during the previous year, i.e., 1-12-1954, to 30-11-1955. Under section 2(6A)(d) of the 1922 Act, 'dividend' includes any distribution by a company on the reduction of its capital to the extent to which the company possesses accumulated profits, whether such accumulated profits have been capitalised or not. In assessing the income of the appellant-company for the assessment year 1956-57, the ITO held that the said dividends were distributed during the accounting year and on that finding he calculated the rebate on super-tax in terms of clause (i)(b) of the second proviso to paragraph D of Part II of the First Schedule to the Finance Act, 1956. The ITO further held that the assessee's accumulated profits at the time of the reduction of the capital from Rs. 25 lakhs to Rs. 15 lakhs were Rs. 8,42,337. On appeal, the AAC accepted the said figure arrived at by the ITO. On further appeal, the Tribunal, for the reasons recorded by it in its order, reduced the figure under the said head by a sum of Rs. 3,61,405.

It was contended on behalf of the assessee that inasmuch as the certificate from the Registrar for the reduction of the capital from Rs. 25 lakhs to Rs. 15 lakhs was obtained on 4-11-1954, the distribution of the dividends should be deemed to have taken place during the year 1953-54 and, therefore, the said dividends were not exigible to tax for the assessment year. The ITO, the AAC and the Tribunal concurrently rejected that plea and held that, as the actual payment to the shareholders of the refund of the capital and the debit in the accounts of the shareholders were effected in the accounting year, the said dividends must be held to have been distributed in the accounting year.

On reference, the High Court gave decision against the assessee.

On appeal :

Section 2(22)( d) creates a legal fiction. This is to enlarge the ken of section. Before applying the deeming provision it has to be seen that conditions precedent for invoking such deeming provision do exist in the facts and circumstances of the case. Such a deeming provision or legal fiction should be narrowly watched, jealously regarded and never to be pressed beyond its true limits. The parameters set within the statute should be strictly examined with reference to the factual matrix of the case. In the instant case, scheme of arrangement resulted in reorganisation of capital. There was no reduction of capital. For reduction of capital Companies Act enumerates procedure laid down in sections 100 to 105. Recourse was not made to this procedure. In effect arrangement in the present case resulted in splitting up capital of the company into two companies. There was no reduction of capital in the aggregate. The shareholding of the individual shareholders were split between two companies. The aggregate of holding of each shareholder in the two companies continued to be the same as was the original share-holding in the parent company.

As such the first requisite of section 2(22 )(d) was not satisfied. Shares were issued to the assessee by foreign company and not by company H of which the assessee was the shareholder. In other words, there was no distribution of shares by the parent company. As such, the second condition laid down under section 2(22)(d ) was also not satisfied.

Thus, apparently, there was no distribution on the reduction of share capital. Therefore, there was no question of utilisation of accumulated profits for the purpose of distribution. As such, the case of the assessee did not fall within the ambit and scope of section 2(22)(a ).

Apropos the contention that jurisdiction under section 263 cannot be assumed on the basis of change of opinion, the issue was considered by the Assessing Officer. He did ask for explanation of the assessee. That explanation was considered. The view taken by the Assessing Officer was in conformity with the decision of the Commissioner (Appeals) in the cases of other shareholders. Therefore, view of the Assessing Officer was definitely a possible view in the matter. Having regard to the facts it could not be said that the view taken by the Assessing Officer was patently erroneous.

For assuming jurisdiction under section 263 it is sine qua non, that the twin conditions must be satisfied, namely, order must be erroneous and it must be prejudicial to the interest of the revenue. The Commissioner must have some cogent material before him to declare the order of the Assessing Officer as erroneous. The order of the Assessing Officer cannot be held to be erroneous merely on the whims and fancy of the Commissioner. In the instant case, the order of the Assessing Officer did not certain with any legal error. As such, it could not be said that the order was erroneous or prejudicial to the interest of the revenue.

Hence, the conditions precedent for invoking jurisdiction under section 263 did not exist in the facts and circumstances of the present case. Accordingly, the order passed under section 263 was quashed.

FACT: The assesee was a shareholder of company H. A foreign company entered into a joint venture with company H in respect of computer business only. The company H was a multi unit company. Under a scheme of arrangement submitted to the High Court, the assessee received certain shares in foreign company. The shares held in company H were declared but the aggregate holding of the assessee remained the same. The assessee received cash towards fractional shares arising on such reconstruction. The assessee sold certain shares received on reconstruction to foreign company and the remaining shares were held by him. For the assessment year 1992-93, the assessee reflected certain amount as long term capital gains in his return. The Assessing Officer made certain queries on the arrangement scheme and completed the assessment under section 143(3). The Commissioner invoked the provisions of section 263 and held that the order of the Assessing Officer was erroneous and prejudicial to the interest of the revenue inasmuch as the benefit received on account of reduction in share capital and distribution of shares to the existing share-holder as well as payment of enhanced consideration could be considered to be deemed dividend under section 2(22)( d) and as such, it was exigible to tax. He, therefore, cancelled the assessment and directed the Assessing Officer frame assessment afresh.

On appeal :

HELD: The purpose of section 2(22 )(d) is to bring within the net of taxation payments made by distribution of assets or money of the company which can be taken to have come from the accumulated profits. This is so as the fiction contained in sub-clause is limited to the extent of the accumulated profits. Where there are no accumulated profits in the company, the fiction cannot be attracted.

Accumulated profits of the company may be utilised by the company for increasing the capital stock or for distributing the same among the share-holders by way of dividend and for reducing the capital. Ordinarily, a company reduces the capital when there is loss or depreciation of assets. In that event, there is no question of distribution of profits to the share-holders. In that eventuality, the shares are only devaluated. But a company may on the pretext of reducing its capital may utilise its accumulated profit to pay back to the shareholders the whole or part of the paid up amounts on the shares. A shareholder, though in form gets back the whole or a part of the capital contributed by him in effect he gets a share of the accumulated profit which, if a straight away course is followed, he should have received as dividend. This is a diversion of profit in the guise of division of capital - a distribution of profit under colour of reduction of capital. The Legislature. therefore, in the interest of the ex chequer, elongated the scope of the definition of "dividend" so as to catch the said payments within the net of taxation.

Before applying the deeming provision it has to be seen that conditions precedent for invoking such deeming provision do exist in the facts and circumstances of the case. Such a deeming provision or legal fiction should be narrowly watched, jealously regarded and never to be pressed beyond its true limits. The parameters set within the statute should be strictly examined with reference to the factual matrix of the case.

However, while approving the Scheme, the Company Court has categorically held that 'this order will not be construed as an order granting exemption from payment of stamp duty or, taxes or, any other charges, if any,payable, as per the relevant provisions of law'. Whenever a Company distributes its profits to its shareholders, the profit so disbursed, will amount to dividend. Clause (d) to section 2 (22) of the Act, demonstrates that if any distribution is made to his shareholders by a Company on the reduction of his capital, it would be a dividend. [Para 25]

In view of the reasons stated for purchasing the shares under the Scheme of Arrangement under Sections 391 to 393 of the Companies Act, Prima-facie there is no merit in the contention of the assessee that the shares purchased pursuant to the order of Company Court would be a capital gain and not to be treated as dividend.

HEADNOTE: Section 2(22)(d) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deemed dividend - Assessment year 1963-64 - Whether a dividend would and should come out of accumulated profits - Held, yes - Whether where company made advance to its share holders in previous years, it must be taken as having come out of profits of previous year and when it had not been established that there had been deductions made from accumulated profits in past when dividend was issued or advances made, same had to be deducted from accumulated profits of year in question - Held, yes

Section 45, read with section 2(47) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Capital Gains - Chargeable as - Assessment years 1963-64 - Whether where company  in which assessee was holding certain shares reduced face value of its share, no capital gains was assessable in hands of assessee as there was no extinguishments of any right of assessee and consequently, there was no transfer within meaning of section 2(47) - Held, yes

FACT: The assessee was a shareholder in a company. During relevant accounting period the company resolved to reduce its capital. The necessary procedure was gone through, the court order was obtained and the reduction was given effect to on 25-5-1962. The result of the reduction was to reduce the value of the share. Consequent on this reduction, there was distribution of assets and money to the shareholders. The company also advanced certain amount to four shareholders in the previous years.

The Tribunal held that the deemed dividends viz., the advances made to the shareholders, assessed in the hands of the various shareholders in the past assessment years, should be deducted from the surplus while determining the ‘accumulated profits’ in the hands of the company. The Tribunal further held that no capital gain was assessable in the hands of the assessee as there was no extinguishment of any right of the assessee and consequently there was no transfer within the meaning of section 2(47), by the assessee of any capital assets for the relevant assessment year.

On reference:

HELD: It is clear on a reading of section 2(22)(d ) that, on distribution, there will be an issue of dividend only to the extent to which the company possesses accumulated profits. The purpose of this section appears to be to bring within the net of taxation payments made by distribution of assets or moneys of the company which can be taken to have come from the accumulated profits. If there was no accumulated profit in the company, the fiction could not be attracted and if the accumulated profit in the company is less than the value of the assets or moneys distributed, the fiction will be applied only to the extent of the available accumulated profit.

The profits of the year of accounting which will be taxed in the assessment year, ‘till the date of distribution’ is also included in the term 'accumulated profits' as defined in section 2(22) by virtue of the Explanation thereto. Apart from the profits of the year on the date of distribution, accumulated profits can take in accumulated profits of the years previous to the previous year as long as the profits accrued before 1-4-1933, are not taken into account. Accumulated profits, therefore, is the amount which has been accumulated from the profits arising from the past performance of the company year by year. It is of course undistributed profit which is implied by the term ‘accumulated’. From the entries in a balance-sheet, it may not be possible at a glance to find out what exactly is the accumulated profit of the company at any given time. Even assuming that the general reserves of the company may reflect accumulated profits, whether the entirety of the general reserves would be accumulated profits cannot be discerned by merely looking at the balance-sheet of the company. In the absence of specific reserves for taxation or other liabilities of the company in relation to its performance in the past years, those liabilities may have to be met from the general reserves. To take the figures from the balance-sheet, therefore, with regard to the accumulated profits would not in all cases be a correct procedure, for the quantum of the general reserves need not represent the accumulated profits. If the liabilities that accrued from year to year had been taken into account year by year and the accumulated profits had been depleted year by year by writing down the accumulated profits and only the balance carried over, the total of the accumulated profits in any given year will be less than in cases where there has been no deduction made for accrued liabilities.

The objection further said that in view of non-disclosure of the bank guarantee amount, the balance sheet did not disclose ‘true and fair view’ of the accounts of the company and, as such, the accounts of the company were not reliable and in view of the glaring facts, there could be no compromise. It would absolutely be correct to say that the compromise and demerger scheme was a package deal and when a party was agreeable to the compromise in a package deal, then such party would be entitled to all the benefits flowing from the scheme. It was also true to say that the statutory liabilities and other liabilities, known or unknown, real or contingent, would have to be suffered by ‘N’ and at that stage, it was not possible to define with reasonable certainty and exact calculation as to what would be the sum total of such liabilities. At the relevant time the amount under the bank guarantee had been paid for or on behalf of Core and if that amount ultimately was to be refunded, then the benefit must go to the party entitled to it under the scheme. It would also be correct to say that if ‘N’ fulfilled the export obligations, then their right to recover the money from the Customs Department would be a right flowing from the scheme and, in fact, the amount to be paid to N would not be an amount, which was to go back to the HDFC Bank. In case, there was no scheme and petitioner fulfilled the export obligations, then Core would be entitled to the refund and HDFC, even at that time, could not say that the money should be paid to them directly. Under the circumstances, the objection raised by HDFC did not merit consideration. [Para 131]

In relation to the objection regarding the share exchange ratio, the petitioners had submitted that none of the objectors-banks were shareholders of the petitioners and, therefore, they were not entitled to raise such objection. Conferral of that benefit upon the shareholders would also have to be appreciated from the viewpoint of the shareholders, who were to get something against nothing and that was persuading them to accept the scheme. . The accumulated profits are to be ascertained on the date of the distribution. But the accumulated profits must be ascertained on the date of the reduction of capital. Thus the two events, namely, the distribution and the reduction of capital must synchronise, and the accumulated profits must also be ascertained at the same point of time. The synchronisation is also obvious on a plain reading of the abridged text 'any distribution on the reduction of capital to the extent of accumulated profits'. In the instant case, the resolution for the reduction of the capital of the company and the consequential refund of the surplus capital to its shareholders took effect on 4-11-1954. Consequently, the distribution of the dividend as defined by section 2(6A)(d) of the 1922 Act, took place on 4-11-1954, i.e., during the previous year corresponding to the assessment year 1955-56. It is true that during the accounting year ending 30-11-1954, the company did not pay any dividends, nor make any book entries with regard to reduction of capital or with regard to refund or payment of surplus capital. But the company incurred on 4-11-1954, the legal liability to make the refunds and the distribution must be deemed to have taken place on 4-11-1954, though no book entries were made and no payments were made on that date. In view of the fact that the distribution took effect on 4-11-1954, the company was bound to make necessary entries in their books on 4-11-1954, showing the reduction of capital, and was also bound to show the reduction in its balance-sheet for the year ending 30-11-1954. Irrespective of its method of book-keeping, the company incurred on 4-4-1954, the legal liability to make the refunds. The method of book-keeping is not relevant, but, were it so, it was pertinent to remember that the accounts of the company were kept on the mercantile basis. That system of accounting brings into debit as expenditure the amount for which a legal liability has been incurred before it is actually disbursed.

Thus, the revenue authorities should have/but in fact have not fixed the amount of the dividend by reference to the accumulated profits on 4-11-1954, when the resolution for reduction of capital became effective, or by reference to the accumulated profits brought forward on 1-12-1953, at the commencement of the accounting year during which the reduction of capital took effect. Instead, the revenue authorities took into account the accumulated profits on 1-12-1954, that is to say, the date of the commencement of the subsequent accounting year during which the dividends were paid.

The revenue authorities rightly assumed that the distribution and the ascertainment of the accumulated profits to the extent of which the distribution is deemed to be dividend under section 2(6A)(d) of the 1922 Act took place during the same accounting year, but they erred in holding that the accounting year commencing on 1-12-1954, was the relevant year.

The High Court was in error in holding that dividends under section 2(6A)(d) of the 1922 Act were distributed during the previous year corresponding to the assessment year 1956-57. The dividends, if any, under section 2(6A)(d) of the 1922 Act were distributed in the previous year corresponding to the assessment year 1955-56.

Note : The case was decided in favour of the revenue.

[Para 34] The provisions of section 77 of the Companies Act, 1956 prohibits a company from purchase of its own shares except by way of actual reduction in capital in accordance with sections 100-104 or section 402 of the Companies Act, 1956. The only exception to this is the newly introduced non obstinate clause under section 77A of the Companies Act, 1956, for buyback of its own shares. The provisions of sections 391-393 are only a single window scheme through which various actions are undertaken. Therefore, the purchase of own shares will have to still relate back to either section 77 read with section 100 or section 77A. There cannot be any purchase of own shares just under sections 391-393 without relate back to section 77 read with sections 100-104 or section 77A of the Companies Act, 1956. Therefore, the transaction of the assessee would either to fall under sections 391-393 read with section 77 and section 100 of the Companies Act, 1956 or sections 391-393 read with section 77A of the Companies Act, 1956. The scheme has clearly states that it is not a buyback under section 77A. Therefore, once the assessee itself specifically states that it is not buyback under section 77A, then, it should automatically fall back to section 77 read with sections 100-104 of the Companies Act, 1956. If sections 100-104 read with section 77 of the Companies Act, 1956 are applied, then said transaction is nothing but reduction of capital and distribution of accumulated profits, and thus, comes within the ambit of provisions of section 2(22)(d) and section 115-O. [Para 37]

In the instant case, the assessee itself has stated that it is not a buyback under section 77A of the Companies Act. In any event under section 77A/68 of the Companies Act, 1956, a company can buyback only 25 per cent of the total paid up share capital and free reserves. In the present case, the conditions prescribed under section 77A of the Companies Act, 1956, are not satisfied, because, the purchase of its own shares by the assessee is more than 25 per cent of the total paid up share capital and free reserves which is evident from the facts brought on record by the authorities, where, it has been observed that 54.70 per cent of capital has been reduced after the scheme was given effect. Therefore, once the buyback is not under section 77A of the Companies Act, 1956, then, it will fall back under sections 391-393 read with sections 100-104 of the Companies Act, 1956, because, without any reference to sections 100-104 of the Companies Act, 1956, no company can buyback its shares under sections 391-393 alone. Therefore, the Assessing Officer & the Commissioner (Appeals) have rightly held that the transactions of purchase of its own shares is nothing but distribution of accumulated profits and reduction of capital which falls under the definition of dividend under section 2(22)(d). [Para 38]

HELD: Reduction of share capital of company is permissible under the Companies Act by following a specific procedure as laid down therein. This decision is taken after affording the individual shareholder to participate in the decision making process wherein they are free to give their views and the majority view or opinion prevails. If the decision to reduce share capital is approved the consequences follows obviously by following the statutory formalities. In the instant case the reduction of share capital in the plaintiff-company has taken place not by such process but as a part of a rehabilitation scheme sanctioned by AAIFR in the process of reviving the plaintiff-company. The sole object while sanctioning or approving a scheme on a company being referred to under SICA is to rehabilitate and if possible to revive the company from the stage for which the company had to be referred to BIFR under SICA. The individual shareholder though had a right to participate in the proceedings before BIFR or AAIFR and express their views but the same was in a limited score unlike their participation to reduce share capital under the Companies Act, 1956 being the act prevalent at the time when reduction of share capital in the plaintiff-company was allowed. A rehabilitation scheme like the one introduced in the plaintiff-company is sanctioned under the provisions of section 18(2)(f) and section 18(4). The scheme becomes binding on an individual shareholder for the purpose of reviving the company till the scheme is successfully worked out or implemented. The scheme is always open to modification to accommodate the difficulties faced in course of implementing the scheme. Any provision including the step approved for reduction of share capital like that in case of the plaintiff remains open till the scheme is successfully worked out. It may so happen that the scheme fails and the company is directed to be wound up. The act of reduction of share capital under a scheme like that in the plaintiff is a contingent act, which fructifies on the successful implementation of the scheme. The reduction of share capital allowed under the scheme, therefore, cannot be said to have achieved finality during the implementation of the scheme. This act of reduction of share capital in the plaintiff-company pursuant to the scheme will crystallize only on the scheme being successfully worked out. [Para 16]

In the instant case the reduction of share capital was brought by way of a Rehabilitation Scheme framed under section 18(2)(f) and section 18(4) and not by following the procedure available under the Companies Act. The BIFR and the AAIFR under the provisions of section 18(2)(f) and section 18(4) are competent to formulate a composite scheme permitting reduction of share capital for rehabilitation of the company. This fact is not in dispute. In such factual background the reduction in share capital permitted under the Rehabilitation Scheme shall continue to hold good till the scheme is in operation or in such time it is successfully implemented. The situation will be different if the implementation is not successful and an order of winding up of the plaintiff-company is ultimately directed. It is also possible that the Rehabilitation Scheme permitting reduction of share capital may be further modified during the course of implementation which may have an effect over the portion of the scheme which permits reduction of share capital. It can, therefore, be said that still the scheme has been successfully implemented, the reduction of share capital permitted under the said scheme does not achieve finality and is subject to being further modified. [Para 20]

FACT: The assessee-company held preference shares in 'R' company, which had in the year 1945 issued shares at a premium and kept the shares premiums so received under the head 'Capital Reserve'. Out of the above capital reserve, the 'R' company paid a sum as dividend on the said preference shares to the assessee. For the assessment year 1954-55, the ITO taxed the said sum in the hands of the assessee as dividend within section 2(6A) of 1922 Act. On appeal, the AAC held that said dividend was not taxable. On appeal, the Tribunal, however, agreed with the ITO. On reference, the High Court upheld the order of the Tribunal.

On appeal to the Supreme Court :

HELD: It is evident from the definition of the word 'dividend' in section 2(6A) of 1922 Act that if a distribution of accumulated profits, whether capitalised or not, entails the release by the company to its shareholder of all or any part of its assets, it is dividend. It was not disputed that the distribution of dividend entailed the release of the assets of 'R' company. It could not be said that the premiums received by the 'R' company were not profits within regulation 97 of Table A of 1913 Act. Previous to the enactment of section 78 of 1956 Act, and the corresponding section in the English Companies Act, it was recognised that a company could distribute premiums received on the issue of shares as dividends.

A company which had issued shares at a premium before the commencement of 1956 Act would by virtue of section 78 of 1956 Act have to open a share premium account and transfer to it the premium so received. If before the commencement of 1956 Act the company had already dealt with the premium in such a way that they had ceased to remain as an identifiable part of the company's reserves, in that event the premiums so dealt with shall be disregarded in determining the sum to be included in the share premium account. If such premiums are to be disregarded for the creation of the share premium account, it means that they fall outside the purview of section 78 of 1956 Act. It has no application to them. If this is so, it is difficult to appreciate how the assessee could utilise this section for the purpose of showing that the premiums which had already been distributed became invested with the character of capital in the hands of the distributing company. It could not be said that for the purpose of income-tax any future application of the share-premium account in one of the ways mentioned in sub-section (2) will be treated as distribution of capital. No such question arose for determination in the instant case. But it was held that section 78 of 1956 Act does not in any way change the taxability of dividends declared out of premiums on shares received by a company before the Act of 1956 came into force. If it was taxable, apart from section 78, it remains so taxable.

In the result, the High Court was justified in disallowing assessee's claim. Hence, the appeal was dismissed.

Note : The case was decided in favour of the revenue.

Further there was no evidence to hold that this reduction of share capital in the particular case meant any return of ‘accumulated profits’ . There was no question in the instant case of any dividend from any subsidiary Indian company within the meaning of Paragraph D of the Finance (No. 2) Act, 1957 and its provisos. The conditions laid down in proviso (i), (ii ) or (iii) of Paragraph D of the Finance (No. 2) Act, 1957, were not present in the instant reference.

section 391 the Court is invested with very wide powers to approve or sanction any scheme of amalgamation, arrangement, compromise or reconstruction. The Court has power to sanction all matters which for their effectuation require a special procedure to be followed under the Act. The only exception to this is the special procedure to be followed under section 101 for reduction of capital since rule 85 of the Court Rules specifically enjoins the following of a special procedure prescribed for reduction of share capital. [Para 19] The opening words of section 77A, viz., "notwithstanding anything, contained in this Act, but subject to the provisions of sub-section (2) of this section and section 77B, a company may purchase its own shares or other specified securities...." show that section 77A is a facilitating provision which enables the companies to buy-back their shares without having to approach the Court under section 391 and sections 100 to 104 subject to compliance with the provisions of sub-sections (2), (3) and (4). Prior to the introduction of section 77A, the only manner in which a company could buy-back its shares was by following the procedure set out under sections 100 to 104 and section 391 which required the calling of separate meetings of each class of shareholders and creditors as well as (if required by the Court) the drawing up of a list of creditors of the company and obtaining of their consent to the scheme for reduction. The legislative intention behind the introduction of section 77A is to provide an alternative method by which a company may buy-back up to 25 per cent of its total paid-up equity capital in any financial year subject to compliance with sub- sections (2), (3) and (4). It does not supplant or take away any part of the pre-existing jurisdiction of the Company Court to sanction a scheme for such reduction under sections 100 to 104 and section 391. [Para 22]

The non obstante clause in section 77A, namely ‘notwithstanding anything contained in this Act....’ only means that notwithstanding the provisions of section 77 and sections 100 to 104, the company can buy-back its shares subject to compliance with the conditions mentioned in that section without approaching the Court under sections 100 to 104 or section 391. There is nothing in the provision of section 77A to indicate that the jurisdiction of the Court under section 391 or 394 has been taken away or substituted. It is well-settled that the exclusion of the jurisdiction of the Court should not readily be inferred; such exclusion should be explicitly or clearly implied. There is nothing in the language of section 77 that gives rise to such an inference. Therefore, section 77A is merely an enabling provision and the Court’s powers under sections 100 to 104 and section 391 are not in any way affected. The conditions provided in section 77A are applicable only to buy-back of shares under section 77A. The conditions applicable to sections 100 to 104 and section 391 cannot be imported into or made applicable to a buy-back under section 77A. Similarly the conditions for a buy-back under section 77A cannot be applied to a scheme under sections 100 to 104 and section 391. The two operate in independent fields. [Para 23]

It is not disputed that reduction in the capital can be effected under section 77 read with sections 100 to 104 and 391 even in the case of buy-back of shares. Even in cases where capital is reduced by optional sale reduction results after the option is exercised to the extent of the shares cancelled. This is as equally a reduction of capital as in the case of compulsory cancellation of shares. There is no distinction between the two on the aspect of the reduction. The word ‘arrangement’ is of wide import and is not restricted to a compulsory purchase or acquisition of shares there is no reason as to why a cancellation of shares and the consequent reduction of capital cannot be covered by section 391 read with section 100 merely because a shareholder is given an option to cancel or to retain his shares. In view of the foregoing discussion, the objection of the appellants based on section 77A must be rejected. [Para 24]

(iii) Whether the scheme sanctioned by the Company Court was contrary to any provisions of law or was unconscionable and unfair and against the interest of the shareholders?

The principal attack against the scheme sanctioned by the Company Judge was that the scheme treated the silence of shareholders as an offer. It was contended that that was contrary to the well-established principles of transfer of shares and that it violated various provisions of various laws such as Companies Act, Depositories Act, and the SEBI and NSDL Regulations. It would be highly unjust to allow the Central Government to raise an objection of such nature at the appellate stage. The draft order of the Company Judge recorded that the Central Government had submitted to the order of the Court. The Judge specifically recorded in the minutes of the order that the Central Government had no objection to the scheme. As indicated earlier, a vast majority of shareholders had exercised their option in accordance with the scheme. In these circumstances, it would be wholly inequitable to entertain such objections at such belated stage. [Para 25]

Resultantly, the appeals were to be dismissed.

headnotes.text: Section 5 of the Income tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 4 of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Income - Accrual of - Assessment year 1935-36 company ‘R’ had accumulated substantial reserve and resolved to capitalize it - It was also decided that capitalized fund would later on be distributed amongst shareholders as bonus share - Company ‘R’ purchased share of company ‘A’ - Later on; it resolved to reduce its capital by returning to shareholder share in company ‘A’, which was confirmed by District Court - Revenue held that whole transaction was illusory and share of company ‘A’ allotted to assessee shareholders had never become capital and it would represent profits of company ‘R’ which would be taxable in hands of assessee - Whether department was competent to go behind order of court confirming reduction of capital and to hold that what was sought to be released and reduced of its share capital was release of profits - Held, No - Whether value of shares of company ‘A’ received by assessee was not liable to be included in his income - Held, yes

Section 45 of the income-tax act, 1961-Capital gains-Chargeable as-Consequent on reduction of share capital effected by assessee-company, company became liable to pay a sum to the shareholders-To discharge its liability, assessee distributed to shareholders shares held by it and at the time of their distribution to shareholders, it revalued them at market price and credited the difference between book value and market value in capital reserve account-Whether difference between book value of shares and the market value at which they were transferred to shareholders was capital gains chargeable to tax as there was transfer of these shares from company to shareholders-Held, on facts, yes

Section 2(22), read with sections 46A, 115-O and 246, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deemed dividend (Clause (d)) - Assessee-company was engaged in business of development of computer software and related services and export - During year 2016, assessee sought order of Court to buy back its own shares - Said scheme got approved by Court and, accordingly, consideration for such buy-back was paid to shareholders - Gain arising to shareholders in course of buy-back was offered to taxation as capital gain under section 46A - Department submitted that buy-back of share was nothing but distribution of accumulated profit and it had to be treated as dividend under section 2(22)(d) and Dividend Distribution Tax at 15 per cent was required to be paid by assessee under section 115-O - Assessee filed writ petition on ground that gain on buy-back of shares could not be categorized as a dividend and it was capital gain as per section 46A - Whether profit on shares purchased pursuant to order of Court would amount to dividend and would not amount to capital gain - Held, yes - Whether since assessee had an appeal remedy under section 246, and attempt had been made by it to bypass said appeal remedy, writ petition failed and same was to be dismissed - Held, yes [Paras 30-32] [In favour of revenue]

Section 2(22)  of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 2(6A) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] read with schedule I, para D, of the Finance (No. 2) Act, 1957 - Deemed dividend - Assessment year 1957-58 - On orders of High Court share capital of company was reduced, and company distributed amounts to shareholders in consequence of such reduction - ITO held that company had accumulated profits and to that extent distribution by company on reduction of share capital would be regarded as dividend - Tribunal held that rebate of super-tax was allowable to assessee under clause (iii) of first proviso to para D of Part II of First Schedule to Finance (No. 2) Act, 1957 - However, there was no evidence to hold that reduction of share capital in particular case meant any return of "accumulated profits" and there was no question in instant case of any dividend from any subsidiary Indian company within meaning of Paragraph D of the Finance (No. 2) Act, 1957, and its provisos - Whether reduction of share capital did not produce any income on which super tax could be levied nor it was dividend within meaning of Act or Paragraph D of Finance (No. 2) Act, 1957 - Held, yes - Whether, therefore, Tribunal was not right in holding that any rebate of super-tax was allowable in sense that no super-tax itself was leviable on reduction of share capital which occurred in facts and circumstances of case - Held, yes

Section 2(22)(d),  read with section 194, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deemed dividend - Assessment year 1963-64 - Whether advances given by company to its shareholders must be treated as dividend for all purposes and would go to reduce accumulated profits of company, whether capitalised or not, whenever such accumulated profits are required to be determined - Held, yes - Whether only that part of distributed amount attributable to accumulated profits alone can be taxed as dividend - Held, yes  Section 45,  read with section 2(22) and 2(47) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Capital gains - Assessable as - Assessment year 1963-64 - Whether amount distributed by a company on reduction of its share capital has two components, viz., distribution attributable to accumulated profits and distribution attributable to capital and to the extent of accumulated profits in hands of company, (whether such accumulated profits are capitalised or not), return to shareholder on reduction of his share capital would be taxable as dividend in his hands and only balance may be subject to tax as capital gains if they accrue - Held, yes - Whether, where assessee had been paid not merely cash but had also been given a property for reduction in value of his shares, while computing capital gains out of total amounts so received including value of property received, portion attributable to accumulated profits would have to be deleted - Held, yes  Section 2(47) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Transfer - Whether transaction of reduction of share capital by company and prorata distribution of amount/assets to shareholders amount to 'transfer' within meaning of section 2(47) - Held, yes

Section 2(22)  of the Income-tax Act, 1961 (Corresponding to section 2(6A)(d) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922 read with Entry 54, List I, Schedule 7 of Government of India Act, 1935 - Deemed dividend - Assessment year 1956-57 - Section 2(6A)(d) was challenged as ultra vires Central Legislature as it had power to make laws only in respect of ‘income’ under Entry 54 but section 2(6A)(d) purported to impose tax on capital on its reduction, even though only to extent of accumulated profits possessed by a company - Whether since real object and effect of section 2(6A)(d) was that distribution by a company on reduction of its capital limited to amount which company possessed as accumulated profits was to be treated as dividend, capital character of company was not being disturbed - Held, yes - Whether since provision was intended to prevent evasion of tax by a company by transferring its profits to capital and then by reducing capital proportionately thereby distributing profits under guise of “capital reduction”, it was within ambit of Entry 54 not only in form but in substance and was not ultra vires Central Legislature - Held, yes - Whether where in case of such distribution although Certificate of reduction capital was granted by Registrar of Companies in year 1954-55 but debits of refund were actually made in accounts of shareholders and refunds actually granted to them in accounting year 1955-56, dividend must be deemed to have been distributed in accounting year 1955-56 and was liable to be assessed in assessment year 1956-57 and not in assessment year 1955-56, notwithstanding accounts of company being maintained on mercantile basis - Held, yes

Section 2(22) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deemed dividend - Assessment year 1989-90 - Assessee was shareholder of company AIPL - There had been two amalgamations whereby group companies including some wholly-owned subsidiaries of company ‘AIPL’ had amalgamated with AIPL under supervision of High Court - Subsequently, during previous year relevant to assessment year 1989-90, AIPL effected reduction of its capital from Rs. 100 per equity share to Rs. 45 per equity share - There was specific provision in Articles of AIPL to effect that capital profits of company could not be distributed - During assessment proceedings, Assessing Officer worked out accumulated profits of AIPL by including capitalised part of share capital issued in exchange of shares of subsidiaries, surplus arising on account of cancellation of shares of subsidiaries held by each other; excess of distribution over book value of shares of certain wholly owned subsidiaries from liquidators; and provision for tax and existing disputed tax liability - He held that payment of Rs. 55 per share on account of reduction of share capital was made out of these accumulated profits and thereby provision of section 2(22)(d) was attracted - Whether where High Court had approved amalga-mations it could not be said that series of amalgamations was carried out as a tax planning device and to avoid capital gains tax - Held, yes - Whether expression ‘accumulated profits’ used in section 2(22)(d) is to be construed as commercial profits computed in accordance with principles of commercial accounting and these profits are not to be treated as equivalent to assessable income - Held, yes - Whether surplus arising on amalgamation of companies results in revenue gain and can be treated as accumulated profits of amalgamated company - Held, no - Whether profits in balance sheet of amalgamating company can be treated as accumulated profits of amalgamated company - Held, no - Whether, insofar as profits of capital nature are concerned arising from sale of capital assets, such profits are to be excluded for purpose of ascertaining accumulated profits under section 2(22) unless such capital profits have been subjected to capital gains under section 45 - Held, yes - Whether, therefore, surplus realised by amalgamating company 
 and capitalised by issue of paid-up capital would not be covered under the expression ‘accumulated profits or capitalised profits’ for purpose of section 2(22)(d) - Held, yes - Whether, therefore, in instant case, Assessing Officer was wrong in working out accumulated profits by including aforementioned surpluses, and reworked profits being negative, provisions of section 2(22)(d) were inapplicable - Held, yes

Section 2(22)(d) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deemed dividend - Assessee held shares in banking company, which was nationalised under the banking companies (Acquisition and Transfer of Undertakings) Act, 1970 - Company continued its business after nationalisation and offered option to shareholders to sell their shares to company itself - Assessee exercised such option - Reduction in share capital was also confirmed by High Court - Whether excess over original cost of shares received by assessee was distribution of accumulated profits by company and was hence taxable as deemed dividend - Held, no

Section 2(22), read with section 115-O, of the Income-tax Act, 1961, articles 10 and 13 of the DTAA between India and Mauritius and sections 391 to 394 of the Companies Act, 1956 - Deemed dividend (Sub-clauses (a) and (d) of section 2(22)) - Assessment year 2017-18 - Assessee-company had purchased its own shares from non-resident shareholders (CTS-USA, MRX-USA and CML-Mauritius) in accordance with 'scheme of arrangement  compromise' sanctioned by High Court as per provisions of sections 391-393 of Companies Act, 1956 - Net effect of scheme was that post-sanction of scheme, entire shareholding of CTS-USA and MRX-USA, were purchased by assessee and shareholding percentage of CML-Mauritius was increased to 99.87 per cent of total paid up capital of assessee company - Assessing Officer held that consideration paid by assessee to its shareholders for purchase of its own shares was liable to tax as deemed dividend under section 2(22), and consequently, assessee was liable for payment of DDT under section 115-O - It was noted that from above restructuring of shareholding pattern of assessee-company, it was clear that there was an artificial shifting of shareholding base from USA to Mauritius solely with aim of claiming DTAA benefits as per India-Mauritius DTAA wherein capital gains on transfer of equity shares was not taxable in India, as per Indian Tax Laws - Further, assessee had paid a sum of certain amount from paid up share capital, a sum of certain amount from general reserves and balance of sum of certain amount from retained earnings - Therefore, it was clear that there was a capital reduction and distribution out of accumulated profit of company to its shareholders - Whether any distribution by a company of accumulated profits, if such distribution entails release by company to its shareholders all of or any part of asset of company would come within definition of 'dividend' under section 2(22) - Held, yes - Whether consideration paid by assessee for purchase of its own shares in accordance with scheme sanctioned by High Court as per provisions of sections 391-393 of Companies Act, 1956, amounted to distribution of accumulated profits which entailed release of all or part of assets of a company on reduction of capital which attracted provisions of section 2(22)(d), and consequently, assessee was liable for payment of Dividend Distribution Tax under section 115-O - Held, yes [Paras 34, 38 and 51] [In favour of revenue]INCOME TAX : Where assessee-company paid consideration for purchase of its own shares from its non-resident shareholders in accordance with scheme sanctioned by High Court as per provisions of sections 391-393 of Companies Act, 1956, since there was a capital reduction and distribution out of accumulated profit of company to its shareholders, same would entail release of all or part of assets of a company on reduction of capital and would attract provisions of section 2(22)(d), and consequently, assessee was liable for payment of DDT under section 115-O

Section 45,  read with section 2(22) and 2(47) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Capital gains - Assessable as - Assessment year 1963-64 - Whether amount distributed by a company on reduction of its share capital has two components, viz., distribution attributable to accumulated profits and distribution attributable to capital and to the extent of accumulated profits in hands of company, (whether such accumulated profits are capitalised or not), return to shareholder on reduction of his share capital would be taxable as dividend in his hands and only balance may be subject to tax as capital gains if they accrue - Held, yes - Whether, where assessee had been paid not merely cash but had also been given a property for reduction in value of his shares, while computing capital gains out of total amounts so received including value of property received, portion attributable to accumulated profits would have to be deleted - Held, yes

Held, yes [Paras 34, 38 and 51] [In favour of revenue]

Section 45, read with  Section 2(47), of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Capital gains - Chargeable as - Whether reduction of share capital resulting in release of assets would attract capital gains in hands of shareholders - Held, yes - Whether, therefore, surplus resulting from surrender of shares in a company was liable to be taxed as capital gain in hands of assessee - Held, yes

Section 2(22) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 2(6A)(a) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Deemed dividend -  Assessment year 1956-57 - Whether expression "income" in entry 54 of List I of Seventh Schedule to Government of India Act, 1935, and corresponding entry 82 of List I of the Seventh Schedule to Constitution of India, shall be widely and liberally construed so as to enable a legislature to provide by law for prevention of evasion of income-tax but there must be a reasonable nexus between item taxed and legislative field delineated - Held, yes - Whether as section 2(6A)(d) of 1922 Act embodies a law to prevent evasion of tax, it falls within ken of entry 54 of List I of Schedule VII to Government of India Act, 1935 - Held, yes - Whether if accumulated profits were distributed, it would satisfy not only definition of 'dividend' in section 2(6A)(d) of 1922 Act but also would bix year in which it would be deemed to be income - Held, yes - Whether dividends may be paid or credited to different shareholders during different accounting years; and shareholders may be assessed in respect of the said payments in different years even so, payments are referable only to declaration of dividends out of profits of a particular year - Held, yes - Assessee company by sanction of High Court reduced its capital from Rs. 50 lakhs to Rs. 15 lakhs and got requisite certificate from Registrar of companies - Noties were issued to shareholders inviting applications for refund and after receipt of applications amounts payable to shareholders were debited in accounts and refunds were actually granted during accounting year 1955, i.e., between 1-12-1954, and 30-11-1955 - Whether amounts were distributed only during accounting year, when amounts were both debited and paid and, therefore, dividends were distributed to shareholders during accounting year, i.e., 1954-55 - Held, yes

Section 115-O, read with  section 246A of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Tax on distributed profits of certain distributed companies - Appellable orders (Scope of) - Assessee sought for an approval of scheme under sections 391 to 393 of Companies Act, 1956, involving purchase of shares from its shareholders - Scheme was approved by Court - In pursuance to same, assessee bought back shares from its shareholders and, accordingly, it was treated as capital gains - Respondent passed impugned order inter alia holding that transactions made in pursuant to buy back arrangement effected as a consequence to approval of Scheme required to be taxed under section 115-O on premise that it would constitute dividend and not capital gain - Against said order, assessee filed writ petition - Single Judge held that there was no merit in assessee's contention that shares purchased pursuant to order of Company Court would be a capital gain and not to be treated as dividend - He, however, dismissed assessee's petition with a liberty to them to file an appeal under section 246A in view of fact that assessee had already deposited a part of amount demanded - Whether, on facts, Single Judge was not right in going to merit while granting liberty to file an appeal - Held, yes - Whether, therefore, findings rendered by Single Judge on nature of transaction and scope under section 115-O were to be set aside - Held, yes - Whether, however, impugned order passed by Single Judge to extent that an appeal could be entertained and decided on merit was justified and, thus, same did not require any interference - Held, yes [Paras 10.4, 11 and 13][Partly in favour of assessee]INCOME TAX: Where there was dispute relating to taxability of transaction of buy back of shares from shareholders by assessee-company in terms of section 115-O, Single Judge while directing assessee to file an appeal before Commissioner (Appeals) under section 246A, was not justified in entering into merits of case so far as taxability under section 115-O was concerned

Section 45, read with section 2(47) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Capital gains - Chargeability of - When a company reduces its share capital by paying off a part of paid up capital in exercise of powers under section 100(1)(c) of the companies act, does it result in extinguishment of right of shareholders to the extent of reduction of face value of shares - Held, yes - Whether any profits or gains arising from such extinguishment are chargeable to income-tax under section 45 - held, yes

Section 271(1)(c) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Penalty - For concealment of income - Assessment year 1974-75 - Assessee-company, with permission of Calcutta High Court, in accordance with provisions of the Companies Act, reduced its share capital by cancelling specified number of fully paid-up equity shares - Assessing Officer was of view that reduction of share capital did not represent a loss incurred by assessee and, therefore, taxed that amount, which was upheld by Tribunal - Assessing Officer also levied penalty under section 271(1)(c) - Whether, on facts, Assessing Officer was justified - Held, no

Section 2(47), read with section 45, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Transfer - Whether reduction of share capital by company paying a part of capital by reducing face value of its share would result in extinguishment of proportionate right in shares held by shareholder so that amount paid by company to shareholder on reduction of share capital would be exigible to capital gains tax in hands of shareholder - Held, yes

Section 256, read with section 28(i) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Reference - Question, of law - Assessee-company held 25,000 shares of face value of Rs. 10 each in company H - Share capital of H was reduced as a result of an order of High Court to 20,000 shares - Revenue authorities including Tribunal disallowed assessee's claim for short-term capital loss of Rs. 5 lakhs - On assessee's application under section 256(1) Tribunal referred to High Court question as to whether assessee was entitled to claim a short-term capital loss of Rs. 5 lakhs on reduction of capital of H sanctioned by High Court - On application under section 256(2) assessee sought to raise certain other questions - Whether question referred by Tribunal was wide enough to cover entire controversy being raised by assessee - Held, on facts, yes

Section 2(22)(e) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deemed dividend - Whether in view of facts stated under head ‘Revision - Of orders prejudicial to interests of revenue’ and as well as facts that there was no reduction of share capital of H and that there was no distribution of shares by parent company, it could be said that case of assessee did not come within ambit of section 2(22) - Held, yes

Section 2(22) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 2(6A) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922], read with section 78 of the Companies Act, 1956 - Deemed dividend - Assessment year 1954-55 - Assessee-company held preference shares in 'R' company which had in year 1945 issued share at a premium and kept share premiums so received under head 'capital reserve' - Out of said capital reserve, 'R' company paid a sum as dividend to assessee - For relevant assessment year, ITO taxed said sum in hands of assessee as dividend with section 2(6A) of 1922 Act - Tribunal as well as High Court upheld ITO's order - Whether if a distribution of accumulated profits, whether capitalised or not, entails release by company to its shareholder of all or any part of its assets, it is dividend - Held, yes - Whether since it could not be said that premiums received by 'R' company were not profits within Regulation 97 of Table A of 1913 Act, ITO, therefore, rightly taxed sum received by assessee as dividend - Held, yes

Section 230 of the Companies Act, 2013 - Compromise and arrangement - A composite scheme of arrangement between petitioner companies was approved by NCLT - Income tax department opposed said scheme on ground that conversion of preference shares into loan would substantially reduce profitability of demerged company, which would act as a tool to avoid and evade taxes - NCLAT by impugned order held that without going to record and without placing any evidence to substantiate allegation by appearing before Tribunal, it was not open to Income-tax department to hold that overall scheme of arrangement was giving undue favour to shareholders of company and resulted into tax avoidance and approval by NCLT to such scheme was not to be interfered with - On appeal before Supreme Court, Joint Commissioner of Income-tax submitted that impugned orders and/or sanction of Scheme might come in way of Department while framing assessment and to that extent, interest of revenue would be affected - However, NCLT as well as NCLAT had already clarified that IT department would be entitled to take out appropriate proceedings for recovery of any tax statutorily due from transferor or transferee company or any other person who was liable for payment of such tax due - Whether therefore, impugned judgment and orders passed by NCLAT as well as NCLT approving scheme could not have been interfered with - Held, yes [Paras 5, 6 and 7]

Section 2(47),  read with section 45, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Transfer - Whether reduction of share capital by company paying a part of capital by reducing face value of its share would result in extinguishment of proportionate right in shares held by shareholder so that amount paid by company to shareholder on reduction of share capital would be exigible to capital gains tax in hands of shareholder - Held, yes

Section 2(45), read with section 56 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 (Corresponding to section 2(15), read with section 12 of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922) read with section 55 of the Super-tax Act, 1920 - Income, profits or gains - Meaning of - Company ‘D’ in which assessee-company was one of shareholders, by special resolution, decided to distribute its accumulated profits in form of additional shares to shareholders - Thus, existing capital of company ‘D’ was increased by creation of new shares which ranked pari passu in all respects with existing ordinary shares of company - Whether, on facts, assessee-company was liable to pay super-tax on value of shares newly issued by ‘D’ company - Held, no
