Need of review of Supreme Court's decision 7. It is, therefore, humbly urged that the Supreme Court may review its judgment in Vijaya Bank Ltd.'s case (supra) in the light of the accounting authorities cited and discussed above. The Accounting Standard-13 of the ICAI has tremendous force when it says that interest/dividend relatable to the pre-acqitisition period must not be viewed as income but has recovery of cost and, therefore, should be viewed as a capital receipt. And capital receipts are not taxable for the simple reason that they do not constitute income. The Supreme Court rightly held where a bank purchased securities at a price with reference to their actual value as well as the interest accrued thereon till the date of purchase, the entire price paid would be in the nature of capital outlay. As a corollary, it follows that when this cost is recovered by way of interest, such recovery, far from being income, is an abatement against the cost originally incurred and should be reduced from the cost of purchase. It is this aspect urged in this article and buttressed by the accounting authorities that craves for reconsideration by the Supreme Court. The Supreme Court held the assessee (Vijaya Bank) to be liable for the entire interest including for the broken period, i.e., the pre-acquisition period. It is submitted that this is not correct. The broken period interest, it is reiterated, is a capital receipt and should be rightly reduced from the cost of securities. This accounting treatment is nothing new. Those familiar with preparing consolidated accounts of the holding company with the accounts of its subsidiary, would know that the proportionate part of pre-acquisition profits of the subsidiary relatable to the holding company's holding in the subsidiary is always reduced from the cost of investment and is never shown as part of reserves and surplus. This analogy should be sufficient to remove the mental block or the mind-set of those who are unable to come round to the view-point that broken period interest is a capital receipt.

Implications for shares

8. The Accounting Standard-13 applies to shares as much as it does to interest-bearing securities. In case of shares, the treatment propounded is likely to be even less palatable to tax administration because it will have the effect of converting dividend into capital gains, and if the holding period is more than 12 months, the investor is going to get away with a host of benefits that come with long-term capital gains - to be specific, a flat rate of 20 per cent tax irrespective of the quantum of gains and section 54F benefit which exempts long-term capital gains from tax if they are ploughed back in a residential house.

Implications for stock-in-trade

9. A dealer in securities is not going to be affected one way or the other, whether he is required to follow the law laid down by the Supreme Court in Vijaya Bank Ltd.'s case (supra) or the one propounded by the accounting standards and endorsed in this article. For, in any case, the entire transaction is revenue in nature. The cost of interest-bearing securities is going to be debited to the profit and loss account and the carrying amount at the end of the financial year, cost or market value, whichever is less, is going to be credited to such account. In the event, interest relating to the broken-period is not an issue at all in his case. It must be made clear that in Vijaya Bank Ltd. 's case (supra), the Supreme Court did not say that in case of a bank purchase of interest-bearing securities will invariably constitute investments. Nor did it say that they will invariably constitute stock-in-trade. This classification will, therefore, be governed by the RBI norms and other accounting considerations which are outside the scope of this article. What is relevant is the Supreme Court's verdict in Vijaya Bank Ltd.'s case (supra) has grave portents for investors.

Private Limited Companies and Unlisted Public Companies can issue bonus shares out of revaluation reserve

Issuance of bonus shares out of revaluation reserve by private Ltd. companies and unlisted public companies has always been a controversial matter. Although such practice is judicially recognized in England, it was not been quite so in India, and a lot of disputes have arisen in this context. But with Apex Court’s decision in the case of Bhagwati Developers v. Pearless General Finance & Investment Co. [2005] 62 SCL 574, wherein it has been held that unlisted companies can issue bonus shares out of revaluation reserve, the matter has come to rest. This article discusses all the issues related to this topic and ends with the suggestion that articles of association of the company must be suitably amended besides fulfilment of other requirements for issue of bonus shares.

INTRODUCTION - BONUS SHARES

1. All the profits earned by the company are normally not distributed as dividend to the shareholders. A part of the earned profit is ploughed back in the business. It is transferred to reserves and/or carried over as a surplus or credit balance in the profit and loss account. This profit remains with the company, and is used in the business as an additional working capital. It may happen that the share capital may remain small, but profits would go on increasing. The reserves will also increase. In such a case, the profit and dividend would appear unduly large in comparison to the share capital, though in fact the working funds may be much larger than the share capital. Under such circumstances, the company may opt to issue bonus shares. By issuing bonus shares, a part of the reserves and the balance in the profit and loss account are capitalized. They are converted into share capital. These shares are, therefore, not issued for cash. Bonus shares are generally defined as additional shares of a company’s share capital distributed to its shareholders without their having to pay for them. Bonus shares are also known as scrip dividend.

Regulations 96 and 97 of Table A deal with the capitalization of profits and reserves. However, these 2 regulations do not specifically provide for capitalization of revaluation reserves.

Current Judicial Trends

3. There are a few advance rulings and judicial decisions on the subject. However, due to the inherent infirmity of advance rulings, these may only be relied upon in a persuasive manner rather than a binding capacity. Further, the insertion of section 56(1)(viia ) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 from the assessment year 2010-11 also overturns most established judge made law in one fell swoop.

Nevertheless, let us examine the major decisions to determine the line of judicial thinking on this issue.

(a) Amiantit International Holding Ltd. In re [2010] 189 Taxman 149 (AAR - New Delhi)

This is so far the only the AAR dealing directly with the issue. The crux of the matter is that a Bahrain based company transferred shares of its Indian based subsidiary to its cyprus associate enterprise without any consideration pursuant to a corporate restructuring. Since the situs of incorporation of the company whose shares are transferred is India, the Indian revenue authorities have the jurisdiction to tax the transaction.

The main issue decided by the AAR is whether in case of shares transferred to an associated enterprise, the Indian TPP would apply.

The AAR in a well-reasoned judgment ruled that since the transfer is without consideration, there is no question of applying the touch stone of the ‘arms length price’ to determine a capital gain which could not be computed and, hence, ruled that the authorities could not ram the TPP down the assessee’s throat and tax an income which is not there. The Supreme Court’s decision in CIT v. B.C. Srinivasa Shetty [1981] 128 ITR 294/5 Taxman 1 which has laid down that in case the computation provision fails the charging section also fails seems to have been applied by the AAR notwithstanding the fact that the giver and recipient of the shares are associated enterprises.

However, it needs to be borne in mind that the Finance Act, 2010 has inserted section 56(2)(viia) which taxes receipt of shares at the difference between the fair market value and consideration in the hands of the recipient as ‘income from other sources’. The fair market value determination may certainly involve the principle of ‘arms length’ valuation and, hence, imply a backdoor application of the TPP in a modified form.

(b) Dana Corporation, In re [2010] 186 Taxman 187 (AAR - New Delhi)

This is another ruling which deals with a similar issue. In this case, the US parent entity files for bankruptcy under Chapter 11 and as a result of the bankruptcy proceedings an independent private equity player infuses capital in exchange for an integral package of assets and liabilities which involves shares of a merged US entity. As a result, indirect control and ownership of Indian subsidiaries is transferred to the private equity player.

The question before the AAR is whether such transfer of indirect control would constitute a gain in the hands of the private equity player and, hence, application of the arms length provisions to determine the costs of acquisition.

The AAR in this case also ruled that since the shares are transferred indirectly and also as part of a package where it is argued that the liabilities are more than the assets, no direct cost could be attributable to them. Hence, once again the computation provisions fail and, hence, the charging section would also fail and the TPP would not have any application.

Having said this, it is pertinent to note that the current vodafone controversy also has at its core the capital gains on indirect control and transfer of shares of an Indian subsidiary company and the AAR seems to have disregarded this aspect in its ruling.

(c) Star Television Entertainment Ltd., In re [2010] 188 Taxman 206 (AAR - New Delhi)

The Star Ruling also has similar facts but shares of an Indian company are transferred indirectly by virtue of corporate reorganization, here too the AAR rules that no tax is leviable since the computation provisions have failed and that the TPP are held not applicable.

Deemed short-fall in receipt of share premium couldn't be charged to tax: High Court

PRADEEP S. SHAH

CA

INTRODUCTION

1. In Vodafone India Services (P.) Ltd. v. Union of India [2014] 50 taxmann.com 300 (Bom.) case, Tax Department so to say innovated 'income' by applying Transfer pricing provisions [Chapter X ('the Chapter' or 'Chapter X') of the Income tax Act, 1961 ("the Act")] to the issue of shares by a wholly owned subsidiary to the holding company, inter alia, by treating the alleged shortfall in the premium as an income.

The mystery was unfolded by the High Court through simple application of the basic principles of interpretation to the simple facts.

The Court decided the issue while exercising its writ jurisdiction and, obviously, it did not comment on the facts. However, it has set out the facts (para 6 of the Order) in details, to appreciate the issue.

FACTS OF THE VODAFONE'S CASE

2. It would be quite interesting to note the manner in which the facts (set out broadly) were considered by the Department to invoke Chapter X:

Vodafone India Services (P.) Ltd. 'the company' (issuing shares at a premium) was a wholly owned subsidiary of a foreign company.

It issued shares to the holding company at certain premium (apparently, to comply with the requirements stipulated under applicable law).

Tax Department felt that the provisions of Chapter X would apply. For that purpose:

Issue of shares was treated as an International transaction;

Issue price was tested;

Net asset based valuation method was applied; and

Arm's length price or ALP was sought to be derived.

The authorities (AO and/or TPO and/or DRP)1 worked out the value of the shares based on net assets value. While doing that, "transfer pricing adjustments" made in the earlier years were added to the net assets by treating them as "off balance sheet" items and, accordingly, the value of share was worked out at a substantially higher amount.

The difference considered or alleged as shortfall in the premium (''the Shortfall") was treated as an income of the subsidiary; though premium itself was not considered as income.

Further, the shortfall was deemed as a loan by subsidiary to the holding company and interest which could have been earned on such deemed loan was also treated as income.

The case was defended by Solicitor General on a different ground before the High Court and it was treated as a 'benefit' to the holding company resulting in cost to the subsidiary.

3. FICTION VIS-À-VIS FACTS OF VODAFONE'S CASE

The premium2 amount itself was not considered as income. Only the Shortfall, by applying the so-called ALP, was treated as an income.

Net asset value usually is determined on the basis of the assets/liabilities reflected in the audited financial statements. Even the Act, although for a different purpose, provides for determination of net asset value having regard to the balance sheet as at specified date, without any adjustment of any 'off-balance-sheet' items.

However, in this case the adjustments were considered of 'off-balance-sheet' items and were added to the net asset value to determine the shortfall, which should have been charged as premium for the issue of shares. Apparently, it was not examined whether such notional income was represented by an asset or not?

Chapter X permits valuation of income at ALP. However, it does not provide for adjustment thereof in the books of account or financial statements or otherwise for any other purpose whatsoever. To put it differently, the Chapter authorises the adoption of ALP only for the limited purpose of determining taxable income arising from an international transaction.

The shortfall, if any, was based on valuation of the company as a whole. Now, that value for the holding company, whatever might have been the number of shares and whether these were issued at a premium or at par would have remained the same.

The alternate ground taken treated the shortfall as benefit and, in turn, cost. Thus, factually, different positions were adopted by the authorities and by the authority representing them before the High Court.

While considering and arguing the alternate ground, apparently, a material fact was missed. How, where, to whom and what was the benefit, if any? It would dependent on the differential, if any. When the entire value belonged to the holding company, before or after the issue of shares, where was the difference or what was the benefit? The holder of all the shares; the assets; and the value, as such, did not change. If so, the benefit would not arise. The entire value of the company (considered for determining the Shortfall) before and after the fresh issue always belonged to the holding company.

5. ARGUMENTS BEFORE THE HIGH COURT 6. HIGH COURT'S VERDICT

The Bombay High Court held that on the facts of the present case, issue of shares at a premium by VISL to its non-resident AE does not give rise to any income from an admitted international transaction and thus, Indian Transfer Pricing provisions are not applicable for the following reasons:

Income arising from an international transaction is a pre-condition for application of Transfer Pricing provisions. Further, the Act defines the term income in an inclusive manner. Income, in its normal meaning, will not include capital receipts unless specifically provided. The amounts received on issue of share capital including the premium are on capital account. In this case, what is being sought to be taxed is capital forgone i.e. not received from a non-resident in the form of short premium. Therefore, absent express legislation, an amount received, accrued or arising on capital account transactions cannot be subjected to tax as income.

The High Court further held that the transaction on capital account or on account of restructuring would become taxable to the extent it impacts income i.e., under-reporting of interest received/over reporting of interest paid or claiming of depreciation. It is that income (and not the capital receipt) which is to be determined having regard to the ALP under the Transfer Pricing provisions.

The Transfer Pricing provisions are brought into statute books to ensure that the transaction is taxed only on the income computed as per the ALP of the transaction and to ensure that there is no manipulation of prices/consideration between AEs.

In any case, the entire exercise of taxing the amounts allegedly not received as share premium fails, as no tax is charged on the amount received as share premium.

Neither the capital receipts received by VISL on issue of equity shares to its AE nor the shortfall between the alleged FMV of its equity shares and the issue price of the equity shares can be considered as income within the meaning of the expression as defined in the Act and hence not subject to Transfer Pricing provisions in India.

The reasoning that if the ALP were received, the Taxpayer would be able to invest the same and earn income, proceeds on a mere surmise/assumption and that this cannot be the basis of taxation.

The Tax Authorities relied on this section to argue that differences between the ALP and the price charged for issue of shares is the benefit conferred upon the holding company.

Relying on section 92(2) of the Act is misplaced. Section 92(2) of the Act, which deals with a situation where two or more AEs enter into an arrangement whereby they are to receive any benefit, service or facility then the allocation, apportionment or contribution of the corresponding cost or expenditure is to be determined for each AE based on ALP, is meant to cover cases of cost sharing arrangements and/or cost contribution arrangements. Section 92(2) would have no application in cases like the present one, where there is no occasion to allocate, apportion or contribute any cost and/or expenses between the Taxpayer and its AE. Ignoring words in a statute to achieve a predetermined objective is not permissible and the same would amount to re-drafting the legislation, which is beyond the jurisdiction of the Courts.

The contention of the Tax Authorities that in view of the Transfer Pricing provisions, notional income is to be taxed and real income is not relevant is unacceptable. The entire exercise of determining the ALP is only to arrive at the real income earned.

Even income arising from international transactions between AEs must satisfy the test of income per se under the Act and must find its home under one of the charging provisions. It is a re-computation exercise to be carried out only when income arises in case of an international transaction between AEs. It does not warrant recomputation of a consideration received/given on capital account except in cases of interest paid/received on loans taken/given, depreciation taken on machinery, etc. Therefore, in the absence of a charging provision to tax issue of shares at a premium to a non-resident, the occasion to invoke the computational Transfer Pricing provisions does not arise.

Further, in view of inclusion of issue of shares, by a company to another resident, at a price in excess of FMV in the definition of income under the Act, there is conscious intention of the Parliament to not tax amounts received from a non-resident for issue of shares, as it would discourage capital inflow from abroad.

7. CONCLUSION

In the backdrop of the present Government's initiative to bring in foreign investment, this decision from the Bombay High Court's is a landmark. The High Court has been rightly able to distinguish between the 'income' per se and the capital which is primarily the source to earn income. One important take away from the decision is the High Court's acknowledgement that mere reporting of an international transaction out of abundant caution would not make the same taxable if there is no income arising from such international transaction.

Annual accounts under the Companies Act 3. The Companies Act, 1956 ('the Act') imposes a duty (a) on the auditors to audit the accounts and to make a report thereon to the shareholders, and (b) on the Board of directors of the company to lay the annual accounts duly audited before get them adopted by the shareholders and at an annual general meeting (A.G.M.).

Section 211 of the Act dealing with the form and contents of the balance-sheet and profits and loss account provides that the balance-sheet and the profit and loss account shall give a true and fair view of the state of affairs of the company at the end of the financial year and of the profit or loss of the company for the financial year. The true and fair view contemplates that the reasonable expectations of readers of accounts are duly met. Accounting standards create a prima facie presumption that accounts which do not comply with them are not true and fair. Financial statements should not give any misleading impression or picture. Non-compliance with the provisions of the said section is an offence punishable under it. Thus, the balance-sheet and the profit and loss account, once they are audited by the company's auditor and adopted by the shareholders at the A.G.M., are given high sanctity. Failure to give a true and fair view in respect thereof amounts to breach of trust to shareholders, creditors and others relying on these documents and leads to penal consequences as mentioned above.

Failure to make provision for tax on distributed profits

4. It is noticed that some companies, not being fully conversant with the provisions of section 115-O and its effect, fail to make any provision for tax on distributed profits in their annual accounts for the Financial year 1996-97. The department of Company Affairs (the department) has ex-pressed the view that failure to make provision for taxation and proposed dividends would not disclose true and fair view of the state of affairs of the Company-Department's Letter No. 3/124/75-CL-VI dated July9, 1975. Accounts placed before the shareholders without making any provision for tax as aforesaid cannot be said to give a true and fair view of the state of affairs or profit (or loss) of the company for the said year as required by section 211, and this would attract the penalty as mentioned in the said section. Ways and means will have to be found out to overcome the difficulty which have arisen in the matter.

Revision of annual accounts - When permissible

5. The Act does not contain any provision regarding the reopening and revision of the annual accounts. The working group on the Companies Act has not also made any suggestion on the subject.

The department as well as the Institute of Chartered Accountants of India (ICAI), the professional body dealing with chartered accountants, has consistently expressed the view that it is open to the Board of directors of a company to revise the annual accounts and to re-submit the same to the auditor for his report thereon, so long as the original accounts have not been placed before and adopted by the shareholders at the A.G.M. Auditor's report on the revised accounts will be in substitution of his earlier report on the original accounts.

The department has also expressed the view that a company cannot reopen and revise its accounts after their adoption at the A.G.M. ICAI has also 'decided that the re-opening or rectification of accounts after they have been adopted at the annual general meeting should not be permitted under any circumstances'. In other words, once the accounts are adopted at the A.G.M. they are treated as sacrosanct and unalterable in any case. It is considered that there seems to be no warrant to take such a rigid view of the matter.

Department's clarification

6. In 1987 in partial modification of its aforesaid view the Department clarified that a company could re-open and revise its accounts even after their adoption in the annual general meeting in order to comply with technical requirements of taxation laws [Department's letter to ICAI dated August 19, 1987]. In such an event the revised annual accounts would be required to be adopted at the subsequent A.G.M. and thereafter filed with the Registrar of Companies as required by the Companies Act.

Probably the query raised by the department related to technical requirements of taxation laws and, hence, the department expressed the view in the matter as aforesaid. There seems to be no justification to take such a restricted view that a company can revise and re-open its accounts only for the limited purpose aforesaid. It is considered that re-opening and revision of accounts is permissible in all cases where directors discover that accounts presented by them are defective and they should be corrected. Appropriate rules or regulations made by the department on the subject would clarify the position in the matter.

DISTRIBUTION ON REDUCTION OF COMPANY'S SHARE CAPITAL [SECTION 2(22)(d)]

Constitutional validity - Provision is constitutionally valid [Punjab Distilling Industries Ltd. v. CIT [1965] 57 ITR 1 (SC)].

Consists of two components - The amount distributed by a company on reduction of its share capital has two components, i.e., distribution attributable to accumulated profits and distribution attributable to capital (except capitalised profits) [CIT v. G. Narasimhan [1999] 102 Taxman 66 (SC)].

Date of resolution is relevant in ascertaining accumulated profits - The date of the resolution for the reduction of capital, and not the several dates of payments to the shareholders, is the date for ascertaining the quantum of accumulated profits [Punjab Distilling Industries Ltd. v. CIT [1965] 57 ITR 1 (SC)].

No deduction as to face value of shares - Entire amount received by shareholder on purchase by company of shares pursuant to scheme of reduction of capital would constitute 'divided' without deducting face value of shares [CIT v. Jai Hind Investment Industries (P.) Ltd. [1992] 62 Taxman 361 (Cal.)].

PAYMENT BY WAY OF LOAN/ADVANCE TO SPECIFIED BENEFICIAL SHAREHOLDERS OR TO ITS RELATED CONCERN [SECTION 2(22)(e)]

Constitutional validity - Provision of section 2(22)(e) is not beyond the legislative competence of the Legislature. It also does not contravene the rights conferred under Articles 19(1)(f) and 19(1)(g) of the Constitution of India [Navnit Lal C. Javeri v. K. K. Sen, Appellate Asstt. CIT [1965] 56 ITR 198 (SC)].

Provision to be strictly interpreted - The dividend, taken note of by this provision, is a deemed dividend and not a real dividend. Loan or payment made by the company to its shareholder is actually not a dividend. In fact, such a loan has to be returned by the shareholder to the company. It does not become income of the shareholder. Notwithstanding the same, for certain purposes, the Legislature has deemed such a loan or payment as dividend and made it taxable at the hands of the said shareholder. It is, therefore, not in dispute that such a provision which is a deemed provision and fictionally creates certain kinds of receipts as dividends, is to be given strict interpretation [Gopal & Sons (HUF) v. CIT [2017] 77 taxmann.com 71/245 Taxman 48 (SC)].

To the extent of accumulated profits, entire payment made by company and not merely proportionate to shareholdings of assessee shareholder should be deemed as dividend in hands of shareholder [CIT v. Mayur Madhukant Mehta [1972] 85 ITR 230 (Guj.)].

DIMINUTION OF CAPITAL DOES NOT CONSTITUTE REDUCTION OF CAPITAL

As per section 61(1)(e) of Companies Act, 2013 [Corresponding to section 94(1)(e) of the 1956 Act], a company can cancel shares which have not been taken or agreed to be taken by any person, and diminish the amount of its share capital by the amount so cancelled.

Section 61(2) of Companies Act, 2013 [Corresponding to section 94(3) of the 1956 Act] states that such cancellation is not 'reduction of capital'.

The section is applicable only to change in memorandum. The Memorandum specifies only 'Authorised Capital'. Hence, only 'Authorised Capital' can be cancelled under this section.

Such reduction in authorised capital in Memorandum is not likely to be of much use, as stamp duty paid on authorised capital will not be refunded. Hence, this provision is hardly used.

If any part of capital is returned, it is not 'deemed dividend' [see CIT v. Urmila Ramesh (1998) 230 ITR 422 = 96 Taxman 533 (SC)].

Dividend Distribution Tax will be payable on such dividend.

Narasimhan (1999) 102 Taxman 66 (SC), it was held that amount distributed by a company on reduction of its share capital has two components - distribution attributable to accumulated profits and distribution attributed to capital (except capitalised profits). To the extent of accumulated profits in the hands of company (whether capitalised or not), the return to the shareholder on reduction of its share capital is a return of such accumulated profits. This part would be taxable as dividend. The balance may be subject to tax as capital gains that accrue.

Capital Gains*

Buy back of shares

5.1 Section 77A of the Companies Act, 1956 permits a company to buy back its own shares upon fulfilment of the prescribed conditions. It has tax implications and broadly, there were two views :

◆ As per one view, utilisation of accumulated profits for the buy back, entailing reduction of capital, could amount to dividend attracting tax @ 10% under section 115-O of the Act in the hands of the company.

◆ As per the other view, the company is not liable to dividend tax inasmuch as the purchase of its own shares does not amount to reduction in capital and only the shareholders are liable to pay tax on the gains, if any.

To set the controversy at rest, the Finance Act, 1999 has made the following provisions :

(a) The payment made by a company for purchase of share would not constitute dividend [vide section 2(22)(iv)]; and

(b) Shareholders would be chargeable to capital gains tax (by inserting section 46A).

5.1-1 Dividend - Section 2(22) of the Act defines dividend inclusively. After listing the distribution or payment amounting to dividend, it lists certain distribution or payment not constituting dividend. In that list, the payment made by a company on purchase of its own shares from shareholder in terms of section 77A of the Companies Act, 1956 has been added [vide, sub-clause (iv)] meaning that such payment would not constitute dividend. Accordingly, the provisions of section 115-O of the Act would not apply.

However, this provision would not apply in respect of buy back of any shares or other securities by the company under any other provisions of the Companies Act, 1956 (i.e., other than section 77A) under any scheme of arrangement (e.g. an order under section 402 of the Companies Act, 1956) or otherwise. Accordingly, any payment made by the company in such a case for such purchase may constitute dividend within the meaning of section 2(22) of the Act.

5.1-2 Section 46A - The section provides as follows :

◆ When a shareholder or holder of other specified securities receives any consideration from a company,

◆ Upon purchase of its own shares or securities by the company,

◆ The difference between cost of acquisition and purchase price of shares or securities paid by the company would constitute capital gains,

◆ In computing the capital gains, section 48 should be given effect to,

◆ The gain would be chargeable to tax in the year of purchase and

◆ For the purpose, the other securities have the same meaning as assigned in Explanation to section 77A of the Companies Act, 1956.

5.1-2a Necessity - Shares or securities do constitute capital asset. It is settled law that upon purchase by the company, there is a transfer of shares [Anarkali Sarabhai v. CIT[1997] 224 ITR 422 (SC)]. Accordingly, any gain arising therefrom is chargeable to tax as capital gains or otherwise. Further, there was no controversy that a shareholder was liable to capital gains tax. Also, the question of reducing accumulated profit considered as dividend in computing the capital gain would not arise in view of the amendment made in section 2(22). In the circumstances, the need for a separate provision was not there. Also, the need for including other specified securities in the provision is also not clear.

5.1-2b Meaning of ‘shareholder’ or ‘holder’ - The Supreme Court in Howrah Trading Co. Ltd. v. CIT[1959] 36 ITR 215, 219-220] held that a shareholder or holder, means, a member, i.e., a person whose name is entered in the register of members. Accordingly, a beneficial owner of shares, say, a firm who holds shares through its partners, would not be considered as a shareholder. Buy back of shares

5.1 Section 77A of the Companies Act, 1956 permits a company to buy back its own shares upon fulfilment of the prescribed conditions. It has tax implications and broadly, there were two views :

♦

As per one view, utilisation of accumulated profits for the buy back, entailing reduction of capital, could amount to dividend attracting tax @ 10% under section 115-O of the Act in the hands of the company.

♦

As per the other view, the company is not liable to dividend tax inasmuch as the purchase of its own shares does not amount to reduction in capital and only the shareholders are liable to pay tax on the gains, if any.

To set the controversy at rest, the Finance Act, 1999 has made the following provisions :

(a)

The payment made by a company for purchase of share would not constitute dividend [vide section 2(22)(iv)]; and

(b)

Shareholders would be chargeable to capital gains tax (by inserting section 46A).

5.1-1 Dividend - Section 2(22) of the Act defines dividend inclusively. After listing the distribution or payment amounting to dividend, it lists certain distribution or payment not constituting dividend. In that list, the payment made by a company on purchase of its own shares from shareholder in terms of section 77A of the Companies Act, 1956 has been added [vide, sub-clause (iv)] meaning that such payment would not constitute dividend. Accordingly, the provisions of section 115-O of the Act would not apply.

However, this provision would not apply in respect of buy back of any shares or other securities by the company under any other provisions of the Companies Act, 1956 (i.e., other than section 77A) under any scheme of arrangement (e.g. an order under section 402 of the Companies Act, 1956) or otherwise. Accordingly, any payment made by the company in such a case for such purchase may constitute dividend within the meaning of section 2(22) of the Act.

5.1-2 Section 46A - The section provides as follows :

♦

When a shareholder or holder of other specified securities receives any consideration from a company,

♦

Upon purchase of its own shares or securities by the company,

♦

The difference between cost of acquisition and purchase price of shares or securities paid by the company would constitute capital gains,

♦

In computing the capital gains, section 48 should be given effect to,

♦

The gain would be chargeable to tax in the year of purchase and

♦

For the purpose, the other securities have the same meaning as assigned in Explanation to section 77A of the Companies Act, 1956.

5.1-2a NECESSITY - Shares or securities do constitute capital asset. It is settled law that upon purchase by the company, there is a transfer of shares [Anarkali Sarabhai v. CIT [1997] 224 ITR 422 (SC)]. Accordingly, any gain arising therefrom is chargeable to tax as capital gains or otherwise. Further, there was no controversy that a shareholder was liable to capital gains tax. Also, the question of reducing accumulated profit considered as dividend in computing the capital gain would not arise in view of the amendment made in section 2(22). In the circumstances, the need for a separate provision was not there. Also, the need for including other specified securities in the provision is also not clear.

5.1-2b MEANING OF 'SHAREHOLDER' OR 'HOLDER' - The Supreme Court in Howrah Trading Co. Ltd. v. CIT [1959] 36 ITR 215, 219-220] held that a shareholder or holder, means, a member, i.e., a person whose name is entered in the register of members. Accordingly, a beneficial owner of shares, say, a firm who holds shares through its partners, would not be considered as a shareholder. Similarly, the holder of specified security would mean the person whose name is entered in the register or record maintained by the company and not the beneficial owner.

Prima facie in such a case, (i.e., a beneficial owner), the provisions of section 46A may not apply, unless, a view is taken that in the context of section 46A, the shareholder could mean a person who receives the price for the buy back from the company. Apart from that, assuming for a moment section 46A cannot apply in case of a beneficial owner, taxation of gain on buy back cannot be ruled out under section 45. This is because where the special provision does not apply, the general provision can always apply.

1.23.11 Applicability to Court sanctioned schemes A question that arises is whether the provisions of Chapter XA would apply to a transaction or a scheme approved by a Court. To illustrate, an amalgamation or demerger is effective only upon the order of the High Court under section 394 of the Companies Act, 1956. Can such Court approved scheme be declared as an IAA? According to one view, this is permissible:

(a) the definition of arrangement is very wide and includes schemes; hence, on a literal reading, even a Court approved Scheme could be considered as an arrangement.

(b) the following cases show that a Court approved scheme could be challenged on the ground of tax avoidance:

(i) Marshall Sons & Co. (India) Ltd. v. ITO [1996] 89 Taxman 619/[1997] 223 ITR 809 (SC)

"We, however, make it clear that we have not expressed any opinion on the plea of learned counsel for the Revenue that the amalgamation itself is a device designed to evade the taxes legitimately payable by the subsidiary company. If the income-tax authorities think that they are entitled to raise this question in the proceedings under the Income-tax Act, it is open to them to do so by way of a separate proceeding according to law."

In the context of spin off prior to introduction of demerger provisions with effect from assessment year 2000-01, the Tribunal observed that if the transaction is for the purposes of avoiding any tax, then the Capital Gain may be liable.

(c) The Ministry of Finance has also clarified as follows :

"The approval of High Court or Supreme Court is with specific objective and may not take into account tax avoidance issues and circumstances which are relevant at the time of GAAR" (para 15.31 of the SC Report)

According to the other view, a duly approved scheme cannot be challenged subsequently on the ground that it was effected as a tax planning device.

(a) See Asstt. CIT v. Gautam Sarabhai Trust No. 23 [2002] 81 ITD 677 (Ahd. - Trib.)

"Various amalgamations and mergers have been duly approved by the High Court and after such amalgamations have been sanctioned as made in conformity with the requirements under the Companies Act, no such allegation of tax planning or tax evasion can be levelled by the Revenue against the assessee. 1.10-1 Certain decisions relating to 'depreciation' - Note the following—

The Delhi Tribunal in SAIL v. DCIT (1991) 38 ITD 193, under the provisions of section 115J held that for the purposes of working out permissible adjustment of the lower of depreciation or loss, profits made in the earlier year cannot be ignored. The losses or the depreciation must be set off against earlier years' profits. In Geetanjali Woollens Pvt. Ltd. v. ACIT [1994] 50 ITD 558 the Ahmedabad Tribunal took a view that in determining, amount of loss or depreciation, to be set off, the amount already not set off in the past can only be considered.

The Chandigarh Bench of Income-tax Appellate Tribunal in ITO v. Parbhat Forging Pvt. Ltd [1991] 38 ITD 319 held that unprovided depreciation in respect of the past cannot be adjusted. While holding so, it also considered provisions similar to section 205 which were incorporated in section 115J of the Act.

Section 115JA does not have a similar provision. Now, what is permissible is reduction of the lower of brought forward loss or unabsorbed depreciation, as per books of account. This does imply that the loss or the depreciation must have been reflected in the books of account. In case of a company, which was incurring loss, depreciation may not have been provided at all.

Accordingly, in the year of profit, if it also provides for depreciation in respect of earlier years, then in computing the book profit, whether any adjustment can be made in respect of unprovided depreciation of earlier years ?

Having regard to the provisions, under the Explanation below section 115JA(2)no such adjustment can be made.

However, it may be pointed out that, as discussed earlier, a bench of Tribunal has taken a different view. Possibly, the different view could be contested on the ground that the provision for depreciation is a legal requirement, before declaring any dividends, and therefore in terms of the statute, the provision was made and therefore should not be a subject matter of adjustment.

The Cochin Bench of the Tribunal in Apollo Tyres Ltd v. DCIT [1992] 43 ITD 464 was concerned with a case where assessee provided for extra shift depreciation an its accounts, pursuant to insertion of Schedule XIV to the said Act. It was observed by the Tribunal that in view of the statutory amendment, the assessee was legally bound to provide for arrears of such extra shift depreciation. Further, this was in accordance with the provisions of the Schedule. Apart from that there was no earmarked adjustment for the provision. Accordingly, in computing book profit, an adjustment in respect thereof cannot be made.

In Bombay Tyres International Ltd v. DCIT[1994] 51 ITD 339, the company had changed the method of depreciation from straight line to WDV method based on technical or other evaluation and provided for the same in the accounts. The Bombay Tribunal took a view that change was bona fide based on recommendation of financial and technical personnel; it was a valid change and as per legal or accounting requirement as inferred, it was appropriate and not a colourable device. It took a view that the arrears pertained to a provision of an ascertained and known liability and therefore did not constitute reserve. Having regard to decision of Special Bench in Sutlej case (supra), the adjustment made by the department was not permitted.

In Beta Napthol Pvt. Ltd. v. DCIT [1994] 50 TTJ 375, Indore Bench of the Tribunal with reference to change in method of depreciation and section 115J has taken a view that an assessee is entitled to change method of depreciation and also entitled to claim extra depreciation as arrears of past.

Finance Act, 1999

Buy back of shares

5.1 Section 77A of the Companies Act, 1956 permits a company to buy back its own shares upon fulfilment of the prescribed conditions. It has tax implications and broadly, there were two views :

As per one view, utilisation of accumulated profits for the buy back, entailing reduction of capital, could amount to dividend attracting tax @ 10% under section 115-O of the Act in the hands of the company.

As per the other view, the company is not liable to dividend tax inasmuch as the purchase of its own shares does not amount to reduction in capital and only the shareholders are liable to pay tax on the gains, if any.

To set the controversy at rest, the Finance Act, 1999 has made the following provisions :

(a)

The payment made by a company for purchase of share would not constitute dividend [vide section 2(22)(iv)]; and

(b)

Shareholders would be chargeable to capital gains tax (by inserting section 46A).

5.1-1 Dividend - Section 2(22) of the Act defines dividend inclusively. After listing the distribution or payment amounting to dividend, it lists certain distribution or payment not constituting dividend. In that list, the payment made by a company on purchase of its own shares from shareholder in terms of section 77A of the Companies Act, 1956 has been added [vide, sub-clause (iv)] meaning that such payment would not constitute dividend. Accordingly, the provisions of section 115-O of the Act would not apply.

However, this provision would not apply in respect of buy back of any shares or other securities by the company under any other provisions of the Companies Act, 1956 (i.e., other than section 77A) under any scheme of arrangement (e.g. an order under section 402 of the Companies Act, 1956) or otherwise. Accordingly, any payment made by the company in such a case for such purchase may constitute dividend within the meaning of section 2(22) of the Act.

5.1-2 Section 46A - The section provides as follows :

When a shareholder or holder of other specified securities receives any consideration from a company,

Upon purchase of its own shares or securities by the company,

The difference between cost of acquisition and purchase price of shares or securities paid by the company would constitute capital gains,

In computing the capital gains, section 48 should be given effect to,

The gain would be chargeable to tax in the year of purchase and

For the purpose, the other securities have the same meaning as assigned in Explanation to section 77A of the Companies Act, 1956.

5.1-2a NECESSITY - Shares or securities do constitute capital asset. It is settled law that upon purchase by the company, there is a transfer of shares [Anarkali Sarabhai v. CIT [1997] 224 ITR 422 (SC)]. Accordingly, any gain arising therefrom is chargeable to tax as capital gains or otherwise. Further, there was no controversy that a shareholder was liable to capital gains tax. Also, the question of reducing accumulated profit considered as dividend in computing the capital gain would not arise in view of the amendment made in section 2(22). In the circumstances, the need for a separate provision was not there. Also, the need for including other specified securities in the provision is also not clear.

5.1-2b MEANING OF 'SHAREHOLDER' OR 'HOLDER' - The Supreme Court in Howrah Trading Co. Ltd. v. CIT [1959] 36 ITR 215, 219-220] held that a shareholder or holder, means, a member, i.e., a person whose name is entered in the register of members. Accordingly, a beneficial owner of shares, say, a firm who holds shares through its partners, would not be considered as a shareholder. Similarly, the holder of specified security would mean the person whose name is entered in the register or record maintained by the company and not the beneficial owner.

Prima facie in such a case, (i.e., a beneficial owner), the provisions of section 46A may not apply, unless, a view is taken that in the context of section 46A, the shareholder could mean a person who receives the price for the buy back from the company. Apart from that, assuming for a moment section 46A cannot apply in case of a beneficial owner, taxation of gain on buy back cannot be ruled out under section 45. Where absence of mala fide would not by itself entitle a company to an order under section 101(3) or deny a creditor an order under section 101(2)(c), the presence of it may well be an important factor to deny an order to the company. In relation to the applicability of the clause to the amalgamated company or the resulting company, there could be two possible views when shares are issued pursuant to amalgamation or demerger of a resident amalgamating/demerged company, respectively.

As per one view, the clause would apply, inter alia, for the following reasons:

♦ Under the scheme of amalgamation or demerger, the amalgamated company or the resulting company issues shares to the shareholders of the amalgamating company or the demerged company, in consideration for vesting of the undertaking [apart from the applicable provisions of the Act, like, definition of demerger, exemption to the shareholders etc., a reference may be made to a decision of Supreme Court in Hindustan Lever v. State of Maharashtra [2003] 117 Comp. Cas. 758, where it was observed that once the shareholders of the transferee company receive the consideration it would be deemed as if the owner has received the consideration (page 774)].

♦ Further, as held by Supreme Court in Hindustan Lever v. State of Maharashtra [2003] 117 Comp. Cas. 758, the amalgamation is a compromise or arrangement between the parties, which, inter alia, includes the amalgamated company issuing the shares and the shareholders of the amalgamating company, which is supervised by the court, in terms of the provisions of the Companies Act, 1956. In other words, there is an agreement or arrangement, inter alia, by and between the amalgamated company issuing the shares and the shareholders of the amalgamating company. The Clause contemplates the issue of shares and the receipt of consideration from a resident person and it is fulfilled in case of amalgamation.

♦ The Clause applies to any consideration, whether in cash or in kind or whether at the instance of the company or otherwise.

♦ The Clause applies to any consideration whether received from the person to whom the shares are issued or otherwise.

♦ The events attracting tax are present, namely, receipt of consideration and issue of shares.

♦ Whether the issue triggers consideration or otherwise is of no relevance.

As per the other view, the clause cannot apply, inter alia, for the following reasons:

♦ The objective of insertion of the provision is relevant for determining the true scope and ambit of the provision.

♦ The objective is to tax 'conversion of unaccounted' money and accordingly include within its scope only such transactions, which facilitate such conversion.

♦ The issue of shares is not to invite subscription by the persons to whom an offer is made. The issue of shares is to give effect to the amalgamation or the demerger, as per the mutual agreement and the Court order. In other words, the issue of shares does not trigger any consideration; in fact, the obligation to give consideration, triggers the issue of shares.

♦ The clause contemplates 'receipt' of the consideration for the shares from a resident person. In other words, it contemplates a transaction between a resident person and the company issuing the shares. In case of an amalgamation or a demerger, the consideration, which would be the undertaking along with all its assets and liabilities is in the form of vesting by the amalgamating or the demerged company; whereas, the shares are issued to its shareholders. Thus, it is a tripartite arrangement not contemplated by the Clause.

In such a case, such setting apart does not constitute a provision within the meaning assigned to it by the Schedule; but, in fact constitutes a reserve as defined in the Schedule. Thus, though it is called a provision, it is a reserve. Therefore, irrespective of the nomenclature, the amount so set apart has to be added back to the profits in terms of Explanation defining book profits.

1.9-2a RESERVES ADJUSTMENT UNDER EXPLANATION (i) - Explanation (i) requires reduction of amount withdrawn from any reserve or provision, if it is credited to profit and loss account.

Such reduction can be made in respect of any reserves or provisions created in respect of any year relevant to assessment year 1997-98 and thereafter only when the amount of such reserves or provision was added back under Explanation (b).

Accordingly, if any reserve has been created in any earlier year and if that is credited to profit and loss account, the adjustment, by way of reduction, under, this Explanation can be made.

1.9-2b CREDIT TO CAPITAL RESERVE - The Special bench of the Tribunal (Calcutta) in Sutlej Cotton Mills Ltd. v. ACIT [1993] 45 ITD 22 was concerned with an adjustment not specifically permitted by section 115J of the Act. The company in that case had revalued its fixed assets in earlier years. In the subsequent year, it revalued all its quoted investments at market value. The difference on revaluation of these shares was credited to capital reserve account. In the next year, relevant to assessment year 1988-89, it sold certain shares. The sale proceeds were not credited to profit and loss account; but were adjusted in the asset account and/or capital reserve account. In the assessment proceedings, the Assessing Officer took a View that the objective of revaluation was to defraud revenue and avoidance of tax under section 115J by changing method of valuation. In the appellate proceedings, the Appellate Authority held that the treatment was not in accordance with para 3(xii)(a)of the Schedule which read as follows:

"Profits or losses on investments showing distinctly the extent of the profits or losses earned or incurred on account of membership of a partnership firm to the extent not adjusted from any previous provision or reserve." [Emphasis supplied]

On the aforesaid facts, the Tribunal held as follows :

The requirement of the Schedule show that it is concerned with the result of the working of the company. Thus, it cannot be directly concerned with changes in capital structure. Profit on realisation of capital assets will not be an item of income.

Company had followed a consistent practice in relation to revaluation of capital assets. The practice adopted was in accordance with para 3(xii)(a) referred above, as a credit to Profit & Loss Account was required to be taken to the extent not adjusted, as provided therein. The practice followed by the company was a sound accounting practice as the profit was not available for distribution. Accordingly, the profit realised cannot form part of book profit.

As per Explanation below section 115J(1A) providing for adjustments, only the permitted adjustments can be made. Beyond that, book profit cannot be adjusted. For the purpose, even section 145 cannot be applied. Accordingly, the Assessing Officer was bound to proceed with computation of book profit as shown in the Profit and Loss Account.

As far as valuation of assets, etc., is concerned, really it cannot be compared with the method of valuation in relation to stock in trade. In any case, section 145 does not apply to revaluation of fixed assets.

The Assessing Officer cannot disturb reserve, which has been adjusted in accordance with requirement of the Schedule and as per the para referred above.

This was not a device for avoidance of tax.

Provisions of section 45, deeming capital gains as income, cannot apply to book profit under section 115J on account of non obstante clause. This is because a deemed income cannot be included as part of book profit.

Share buybacks raise a characterisation issue under the DTAAs. The central issue is whether the gain or income arising in the hands of the shareholder should be treated as a dividend, a capital gain, or other income. This characterisation is critical because it determines which article of the DTAA applies and, consequently, which country retains the right to tax such income. The OECD Model Convention defines "dividends" under Article 10(3) to mean income from shares, jouissance shares or jouissance rights, mining shares, founders' shares or other rights that are not debt-claims but participate in profits, as well as income from other corporate rights which is subjected to the same taxation treatment as income from shares by the laws of the state of which the company making the distribution is a resident. This definition is broad and explicitly connects the characterisation of dividend income to the domestic law of the source state. Paragraph 28 of the OECD Commentary on Article 10 addresses situations involving redemption, liquidation, and disguised distributions of profits, and notes that where the domestic law of the source state treats the amounts paid to a shareholder on buyback as a distribution of profits, such amounts fall within the definition of dividends under Article 10.

Para 31 of the OCED Model Commentary on Article 13 provides that if shares are alienated by a shareholder in connection with the liquidation of the issuing company or the redemption of shares or reduction of paid-up capital of that company, the difference between the proceeds obtained by the shareholder and the par value of the shares may be treated in the State of which the company is a resident as a distribution of accumulated profits and not as a capital gain. The Article does not prevent the State of residence of the company from taxing such distributions at the rates provided for in Article 10. Where the domestic law of the source country does not treat the buyback proceeds as dividend income but instead characterises the transaction as a sale or transfer of a capital asset, Article 13 of the treaty on Capital Gains would apply.

In simple terms, the treatment of share buybacks under a DTAA is not governed by a single universal rule but depends critically on the characterisation of the proceeds under the domestic law of the source state, the specific treaty language, and the model convention on which the bilateral treaty is based. Where domestic law treats buyback proceeds as a deemed dividend or distribution of profits, Article 10 applies, and the source state retains the tax rights. Where domestic law treats income from share buybacks as capital gains, the classification should be the same under the DTAA unless a treaty provides otherwise. Regardless of characterisation, taxpayers must remain mindful of anti-avoidance provisions such as the PPT, which may override treaty benefits where arrangements lack sufficient commercial substance.

6.2-5h Taxable in the hands of the shareholder - The capital gains computed under section 69 shall be taxable in the hands of the shareholder. The term 'shareholder' is not specifically defined in either the Income-tax Act or the Companies Act. However, section 2(55) of the Companies Act, 2013 defines 'member' as a person whose name is entered in the register of members of the company. Additionally, a person who holds shares in a company and whose name is recorded as a beneficial owner in the depository's records is considered a member.

For income tax purposes, the term 'shareholder' generally refers to a registered shareholder. A beneficial owner whose name does not appear in the register of shareholders is not considered a 'shareholder'11.

According to the Prohibition of Benami Property Transactions Act, 1988 ("Benami Act"), it is not permissible for a person to be a shareholder when the beneficial owner of those shares is some other person. However, section 2(9) of the Benami Act provides certain exceptions where the shareholder may be a different person from the beneficial owner, subject to specific conditions:

A shareholder who is the Karta of an HUF, with the beneficial owner being the HUF itself.

A shareholder acting in a fiduciary capacity, such as a trustee, executor, partner, director, depository, or depository participant, with the beneficial owner being the Trust, estate, partnership firm, company, or demat account holder.

A shareholder who is an individual, with the beneficial owner being his or her spouse or child.

A shareholder who is an individual, with the beneficial owner being his or her brother, sister, or lineal ascendant or descendant, as joint owners.

The Supreme Court, in Howrah Trading Co. Ltd. v. CIT [1959] 36 ITR 215 (SC), held that a shareholder means a person whose name is entered in the register of members. Thus, a beneficial owner, such as a firm holding shares through its partners, is not considered a shareholder. Consequently, if shares are held in a fiduciary capacity for another person, the taxability lies with the person who holds the shares as the registered shareholder. However, this principle shall not apply when a depository or depository participant holds shares in a fiduciary capacity for a demat account holder, as the demat account holder is considered the member in relation to the company, not the depository.

Javeri v. K.K. Sen3, the validity of section 12(1B) of the 1922 Act, was questioned. Section 12(1B) provided that a loan made to a shareholder by private-controlled company is taxable as dividend. It was recognized that merely because the loan is taxed as a dividend in the hands of a shareholder, the loan may not cease to be a loan, and that it would be open to the company to recover the loan by resorting to law. The petitioner’s argument was that what is not income is being taxed as ‘income’ and, therefore, it is beyond the legislative competence of the Parliament. (The impugned provision was introduced by the Finance Act, 1955.) The argument was rejected in the following words :

“In dealing with this point, it is necessary to consider what exactly is the connotation of the word ‘income’ used in the relevant entry. It is hardly necessary to emphasize that the entries in the Lists cannot be read in a narrow or restricted sense, and as observed by Gwyer, CJ. in the United Provinces v. Atiqa Begum1, each general word should be held to extend to all ancillary or subsidiary matters which can fairly and reasonably be said to be comprehended in it. What the entries in the Lists purport to do is to confer legislative powers on the respective Legislatures in respect of areas or fields covered by the said entries; and it is an elementary rule of construction that the widest possible construction must be put upon their words. This doctrine does not, however, mean that Parliament can choose to tax as income an item which in no rational sense can be regarded as a citizen’s income. The item taxed should rationally be capable of being considered as the income of a citizen. But in considering the question as to whether a particular item in the hands of a citizen can be regarded as his income or not, it would be inappropriate to apply the tests traditionally prescribed by the Income-tax Act as such...” (p. 1379)

The Court reaffirmed the principles enunciated in Navinchandra Mafatlal’s case (supra), Baldeo Singh’s case (supra) and Balaji’s case (supra).

It is equally relevant to notice that in Baldeo Singh’s case (supra), the validity of section 23A of the 1922 Act was questioned. Section 23A provided that where the ITO is satisfied that in respect of any previous year the profits and gains distributed as dividend by any company within twelve months immediately following the expiry of that previous year are less than 60 per cent of the total income of the company of that previous year [as reduced by the amounts specified in clauses (a), (b) and (c) of sub-section (1)], the ITO shall, unless he is satisfied that having regard to losses incurred by the company in earlier years, or to the smallness of the profits made in the previous year, the payment of a dividend, or a larger dividend than that declared, would be unreasonable, make an order in writing that the company shall, apart from the sum determined as payable by it on the basis of the assessment under section 23 of the 1922 Act, be liable to pay super-tax at the rate specified by sub-section (1) of section 23A. This section was enacted to prevent avoidance of super-tax by shareholders of a company in which the public are not substantially interested. The assessee’s argument was that since the company and shareholders are distinct entities, taxing the shareholders on dividends not distributed by the company, and not received by them, cannot be justified as a tax on income received by shareholders. This argument was repelled on the ground that the obvious intention of section 23A was to prevent evasion of tax, and that Entry 54 in List I of the Seventh Schedule should be read not only as authorising the imposition of a tax, but also as authorising an enactment which prevents the tax imposed being evaded. It was also observed that section 23A dealt with a situation where shareholders did not deliberately distribute the accumulated profits as dividend among themselves and, therefore, provided that these accumulated profits will be deemed to have been distributed to shareholders and tax levied on that basis.

COVERAGE OF SECTION 46(2)

Section 46 deals with capital gains on distribution of assets by companies on liquidation. Section 46(1) provides that notwithstanding anything contained in section 45, where the assets of a company are distributed to its shareholders on its liquidation, such distribution shall not be regarded as a transfer by the company for the purposes of section 45. 6.2 Buy-back of shares will be taxable as capital gains [Section 69 of ITA 2025 (corresponding to Section 46A of ITA 1961)]

The Finance Act, 2026 has made several amendments to the provisions of the ITA 2025 regarding the taxation of buy-back of shares. Under the amended provisions, the sum paid by a domestic company to the shareholders under a buyback shall be treated as capital gains in the hands of the shareholders.

6.2-1 Introduction

Corporate action to buyback shares can serve multiple strategic purposes. Primarily, it's used to increase earnings per share by reducing the number of outstanding shares, often leading to a higher stock price. Additionally, buybacks are a method to return excess cash to shareholders, an alternative to dividend payouts. Companies might also repurchase shares if they believe their stock is undervalued, signalling confidence in the future. Moreover, buybacks can deter hostile takeovers by increasing the company's ownership percentage.

Section 68 of the Companies Act, 2013 gives the company the power to purchase its own securities. It defines a buyback as the purchase of its own shares or other specified securities (i.e., Employee Stock Options or Sweat Equity) by the Company itself.

6.2-2 History of tax on buyback of shares as per the ITA 1961

Before the assessment year 2000-01, the Income Tax Act did not include a special provision for taxing share buybacks. There were two views on the buyback of shares: either it could attract dividend distribution tax, or shareholders would be liable to pay tax on any gains.

To set the controversy at rest, the Finance Act, 1999 inserted section 46A with effect from assessment year 2000-01, which stated that shareholders would be charged to tax on the capital gains arising from the buyback of shares. A corresponding amendment was also made to section 2(22) by inserting clause (iv), which provides that a payment for the purchase of shares does not constitute a dividend. Therefore, the consideration received by a shareholder on the buyback of shares by the company in accordance with section 77A of the Companies Act, 19561 (corresponding to Section 68 of the Companies Act, 2013) was not treated as a dividend. The same was taxed under Section 46A of the Act as capital gains.

Subsequently, the unlisted companies, as part of the tax avoidance scheme, were found resorting to buyback of shares instead of payment of dividends in order to avoid payment of tax by way of DDT, particularly where the capital gains arising to the shareholders were either not chargeable to tax or were taxable at a lower rate under respective Double Taxation Avoidance Agreements. In A Mauritius, In re [2012] 20 taxmann.com 52, the AAR held that only a genuine buyback is excluded from the definition of 'dividend' under section 2(22)(iv) and exempt from DDT under section 115-O. A colourable buyback will attract DDT. In that case, the buyback was held to be a colourable device for tax avoidance, as dividends were distributed in the guise of a buyback to avoid DDT.

Taking a cue from the above decision of the AAR, the Finance Act, 2013 inserted a new Chapter XII-DA, 'Special Provisions relating to tax on distributed income of domestic company for buyback of shares,' consisting of sections 115QA to 115QC, with effect from 1-6-2013. The Finance (No. 2) Act, 2019 extended the levy of tax on the buy-back of shares listed on a recognised stock exchange on or after 5 July 2019 by amending section 115QA.

In November 2022, the Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI) released a consultation paper on a review of the SEBI (Buyback of Securities) Regulations, 2018, proposing various changes to existing buyback norms. One of the proposed changes is to shift the tax burden of buybacks from the company to the shareholders. This proposal was based on the fact that promoters tendered more shares than their pre-buyback holdings, resulting in the company paying taxes not only on shares tendered by the promoters but also on the additional shares tendered by them. These taxes were paid from the company's reserves on behalf of the existing shareholders and promoters at the expense of continuing shareholders. Therefore, it was suggested that the tax burden on buybacks should be shifted to shareholders, as it is with dividend distributions.

6.15-5Eg LOANS AND ADVANCES TO REGISTERED SHAREHOLDERS - Loan or advance allowed to a shareholder is dividend. The shareholder should be a registered shareholder. When, suppose an advance or loan is given to a Hindu undivided family, whose karta is the registered shareholder of the advancing or lending company, the amount, thus, advanced or loaned cannot be taken to be deemed dividend, because the karta is the registered owner, though the beneficial ownership vests with the Hindu undivided family and it is not the registered owner who is getting advance or loan.3

The Finance Act, 1987, however, amended the section by virtue of which, advance or loan to such person as Hindu undivided family would be deemed dividend, if the advance or loan is made after 31-5-1987.

The tax is attracted to the amount, thus, paid to the extent of accumulated profits. Even if the loan or advance is subsequently repaid or adjusted so that no amount is outstanding at the end of the year, it would still be assessed as deemed dividend.5

In Dictionary for Accountants, ‘advance’ has been defined as payment of cash or the transfer of goods for which accounting must be entered by the recipient at some later date.6 Section 2(22)(e) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 makes it clear that any payment by any company of any sum representing a part of the assets by way of advance would come within the mischief of the said section. 6.15-5Ei INTEREST - Income as interest is also taxable under the residuary head. It means income from debt-claims. Debt is a property. It is a chose-in-action and is heritable and assignable and it is treated as property under the transfer of Property Act which calls it ‘actionable claim’. Chose-in-action arising out of contract has two aspects (i) as property, and (ii) as involving a contractual obligation for performance. The property aspect is relevant for purposes of assignment, administration, and taxation and like; the contractual aspect, for performance. The debt being intangible, cannot have location unless except notionally and in order to give it notional position, rules have to be framed along arbitrary lines. In the case of a debt due to a foreigner, the proper law of the contract is to be applied, i.e., the law of the country in which, elements of the contract are most densely grouped and with which factually, the contract is most closely connected.1

FACT: The assessee was shareholder of a company ‘R’ which had substantial reserve, passed a resolution for capitalising the sum standing to the credit of the reserve funds and the capitalized fund was to be distributed amongst the members of the company ‘R’ in effect as bonus shares. On the next day the company ‘R’ resolved to purchase shares in the company ‘A’ out of its capitalized reserve. Later on the company ‘R’ resolved to reduce its capital by returning to the shareholders the shares in the company ‘A’ and this resolution was confirmed by an order of the District Court. As a result of this resolution, certain shares in the Company A were allotted to the assessee. The view which the ITO took was that the whole transaction by the company ‘R’ for the increase and subsequent decrease of its capital and purchase and distribution of company ‘A’ shares was illusory, and that accordingly he could treat the company ‘A’ shares allotted to the assessee as never having become capital, but as their representing profits of the company ’R’. Both the Assistant Commissioner and commissioner agreed with the decision of the ITO

HELD: As soon as the resolution was passed capitalising the reserves, such reserves became capital and could not afterwards be dealt with by the company as income; and subsequently, when the capital was reduced, - which was in the next year, - and part of the proceeds of the capitalised reserves was handed back to the shareholders, that part could only be handed back in the form in which it existed, namely, capital. The ITO, when he said that the whole transaction was illusory, apparently meant that the real motive of the directors in putting forward those various resolutions, and of the shareholders in passing them, was not to increase the capital for any commercial purposes of the Company, but to increase the capital in order that the subsequent distribution among the shareholders of the reserve funds might be in the form of capital and not of income; but the High Court could not go into the question of what was at the back of the mind of the directors or the shareholders.

It was not competent to the Income-tax authorities to go behind the order confirming the reduction of capital made by the District Court and to hold that what was sought to be released and reduced by the Resolution passed by the Company ‘R’ for reduction of its Share Capital was release of profits and not Share Capital.

The assessee was shareholder of a company ‘R’ which had substantial reserve, passed a resolution for capitalising the sum standing to the credit of the reserve funds and the capitalized fund was to be distributed amongst the members of the company ‘R’ in effect as bonus shares. On the next day the company ‘R’ resolved to purchase shares in the company ‘A’ out of its capitalized reserve. Later on the company ‘R’ resolved to reduce its capital by returning to the shareholders the shares in the company ‘A’ and this resolution was confirmed by an order of the District Court. As a result of this resolution, certain shares in the Company A were allotted to the assessee. The view which the ITO took was that the whole transaction by the company ‘R’ for the increase and subsequent decrease of its capital and purchase and distribution of company ‘A’ shares was illusory, and that accordingly he could treat the company ‘A’ shares allotted to the assessee as never having become capital, but as their representing profits of the company ’R’. Both the Assistant Commissioner and commissioner agreed with the decision of the ITO

was illusory, and that accordingly he could treat the Arvind Mills shares allotted to the assessee as never having become capital, but as their representing profits of the Company. In accordance with the spirit of loyalty, which seems to pervade the office of (he Commissioner of Income-tax, the Assistant Commissioner agreed with the decision of the Income-tax Officer, and the Commissioner agreed with the decision of the Assistant Commissioner; and the question is whether the view of the Income-tax Officer is right. The real question, which arises, is whether these 16 shares in the Arvind Mills Co., are income, profits and gains liable to tax under section 4 of the Indian Income-tax Act, but the question is not raised in that form. The questions raised in effect ask whether the transaction, to which I have referred, was illusory, and whether there was any evidence to support the view of the Income-tax Officer to that effect. I have considerable doubt in understanding what is meant by these transactions being illusory. There is no doubt that the original resolution for the increase of capital was passed; it is net suggested that it was not passed by a requisite majority ; and as soon as it was passed, the capital of the Company was increased. As soon as the resolution was passed capitalising the reserves, such reserves became capital and could not afterwards be dealt with by the Company as income; and subsequently, when the capital was reduced,—which was in the next year,—and part of the proceeds of the capitalised reserves was handed back to the shareholders, that part could only be handed back, in the form in which it existed, namely, capital. The Income-tax-Officer, when he says the whole transaction was illusory, apparently means! that the real motive of the directors in putting forward these various resolutions, and of the shareholders in passing them, was not to increase the capital for any commercial purposes of the Company, but to increase the capital in order that the subsequent distribution among the shareholders of the reserve funds might be in the form of capital and not of income; but this Court cannot go into the question of what was at the back of the mind of the directors or the shareholders. Similar questions have arisen under the English Act in Blott's case 8 Tax Cas. 101, and in Fisher's case 10 Tax Cas. 302,—both recent decisions of the House of Lords—, in which it has been definitely established that the principle originally laid down by the House of Lords in Bouch v. Sproule [1887] 12 App. Cas. 385 applies to revenue cases. That principle is that a company has power to declare and determine as against the whole world, whether accumulated reserves shall be treated as capital or income, and if the company determines that they are capital, then they are capital. At the time when the reference was made, there might possibly have been a question whether the principle of these cases applied in India, but that question has definitely been decided in the affirmative by the Privy Council in Commissioner of Income-tax, Bengal v. Mercantile Bank of India, Limited 10 ITC 39. It seems to be that the case cuts from under the Commissioner the only ground on which he might have taken a stand in this reference.

In my opinion, the question raised must be answered as follows : The first question is :

"Whether there is any legal evidence to support the observations of the Assistant Commissioner of Income-tax, in Appeal No. A/193 of 1934-35 that the procedure and the proceedings taken by the Company for increase of capital and for reduction of capital were illusory and were not genuine."

That must be answered in the negative.

The second question is :

"Whether it is competent to the Income-tax authorities to treat as illusory and ungenuine the capitalization of the Reserve Fund and the Machinery Renewal Fund in the share capital of the Company and the reduction of capital determined by appropriate and legal steps taken by the Company."

That must also be answered in the negative.

The third question is :

"Whether in law it is competent to the Income-tax authorities to go behind the order confirming the redaction of capital made by the District Court at Ahmedabad, viz., the Order dated the 24th day of June 1933 and to hold that what was sought to be released and reduced by the Resolution passed by the Company for reduction of its Share Capital was release of profits and not Share Capital?"

That must again be answered in the negative.

The fourth question is :

"Whether in law the 16 shares of the Arvind Mills Limited received by the Petitioner (the assessee) are liable to be included in the petitioner’s (the assessee’s income for the year 1933."

That again must be answered in the negative.
