It is important to bear in mind the following observations of the Supreme Court in the case of CIT v. Sun Engineering Works (P.) Ltd. [1992] 198 ITR 297/64 Taxman 442 (SC)

"It is neither desirable nor permissible to pick out a word or a sentence from the judgment of the Supreme Court divorced from the context of the question under consideration and treat it to be the complete law declared by the court.

The judgment must be read as a whole and the observations from the judgment have to be considered in the light of the questions which were before the court. A decision of the Supreme Court takes its colour from the questions involved in the case in which it is rendered and, while applying the decision to a later case, courts must carefully try to ascertain the true principle laid down by the decision."

It is also advisable to remember the following words of Lord Denning in the matter of applying precedents which have become locus classicus:

[Refer to Sarva Shramik Sanghatana (KV) v. State of Maharashtra [2008] 1 SCC 494 as quoted in para 48 in the case of CIT v. Happy Home Enterprises [2014] 51 taxmann.com 281 (Bom.)]

"Each case depends on its own facts and a close similarity between one case and another is not enough because even a single significant detail may alter the entire aspect, in deciding such cases, one should avoid the temptation to decide cases (as said by Cardozo) by matching the colour of one case against the colour of another. To decide therefore, on which side of the line a case falls, the broad resemblance to another case is not at all decisive."

There is no - in fact there can be no straight jacket formula for any given (ideal or otherwise) situation as factual happenings may differ and even one small difference in facts may completely alter the readymade answer situation. Basic principles taught to us indicate that before analysing a live situation and comparing it with an assumed situation or a decided case-law first find out as to the facts based on which earlier case was decided and what are the facts obtaining in the live situation and what was the point of law then and what is the point of law now-by point of law what is meant is whether any higher authority has decided the case other way after earlier ruling was given or a decision has been given by a jurisdictional High Court now either way or has there been any amendment subsequent to date of last decision or is there any change in assessment year meaning thereby change in law? The point to be considered is - Any change in the thinking of the persons who matter most-the judicial authorities?

To cite an example-

In the case which arose before the Supreme Court in CIT v. R. M. Amin [1977] 106 ITR 368 (SC) the assessee held 192 shares in a private company incorporated in Uganda. That company was not a company falling within the definition of "company" in (then) section 2(17) of the Act. The company went into voluntary liquidation and during 1961, the previous year for the assessment year 1962-63, the assessee received Rs. 1,84,326 in excess of the amount he had paid for those shares. The question was whether the excess of Rs. 1,84,326 was taxable as capital gains in the assessee's hands under section 45 read with section 2(47) of the Act.

The Gujarat High Court held that it was not taxable and on appeal by the Revenue to the Supreme Court it was held as under-

"There was no transfer of capital assets within the meaning of section 2(47). When a shareholder received money representing his shares on the distribution of the net assets of the company in liquidation, he received that money in satisfaction of the right which belonged to him by virtue of his holding the shares and not by any operation of any transaction which amounted to sale, exchange, relinquishment, transfer of a capital asset or extinguishment of any rights in capital assets. But for section 46(2) it would not have been possible to charge tax under the head "Capital gains" on the money or other assets of a company received by its shareholder on its liquidation. Section 46(2) was enacted both with a view to making shareholders liable for payment of tax on capital gains as well as to prescribing the mode of calculating the capital gains to the shareholders on the distribution of assets by a company in liquidation. Since the provisions of section 46(2) applied only to the distribution of assets by such companies in liquidation as were covered by the definition of the word "company" in section 2(17), capital gains tax was not leviable when companies other than those which fell within the definition in section 2(17) distributed assets on liquidation to their shareholders."

The assessee created a development rebate fund to avail of the deduction under section 33. Section 34(3)( a) does not prohibit the assessee from using any amount credited to the fund for the purpose of its business but he cannot utilise the amount for eight years for 'distribution by way of dividends or profits'. If the ITO finds that the assessee has utilised any amount out of the reserve fund for distribution by way of dividends or profits, he can withdraw the allowance given under section 33 by proceeding under section 155.

In the instant case, there was no allegation that the assessee had distributed any dividend out of the amounts standing to the credit of the fund. But the assessee issued bonus shares and for that purpose transferred the amount standing to the credit of the fund to the share capital account. One view is that issue of bonus shares to the shareholders involves a dual operation by which an amount is released to the shareholders from a reserve fund but is retained by the company and applied in payment of the bonus shares which are issued as fully paid up. The shareholders are treated as having paid for the bonus shares and the supposed payments by the shareholders are taken to share capital account from the reserve fund of the Company. In effect, the shareholders have not paid the face value of the bonus shares. It is to all intents and purposes equivalent to distribution of accumulated profits in cash by the company.

The second view is that when bonus shares are issued, an amount equal to the face value of the shares cannot be regarded as having been received by the shareholders. The issuance of bonus shares is nothing but mere capitalisation of the profits of the company in respect of which certificates are issued to the shareholders entitling them to participate in the amount of the reserve but only as part of the capital.

The correct view could be that the profits made by the company may be distributed as dividends or retained by the company as its reserve which may be used for improvement of the company's works, buildings and machinery. That will enable the company to make larger profits. There cannot be any dispute that the shareholders will benefit from the improvements brought about in the profit-making apparatus of the company. Likewise, if the accumulated profits are capitalised and capital base of the company is enlarged, this may enable the company to do its business more profitably. The shareholders will also benefit if the share capital is increased. They may benefit immediately by issue of bonus shares. But neither in the case of improvement in the profit-making apparatus nor in the case of expansion of the share capital of the company, can it be said that the shareholders have received any money from the company. They may have benefited in both the cases. But this benefit cannot be treated as distribution of the amount standing to the credit of any reserve fund of the company to its shareholders.

In fact, the transfer of the amounts standing to the credit of development rebate reserve to the share capital account does not involve any disbursement of money by the company. Nothing comes out of the till of the company to the shareholder. The entire amount of money shown as development rebate reserve is retained by the company in another account. It cannot be said that by the issue of bonus shares, the company has distributed its reserve fund to the shareholders even though it has retained the entire amount with it in the share capital account.

When a shareholder gets a bonus share, the value of the original share held by him goes down. In effect, the shareholder gets two shares instead of the one share held by him and the market value as well as the intrinsic value of the two shares put together will be the same or nearly the same as the value of the original share before the bonus issue.

It appears from the various decisions that issuance of bonus shares does not amount to distribution of accumulated profit of a company. The shareholder derives some benefit by the process of capitalising of the accumulated profits but at the same time, the value of his original shareholding goes down.

Viewed from any angle, it could not be said that in this case the assessee-company had distributed any part of its development rebate reserve fund when it issued the bonus shares. The accumulated profit lying to the credit of the development rebate reserve had been retained by the company. The amount had been transferred to the share capital account. If that was not done, the intrinsic value of the shares held by the shareholders would have been more. After the issue of the bonus shares, the intrinsic value of the original shares had gone down rateably. The accumulated profits of the company had remained with the company in one account or another. In the instant case, neither in form nor in substance, had there been any distribution of profits by the company in making the bonus issue. If the substance and not the form of the transaction was looked to, the issue of bonus shares was in the language of Rowlatt J., 'a bare machinery' for capitalising profits and there was no distribution of profits to the shareholders.

The legal fiction in other words is created in order to enable the revenue to take back that it had given by way of depreciation allowance in preceding years since what was given in preceding years was in excess of that which ought to have been given. Unless this were done, the result would be to recoup the assessee an amount in excess of the real operating cost of the capital asset and, therefore, in order to take back what, had been wrongly allowed in the earlier years, the true character of the receipt is masked and by the legal fiction the receipt is treated as if it were profit for the purpose of computation of the assessable income of the assessee so that it would be brought to tax as such in the hands of the assessee. This being the purpose of the enactment of the legal fiction, the legal fiction must be limited to the field of that purpose; of course, within the framework of that purpose the legal fiction must be given full effect and must be carried to its logical consequence but it cannot be availed of for a different purpose. Having been enacted for the purpose of enabling the revenue to tax the receipt of excess over written down value, as soon as such receipt is taxed the fiction would be exhausted and would not operate in any other field unconnected or unrelated to the purpose for which the fiction is created. It was, therefore, clear that the fiction must be limited to the purpose of computation of the assessable income of the assessee under section 10 of the 1922 Act and it cannot be extended to other provisions such as section 2(6A)(c) of the 1922 Act which are unconnected with the assessment of the assessee and, therefore, unconnected with the purpose for which the fiction is created. It could not therefore by said that the words 'accumulated profits' in section 2(6A)(c) of the 1922 Act include receipt of excess over written down value on sale of capital assets which, though not profit in the accepted connotation of the word, is deemed to be profit by the legal fiction enacted in the second proviso to section 10(2)(vii) of the 1922 Act.

In a taxing statute one has to look merely at what is clearly said. There is no room for any intendment. There is no equity about a tax, there is no presumption as to a tax. General - The expression 'accumulated profits' means profits in the commercial sense and not assessable or taxable profits liable to tax as income under the Act [P. K. Badiani v. Calculation, what to be taken into account and what not - Profits for purpose of ascertaining accumulated profits must be determined after allowing depreciation allowable and allowed under the 1961 Act [Navnitlal C. Current profits could not be included in the expression 'accumulated profits' [Girdhardas & Co. Ltd. v. CIT [1957] 31 ITR 82 (Bom.), affirmed inCIT v. V. Damodaran [1979] 2 Taxman 397 (SC)].

Distribution made to a shareholder of the company out of non-taxable capital gains of the company would not form part of 'accumulated profits' and anything attributable to such capital gain shall not be deemed to be dividend in the hands of the shareholder [CIT v. This would clearly exclude return of a part of the capital by the company from section 2(22) as the same cannot be regarded as profits capable of being capitalised, the return being of the capital itself [CIT v. G. Narasimhan [1999] 102 Taxman 66 (SC)].

As regards the assessability of "distribution of dividend" in the assessment year 1956-57; the controversy linged upon the meaning of the word "distribution" as used in section 2(6A)(d). The word "distribution" connotes "to deal out or bestow in portions or shares among many; to allot or apportion as one’s share." "Distribution" is not merely an act of dividing or apportioning but also dispensing or dealing out. The act of "distribution" has to be actual and not notional; physical and not mental. A resolution or decision to distribute is not "distribution" as there is no giving out, dispensing or disbursement involved. "Distribution" connotes two acts a "division" and "delivery". The word ‘distributed’ occurs in section 16(2). In that section three words are used: "paid, credited or distributed" and, according to well-known canons of statutory interpretation, each expression is to be given a distinct meaning. The word "credited" is used when an entry on the credit side of an account is made. It does not signify actual dealing out. A thing is said to be "paid" when something is given which need not be first apportioned and then disbursed. The word "distributed" is used in the sense of division and delivery. The expression which follows the word "distributed", namely, "deemed to have been . . . distributed" is significant. "Deemed" in this context means "supposed". When a thing is deemed to be distributed, it means that though in fact it is not distributed yet it will be considered or treated as if it had been distributed. If the word "distribute" were to signify a mental decision, or even a book entry, the use of the word "deemed" would perhaps be superfluous. The use of the word "distributed" in section 16(2) suggests that it refers to actual distribution or delivery. In other words, distribution is being considered in the factual and not in the notional sense, and distribution is the sequence of reduction of capital. In the phrase occurring in section 2(6A)(d) "any distribution by a company on the reduction of its capital", the preposition "on" means "after". As the act of distribution is not notional, reduction of capital does not imply contemporaneous distribution. It is a subsequent process after reduction of capital for purpose of contention of the word ‘distribution’ occurring in section 2(6A)(d ), the provisions of section 13 cannot be of any guide. In the instant case, the company sent a circular notice on 5-11-1954, to its shareholders requesting them to send their shares certificates to the company at an early date for necessary endorsement and refund of share capital. They were also informed that the share transfer register of the company would remain closed from 16-11-1954 to 30-11-1954 (inclusive). It may be mentioned that no entry regarding distribution was made in the accounting year which ended on 30-11-1954. In the balance sheet for the period ended 30-11-1954, the directors, in their report to the shareholders, made the following recommendation as to the payment of dividend. "to pay dividend or the year at 7¼% per annum Rs. 1,81,250". Against the words "capital issued, subscribed and paid up", the figure was Rs. 25,00,000 and not Rs. 15,00,000. A personal of this balance sheet did not give any indication either of the reduction of the capital or the consequent distribution of Rs. 15,00,000. Thus, the position shown in the company’s own account books was that the paid-up capital for the period which ended on 30-11-1954, was still Rs. 25,00,000 and this would not have been the case if any steps had been taken to distribute the money on reduction of capital. The fact, however, was that no distribution had taken place even up to 5-6-1955. From this, it was to be concluded that the accumulated profits as dividend were deemed to have been distributed in the assessment year 1956-57, because the debits of refunds were actually made in the accounts of the shareholders and the refunds were actually granted to the shareholders during the accounting period of the assessment year 1956-57. The contention of the assessee-company that the dividend was deemed to have been distributed in the accounting year to 1954-55, corresponding to the assessment year 1955-56, could not prevail and was, therefore, to be rejected notwithstanding the accounts of company being maintained on mercantile basis.

SHAREHOLDER/COMPANY TRANSACTIONS

Whether transactions between company and its shareholders involve transfer is discussed as follows:

4.21-1 Reduction of share capital is 'transfer'

Reduction of share capital by company by reducing face value of its shares and paying off balance to shareholder would result in extinguishment of proportionate right in shares held by shareholder so that amount paid by company to shareholder on reduction of share capital would be exigible to capital gains tax in hands of shareholder - Kartikeya V. Sarabhai v. CIT [1997] 94 Taxman 164 (SC).

Transaction of reduction of share capital by company and pro rata distribution of amount/assets to shareholders amounts to 'transfer' within meaning of section 2(47) - CIT v. G. Narasimhan [1999] 102 Taxman 66 (SC).

[See also Para 4.21-1]

4.21-2 Redemption of preference shares involves 'transfer'

Redemption of preference shares by the company would squarely come within the purview of 'sale, exchange or relinquishment of the asset' - Anarkali Sarabhai v. CIT [1997] 90 Taxman 509 (SC).

[See also Para 4.21-2]

4.21-3 Forfeiture of convertible warrants

Forfeiture of convertible warrant amounts to a transfer within meaning of section 2(47) as there is extinguishment of rights: loss on their forfeiture is allowable as capital loss - CIT v. Chand Ratan Bagri [2011] 10 taxmann.com 129/[2010] 230 CTR (Delhi) 258.

The Bombay High Court in the case of Principal CIT v. Kanaiyalal M. Sheth [2019] 108 taxmann.com 455 (Bom.), following the decision of the Karnataka High Court in the case of Dy. CIT v. BPL Sanyo Finance Ltd. [2009] 312 ITR 63 (Kar.), held that loss suffered by assessee on forfeiture of payment towards convertible warrant due to failure of assessee to pay balance amount on allotment of such warrants was to be allowed as short-term capital loss.

Share warrant is a capital asset and loss generated from its forfeiture is capital loss [Dy. CIT v. Diamond Co. Ltd. [2016] 76 taxmann.com 127/[2017] 162 ITD 131 (Kol - Trib.)

Where assessee issued optionally convertible warrants during relevant year, amount forfeited by it on account of subsequent non-payment of instalments towards warrants issue had to be treated as capital receipt not liable to tax. Prior to the amendments by Finance Act, 2016

(a)

distributed income was defined to mean the consideration paid by the company on buy back of shares as reduced by the amount which was received by the company for issue of such shares;

buyback had been defined to mean the purchase by a company of its own shares in accordance with the provisions of section 77A of the Companies Act, 1956. Thus the definition of buyback did not cover buybacks undertaken by a company under other provisions of the Companies Act, 1956 or the Companies Act, 2013.

Again there could be situations where shares may have been issued by the company in tranches, for different considerations, at different point of time or may have been issued in lieu of existing shares of another company under amalgamation, merger or demerger. In all these cases there was lack of clarity in determination of consideration received by the company at the time of issue of shares being bought back by the company (as per Explanatory Memorandum to Finance Bill, 2016).

In Capgemini India (P.) Ltd., In re [2016] 67 taxmann.com 1 (Bom.) it was held that the Indian company law, as it stood then, permitted a company to buy-back its shares either without Court approval (by adopting procedure of buy-back regulations) or with the Court's approval. If the law permitted a company to follow one of the two methods, it could not be compelled to follow only that method that results in higher tax liability. The Court held that the purchase of shares under section 391 of the Companies Act, 1956 (now section 230 of the Companies Act, 2013) was not covered by section 115QA.

In view of the above, section 115QA has been amended with effect from 1-6-2016 to provide that

(a)

Buyback will mean purchase by a company of its own shares in accordance with the provisions of any law for the time being in force relating to companies [Explanation (i) to section 115QA(1)].

(b)

Distributed income means the consideration paid by the company on buyback of shares as reduced by the amount, which was received by the company for issue of such shares, determined in the manner as may be prescribed [Explanation (ii) to section 115QA(1)].

7.5-1 'Purchase' of shares is a precondition

Even after the amendment in Explanation (i), 'purchase' of shares by a company is a precondition for applicability of section 115QA. If a particular transaction does not result in 'purchase' by the company, then section 115QA is not triggered.

Thus, section 115QA will now apply to buy backs under

(a)

sections 391 to 394 of the Companies Act, 1956 (corresponding to sections 230 to 232 of the Companies Act, 2013);

(b)

section 395 of the Companies Act, 1956 (corresponding to section 235 of the Companies Act, 2013);

(c)

section 402 of the Companies Act, 1956 (corresponding to section 242(2)(b) of the Companies Act, 2013).

7.5-2 Unlisted share is a precondition

Even after the amendment, section 115QA applies only in respect of purchase of unlisted shares. The term 'shares' will include all types of shares including preference shares and convertible preference shares. However, listed shares or convertible debentures are not covered.

7.5-3 Positive distributed income

It appears that the provision envisages positive distributed income. If the consideration paid by the company on buyback of shares is less than the amount received by the company for issue of such shares than the distributed income would be negative and in these circumstances, obviously there will not be any liability under section 115QA.

7.5-4 Reduction of capital

Section 100 of the Companies Act, 1956 (corresponding to section 66(1)(b) of the Companies Act, 2013) provides that a company may reduce the share capital and may 'pay off' any paid up share capital which is in excess of the wants of the company. According to one view, purchase of share under section 77A of the Companies Act, 1956 (corresponding to section 68 of the Companies Act, 2013) and reduction of capital under section 100 pursuant to which shares are 'transferred' to the company are two distinct transactions and such reduction cannot be construed as purchase of shares by the company within the meaning of section 115QA. In Goldman Sachs (India) Securities (P.) Ltd. v. ITO [ITA No. 3726 of 2015, decided on 12-2-2016] (Mum. - Trib.), the Tribunal cited observations from SEBI v. Sterlite Industries (India) Ltd. Section 66 of the Companies Act, 2013/Section 100 of the Companies Act, 1956 - Share capital - Reduction of - Whether before a Court can decline sanction to a scheme of reduction on account of a valuation, an objector to scheme must first show that valuation is ex-facie unreasonable - Held, yes - Whether sanctioning Court has no power or jurisdiction to exercise any appellate functions over scheme; it is not a valuer and it does not have necessary skills or expertise - Held, yes - Whether Court cannot substitute its own opinion for that of shareholders, its jurisdiction is peripheral and supervisory, not appellate - Held, yes - Whether it is impossible to say which of several available valuation models are 'best' or most appropriate - Held, yes - Whether no valuation is to be disregarded merely because it has used one or other of various methods; it must be shown that chosen method of valuation is such as has resulted in an artificially depressed or contrived valuation well below what a fair-minded person may consider reasonable - Held, yes - Whether where in proposed scheme of reduction of share capital of Cadbury India valuation of shares was done by Court appointed valuer and was accepted by overwhelming majority including a bulk of non-promoter minority, scheme was to be sanctioned - Held, yes [Paras 7.1.5, 7.1.7, 7.1.9, 7.1.11  8.1]CL: To disregard a method of valuation of shares in scheme of reduction, it must be shown that chosen method of valuation is such as has resulted in an artificially depressed or contrived valuation well below what a fair-minded person may consider reasonable

ratio of shares between two merging companies was a complex issue requiring technical expertise, however the Court in its supervisory jurisdiction could certainly look into and examine the justification or otherwise of the valuation and exchange ratio proposed and in appropriate cases may lift the veil to see the real purpose. The Company Court exercises jurisdiction which was founded on fairness. While exercising its jurisdiction, the Court was competent to examine the bona fides or fairness of the valuation of shares or the exchange ratio and whether the proposal conforms to commercial morality. It was held that from a careful comparison of the two companies and the business profile of the transferor company and the transferee company it was quite apparent that the exchange ratio proposed in the scheme which was heavily loaded in favour of the shareholders of the transferor company appeared to be unrealistic and illogical. It was held that the transferor company whose shares was under lock out for a long period with accumulated losses and with petition filed in the High Court for voluntary liquidation of the Company could not be valued in the manner projected in the scheme. When objections were raised by the objector and by the Regional Director about the exchange ratio, the explanation given by the petitioners was that the exchange ratio of shares were fixed on the basis of the earning capacity of the transferor company and not on the basis of its net asset value or net worth as was appearing from the balance sheet.

It was held that having regard to the litigation history in the transferee company involving the objector and other related developments and also having regard to the financial status of the transferor company as discussed above, objection raised by the objector and by the Central Government through the Regional Director regarding the exchange ratio of shares between the two companies could not be brushed aside. Accordingly, the Registrar of Companies was directed to work out the exchange ratio in a fair manner through independent experts keeping in view the discussions made and were asked to submit the same to the Court in two months time. Thereafter Court might sanction the scheme with modifications.

2. Heritage Housing Finance Ltd., Inre [2013] 40 taxmann.com 103/[2014] 124 SCL 319 (Cal.)

Similar to the case discussed above was the case of "Heritage Housing Finance Ltd" wherein the Central Government raised an objection that the share exchange ratio as proposed in the said scheme was not fair and reasonable. The petitioner filed petition contending that the Central Government could not raise aforesaid objection when in the shareholders' meeting the entire scheme had been approved unanimously. It was held that the plain reading of the provisions did not postulate the nature of the objection required to be raised by the Central Government but what it provided was that the Court before passing any order ,must take into consideration the representations and/or objections raised by the Central Government. It was held that the Central Government was certainly within their competence to raise the objection as they were required to see that no unfairness and/or unreasonableness to be shown either to the creditors or the class of creditors and/or members or the class of members and public interest, which certainly imbibed itself with the power to question the said share exchange ratio. Therefore, there was no force in the submission of the petitioner that the Central Government could not raise objection to the share exchange ratio. It was therefore directed to the official liquidator to engage a Chartered Accountant from its panel, who should submit the report before the court relating to fairness of the share exchange ratio.

13.11-6-3 two striking aspects relating to alteration and reduction of capital - In regard to the alteration and reduction of share capital, there are two striking aspects to be noticed. 13.11-6-3a Of being fair and equitable - One is that it is open to the Court 1 /Tribunal to examine whether it is fair and equitable though motives are irrelevant, or if it amounts to variation of class rights to confirm whether the majority of that class of shareholders affected has voted in its favour. In Holders Investment Trust Ltd., Re [1971] 2 All ER 289 (Ch. D), confirmation was refused as it appeared that those who approved the scheme did not apply their mind to see as to whether the scheme was good for the class as a whole. In contrast to this decision, in Neale v. City of Bermingham Tramway Co. [1910] 2 Ch. 464, the company passed a resolution to reduce capital with respect to the fully paid ordinary shares proposing to pay the holders from out of accumulated profits, leaving out the holders of partly paid shares; and, the Court was of the view that the section could not be construed as authorizing the return of capital to the whole class of shareholders entitled to share the divisible profits and the resolution was not ultra vires. As an extension of this we find that in issuing unconditional options for company s shares and take-over bids the procedure of alteration of share cpital through decrease and sub-division followed by consolidation and re-division of share capital into shares of larger amount than existing shares, section 94(1)(b) and (d), and their permutation and combination, on the one hand, and reduction of share capital under section 100 on the other, have been employed to produce startling results of dumping the existing shareholders to the advantage of the option-holders or vice-versa through dilution or impregnation of the potentials of voting on the strength of the shares. Thus, in Forsayth Oil & Gas NL v. Livia Pty. Ltd. [1985] BCLC 378 (PC), an option, free of any condition like adjustment or proportionality , was given at Aus. dollar one nominal value, and then the value of the share capital was decreased or devalued to 2.5% as also the nominal value of each of the shares, and next, such shares were consolidated ten into one with a nominal value of 0.25 cents. Following the decision in Hirsch & Co. v. Burns [1897] 77 LT 377 (HL), the Court pointed out that if the company had increased its capital and thereby diluted the potential rights of the option-holders the existing shareholders would not have complained and accordingly the reorganization and consolidation of the company s share capital could not modify the option-holders rights, in the absence of any express term in that behalf, though it disadvantaged the existing shareholders by tilting in favour of the option-holders, and that the option-holders were entitled to exercise their option.

13.11-6-3b It offending the minimum capital norm - The other is new, arising out of the minimum paid-up capital requirement norm of five lakh rupees for a public company introduced in section 3 by the Amending Act, 2000. Let us suppose that a public company limited by shares succeeds to get the Court s 1/Tribunal s order of confirmation in the ordinary course for reduction of its share capital, to Rs. 2.5 lakh and produces the order and the minute of reduction to the Registrar for registration under section 103 of the Act. Under such circumstances, the Registrar ought to refuse to register as the order confirming the reduction of share capital, say to Rs. 2.5 lakh (paid-up) for example, would be inconsistent with the requirement of section 3(1)(iv)( b) of the Act requiring Rs. 5 lakh (present limit) as the minimum paid-up capital for a public company. Then, should such a company seek to be re-registered as a private company limited by shares under section 32 of the Act first before registering the Court s 1/Tribunal s order, will be the question that arises. Or, does this open up into yet a new way of conversion of a public company into a private company comes out as a related question.

Capital Gains*

Buy back of shares

5.1 Section 77A of the Companies Act, 1956 permits a company to buy back its own shares upon fulfilment of the prescribed conditions. It has tax implications and broadly, there were two views :

◆ As per one view, utilisation of accumulated profits for the buy back, entailing reduction of capital, could amount to dividend attracting tax @ 10% under section 115-O of the Act in the hands of the company.

◆ As per the other view, the company is not liable to dividend tax inasmuch as the purchase of its own shares does not amount to reduction in capital and only the shareholders are liable to pay tax on the gains, if any.

To set the controversy at rest, the Finance Act, 1999 has made the following provisions :

(a) The payment made by a company for purchase of share would not constitute dividend [vide section 2(22)(iv)]; and

(b) Shareholders would be chargeable to capital gains tax (by inserting section 46A).

5.1-1 Dividend - Section 2(22) of the Act defines dividend inclusively. After listing the distribution or payment amounting to dividend, it lists certain distribution or payment not constituting dividend. In that list, the payment made by a company on purchase of its own shares from shareholder in terms of section 77A of the Companies Act, 1956 has been added [vide, sub-clause (iv)] meaning that such payment would not constitute dividend. Accordingly, the provisions of section 115-O of the Act would not apply.

However, this provision would not apply in respect of buy back of any shares or other securities by the company under any other provisions of the Companies Act, 1956 (i.e., other than section 77A) under any scheme of arrangement (e.g. an order under section 402 of the Companies Act, 1956) or otherwise. Accordingly, any payment made by the company in such a case for such purchase may constitute dividend within the meaning of section 2(22) of the Act.

5.1-2 Section 46A - The section provides as follows :

◆ When a shareholder or holder of other specified securities receives any consideration from a company,

◆ Upon purchase of its own shares or securities by the company,

◆ The difference between cost of acquisition and purchase price of shares or securities paid by the company would constitute capital gains,

◆ In computing the capital gains, section 48 should be given effect to,

◆ The gain would be chargeable to tax in the year of purchase and

◆ For the purpose, the other securities have the same meaning as assigned in Explanation to section 77A of the Companies Act, 1956.

5.1-2a Necessity - Shares or securities do constitute capital asset. It is settled law that upon purchase by the company, there is a transfer of shares [Anarkali Sarabhai v. CIT[1997] 224 ITR 422 (SC)]. Accordingly, any gain arising therefrom is chargeable to tax as capital gains or otherwise. Further, there was no controversy that a shareholder was liable to capital gains tax. Also, the question of reducing accumulated profit considered as dividend in computing the capital gain would not arise in view of the amendment made in section 2(22). In the circumstances, the need for a separate provision was not there. Also, the need for including other specified securities in the provision is also not clear.

5.1-2b Meaning of ‘shareholder’ or ‘holder’ - The Supreme Court in Howrah Trading Co. Ltd. v. CIT[1959] 36 ITR 215, 219-220] held that a shareholder or holder, means, a member, i.e., a person whose name is entered in the register of members. Accordingly, a beneficial owner of shares, say, a firm who holds shares through its partners, would not be considered as a shareholder. Similarly, the holder of specified security would mean the person whose name is entered in the register or record maintained by the company and not the beneficial owner.

Prima facie in such a case, (i.e., a beneficial owner), the provisions of section 46A may not apply, unless, a view is taken that in the context of section 46A, the shareholder could mean a person who receives the price for the buy back from the company. Apart from that, assuming for a moment section 46A cannot apply in case of a beneficial owner, taxation of gain on buy back cannot be ruled out under section 45. This is because where the special provision does not apply, the general provision can always apply.

Realised and unrealised profit

28.5-5 There are two views about the general meaning of ‘realised’ and ‘unrealised’ profit: the one obvious relates to revenues or gains or losses on assets sold as ‘realised’, and unsold as ‘unrealised’; the other is that the said view on unrealised profit does not hold good in every case and the assets remaining unsold as on the date of the balance sheet also figure as ‘realised’, as for example may be seen in the manner how finished stocks and work-in-progress are valued in accounts, namely, ‘at least of cost or net realizable value’ basis which tends to tilt the profit or loss and which enters into the computation of net profit or loss in the profit and loss account drawn as per Schedule VI. Taking this argument further, it will be seen that in division of undertaking and demergers, which the Company Law does not restrict (that role falls to the Competition Act, 2002), revaluation of fixed assets is a necessary incident of the process and the excess value on revaluation over the book value of the fixed assets forms a non-cash unrealized asset, but if those very assets are distributed as dividend, the unrealized excess value of the fixed assets on their revaluation has to form part of the ‘distributable profit’ treating as realized profit, and this has been recognized and allowed under section 276 of the 1985 English Act, in line with the decision in Dimbula Valley (Ceylon) Tea Co. Ltd. v. Laurie (1961) All ER 769, that a revaluation of unrealized fixed assets could be capitalized as equity shares, though it was done in that case to reduce the chances of participating preference shareholders in their participation in the surplus of assets in winding up that was upheld.

Revaluation reserve is not available to be capitalised as bonus

28.5-6 In India, however, that is not the law both for Regulation by DCA and the SEBI, and revaluation reserve cannot be capitalized as fully paid-up bonus shares though by the principles of accounting as such there is no objection to it if the revaluation was done universally for all fixed assets and by the approved valuers duly off-setting the loss on diminished values of some fixed assets, if any on revaluation.

When there is an issue of bonus shares, money remains with company and nothing comes to shareholders as there is no transfer of property, and thus, provisions of section 56(2)(vii)(c) are not attracted. The issue which arises for consideration in this appeal is 'as to whether the fair market value of bonus shares computed as per Rule 11U and Rule 11UA of the Income-tax Rules can be considered as income from other sources as per section 56(2)(vii) of the Act. A careful scrutiny of section 56(2)(vii) of the Act contemplates two contingencies firstly, where the property is received without consideration and secondly, where it is received for consideration less than the fair market value. The issue of bonus shares by capitalization of reserves is merely a reallocation of the companies funds. There is no inflow of fresh funds or increase in the capital employed, which remains the same. The total funds available with the company remains the same and issue of bonus shares does not result in any change in respect of capital structure of the company. Thus, there is no addition or alteration to the profit making apparatus and the total funds available with the company remain the same. In substance, when a shareholder gets a bonus shares, the value of the original share held by him goes down and the market value as well as intrinsic value of two shares put together will be the same or nearly the same as per the value of original share before the issue of bonus shares. Thus, any profit derived by the assessee on account of receipt of bonus shares is adjusted by depreciation in the value of equity shares held by him. In the instant case, there is no material on record to infer that bonus shares have been transferred with an intention to evade tax, which is the object of the provision in question. Therefore, the CIT (Appeals) as well as the tribunal have rightly held that when there is an issue of bonus shares, the money remains with the company and nothing comes to the shareholders as there is no transfer of the property and the provisions of section under section 56(2)(vii)(c) of the Act are not attracted to the fact situation of the case. Section 46A

Finance Act, 1999

Buy back of shares

5.1 Section 77A of the Companies Act, 1956 permits a company to buy back its own shares upon fulfilment of the prescribed conditions. It has tax implications and broadly, there were two views :

♦

As per one view, utilisation of accumulated profits for the buy back, entailing reduction of capital, could amount to dividend attracting tax @ 10% under section 115-O of the Act in the hands of the company.

♦

As per the other view, the company is not liable to dividend tax inasmuch as the purchase of its own shares does not amount to reduction in capital and only the shareholders are liable to pay tax on the gains, if any.

To set the controversy at rest, the Finance Act, 1999 has made the following provisions :

(a)

The payment made by a company for purchase of share would not constitute dividend [vide section 2(22)(iv)]; and

(b)

Shareholders would be chargeable to capital gains tax (by inserting section 46A).

5.1-1 Dividend - Section 2(22) of the Act defines dividend inclusively. After listing the distribution or payment amounting to dividend, it lists certain distribution or payment not constituting dividend. In that list, the payment made by a company on purchase of its own shares from shareholder in terms of section 77A of the Companies Act, 1956 has been added [vide, sub-clause (iv)] meaning that such payment would not constitute dividend. Accordingly, the provisions of section 115-O of the Act would not apply.

However, this provision would not apply in respect of buy back of any shares or other securities by the company under any other provisions of the Companies Act, 1956 (i.e., other than section 77A) under any scheme of arrangement (e.g. an order under section 402 of the Companies Act, 1956) or otherwise. Accordingly, any payment made by the company in such a case for such purchase may constitute dividend within the meaning of section 2(22) of the Act.

5.1-2 Section 46A - The section provides as follows :

♦

When a shareholder or holder of other specified securities receives any consideration from a company,

♦

Upon purchase of its own shares or securities by the company,

♦

The difference between cost of acquisition and purchase price of shares or securities paid by the company would constitute capital gains,

♦

In computing the capital gains, section 48 should be given effect to,

♦

The gain would be chargeable to tax in the year of purchase and

♦

For the purpose, the other securities have the same meaning as assigned in Explanation to section 77A of the Companies Act, 1956.

5.1-2a NECESSITY - Shares or securities do constitute capital asset. It is settled law that upon purchase by the company, there is a transfer of shares [Anarkali Sarabhai v. CIT [1997] 224 ITR 422 (SC)]. Accordingly, any gain arising therefrom is chargeable to tax as capital gains or otherwise. Further, there was no controversy that a shareholder was liable to capital gains tax. Also, the question of reducing accumulated profit considered as dividend in computing the capital gain would not arise in view of the amendment made in section 2(22). In the circumstances, the need for a separate provision was not there. Also, the need for including other specified securities in the provision is also not clear.

5.1-2b MEANING OF 'SHAREHOLDER' OR 'HOLDER' - The Supreme Court in Howrah Trading Co. Ltd. v. CIT [1959] 36 ITR 215, 219-220] held that a shareholder or holder, means, a member, i.e., a person whose name is entered in the register of members. Accordingly, a beneficial owner of shares, say, a firm who holds shares through its partners, would not be considered as a shareholder. Similarly, the holder of specified security would mean the person whose name is entered in the register or record maintained by the company and not the beneficial owner.

Prima facie in such a case, (i.e., a beneficial owner), the provisions of section 46A may not apply, unless, a view is taken that in the context of section 46A, the shareholder could mean a person who receives the price for the buy back from the company. Apart from that, assuming for a moment section 46A cannot apply in case of a beneficial owner, taxation of gain on buy back cannot be ruled out under section 45. This is because where the special provision does not apply, the general provision can always apply.

However, a share premium account or a capital redemption reserve account can be applied only in the paying up of un-issued shares to be issued to members of the company as fully paid bonus shares to the members according to their respective entitlements but not as a gift, CIT v. This accords with the Proviso to section 205(3), saying that the requirement of the Act for payment of dividend in cash in no way prohibits the capitalization of profits or reserves of a company for the purpose of issuing fully paid-up bonus shares or paying up any amount for the time being unpaid on any shares held by the members of the company. The effect of issue of bonus shares from general reserves is to seal off the chances of the amounts being available for distribution as dividend permanently by conversion into share capital without contribution from the shareholders. According to the decision of Supreme Court in Shree Gopal Paper Mills Ltd. v. For issue of bonus shares, see discussion in Ch 20.

In general, if there is a provision in the articles corresponding to Regulations 96 and 97 of Table A - which only deal with capitalization of profits—any company limited by shares may capitalise profits available for distribution as dividend by issue of fully paid bonus shares and issue the same to the existing members pro rata. From the DCA Circular 9/1994 dated 6-9-1994 it would appear that the guidelines for issue of bonus shares issued by SEBI under the SEBI (DIP) Guidelines, 2000 for listed companies are applicable to all companies—that is to say, that bonus shares are to be issued out of free general reserves built out of genuine profits or share (securities?) premium account collected in cash, but not out of reserves created by revaluation of fixed assets. Issue of bonus shares has the effect of reducing the share value proportionately in the ratio of its issue, Chandrakant Mulraj v. Tata Engg. & Locomotive Co. Ltd. [1985] 58 Comp. Cas. 320 (Bom.); and the character of bonus shares in the hands of the shareholders is capital but not dividend : IRC v. Blott (1921) 2 AC 171 (HL).

4. Capital profits can be utilised for writing off intangible assets like the preliminary expenses, share/debenture issue expenses, goodwill, etc.

The share premium account can be applied for the following purposes as directed by section 78 of the Companies Act, 1956 :

In exceptional cases, dividend may be paid out of capital reserves (i.e., capital profits).

The Delhi High Court had also allowed utilization of capital reserve to set off loss.

When capital reserve can be distributed as dividend

5. Capital reserve is not generally used for distribution of dividend. As a general rule, dividend is paid from current years’ profit. In exceptional cases, dividend may be paid out of capital reserves (i.e., capital profits) if the following conditions are fulfilled:

(a) The company’s articles of association permit such distribution,

(b) the surplus should be realized cash surplus, and

(c) such surplus should remain after proper revaluation of all fixed assets, in the manner provided in Accounting Standard AS-10.

AO passed an assessment order limiting the deduction under Section 44C to 5% of the gross total income. The matter reached before the Supreme Court.

The Supreme Court held that to be brought within the ambit of Section 44C, two broad conditions must be satisfied: (i) The assessee claiming the deduction must be a non-resident; and (ii) The expenditure in question must strictly fall within the definition of 'head office expenditure' as provided in the Explanation to the Section. The Explanation prescribes a tripartite test to determine if an expense qualifies as 'head office expenditure' - (i) The expenditure was incurred outside India; (ii) The expenditure is in the nature of 'executive and general administration' expenses; and (iii) The said executive and general administration expenditure is of the specific kind enumerated in clauses (a), (b), or (c) respectively of the Explanation, or is of the kind prescribed under clause (d).

This means that even if such head office expenditure can be allowed as a deduction under Section 37(1), it would not be permitted if it exceeds the ceiling limit set under Section 44C. Section 44C of the Income Tax Act does not create a distinction between common and exclusive head office expenditure. It applies to 'head office expenditure' regardless of whether it is common expenditure or expenditure incurred exclusively for the Indian branches. The term 'attributable' in Clause (c) does not create a statutory distinction between 'common' and 'exclusive' expenditure.

Thus, the question of law is answered in favour of the Revenue, and it was held that Section 44C applies to 'head office expenditure' regardless of whether it is common expenditure or expenditure incurred exclusively for the Indian branches.

5. Reduction in share capital of subsidiary & subsequent reduction in shareholding is 'transfer' under Section 2(47): SC

Jupiter Capital (P.) Ltd. v. Principal Commissioner of Income-tax [2025] 170 taxmann.com 305 (SC)

The assessee held shares in an Indian company. The company filed a petition before the High Court for a reduction of its share capital to set off the loss against the paid-up equity share capital. The High Court ordered for a reduction in the share capital of the company. The assessee's share was reduced proportionately, and the company paid an amount to the assessee as consideration. During the year, the assessee claimed a long-term capital loss accrued on the reduction in share capital from the sale of shares of such company.

However, the Assessing Officer (AO) contended that although the number of shares got reduced by virtue of reduction in share capital of the company, yet the face value of each share as well as shareholding pattern remained the same. Thus, reduction in shares of the subsidiary company did not result in the transfer of a capital asset as envisaged in section 2(47).

The matter reached before the Supreme Court.

The Supreme Court held that section 2(47) is an inclusive definition providing that relinquishment of an asset or extinguishment of any right therein amounts to a transfer of a capital asset. While the taxpayer continues to remain a shareholder of the company even with the reduction of share capital, it could not be accepted that there was no extinguishment of any part of his right as a shareholder qua the company.

The expression 'extinguishment of any right therein' is of wide import. It covers every possible transaction which results in the destruction, annihilation, extinction, termination, cessation or cancellation, by satisfaction or otherwise, of all or any of the bundle of rights, qualitative or quantitative, which the assessee has in a capital asset, whether such asset is corporeal or incorporeal.

In the instant case, the face value per share remained the same before the reduction of share capital and after the reduction of share capital. However, as the total number of shares were reduced.

Relying upon the decision in case of Kartikeya V. Sarabhai v. Commissioner of Income Tax reported in (1997) 7 SCC 524, it was held that reduction of right in a capital asset would amount to 'transfer' under section 2(47). Sale is only one of the modes of transfer envisaged by section 2(47). Relinquishment of any rights in it, which may not amount to sale, can also be considered as transfer and any profit or gain which arises from the transfer of such capital asset is taxable under section 45.

Also, a company under section 66 of the Companies Act, 2013 has a right to reduce the share capital, and one of the modes which could be adopted is to reduce the face value of the preference share. When as a result of the reducing of the face value of the share, the share capital is reduced, the right of the preference shareholder to the dividend or his share capital and the right to share in the distribution of the net assets upon liquidation is extinguished proportionately to the extent of reduction in the capital. Such a reduction of the right of the capital asset clearly amounts to a transfer within the meaning of section 2(47).

Thus, it was held that the reduction in share capital of the subsidiary company and subsequent proportionate reduction in the shareholding of the assessee would be squarely covered within the ambit of the expression 'sale, exchange or relinquishment of the asset' used in section 2(47).

1.10-1 Certain decisions relating to 'depreciation' - Note the following—

The Delhi Tribunal in SAIL v. DCIT (1991) 38 ITD 193, under the provisions of section 115J held that for the purposes of working out permissible adjustment of the lower of depreciation or loss, profits made in the earlier year cannot be ignored. The losses or the depreciation must be set off against earlier years' profits. In Geetanjali Woollens Pvt. Ltd. v. ACIT [1994] 50 ITD 558 the Ahmedabad Tribunal took a view that in determining, amount of loss or depreciation, to be set off, the amount already not set off in the past can only be considered.

The Chandigarh Bench of Income-tax Appellate Tribunal in ITO v. Parbhat Forging Pvt. Ltd [1991] 38 ITD 319 held that unprovided depreciation in respect of the past cannot be adjusted. While holding so, it also considered provisions similar to section 205 which were incorporated in section 115J of the Act.

Section 115JA does not have a similar provision. Now, what is permissible is reduction of the lower of brought forward loss or unabsorbed depreciation, as per books of account. This does imply that the loss or the depreciation must have been reflected in the books of account. In case of a company, which was incurring loss, depreciation may not have been provided at all.

Accordingly, in the year of profit, if it also provides for depreciation in respect of earlier years, then in computing the book profit, whether any adjustment can be made in respect of unprovided depreciation of earlier years ?

Having regard to the provisions, under the Explanation below section 115JA(2)no such adjustment can be made.

However, it may be pointed out that, as discussed earlier, a bench of Tribunal has taken a different view. Possibly, the different view could be contested on the ground that the provision for depreciation is a legal requirement, before declaring any dividends, and therefore in terms of the statute, the provision was made and therefore should not be a subject matter of adjustment.

The Cochin Bench of the Tribunal in Apollo Tyres Ltd v. DCIT [1992] 43 ITD 464 was concerned with a case where assessee provided for extra shift depreciation an its accounts, pursuant to insertion of Schedule XIV to the said Act. It was observed by the Tribunal that in view of the statutory amendment, the assessee was legally bound to provide for arrears of such extra shift depreciation. Further, this was in accordance with the provisions of the Schedule. Apart from that there was no earmarked adjustment for the provision. Accordingly, in computing book profit, an adjustment in respect thereof cannot be made.

In Bombay Tyres International Ltd v. DCIT[1994] 51 ITD 339, the company had changed the method of depreciation from straight line to WDV method based on technical or other evaluation and provided for the same in the accounts. The Bombay Tribunal took a view that change was bona fide based on recommendation of financial and technical personnel; it was a valid change and as per legal or accounting requirement as inferred, it was appropriate and not a colourable device. It took a view that the arrears pertained to a provision of an ascertained and known liability and therefore did not constitute reserve. Having regard to decision of Special Bench in Sutlej case (supra), the adjustment made by the department was not permitted.

In Beta Napthol Pvt. Ltd. v. DCIT [1994] 50 TTJ 375, Indore Bench of the Tribunal with reference to change in method of depreciation and section 115J has taken a view that an assessee is entitled to change method of depreciation and also entitled to claim extra depreciation as arrears of past.

Finance Act, 1999

Buy back of shares

5.1 Section 77A of the Companies Act, 1956 permits a company to buy back its own shares upon fulfilment of the prescribed conditions. It has tax implications and broadly, there were two views :

As per one view, utilisation of accumulated profits for the buy back, entailing reduction of capital, could amount to dividend attracting tax @ 10% under section 115-O of the Act in the hands of the company.

As per the other view, the company is not liable to dividend tax inasmuch as the purchase of its own shares does not amount to reduction in capital and only the shareholders are liable to pay tax on the gains, if any.

To set the controversy at rest, the Finance Act, 1999 has made the following provisions :

(a)

The payment made by a company for purchase of share would not constitute dividend [vide section 2(22)(iv)]; and

(b)

Shareholders would be chargeable to capital gains tax (by inserting section 46A).

5.1-1 Dividend - Section 2(22) of the Act defines dividend inclusively. After listing the distribution or payment amounting to dividend, it lists certain distribution or payment not constituting dividend. In that list, the payment made by a company on purchase of its own shares from shareholder in terms of section 77A of the Companies Act, 1956 has been added [vide, sub-clause (iv)] meaning that such payment would not constitute dividend. Accordingly, the provisions of section 115-O of the Act would not apply.

However, this provision would not apply in respect of buy back of any shares or other securities by the company under any other provisions of the Companies Act, 1956 (i.e., other than section 77A) under any scheme of arrangement (e.g. an order under section 402 of the Companies Act, 1956) or otherwise. Accordingly, any payment made by the company in such a case for such purchase may constitute dividend within the meaning of section 2(22) of the Act.

5.1-2 Section 46A - The section provides as follows :

When a shareholder or holder of other specified securities receives any consideration from a company,

Upon purchase of its own shares or securities by the company,

The difference between cost of acquisition and purchase price of shares or securities paid by the company would constitute capital gains,

In computing the capital gains, section 48 should be given effect to,

The gain would be chargeable to tax in the year of purchase and

For the purpose, the other securities have the same meaning as assigned in Explanation to section 77A of the Companies Act, 1956.

5.1-2a NECESSITY - Shares or securities do constitute capital asset. It is settled law that upon purchase by the company, there is a transfer of shares [Anarkali Sarabhai v. CIT [1997] 224 ITR 422 (SC)]. Accordingly, any gain arising therefrom is chargeable to tax as capital gains or otherwise. Further, there was no controversy that a shareholder was liable to capital gains tax. Also, the question of reducing accumulated profit considered as dividend in computing the capital gain would not arise in view of the amendment made in section 2(22). In the circumstances, the need for a separate provision was not there. Also, the need for including other specified securities in the provision is also not clear.

5.1-2b MEANING OF 'SHAREHOLDER' OR 'HOLDER' - The Supreme Court in Howrah Trading Co. Ltd. v. CIT [1959] 36 ITR 215, 219-220] held that a shareholder or holder, means, a member, i.e., a person whose name is entered in the register of members. Accordingly, a beneficial owner of shares, say, a firm who holds shares through its partners, would not be considered as a shareholder. Similarly, the holder of specified security would mean the person whose name is entered in the register or record maintained by the company and not the beneficial owner.

Prima facie in such a case, (i.e., a beneficial owner), the provisions of section 46A may not apply, unless, a view is taken that in the context of section 46A, the shareholder could mean a person who receives the price for the buy back from the company. Apart from that, assuming for a moment section 46A cannot apply in case of a beneficial owner, taxation of gain on buy back cannot be ruled out under section 45. This is because where the special provision does not apply, the general provision can always apply.

In the light of the recent decision, an academic analyses is made on authority/jurisdiction of the sanctioning court in an application for approving the scheme of arrangement.

The term 'sanctioning court' and Tribunal has been used in the article interchangeably.

Facts of the case

'Reliance Jio Infocomm Limited'- Demerged/ Transferor Company, 'Jio Digital Fibre Private Limited'- Resulting Company and 'Reliance Jio Infratel Private Limited'- Transferee Company moved a joint petition under Sections 230-232 of the Companies Act, 2013, seeking sanction of the Composite Scheme of Arrangement amongst themselves and their respective shareholders and Creditors.

Hon'ble National Company Law Tribunal (NCLT) vide order dated 11th January 2019 directed the Regional Director, North Western Region to make a representation under Section 230(5) of the Companies Act, 2013 and the Income Tax Department to file representation.

Aggrieved by the impugned order which was pronounced on 20th March 2019 sanctioning the Scheme, the Joint Commissioner of Income Tax (OSD), Circle (3)(3)-1, Mumbai and the income Tax Officer, Ward 3(3)-1, Mumbai has preferred an appeal before the Hon'ble National Company Law Appellate Tribunal (NCLAT).

Composite scheme of arrangement in brief

'Reliance Jio Infocomm Limited' had issued 1,300 preference shares of Rs. 10 each at a premium of Rs. 40 each to its holding company, 'Reliance Industries Ltd.' (RIL), aggregating to Rs. 65,000 crore. These funds were inter alia utilized for investment in the optic fiber and tower infrastructure undertakings.

Under the Scheme, amongst other, the preference share capital and corresponding share premium would be cancelled and converted into an equivalent amount of loans from 'Reliance Industries Ltd.' to 'Reliance Jio Infocomm Limited' (Rs. 7,822 crore), 'Jio Digital Fibre Private Limited' (Rs. 45,342 crore) and 'Reliance Jio Infratel Private Limited' (Rs.11,836 crore).

In brief, preference share capital including its premium amount was converted to equivalent amount of loans though composite scheme of arrangement.

Legal Issues before the Tribunal

A plain reading the instant case of Reliance Jio bring to the mind the following aspects –

(i)

Power of the sanctioning court.

(ii)

Whether preference shares including its premium can be cancelled and converted into loans.

(iii)

Whether Income Tax department can raise objection that scheme was used as a tool to evade and avoid tax.

(iv)

In the instant case, preference shares including premium amount was worth Rs.65,000 crore was converted into loans through composite scheme of arrangement.

Power of the Court/Tribunal

In order to reduce the burden of the High Courts, the Companies Act, 2013 has rightfully shifted the power to approve the scheme arrangement to Tribunal.

A plain reading of Section 230 inter alia reveals that where majority of persons representing three-fourths in value of the creditors/class of creditors or members/class of members agree to any compromise or arrangement and if it is sanctioned by the Tribunal by an order, the same shall be binding on the Company, members and creditors, as the case may be.

All that the Tribunal was called upon to examine was whether the settlement consideration was liable to be construed as capital gains or taxed as 'profits in lieu of salary'. Relevant Factors for order under section 101: The financial position of the company is relevant for an order of confirmation under section 103(1), and there is a distinction between dispensing with the procedure under section 101 and dispensing with the provisions of section 101(2). Where absence of mala fide would not by itself entitle a company to an order under section 101(3) or deny a creditor an order under section 101(2)(c), the presence of it may well be an important factor to deny an order to the company. Even where the Court settles the list of the creditors under section 101(2)(b ) it needs to pass an order for payment of security under section 101(2)(c) only in favour of those creditors who did not consent to the reduction. Section 101(2)(c)( ii) only provides the procedure for fixing an amount of security and it does not contemplate a final, determinative and precise adjudication of a creditor s claim. The proceeding under section 101 in its very nature indicates that it does not contemplate a full fledged trial of the creditor s claim, and in the exercise of the powers under section 101 the court is not entitled to pay over the amount to the creditors but only to secure their claim - Hindustan Dorr Oliver Ltd., In re [2002] 40 SCL 521 (Bom.).

Redemption of preference shares and reduction of capital: Redemption of preference shares may be made in two ways: one under section 80 and the other under section 100. If the company lawfully decides to pay off preference shares, the Court will not refuse to confirm reduction of capital - Scottish Insurance Corpn. Ltd. v. Wilsones Clyde Coal Co. Ltd. Loss on reduction: The loss falls on those who would otherwise bear it on a winding up, London New York Investment Corpn., In re [1895] 2 Ch. 860 (Ch.D). 17. Reopening of cases of Rahul Gandhi and Sonia Gandhi is valid as they failed to disclose shares allotted in excess of FMV: HC

[Sonia Gandhi v. ACIT [2018] 97 taxmann.com 150 (Delhi)]

The assessees, Mr. Rahul Gandhi and Mrs. Sonia Gandhi, extended a loan to the National Herald to write off the accumulated debts and recommence the newspaper publication. The said loan was assigned by the assessee to a newly incorporated non-profit company 'Young India' (YI) and in lieu of that they were allotted shares of YI. However, in Income-tax returns, they failed to pay tax on the shares allotted by Young India. The assessees argued that the allotment of shares did not trigger any taxing event. It was also argued that since they were shareholders of a non-profit and charitable company, they were under no obligation to disclose the value of shares.

The High Court held in favour of revenue that sub-clause (ii) of clause (c) of Section 56(2) provides that if certain shares or property are acquired at a price which is less than its aggregate fair market value by an amount exceeding Rs. 50,000, the fair market value as reduced by the considered paid shall be charged to tax. In the instant case, the assessee bought the shares at Rs. 100 per share which could not be deemed as its fair market value. The assesse had nowhere disclosed the fair market value of such shares and had not recorded the facts relating to above taxing event. Further, it couldn't be held that the individual was exempted altogether from disclosing her or his interest in the acquisition of shares merely because shares were of not-for-profit Company. Therefore, the AO was justified in reopening the cases.

For the purposes of taxation, with a view to provide tax neutral reorganisation or restructuring of businesses, exemption is provided by the Act. While referring to the transaction, some of the provisions of the Act suggest that in consideration of the vesting of the undertaking and/or its assets and liabilities, shares are issued to the shareholders of the amalgamating company or the demerged company.

In case of amalgamated company or the resulting company, the undertaking passes to it and it issues the shares, which, as such, does not result in to any profit or gain and, therefore, presently, no provision is made in the Act in that behalf. For the purposes of calculation of cost of the assets of the undertaking, suitable provisions are made in the Act.

In relation to the applicability of the clause to the amalgamated company or the resulting company, there could be two possible views when shares are issued pursuant to amalgamation or demerger of a resident amalgamating/demerged company, respectively.

As per one view, the clause would apply, inter alia, for the following reasons:

♦ Under the scheme of amalgamation or demerger, the amalgamated company or the resulting company issues shares to the shareholders of the amalgamating company or the demerged company, in consideration for vesting of the undertaking [apart from the applicable provisions of the Act, like, definition of demerger, exemption to the shareholders etc., a reference may be made to a decision of Supreme Court in Hindustan Lever v. State of Maharashtra [2003] 117 Comp. Cas. 758, where it was observed that once the shareholders of the transferee company receive the consideration it would be deemed as if the owner has received the consideration (page 774)].

♦ Further, as held by Supreme Court in Hindustan Lever v. State of Maharashtra [2003] 117 Comp. Cas. 758, the amalgamation is a compromise or arrangement between the parties, which, inter alia, includes the amalgamated company issuing the shares and the shareholders of the amalgamating company, which is supervised by the court, in terms of the provisions of the Companies Act, 1956. In other words, there is an agreement or arrangement, inter alia, by and between the amalgamated company issuing the shares and the shareholders of the amalgamating company. The Clause contemplates the issue of shares and the receipt of consideration from a resident person and it is fulfilled in case of amalgamation.

♦ The Clause applies to any consideration, whether in cash or in kind or whether at the instance of the company or otherwise.

♦ The Clause applies to any consideration whether received from the person to whom the shares are issued or otherwise.

♦ The events attracting tax are present, namely, receipt of consideration and issue of shares.

♦ Whether the issue triggers consideration or otherwise is of no relevance.

As per the other view, the clause cannot apply, inter alia, for the following reasons:

♦ The objective of insertion of the provision is relevant for determining the true scope and ambit of the provision.

♦ The objective is to tax 'conversion of unaccounted' money and accordingly include within its scope only such transactions, which facilitate such conversion.

♦ The issue of shares is not to invite subscription by the persons to whom an offer is made. The issue of shares is to give effect to the amalgamation or the demerger, as per the mutual agreement and the Court order. In other words, the issue of shares does not trigger any consideration; in fact, the obligation to give consideration, triggers the issue of shares.

♦ The clause contemplates 'receipt' of the consideration for the shares from a resident person. In other words, it contemplates a transaction between a resident person and the company issuing the shares. In case of an amalgamation or a demerger, the consideration, which would be the undertaking along with all its assets and liabilities is in the form of vesting by the amalgamating or the demerged company; whereas, the shares are issued to its shareholders. Thus, it is a tripartite arrangement not contemplated by the Clause.

The user of the phrase 'by whatever name called' signifies that the nomenclature given to an amount is of no importance or relevance. If the amount set apart represents a reserve within the meaning of the Schedule, it has to be added back to the net profit.

To illustrate, a company may follow a practice of providing doubtful debts on ad hoc basis and it may be named as 'provision for doubtful debts'. In fact, there may not be any doubtful debts. In other words, the sundry debtors may be realisable at the value stated. In such a case, such setting apart does not constitute a provision within the meaning assigned to it by the Schedule; but, in fact constitutes a reserve as defined in the Schedule. Thus, though it is called a provision, it is a reserve. Therefore, irrespective of the nomenclature, the amount so set apart has to be added back to the profits in terms of Explanation defining book profits.

1.9-2a RESERVES ADJUSTMENT UNDER EXPLANATION (i) - Explanation (i) requires reduction of amount withdrawn from any reserve or provision, if it is credited to profit and loss account.

Such reduction can be made in respect of any reserves or provisions created in respect of any year relevant to assessment year 1997-98 and thereafter only when the amount of such reserves or provision was added back under Explanation (b).

Accordingly, if any reserve has been created in any earlier year and if that is credited to profit and loss account, the adjustment, by way of reduction, under, this Explanation can be made.

1.9-2b CREDIT TO CAPITAL RESERVE - The Special bench of the Tribunal (Calcutta) in Sutlej Cotton Mills Ltd. v. ACIT [1993] 45 ITD 22 was concerned with an adjustment not specifically permitted by section 115J of the Act. The company in that case had revalued its fixed assets in earlier years. In the subsequent year, it revalued all its quoted investments at market value. The difference on revaluation of these shares was credited to capital reserve account. In the next year, relevant to assessment year 1988-89, it sold certain shares. The sale proceeds were not credited to profit and loss account; but were adjusted in the asset account and/or capital reserve account. In the assessment proceedings, the Assessing Officer took a View that the objective of revaluation was to defraud revenue and avoidance of tax under section 115J by changing method of valuation. In the appellate proceedings, the Appellate Authority held that the treatment was not in accordance with para 3(xii)(a)of the Schedule which read as follows:

"Profits or losses on investments showing distinctly the extent of the profits or losses earned or incurred on account of membership of a partnership firm to the extent not adjusted from any previous provision or reserve." [Emphasis supplied]

On the aforesaid facts, the Tribunal held as follows :

The requirement of the Schedule show that it is concerned with the result of the working of the company. Thus, it cannot be directly concerned with changes in capital structure. Profit on realisation of capital assets will not be an item of income.

Company had followed a consistent practice in relation to revaluation of capital assets. The practice adopted was in accordance with para 3(xii)(a) referred above, as a credit to Profit & Loss Account was required to be taken to the extent not adjusted, as provided therein. The practice followed by the company was a sound accounting practice as the profit was not available for distribution. Accordingly, the profit realised cannot form part of book profit.

As per Explanation below section 115J(1A) providing for adjustments, only the permitted adjustments can be made. Beyond that, book profit cannot be adjusted. For the purpose, even section 145 cannot be applied. Accordingly, the Assessing Officer was bound to proceed with computation of book profit as shown in the Profit and Loss Account.

As far as valuation of assets, etc., is concerned, really it cannot be compared with the method of valuation in relation to stock in trade. In any case, section 145 does not apply to revaluation of fixed assets.

The Assessing Officer cannot disturb reserve, which has been adjusted in accordance with requirement of the Schedule and as per the para referred above.

This was not a device for avoidance of tax.
