Share buybacks raise a characterisation issue under the DTAAs. The central issue is whether the gain or income arising in the hands of the shareholder should be treated as a dividend, a capital gain, or other income. This characterisation is critical because it determines which article of the DTAA applies and, consequently, which country retains the right to tax such income. The OECD Model Convention defines "dividends" under Article 10(3) to mean income from shares, jouissance shares or jouissance rights, mining shares, founders' shares or other rights that are not debt-claims but participate in profits, as well as income from other corporate rights which is subjected to the same taxation treatment as income from shares by the laws of the state of which the company making the distribution is a resident. This definition is broad and explicitly connects the characterisation of dividend income to the domestic law of the source state. Paragraph 28 of the OECD Commentary on Article 10 addresses situations involving redemption, liquidation, and disguised distributions of profits, and notes that where the domestic law of the source state treats the amounts paid to a shareholder on buyback as a distribution of profits, such amounts fall within the definition of dividends under Article 10.

Para 31 of the OCED Model Commentary on Article 13 provides that if shares are alienated by a shareholder in connection with the liquidation of the issuing company or the redemption of shares or reduction of paid-up capital of that company, the difference between the proceeds obtained by the shareholder and the par value of the shares may be treated in the State of which the company is a resident as a distribution of accumulated profits and not as a capital gain. The Article does not prevent the State of residence of the company from taxing such distributions at the rates provided for in Article 10. Where the domestic law of the source country does not treat the buyback proceeds as dividend income but instead characterises the transaction as a sale or transfer of a capital asset, Article 13 of the treaty on Capital Gains would apply.

In simple terms, the treatment of share buybacks under a DTAA is not governed by a single universal rule but depends critically on the characterisation of the proceeds under the domestic law of the source state, the specific treaty language, and the model convention on which the bilateral treaty is based. Where domestic law treats buyback proceeds as a deemed dividend or distribution of profits, Article 10 applies, and the source state retains the tax rights. Where domestic law treats income from share buybacks as capital gains, the classification should be the same under the DTAA unless a treaty provides otherwise. Regardless of characterisation, taxpayers must remain mindful of anti-avoidance provisions such as the PPT, which may override treaty benefits where arrangements lack sufficient commercial substance.

6.2-5h Taxable in the hands of the shareholder - The capital gains computed under section 69 shall be taxable in the hands of the shareholder. The term 'shareholder' is not specifically defined in either the Income-tax Act or the Companies Act. However, section 2(55) of the Companies Act, 2013 defines 'member' as a person whose name is entered in the register of members of the company. Additionally, a person who holds shares in a company and whose name is recorded as a beneficial owner in the depository's records is considered a member.

For income tax purposes, the term 'shareholder' generally refers to a registered shareholder. A beneficial owner whose name does not appear in the register of shareholders is not considered a 'shareholder'11.

According to the Prohibition of Benami Property Transactions Act, 1988 ("Benami Act"), it is not permissible for a person to be a shareholder when the beneficial owner of those shares is some other person. However, section 2(9) of the Benami Act provides certain exceptions where the shareholder may be a different person from the beneficial owner, subject to specific conditions:

A shareholder who is the Karta of an HUF, with the beneficial owner being the HUF itself.

A shareholder acting in a fiduciary capacity, such as a trustee, executor, partner, director, depository, or depository participant, with the beneficial owner being the Trust, estate, partnership firm, company, or demat account holder.

A shareholder who is an individual, with the beneficial owner being his or her spouse or child.

A shareholder who is an individual, with the beneficial owner being his or her brother, sister, or lineal ascendant or descendant, as joint owners.

The Supreme Court, in Howrah Trading Co. Ltd. v. CIT [1959] 36 ITR 215 (SC), held that a shareholder means a person whose name is entered in the register of members. Thus, a beneficial owner, such as a firm holding shares through its partners, is not considered a shareholder. Consequently, if shares are held in a fiduciary capacity for another person, the taxability lies with the person who holds the shares as the registered shareholder. However, this principle shall not apply when a depository or depository participant holds shares in a fiduciary capacity for a demat account holder, as the demat account holder is considered the member in relation to the company, not the depository.

Javeri v. K.K. Sen3, the validity of section 12(1B) of the 1922 Act, was questioned. Section 12(1B) provided that a loan made to a shareholder by private-controlled company is taxable as dividend. It was recognized that merely because the loan is taxed as a dividend in the hands of a shareholder, the loan may not cease to be a loan, and that it would be open to the company to recover the loan by resorting to law. The petitioner’s argument was that what is not income is being taxed as ‘income’ and, therefore, it is beyond the legislative competence of the Parliament. (The impugned provision was introduced by the Finance Act, 1955.) The argument was rejected in the following words :

“In dealing with this point, it is necessary to consider what exactly is the connotation of the word ‘income’ used in the relevant entry. It is hardly necessary to emphasize that the entries in the Lists cannot be read in a narrow or restricted sense, and as observed by Gwyer, CJ. in the United Provinces v. Atiqa Begum1, each general word should be held to extend to all ancillary or subsidiary matters which can fairly and reasonably be said to be comprehended in it. What the entries in the Lists purport to do is to confer legislative powers on the respective Legislatures in respect of areas or fields covered by the said entries; and it is an elementary rule of construction that the widest possible construction must be put upon their words. This doctrine does not, however, mean that Parliament can choose to tax as income an item which in no rational sense can be regarded as a citizen’s income. The item taxed should rationally be capable of being considered as the income of a citizen. But in considering the question as to whether a particular item in the hands of a citizen can be regarded as his income or not, it would be inappropriate to apply the tests traditionally prescribed by the Income-tax Act as such...” (p. 1379)

The Court reaffirmed the principles enunciated in Navinchandra Mafatlal’s case (supra), Baldeo Singh’s case (supra) and Balaji’s case (supra).

It is equally relevant to notice that in Baldeo Singh’s case (supra), the validity of section 23A of the 1922 Act was questioned. Section 23A provided that where the ITO is satisfied that in respect of any previous year the profits and gains distributed as dividend by any company within twelve months immediately following the expiry of that previous year are less than 60 per cent of the total income of the company of that previous year [as reduced by the amounts specified in clauses (a), (b) and (c) of sub-section (1)], the ITO shall, unless he is satisfied that having regard to losses incurred by the company in earlier years, or to the smallness of the profits made in the previous year, the payment of a dividend, or a larger dividend than that declared, would be unreasonable, make an order in writing that the company shall, apart from the sum determined as payable by it on the basis of the assessment under section 23 of the 1922 Act, be liable to pay super-tax at the rate specified by sub-section (1) of section 23A. This section was enacted to prevent avoidance of super-tax by shareholders of a company in which the public are not substantially interested. The assessee’s argument was that since the company and shareholders are distinct entities, taxing the shareholders on dividends not distributed by the company, and not received by them, cannot be justified as a tax on income received by shareholders. This argument was repelled on the ground that the obvious intention of section 23A was to prevent evasion of tax, and that Entry 54 in List I of the Seventh Schedule should be read not only as authorising the imposition of a tax, but also as authorising an enactment which prevents the tax imposed being evaded. It was also observed that section 23A dealt with a situation where shareholders did not deliberately distribute the accumulated profits as dividend among themselves and, therefore, provided that these accumulated profits will be deemed to have been distributed to shareholders and tax levied on that basis.

COVERAGE OF SECTION 46(2)

Section 46 deals with capital gains on distribution of assets by companies on liquidation. Section 46(1) provides that notwithstanding anything contained in section 45, where the assets of a company are distributed to its shareholders on its liquidation, such distribution shall not be regarded as a transfer by the company for the purposes of section 45. The company hence need not pay tax on any capital gain by making computation on such distribution.

Section 46(2) says that where a shareholder on the liquidation of a company receives any money or other assets from the company, he shall be chargeable to income-tax under the head 'Capital gains', in respect of the money so received or the market value of the other assets on the date of distribution, as reduced by the amount assessed as dividend under section 2(22)(c) and the sum so arrived at shall be deemed to be the full value of consideration for the purpose of section 48.

6.2 Buy-back of shares will be taxable as capital gains [Section 69 of ITA 2025 (corresponding to Section 46A of ITA 1961)]

The Finance Act, 2026 has made several amendments to the provisions of the ITA 2025 regarding the taxation of buy-back of shares. Under the amended provisions, the sum paid by a domestic company to the shareholders under a buyback shall be treated as capital gains in the hands of the shareholders.

6.2-1 Introduction

Corporate action to buyback shares can serve multiple strategic purposes. Primarily, it's used to increase earnings per share by reducing the number of outstanding shares, often leading to a higher stock price. Additionally, buybacks are a method to return excess cash to shareholders, an alternative to dividend payouts. Companies might also repurchase shares if they believe their stock is undervalued, signalling confidence in the future. Moreover, buybacks can deter hostile takeovers by increasing the company's ownership percentage.

Section 68 of the Companies Act, 2013 gives the company the power to purchase its own securities. It defines a buyback as the purchase of its own shares or other specified securities (i.e., Employee Stock Options or Sweat Equity) by the Company itself.

6.2-2 History of tax on buyback of shares as per the ITA 1961

Before the assessment year 2000-01, the Income Tax Act did not include a special provision for taxing share buybacks. There were two views on the buyback of shares: either it could attract dividend distribution tax, or shareholders would be liable to pay tax on any gains.

To set the controversy at rest, the Finance Act, 1999 inserted section 46A with effect from assessment year 2000-01, which stated that shareholders would be charged to tax on the capital gains arising from the buyback of shares. A corresponding amendment was also made to section 2(22) by inserting clause (iv), which provides that a payment for the purchase of shares does not constitute a dividend. Therefore, the consideration received by a shareholder on the buyback of shares by the company in accordance with section 77A of the Companies Act, 19561 (corresponding to Section 68 of the Companies Act, 2013) was not treated as a dividend. The same was taxed under Section 46A of the Act as capital gains.

Subsequently, the unlisted companies, as part of the tax avoidance scheme, were found resorting to buyback of shares instead of payment of dividends in order to avoid payment of tax by way of DDT, particularly where the capital gains arising to the shareholders were either not chargeable to tax or were taxable at a lower rate under respective Double Taxation Avoidance Agreements. In A Mauritius, In re [2012] 20 taxmann.com 52, the AAR held that only a genuine buyback is excluded from the definition of 'dividend' under section 2(22)(iv) and exempt from DDT under section 115-O. A colourable buyback will attract DDT. In that case, the buyback was held to be a colourable device for tax avoidance, as dividends were distributed in the guise of a buyback to avoid DDT.

Taking a cue from the above decision of the AAR, the Finance Act, 2013 inserted a new Chapter XII-DA, 'Special Provisions relating to tax on distributed income of domestic company for buyback of shares,' consisting of sections 115QA to 115QC, with effect from 1-6-2013. The Finance (No. 2) Act, 2019 extended the levy of tax on the buy-back of shares listed on a recognised stock exchange on or after 5 July 2019 by amending section 115QA.

In November 2022, the Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI) released a consultation paper on a review of the SEBI (Buyback of Securities) Regulations, 2018, proposing various changes to existing buyback norms. One of the proposed changes is to shift the tax burden of buybacks from the company to the shareholders. This proposal was based on the fact that promoters tendered more shares than their pre-buyback holdings, resulting in the company paying taxes not only on shares tendered by the promoters but also on the additional shares tendered by them. These taxes were paid from the company's reserves on behalf of the existing shareholders and promoters at the expense of continuing shareholders. Therefore, it was suggested that the tax burden on buybacks should be shifted to shareholders, as it is with dividend distributions.

Consequently, while the RBI determined value is the minimum fair value, the CBDT determined value is the maximum fair value, of the issued shares. The RBI and CBDT valuations, being derived from different bases (DCF value as per the issuing company and the taxman respectively), will not converge. The starting point of the divergence is the issue of shares to the non-resident which will be based on the RBI guidelines. Thereafter the taxman enters the picture, determines that the shares have been undervalued when they were issued and seeks to tax the alleged discount. Both RBI and the CBDT, being apex bodies of the Government – and indeed of the same Ministry of Finance – there should not be such a divergence between the valuations of these two bodies. The valuations can at most vary by 10-20% but more than that means one of the apex bodies are not doing their job correctly and causing loss to the nation, either by giving up foreign exchange or taxes due to the country. A variation of 1850% in the Shell India/Netherlands case indicates a very basic disconnect between two apex government bodies to whom the share issuer and the non-resident share allottee are subject. Issuers of shares to non-residents and their allottees should not be made victims of separate valuation methodologies of different arms of the Government. This calls for serious and urgent review at the highest levels of the Government.

What is the rationale for issuing shares at a discount to the overseas parent?

Where the taxman alleges that an Indian company has issued shares to its 100% overseas parent at a discount, a fundamental question arises as to why the subsidiary should attempt to do so? A 100% parent can control the subsidiary by the fact of its shareholding percentage and would not be bothered about the number of shares it holds in the subsidiary. If shares are undervalued and issued, more number of shares are issued, compared to a situation where lesser number of shares are issued when the shares are priced higher. In both situations, the shareholding still remains 100% in the subsidiary. What is therefore to be gained by issuing shares at a discount, when the shares are meant to be permanently held by the parent as part of its group structure and not meant to be disposed of soon after allotment? To take the Shell India/Netherlands example, Shell India could have, instead of inviting any tax scrutiny/liability by issuing 87 crore shares at an undervalued price of Rs. 10 each i.e. Rs. 870 crores, have easily issued 4.7 crore shares (of Rs. 10 par value) at an issue price of Rs. 185 and collected the same amount of Rs. 870 crores that it required for its operations. If Shell Netherlands was the sole parent company controlling Shell India, this control could have been equally exercised in the same manner with 4.7 crore shares as with 87 crore shares. Hence, the motive for seeking to undervalue the issue of shares by Shell India to Shell Netherlands needs to be fundamentally established by the taxman, before seeking to establish the quantum of undervaluation. If no motive can be established, the attempts to tax the undervaluation lacks substance and would amount to taking advantage of a technicality.

Capital Reserve can be Used to Set off Loss, with Company Court’s Approval

S. VENUGOPALAN

The author is a Company Secretary.

The author here deals with the issue as to when capital reserve can be used to set off losses. The highlights of the article are the definition of ‘capital reserve’, circumstances in which it is created and its utilisation. In this context, the author has analysed the judgment of the Delhi High Court in Allianz Capital & Management Services Ltd., In re [2005] 63 SCL 496 wherein it has been held that after obtaining the Government’s approval, capital profits can be used to set off loss, and submits that this decision is binding within jurisdiction of the Delhi High Court only.

What is capital reserve

1. Reserve is profit retained or ploughed back in the business and accumulated over the years. Reserves are of two kinds (1) Revenue reserve and (2) Capital reserve. A reserve created out of trading profits is revenue reserve.

A reserve which is created out of capital profits is a capital reserve. The Companies Act, 1956 does not directly define the term ‘capital reserve’. But according to Part III of Schedule VI of the Act, "the expression ‘capital reserve’ shall not include any amount regarded as free for distribution through the profit and loss account; and the expression ‘revenue reserve’ shall mean any reserve other than a capital reserve." In reality, the capital reserve is at time distributable as dividends among shareholders. But normally, it is not so distributed. The capital reserve is not created by transferring the profit through the appropriation account as is the case of the revenue or the general reserve. But, it is created out of the profits of a capital nature.

A reserve which is created out of capital profits is a capital reserve.

How a capital reserve is created

2. The capital reserve is created out of the capital profits. Some of the circumstances under which the capital reserve is created are as under:

(a) Premiums received on the issue of shares and debentures are capital profits. They are considered as the capital reserve.

(b) Balance to the credit of forfeited shares account after the re-issue of such forfeited shares is transferred to the capital reserve.

(c) Profit on the redemption of debentures at a discount is considered as a capital profit and is transferred to the capital reserve.

(d) When on purchase of a business the purchase price is less than the value of the net assets acquired, the difference is normally transferred to the capital reserve.

(e) Similarly the profits prior to the incorporation of the limited company are considered capital profits and are transferred to the capital reserve.

(f) Profits which are of an exceptional nature and which have not been earned during the regular course of business are at times considered as capital profits and are transferred to the capital reserve. But it is not so treated always.

(g) Where the company sells its fixed assets at an amount which is higher than their cost, the excess over cost is considered as a capital profit. This profit is not earned during the regular course of business. Hence, such profits are normally transferred to the capital reserve.

(h) Sometimes a company may revalue its fixed assets as a result of appreciation in their value. The amount of appreciation is normally transferred to the capital reserve. Revaluation of fixed assets is made by following the Accounting Standard-10 accounting for fixed assets. Revaluation of assets should be done of a class of assets and not individual assets.

(i) If directed by the articles of association, certain profits may not be available for distribution among shareholders. In other words, such profits are not free for distribution through the profit and loss account. Such profits are transferred to the capital reserve.

(j) Certain capital gains and other items of profits which are not regarded as available for distribution as dividend are transferred to the capital reserve. (Adapted from Auditing Principles and Practice by V.H Krishnadwala pg. 2.265)

Disclosure of capital reserve in the balance sheet

3. According to Part I of Schedule VI to the Act, the capital reserve should be shown as a separate item under the head ‘Reserves and surplus’. It should not be mixed up with the revenue reserves. The share premium account is a capital profit, but it is shown as a separate item in the balance sheet.

Utilisation of capital profits (and hence the capital reserve)

4. Capital profits can be utilised for writing off intangible assets like the preliminary expenses, share/debenture issue expenses, goodwill, etc.

The share premium account can be applied for the following purposes as directed by section 78 of the Companies Act, 1956 :

(a) in paying up unissued shares of the company to be issued to its shareholders as fully paid bonus shares,

(b) in writing off preliminary expenses,

DEFINITION OF BONUS SHARES

1. Occasionally, in the case of a successful company, large reserves may have been accumulated out of profits as a result of the directors’ policy not to distribute the whole of the profits, but to lay aside something to enable the company to meet any unforeseen contingency that may arise in the future or to serve as working capital to cope with the increasing business. Besides, the reserve fund may have been accumulated far in excess of the present or the future needs of the company, and it would then be deemed desirable to give benefit of a part of such reserve to the existing shareholders by way of compensation for the loss of dividends which they had suffered. This desire on the part of the directors can be given effect to by a bonus to shareholders payable from out of reserve fund being proposed by the former and sanctioned by the general meeting of shareholders. However, instead of paying cash and depleting the financial resources of the company, such bonus may be satisfied by the issue of additional shares considered as fully or partly paid up. Thus, the company is enabled to capitalize a part of its reserves by issuing bonus shares in lieu of cash.

The capitalizing of reserves by the above method benefits the company inasmuch as the past accumulated profits are permanently retained in the business. Further, the share capital is, thus, adjusted to a figure more on a level with the actual capital employed in the undertaking. Where the profits and the consequent dividends are large in comparison with the company’s paid-up capital, the inference of profiteering is very strong; but where the paid-up capital is increased by the issue of bonus shares, although the profits will remain round about the previous level, the percentage of dividend must necessarily be reduced, and yet the actual return to the individual shareholder will remain the same. The shareholders have no occasion to be dissatisfied with such a procedure, as they can easily realize their bonus shares, if they so wish to. Besides, the fact that the company was enabled to issue bonus shares out of the accumulated reserves will tend to bring up the market value of those shares at a premium. While examining taxation of any transaction, normally, a two-stepped approach is adopted. The first step is to examine whether the transaction is giving rise to 'income' under the applicable tax laws and whether that income is liable to taxation in that particular jurisdiction. If the answer to these questions is yes, then the income needs to be characterized in accordance with the tax law, as there may be differences in approach of taxing different types of income. The second step concerns valuation/quantification of the transaction under consideration. If the parties to the transaction are associated enterprises, then the quantification of income has to be in accordance with the transfer pricing regulations. Recently, this basic approach of taxation has been a subject matter of intense discussion in India, for the reason that the tax department took a position that shares infused at a price lower than the arm's length price (as determined by the tax department), would give rise to income taxable in India.

The prime contention of the tax department is that the difference between the arm's length price of shares (so determined) and the price at which shares were issued by an Indian company to the associated enterprise (AE), is income liable to taxation in India. In some cases, the said shortfall (i.e. difference between the issue price and the arm's length price so determined) was also considered as an amount outstanding with the AE i.e. loan recoverable from the AE, requiring additional payment of interest to the Indian company.

Expectedly, the additions made by the tax authorities has drawn loud protest from the business community, particularly foreign investors interested in investing in India. It is argued that infusion of shares is an investment and cannot be held to be income neither as per international understanding, nor as per the Indian taxation law. This issue is yet to be decided by an Income Tax Appellate Tribunal (ITAT) or higher judicial bodies. In this Article, the authors have analyzed various aspects of this controversy.

1. ISSUE BEFORE THE BOMBAY HIGH COURT

The question of taxability of share infusion was recently raised before the Bombay High Court in the case of Vodafone India Services Private Limited (VISPL) by way of a Writ Petition1. The brief facts of the case were that, VISPL, a wholly owned subsidiary of Vodafone Tele Services (India) Holdings Limited, Mauritius, during Financial Year 2008-09, issued 2,89,224 equity shares to the latter. The price charged per share was INR 8,601 (INR 10 being the face value plus a premium of INR 8,591per share), which was determined in accordance with the method prescribed by the Capital Issues Control Act, 1947. The total consideration for this issue of shares thus recorded in the books of account of VISPL was INR 2,463.8 Million.

This transaction of issue of shares was disclosed to the tax department by VISPL in the Accountants Report (i.e. Form No. 3CEB) by way of a note, which stated that issue of shares having no bearing on the income is being reported only as a matter of abundant caution.

During the course of audit proceedings, the Assessing Officer (AO) referred the determination of arm's length price of the aforesaid transaction to the Transfer Pricing Officer (TPO). The TPO opined that the valuation of shares needs to be carried out on Net Asset Value basis, after considering the transfer pricing adjustments in preceding years.

Accordingly, the TPO computed the arm's length price of each share at INR 53,775, resulting in shortfall of INR 13,089.1 Million appurtenant to the issue price of shares. This shortfall was also treated as a deemed loan given by VISPL to Vodafone Tele Services (India) Holdings Limited, Mauritius and hence a notional interest @ 13.50% per annum was charged additionally.

Consequently, the TPO made a total transfer pricing adjustment of INR 13,970 Million (INR 13,089 Million on account of shortfall in issue price, plus an interest of INR881 Million). The AO, based on the order of the TPO, passed a draft assessment order, proposing to add INR 13,970 Million to the total income of VISPL.

This addition proposed by the AO, was challenged by VISPL before the Bombay High Court by way of a Writ Petition. The objections in the Writ Petition were related only to the issue of jurisdiction/applicability of Chapter X (i.e. the Indian Transfer Pricing Regulations) on issue of share capital. The questions put forth by VISPL in the Writ Petition were as follows:

1.

Whether the existence of a potentially taxable income or an expenditure (capital or revenue) that impacts computation of taxable income is a sine qua non for the invocation of jurisdiction under Chapter X?

2.

Whether Chapter X confers the jurisdiction to:

The ruling reinforces the fundamental principles for interpretation of fiscal statutes which ought to be read practically by resolving the ambiguities of legal construction, in favour of the tax payers. Azadi Bachao Andolan [2003] 263 ITR 706/ 132 Taxman 373 (SC) The Apex Court clearly held that legitimate tax planning cannot be challenged merely on the basis of assumed underlying intentions of tax evasion. The Court, commenting on the McDowell’s decision whilst referring to various other judgments, agreed that not every action or inaction on the part of the taxpayer, which results in reduction of tax liability, must be viewed with suspicion. Taxpayers are free to carry out any trade/activity or plan their affairs with circumspection, within the framework of law, unless the same falls in the category of a colourable device without substance. So principally, the right of taxpayer to ‘plan’ his transactions to mitigate tax liability cannot be questioned only because it is ‘tax advantage’ provided ‘economic substance’ is demonstrated in the same. However, if the motive of the tax avoidance is seen to outweigh the purpose of the transaction evidenced and evaluated with factual aspects, the Courts in India more likely than not will tread the path of assuming that ‘substance over form’ should prevail and the transaction should be challenged.

Conclusion

6. In the case of Walfort Share & Stock Brokers (P.) Ltd. (supra ), the Supreme Court of India has reiterated that tax planning is perfectly valid, since it is within the four corners of law. However, the revenue department has time and again attemp-ted to tax legally permissible transactions as tax avoidance mechanism. The Government of India is in the process to introduce the Direct Taxes Code. The Direct Taxes Code proposes to introduce a General Anti Avoidance Rule (‘GAAR’), which could empower tax authorities to re-characterize a transaction entered into by a taxpayer and the income therefrom. The GAAR provisions are proposed to override the other provisions of the DTC. Currently tax planning is considered as legal in light of the Azadi Bachao Andolan’s case (supra). However, it remains to be seen how GAAR would impact tax planning by taxpayers, including in cases of dividend stripping.

Section 56(2)(viib) of the Act is another provision which deals with issue of shares. The purpose of introducing this provision was explained in the Memorandum explaining the Finance Bill as follows:

'Section 56(2) provides for the specific category of incomes that shall be chargeable to income-tax under the head Income from other sources.

It is proposed to insert a new clause in section 56(2). The new clause will apply where a company, not being a company in which the public are substantially interested, receives, in any previous year, from any person being a resident, any consideration for issue of shares. In such a case if the consideration received for issue of shares exceeds the face value of such shares, the aggregate consideration received for such shares as exceeds the fair market value of the shares shall be chargeable to Income-tax under the head "Income from other sources. However, this provision shall not apply where the consideration for issue of shares is received by a venture capital undertaking from a venture capital company or a venture capital fund.'

In summary, the object of section 56(2)(viib) of the Act is to tax the excess premium received by a company on account of issue of shares. This provision seeks to cover situations, where a company receives from a 'resident' any consideration in excess of the fair market value of shares. Obviously, this will not be applicable to the situation where shares are issued by an Indian company to a non-resident at a price lower than fair market value.

2. IS SHARE INFUSION AN 'INTERNATIONAL TRANSACTION'?

Section 922 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 (the Act) requires that any income, allowance for any expenses (including allocations) and allowance for any interest, arising out of international transactions should be computed having regard to the arm's length price.

The question is whether share infusion falls within the definition of the term 'international transaction' under section 92B of the Act. It may be mentioned that the term 'international transaction' as originally defined covered a wide gamut of transactions (including transactions having a bearing on assets) entered into between two associated enterprises (out of which, at least one should be a non-resident). By the Finance Act, 2010, an explanation was added to further extend the scope of this term. This extended definition was made retrospectively effective from the day the Indian Transfer Pricing Regulations were introduced i.e. April 1, 2001.

This extended definition includes a clause, which reads as follows:

'(e) a transaction of business restructuring or reorganisation, entered into by an enterprise with an associated enterprise, irrespective of the fact that it has bearing on the profit, income, losses or assets of such enterprises at the time of the transaction or at any future date'

The term 'business restructuring' or 'reorganisation' have not been defined in the Act and hence prone to a wider interpretation. It is possible that the tax department may seek to infer that these terms cover any change in shareholding, including share infusion. Even without resorting to the extension of the definition, a view is possible that 'share' is a form of an 'assets' and hence, any change in the value of shares, would impact the assets of a taxpayer. Therefore, it can be said that share infusion stands covered by the original definition of the term international transaction.

It requires that income, expense and interest in relation to an international transaction should be computed having regard to the arm's length price. Thus, the primary question is: whether infusion of share capital can be regarded as income?

Doctrine of Unjust Enrichment

8. The resolution plan cannot provide for extinguishment of the liability of the corporate debtor in respect of amounts deducted or collected as fiduciary of the statutory authorities. One example is tax deducted at source; other common example is indirect tax.

Such an amount cannot be said to be forming a part of the estate of the corporate debtor. The resolution applicant who submits resolution plan intends to acquire the corporate debtor at the best (read, lowest) possible price. However, extinguishment of amounts as aforesaid will lead to what is commonly referred to as "unjust enrichment" of the shareholders of the acquirer, that too at the cost of the persons who suffered taxes.

9. As is evident from the discussion so far, plans or schemes approved under statutes have been given overriding effect, so as to be called "a statutory magic"; however, a pre-condition is that the same shall "legitimately" bind those who dissented to the scheme/plan. A statutory creditor who was not even provided an opportunity to be there in the meeting of creditors for approval and rejection of the resolution plan cannot be excluded in entirety and denied the right to be repaid. A plan framed under one statute cannot prevail over another statute.It may also be noted here that the conflict here is between two classes of creditors. A class of creditors cannot extinguish the rights of other class of creditors.

Therefore, the following may be concluded as regards statutory dues –

(i)

Statutory dues cannot be reduced or extinguished without seeking consent of the concerned authority. The authority shall be given a right to object to the provisions of the resolution plan affecting its right to receive statutory dues. It is opined that a public notice shall be issued by the resolution applicant asking for objections against the resolution plan.

(ii)

The above holds true even if statutory dues are deferred or scheduled to paid in tranches.

(iii)

The resolution plan shall, at bare minimum, provide for payment of liquidation value due towards statutory dues. The plan cannot go beyond such minimum level. See "Guide to Liquidation Value under the Insolvency Code"7, by Sikha Bansal.

(iv)

In case of statutory arrears, the retention of which leads to unjust enrichment of the corporate debtor, waiver/extinguishment is not possible.

The administrators of the law in their usual fashion adopted a harsh and adverse interpretation so as to tax even genuine receipts without consideration and extort taxes thereon.

The confusion has been even more confounded on cross-border receipts without consideration or at less than fair market value due to several factors like reorganizations and restructurings due to the warp and weft of DTAA provisions, the regular income-tax provisions and the special transfer pricing provisions (TPP) embodied in sections 92 to 92F (and relevant rules) of the Domestic Income-tax Act. A further complication in the matter is that most double taxation treaties are silent on the issue of gifts and club them with other income, which is generally taxed in either the source or residence country.

This amendment in section 56(2)(viia) of the Act seeks to tax shares received by a firm or company in which the ‘public are not substantially interested’ as per section 2(18) of the Act. This amendment takes effect from June 1, 2010 and throws up the following issues from a cross-border tax perspective:

u How far would deeming provisions introduced in the assessment year 2010-11 for receipt of shares by an unlisted company in section 56(2)(viia) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 apply in cases of such cross-border receipts of securities deemed as ‘gifts’?

u What would be the course of action when the receipt is classified in a different manner in the two jurisdictions of the donor and receiver?

u What is the remedy when the residential status of the receiver is different under the two jurisdictions (e.g. US law takes the situs of the shareholder as residential jurisdiction while Indian law treats the situs of incorporation of the company as residential jurisdictions)?

u Does the market value of a gift (essentially without consideration) have to be tested on the anvil of ‘arms length price’ to determine its taxability?

u Whether withholding tax would apply on such receipts?

These are only some of the issues in this new and nascent area of the law and the only thing that may be said with certainty is that there will be many more uncertainties as the law meanders through the banks of judicial decisions.

Interplay with newly introduced section 56(2)(viia ) with DTAA and TPP

2. An important point to note in this context is that the TPP are procedural and methodology driven (best method, comparisons, tested party, FAR analysis) while the provisions embodied under section 56(1)(viia) are ‘consideration driven’ (i.e., take the fair market value as the starting point of the computation of income). Another difference to note is that the TPP generally apply to business income while the section 56 provisions apply to income from other sources.

Thus, such a company receiving shares (by any method except for the exempted methods laid out in Act) will be taxed on the difference between the consideration and the ‘fair market value’ of the shares. Such difference will be taxed under the head ‘income from other sources’. It is worth noting that the Finance Minister in his budget speech used the term ‘transfer of shares’ while the amendment in the Finance Act, 2010 uses the term ‘receives’, thereby lending credence to the old adage that ‘there is many a slip bewixt the cup and the lip’. This amendment applies to residents and non-residents alike.

This intended amendment creates conflict and confusion particularly in the area of cross-border taxation in the following areas :

u The TPP will now be made applicable to such receipt of shares, even on a foreign business reorganization or bankruptcy proceedings since the difference between consideration (even though not ascertainable) and fair market value will be taxable. u If a company receives shares and is taxed under the head ’Income from other sources’, tax credits under the corresponding head of the relevant treaty which India has with the home jurisdiction of such company may not be easily availed of.

u Valuation in relation to cross-border receipts is an important issue and brings one back to the bogey of ‘arms length’ and, thus, virtually guaranteeing a backdoor application of the TPP.

Issuing bonus shares out of revaluation reserve 6.1 Existing prohibition - Section M of the SEBI Guidelines for Disclosure and Investor Protection does not allow issue of bonus shares out of the Revaluation reserve. This prohibition is applicable to listed companies. The Department of Company Affairs vide its Circular No. 9/94 (Circular Letter No. 17/32/93 - CL V dated September 6,1994) has also prohibited issue of bonus shares out of revaluation reserve by the existing private/ closely-held and unlisted companies.

The Guidance note on availability of revaluation reserve for issue of bonus shares issued by the ICAI (Published in November 1994 issue of the Chartered Accountant) argues that the excess of the revalued amount over the net book value of fixed assets, which is credited to revaluation reserve, is created as a result of book adjustment only. The revaluation reserve does not result from an arm's length transaction; it represents an expert's perception of value. The revaluation reserve thus does not represent realised gain.

The ICAI Guidance Note also states that share capital represents money or money's worth received from the owners and capitalisation of earned profits or other gains arising out of arm's length transactions. It is a cardinal principle that only such profits as are earned or the relevant capital receipts (e.g. share premium) as are realised, can be capitalised.

6.2 Expert's value perception - So long as the expert's perception of the fair value of a fixed asset is judicious, there is nothing wrong in depending on such valuation, in case the upper limit of revaluation is restricted to the net recoverable amount. Substitution of historical cost becomes necessary when it materially differs from the fair value of the fixed assets. A going concern may not think of disposing of a particular asset, still the increase in value of the asset, although unrealised, cannot be denied. Since the revaluation reserve forms part of the shareholders' funds, it should be treated as a free reserve.

6.3 Arm's length transactions and business income -The concept of arm's length relationship is altogether irrelevant in this context. The reported net profit of an entity is not necessarily the result of arm's length transactions. Also it is not necessary for the purpose of a bonus issue to consider to what extent the accumulated surplus of the entity has resulted from arm's length transactions.

6.4 Unrealised gain - Of course, the revaluation reserve represents unrealised gain. But it represents real gain and cannot be treated as a fictitious gain. Accordingly, the shareholders should not be denied the right to utilise any such real gain in the manner they want. It is not unknown to the shareholders that such a bonus issue, if any, results from unrealised gain.

6.5 Accounting effect of bonus issue - Presently, many companies take a transfer from the revaluation reserve to the extent of additional depreciation. To that extent profit is inflated every year and the revaluation reserve is converted into the so called 'earned profit'. It is just a matter of time to convert revaluation reserve into 'earned profit' and as soon as the conversion is complete there is no bar on utilising such 'earned profit' for issuing bonus shares.

In case the revaluation reserve is utilised for a bonus issue, the company would have no choice but to charge additional depreciation out of profit.

6.6 Corporate freedom - One of the basic tenets of economic liberalisation is reduction/elimination of bureaucratic interference on the activities of private entrepreneurs. Corporate management should be given freedom to adopt a suitable financial management policy. A bonus issue out of the revaluation reserve will not generally be supported by increase in the earning capacity. However, the management will not find difficulty in maintaining the dividend rate in real terms. A decline in post-equity pricewill have no effect in real terms, since this book adjustment has no effect on the earnings of the entity.

Introduction:

Reduction of share capital is a process by which a company decreases it's issued, subscribed, or paid-up share capital. This can be undertaken for various purposes, including restructuring, correcting an overcapitalized balance sheet, or returning excess funds to shareholders. Under the Companies Act, 2013, the reduction of share capital requires the approval of the National Company Law Tribunal (NCLT) as per the provisions of the mentioned in the Act.

Legal Framework:

The reduction of share capital is governed by Section 66 of the Companies Act, 2013 read with The National Company Law Tribunal (Procedure for reduction of share capital of Company) Rules, 2016 which lays down the procedures, requirements, and conditions for reducing share capital.

Reasons for Reduction of Share Capital:

Reduction of share capital can be carried out for various reasons, including but not limited to:

1. Return of Excess Paid-up Capital:

When the company has surplus paid-up capital that is not being utilized, it can be returned to shareholders. This is beneficial as dividends are paid on paid-up capital, and retaining unnecessary capital increases the company's financial burden.

2. Cancellation of Uncalled Share Capital:

Share capital that has been issued but not called for payment can be cancelled to streamline the company's capital structure and reflect actual capital requirements. For example, partly paid shares can be made fully paid without calling for balance call money and accordingly reducing the face value of shares.

3. Cancellation of Unpaid Share Capital:

The unpaid portion of the share capital that shareholders are yet to pay can be cancelled to reduce liabilities and simplify financial accounts.

4. Adjustment for Capital Lost or Diminished:

When the company's assets lose value (reflected as a reduction in book value), the company can adjust its share capital by returning the reduced amount to shareholders. This aligns the share capital with the actual value of the company's assets.

Procedure for Reduction of Share Capital:

Board Meeting & Special Resolution

Board Approval: The Company's Board of Directors must approve the proposal to reduce share capital.

Special Resolution: A special resolution (approved by at least 75% of shareholders) must be passed at a general meeting to approve the reduction. The resolution should specify the method and extent of the reduction.

Filing of Application for Reduction of Share Capital with NCLT:

Form and Fee:

An application to the Tribunal for confirming a reduction of share capital must be made in Form RSC-1, along with the applicable fee as prescribed in the fee schedule i.e., Rs. 5000/-

Accompanying Documents:

The application should be accompanied by the following documents:

Special resolution copy.

Memorandum of association and articles of association.

List of Creditors: A list, certified by the Managing Director (or two directors), showing creditor details (name, address, amounts owed), dated no more than 15 days before filing.

Auditor's Certificate on Creditor List: A certificate from the company's auditor verifying the accuracy of the creditor list.

No Arrears Declaration: A certificate from the auditor and a director's declaration confirming that the company has no pending deposits or interest arrears.

Accounting Treatment Compliance: A certificate from the auditor confirming that the proposed accounting treatment for share capital reduction complies with Section 133 of the Companies Act or relevant provisions.

Issuance of Notices and Directions by NCLT for Reduction of Share Capital:

Notice by Tribunal:

Within 15 days of receiving the application (Form RSC-1), the Tribunal will issue notices or direct that notice to be given in:

Form RSC-2: To the Central Government and Registrar of Companies (RoC) in all cases.

Form RSC-2: To SEBI, if the company is listed.

And Direct the Company to send Notices to each creditor (as per the submitted list) must be within 7 days of the Tribunal's direction in form Form RSC-3. The notice will include:

Details of the proposed reduction of share capital including an amount.

The amount owed to the creditor or contingent claim, if any.

A deadline for sending objections.

Public Notice:

The Tribunal will direct the company to publish a notice in Form RSC-4 within 7 days from the directions given by the tribunal in:

A widely circulated English newspaper.

A widely circulated vernacular newspaper in the state of the registered office.

The company's website (if applicable).

The notice will invite creditor objections and provide hearing details.

The notice must mention:

The amount of share capital reduction.

Locations where the creditor list can be inspected.

The deadline (fixed by the Tribunal) for submitting objections.

3.1 The Shell controversy - The controversy fundamentally revolves around taxation on the undervaluation of shares issued by Shell India to its overseas group entity, more specifically under the extant Indian TP regulations and seeks to tax Shell India on alleged issuance of shares at a discounted rate. Shell India, having diversified businesses in India, was issued with TP notices from the tax authority alleging that the Company had undervalued its shares while raising money from the Shell group entity during the financial year 2008-09. Shell India issued 870 million equity shares at INR 10 each (which was the par value) to Shell Gas BV. During TP audit, the TPO asked Shell India to justify the pricing of the equity shares issued to Shell Gas BV. In response, Shell India justified the price of the equity shares based on discounted cash flow ("DCF"), as provided under the Indian foreign exchange regulations and the value per share was determined at INR 6.93.

The TPO re-computed the price per share, using DCF method, but at INR 183.44 and held that Shell India had transferred its equity shares to its overseas group entity at a price below their fair market value. The difference in valuation so arrived by TPO was branded as a 'loan' advanced by Shell India to its overseas group entity. While doing so, the TPO also alleged that Shell India ought to have charged interest on the same, thereby resulting in an overall adjustment to the tune of INR 152bn (equivalent to USD 2.8bn). Consequently, the TPO imposed tax on the short receipt of share capital as well as a notional return calculated on such short receipt.

To challenge the constitutional, jurisdictional, legality, validity and judicial propriety of the TP order, Shell India filed a writ petition before the Hon'ble Bombay High Court. In its grounds of appeal, Shell India mentioned that the action of the tax authority was based on misrepresentation of the fact and hence, was confiscatory in nature. It further stated that the adjustment on account of re-characterization of transaction was not permitted in Indian TP regulations and such an action showed arbitrariness and was unfair besides being illegal and had disregarded the fact that as per the corporate and regulatory framework and laws, the alleged shortfall (i.e., so called share premium) could never be received by Shell India as the shares were issued at par value.

This matter is yet to be adjudicated by the Hon'ble High Court and would not be apt to comment on the righteousness of the case or any facts thereto.

9. Exemption to be given on transfer of shares held as stock-in-trade in the scheme of amalgamation

As per Section 70(1)(f) of the ITA 2025 [Corresponds to Section 47(vii) of the ITA 1961], any transfer of a capital asset, such as shares held by a shareholder in the amalgamating company (transferor), under a scheme of amalgamation is not regarded as a transfer, provided the specified conditions are satisfied. Thus, no tax implication arises in the hands of the shareholder at the time of allotment of shares of the amalgamated company (transferee) in lieu of shares held as a capital asset in the amalgamating company (transferor).

The above exemption is available only when the shareholders hold the shares as capital assets. If such shares are held as stock-in-trade, no exemption is provided, and profits and gains arising from the transfer of shares will be chargeable to tax under the head 'profits and gains from business and profession'.

This differential tax treatment, based solely on the nature of the investment made by shareholders, is arbitrary. Thus, it is recommended that the government bring parity and amend Section 70(1)(f) to extend the exemption to shares held as stock-in-trade.

Need of review of Supreme Court's decision 7. It is, therefore, humbly urged that the Supreme Court may review its judgment in Vijaya Bank Ltd.'s case (supra) in the light of the accounting authorities cited and discussed above. The Accounting Standard-13 of the ICAI has tremendous force when it says that interest/dividend relatable to the pre-acqitisition period must not be viewed as income but has recovery of cost and, therefore, should be viewed as a capital receipt. And capital receipts are not taxable for the simple reason that they do not constitute income. The Supreme Court rightly held where a bank purchased securities at a price with reference to their actual value as well as the interest accrued thereon till the date of purchase, the entire price paid would be in the nature of capital outlay. As a corollary, it follows that when this cost is recovered by way of interest, such recovery, far from being income, is an abatement against the cost originally incurred and should be reduced from the cost of purchase. It is this aspect urged in this article and buttressed by the accounting authorities that craves for reconsideration by the Supreme Court. The Supreme Court held the assessee (Vijaya Bank) to be liable for the entire interest including for the broken period, i.e., the pre-acquisition period. It is submitted that this is not correct. The broken period interest, it is reiterated, is a capital receipt and should be rightly reduced from the cost of securities. This accounting treatment is nothing new. Those familiar with preparing consolidated accounts of the holding company with the accounts of its subsidiary, would know that the proportionate part of pre-acquisition profits of the subsidiary relatable to the holding company's holding in the subsidiary is always reduced from the cost of investment and is never shown as part of reserves and surplus. This analogy should be sufficient to remove the mental block or the mind-set of those who are unable to come round to the view-point that broken period interest is a capital receipt.

Implications for shares

8. The Accounting Standard-13 applies to shares as much as it does to interest-bearing securities. In case of shares, the treatment propounded is likely to be even less palatable to tax administration because it will have the effect of converting dividend into capital gains, and if the holding period is more than 12 months, the investor is going to get away with a host of benefits that come with long-term capital gains - to be specific, a flat rate of 20 per cent tax irrespective of the quantum of gains and section 54F benefit which exempts long-term capital gains from tax if they are ploughed back in a residential house.

Implications for stock-in-trade

9. A dealer in securities is not going to be affected one way or the other, whether he is required to follow the law laid down by the Supreme Court in Vijaya Bank Ltd.'s case (supra) or the one propounded by the accounting standards and endorsed in this article. For, in any case, the entire transaction is revenue in nature. The cost of interest-bearing securities is going to be debited to the profit and loss account and the carrying amount at the end of the financial year, cost or market value, whichever is less, is going to be credited to such account. In the event, interest relating to the broken-period is not an issue at all in his case. It must be made clear that in Vijaya Bank Ltd. 's case (supra), the Supreme Court did not say that in case of a bank purchase of interest-bearing securities will invariably constitute investments. Nor did it say that they will invariably constitute stock-in-trade. This classification will, therefore, be governed by the RBI norms and other accounting considerations which are outside the scope of this article. What is relevant is the Supreme Court's verdict in Vijaya Bank Ltd.'s case (supra) has grave portents for investors.

Private Limited Companies and Unlisted Public Companies can issue bonus shares out of revaluation reserve

Issuance of bonus shares out of revaluation reserve by private Ltd. companies and unlisted public companies has always been a controversial matter. Although such practice is judicially recognized in England, it was not been quite so in India, and a lot of disputes have arisen in this context. But with Apex Court’s decision in the case of Bhagwati Developers v. Pearless General Finance & Investment Co. [2005] 62 SCL 574, wherein it has been held that unlisted companies can issue bonus shares out of revaluation reserve, the matter has come to rest. INTRODUCTION - BONUS SHARES

1. All the profits earned by the company are normally not distributed as dividend to the shareholders. A part of the earned profit is ploughed back in the business. It is transferred to reserves and/or carried over as a surplus or credit balance in the profit and loss account. This profit remains with the company, and is used in the business as an additional working capital. It may happen that the share capital may remain small, but profits would go on increasing. The reserves will also increase. In such a case, the profit and dividend would appear unduly large in comparison to the share capital, though in fact the working funds may be much larger than the share capital. Under such circumstances, the company may opt to issue bonus shares. By issuing bonus shares, a part of the reserves and the balance in the profit and loss account are capitalized. They are converted into share capital. These shares are, therefore, not issued for cash. Bonus shares are generally defined as additional shares of a company’s share capital distributed to its shareholders without their having to pay for them. Bonus shares are also known as scrip dividend.

The question before the AAR is whether such transfer of indirect control would constitute a gain in the hands of the private equity player and, hence, application of the arms length provisions to determine the costs of acquisition.

The AAR in this case also ruled that since the shares are transferred indirectly and also as part of a package where it is argued that the liabilities are more than the assets, no direct cost could be attributable to them. Deemed short-fall in receipt of share premium couldn't be charged to tax: High Court

PRADEEP S. SHAH

CA

INTRODUCTION

1. In Vodafone India Services (P.) Ltd. v. Union of India [2014] 50 taxmann.com 300 (Bom.) case, Tax Department so to say innovated 'income' by applying Transfer pricing provisions [Chapter X ('the Chapter' or 'Chapter X') of the Income tax Act, 1961 ("the Act")] to the issue of shares by a wholly owned subsidiary to the holding company, inter alia, by treating the alleged shortfall in the premium as an income.

The mystery was unfolded by the High Court through simple application of the basic principles of interpretation to the simple facts.

The Court decided the issue while exercising its writ jurisdiction and, obviously, it did not comment on the facts. However, it has set out the facts (para 6 of the Order) in details, to appreciate the issue.

FACTS OF THE VODAFONE'S CASE

2. It would be quite interesting to note the manner in which the facts (set out broadly) were considered by the Department to invoke Chapter X:

Vodafone India Services (P.) Ltd. 'the company' (issuing shares at a premium) was a wholly owned subsidiary of a foreign company.

It issued shares to the holding company at certain premium (apparently, to comply with the requirements stipulated under applicable law).

Tax Department felt that the provisions of Chapter X would apply. For that purpose:

Issue of shares was treated as an International transaction;

Issue price was tested;

Net asset based valuation method was applied; and

Arm's length price or ALP was sought to be derived.

The authorities (AO and/or TPO and/or DRP)1 worked out the value of the shares based on net assets value. While doing that, "transfer pricing adjustments" made in the earlier years were added to the net assets by treating them as "off balance sheet" items and, accordingly, the value of share was worked out at a substantially higher amount.

The difference considered or alleged as shortfall in the premium (''the Shortfall") was treated as an income of the subsidiary; though premium itself was not considered as income.

Further, the shortfall was deemed as a loan by subsidiary to the holding company and interest which could have been earned on such deemed loan was also treated as income.

The case was defended by Solicitor General on a different ground before the High Court and it was treated as a 'benefit' to the holding company resulting in cost to the subsidiary.

3. FICTION VIS-À-VIS FACTS OF VODAFONE'S CASE

The premium2 amount itself was not considered as income. Only the Shortfall, by applying the so-called ALP, was treated as an income.

Net asset value usually is determined on the basis of the assets/liabilities reflected in the audited financial statements. Even the Act, although for a different purpose, provides for determination of net asset value having regard to the balance sheet as at specified date, without any adjustment of any 'off-balance-sheet' items.

However, in this case the adjustments were considered of 'off-balance-sheet' items and were added to the net asset value to determine the shortfall, which should have been charged as premium for the issue of shares. Apparently, it was not examined whether such notional income was represented by an asset or not?

Chapter X permits valuation of income at ALP. However, it does not provide for adjustment thereof in the books of account or financial statements or otherwise for any other purpose whatsoever. To put it differently, the Chapter authorises the adoption of ALP only for the limited purpose of determining taxable income arising from an international transaction.

The shortfall, if any, was based on valuation of the company as a whole. Now, that value for the holding company, whatever might have been the number of shares and whether these were issued at a premium or at par would have remained the same.

The alternate ground taken treated the shortfall as benefit and, in turn, cost. Thus, factually, different positions were adopted by the authorities and by the authority representing them before the High Court.

While considering and arguing the alternate ground, apparently, a material fact was missed. How, where, to whom and what was the benefit, if any? It would dependent on the differential, if any. When the entire value belonged to the holding company, before or after the issue of shares, where was the difference or what was the benefit? The holder of all the shares; the assets; and the value, as such, did not change. If so, the benefit would not arise. The entire value of the company (considered for determining the Shortfall) before and after the fresh issue always belonged to the holding company.

5. ARGUMENTS BEFORE THE HIGH COURT 6. HIGH COURT'S VERDICT

The Bombay High Court held that on the facts of the present case, issue of shares at a premium by VISL to its non-resident AE does not give rise to any income from an admitted international transaction and thus, Indian Transfer Pricing provisions are not applicable for the following reasons:

Income arising from an international transaction is a pre-condition for application of Transfer Pricing provisions. Further, the Act defines the term income in an inclusive manner. Income, in its normal meaning, will not include capital receipts unless specifically provided. The amounts received on issue of share capital including the premium are on capital account. In this case, what is being sought to be taxed is capital forgone i.e. not received from a non-resident in the form of short premium. Therefore, absent express legislation, an amount received, accrued or arising on capital account transactions cannot be subjected to tax as income.

The High Court further held that the transaction on capital account or on account of restructuring would become taxable to the extent it impacts income i.e., under-reporting of interest received/over reporting of interest paid or claiming of depreciation. It is that income (and not the capital receipt) which is to be determined having regard to the ALP under the Transfer Pricing provisions.

The Transfer Pricing provisions are brought into statute books to ensure that the transaction is taxed only on the income computed as per the ALP of the transaction and to ensure that there is no manipulation of prices/consideration between AEs.

In any case, the entire exercise of taxing the amounts allegedly not received as share premium fails, as no tax is charged on the amount received as share premium.

Neither the capital receipts received by VISL on issue of equity shares to its AE nor the shortfall between the alleged FMV of its equity shares and the issue price of the equity shares can be considered as income within the meaning of the expression as defined in the Act and hence not subject to Transfer Pricing provisions in India.

The reasoning that if the ALP were received, the Taxpayer would be able to invest the same and earn income, proceeds on a mere surmise/assumption and that this cannot be the basis of taxation.

The Tax Authorities relied on this section to argue that differences between the ALP and the price charged for issue of shares is the benefit conferred upon the holding company.

Relying on section 92(2) of the Act is misplaced. Section 92(2) of the Act, which deals with a situation where two or more AEs enter into an arrangement whereby they are to receive any benefit, service or facility then the allocation, apportionment or contribution of the corresponding cost or expenditure is to be determined for each AE based on ALP, is meant to cover cases of cost sharing arrangements and/or cost contribution arrangements. Section 92(2) would have no application in cases like the present one, where there is no occasion to allocate, apportion or contribute any cost and/or expenses between the Taxpayer and its AE. Ignoring words in a statute to achieve a predetermined objective is not permissible and the same would amount to re-drafting the legislation, which is beyond the jurisdiction of the Courts.

The contention of the Tax Authorities that in view of the Transfer Pricing provisions, notional income is to be taxed and real income is not relevant is unacceptable. The entire exercise of determining the ALP is only to arrive at the real income earned.

Even income arising from international transactions between AEs must satisfy the test of income per se under the Act and must find its home under one of the charging provisions. It is a re-computation exercise to be carried out only when income arises in case of an international transaction between AEs. It does not warrant recomputation of a consideration received/given on capital account except in cases of interest paid/received on loans taken/given, depreciation taken on machinery, etc. Therefore, in the absence of a charging provision to tax issue of shares at a premium to a non-resident, the occasion to invoke the computational Transfer Pricing provisions does not arise.

Further, in view of inclusion of issue of shares, by a company to another resident, at a price in excess of FMV in the definition of income under the Act, there is conscious intention of the Parliament to not tax amounts received from a non-resident for issue of shares, as it would discourage capital inflow from abroad.

7. CONCLUSION

In the backdrop of the present Government's initiative to bring in foreign investment, this decision from the Bombay High Court's is a landmark. The High Court has been rightly able to distinguish between the 'income' per se and the capital which is primarily the source to earn income. One important take away from the decision is the High Court's acknowledgement that mere reporting of an international transaction out of abundant caution would not make the same taxable if there is no income arising from such international transaction.

Annual accounts under the Companies Act 3. The Companies Act, 1956 ('the Act') imposes a duty (a) on the auditors to audit the accounts and to make a report thereon to the shareholders, and (b) on the Board of directors of the company to lay the annual accounts duly audited before get them adopted by the shareholders and at an annual general meeting (A.G.M.).

Section 211 of the Act dealing with the form and contents of the balance-sheet and profits and loss account provides that the balance-sheet and the profit and loss account shall give a true and fair view of the state of affairs of the company at the end of the financial year and of the profit or loss of the company for the financial year. The true and fair view contemplates that the reasonable expectations of readers of accounts are duly met. Accounting standards create a prima facie presumption that accounts which do not comply with them are not true and fair. Financial statements should not give any misleading impression or picture. Non-compliance with the provisions of the said section is an offence punishable under it. Thus, the balance-sheet and the profit and loss account, once they are audited by the company's auditor and adopted by the shareholders at the A.G.M., are given high sanctity. Failure to give a true and fair view in respect thereof amounts to breach of trust to shareholders, creditors and others relying on these documents and leads to penal consequences as mentioned above.

Failure to make provision for tax on distributed profits

4. It is noticed that some companies, not being fully conversant with the provisions of section 115-O and its effect, fail to make any provision for tax on distributed profits in their annual accounts for the Financial year 1996-97. The department of Company Affairs (the department) has ex-pressed the view that failure to make provision for taxation and proposed dividends would not disclose true and fair view of the state of affairs of the Company-Department's Letter No. 3/124/75-CL-VI dated July9, 1975. Accounts placed before the shareholders without making any provision for tax as aforesaid cannot be said to give a true and fair view of the state of affairs or profit (or loss) of the company for the said year as required by section 211, and this would attract the penalty as mentioned in the said section. Ways and means will have to be found out to overcome the difficulty which have arisen in the matter.

Revision of annual accounts - When permissible

5. The Act does not contain any provision regarding the reopening and revision of the annual accounts. The working group on the Companies Act has not also made any suggestion on the subject.

The department as well as the Institute of Chartered Accountants of India (ICAI), the professional body dealing with chartered accountants, has consistently expressed the view that it is open to the Board of directors of a company to revise the annual accounts and to re-submit the same to the auditor for his report thereon, so long as the original accounts have not been placed before and adopted by the shareholders at the A.G.M. Auditor's report on the revised accounts will be in substitution of his earlier report on the original accounts.

The department has also expressed the view that a company cannot reopen and revise its accounts after their adoption at the A.G.M. ICAI has also 'decided that the re-opening or rectification of accounts after they have been adopted at the annual general meeting should not be permitted under any circumstances'. In other words, once the accounts are adopted at the A.G.M. they are treated as sacrosanct and unalterable in any case. It is considered that there seems to be no warrant to take such a rigid view of the matter.

Department's clarification

6. In 1987 in partial modification of its aforesaid view the Department clarified that a company could re-open and revise its accounts even after their adoption in the annual general meeting in order to comply with technical requirements of taxation laws [Department's letter to ICAI dated August 19, 1987]. In such an event the revised annual accounts would be required to be adopted at the subsequent A.G.M. and thereafter filed with the Registrar of Companies as required by the Companies Act.

Probably the query raised by the department related to technical requirements of taxation laws and, hence, the department expressed the view in the matter as aforesaid. There seems to be no justification to take such a restricted view that a company can revise and re-open its accounts only for the limited purpose aforesaid. It is considered that re-opening and revision of accounts is permissible in all cases where directors discover that accounts presented by them are defective and they should be corrected. Appropriate rules or regulations made by the department on the subject would clarify the position in the matter.

(a) The element names in this para have been aligned with the nomenclature used in the Revised Schedule VI.

(b) All figures for the computation of Value Addition and Distribution of Earnings would flow from the audited Profit & Loss Account of the company.

(c) It is advisable to prepare a statement drawing the figures from the audited Profit & Loss Account showing details of individual elements. The resultant balance in the statement after consideration of all incomes, expenses, Income Tax, Dividend and transfer of undistributed profits to reserves should be equal to zero. Export Incentives - The Government of India provides various incentives & facilities to the exporter. These export incentives and facilities are as follow.

♦ Duty Drawback (DBK)

♦ Duty Entitlement Passbook Scheme (DEPB)

♦ Focus Market Scheme (FMS)

♦ Focus Product Scheme (FPS).

♦ Duty Exemption Scheme

♦ Vishesh Krishi and Gram Udyog Yojna (VKGUY)

♦ Marketing Development Assistance (MDA)

♦ Export Promotion Capital Goods Scheme

♦ Served from India Scheme

♦ Exchange earner Foreign Currency Account (EEFC Account)

(f) Cost of other bought-out inputs of company would include expenses incurred for purchase of all types of bought out services like Telephone, Postage, Printing & Stationery, Rates & Taxes, Travelling Expenses, Rent, Insurance, Freight, outside conversion charges (if not included in cost of materials and used as input for further processing), audit fees, commission charges, brokerage, discount etc. In other words, Employee Cost and Benefits, Depreciation, Borrowing Costs and other Non-Cost Items of expenses shall not be included here.

(g) Distribution of Earnings:

(i) Employees as salaries & wages, retirement benefits and others - This would include all items considered under Employee Benefits Expense in the Profit & Loss Account. Items to be considered shall include salaries, wages, contribution to provident and other funds, contribution to gratuity, other retirement benefits, medical benefits, staff welfare expenses etc.

(ii) Shareholders as Dividend - The proposed dividend, if any, payable to shareholders to be provided here. The dividend would include dividend payable on all types of shares.

(iii) Funds Retained by Company - This would mean Depreciation and Amortization Expense charged to the Profit & Loss Account during the year and undistributed surplus in Profit & Loss Account transferred to Reserves arising out of the current year profits after payment of tax and dividend.

(iv) Government as Taxes - This would include Income Tax including taxes on dividend (if borne by the company) - both current and deferred, Wealth Tax, difference between Excise Duty Paid and Excise Duty recovered.

(v) Other Distribution of Earnings would include all non-cost expenses available on the face of the Profit and Loss Account, e.g., Loss on sale of capital assets and investments, Loss/gain on forex, bad debts, stores/stocks written off, Demurrage, Fines and Penalties to statutory authorities, prior period expenses etc. Exceptional Items, if any, and Financial Costs considered in Profit & Loss Account would also be included here.

(vi) Total Distribution of Earnings - This is to be computed as sum total of [Employees as salaries & wages, retirement benefits etc. + Shareholders as Dividend + Government as Taxes + Other Distribution of Earnings]. This will be equal to "Earnings available for Distribution" computed above.

50. (1) For the purposes of section 72(5)89, the amount chargeable to income-tax as income of specified entity under section 67(10)87, shall be attributed to capital asset remaining with the specified entity in the manner provided in this rule.
