6. We are of the view that the Tribunal has taken a correct view in this matter. 7. Section 2(22) has defined 'dividend' and has given an extended meaning to the usual connotation of the word by including certain provisions in sub-clauses (b), (c), (d) and (e). This extended meaning has obviously been given to prevent any attempt by the company to distribute its reserve by profits in such a way as to not fall within the extended meaning of the word 'dividend' and thereby to avoid payment of any tax on these amounts. If this object is borne in mind, then there will be no difficulty in construing the provisions of section 2( 22)(d) . According to the sub-clause, any distribution to its shareholders by a company will be treated as dividend, if such distribution is made on the reduction of its capital to the extent to which the company possesses accumulated profits, whether such accumulated profits have been capitalised or not. The scope of the sub-clause was considered by the Supreme Court in the case of Punjab Distilling Industries Ltd. v. CIT [1965] 57 ITR 1. In this judgment Subba Rao, J. (as His Lordship then was) pointed out that the accumulated profits of a company may be utilised in the following three ways, viz., (1) for increasing the capital stock; (2) for distributing the same among the shareholders by way of dividends, and (3) for reducing the capital. Ordinarily a company reduces the capital; when there is loss or depreciation of assets. In that event there is no question of distribution of profits to the share-holders, but the shares are only devaluated. But a company may, on the pretext of reducing its capital, utilise its accumulated profits to pay back to the shareholders the whole or a part of the paid-up amounts on the shares. A shareholder, though in form, gets back the whole or a part of the capital contributed by him, in effect gets a share of the accumulated profits which, if a straight-forward course was followed, he should have received as dividend. This is a division of profits under the guise of division of capital, a distribution of profits under the colour of reduction of capital. If this was permitted, there would be evasion of super tax, the extent of the evasion depending upon the prevalence of the evil. The Legislature, presumably in the interest of the exchequer, has enlarged the definition of dividend to catch the said payments within the net of taxation. By doing so, it is really taxing the profits in the hands of the shareholders, though they are receiving the said profits under the cloak of capital. Subba Rao, J. further pointed out that distribution is a culmination of a process. Firstly, there will be a resolution by the general body of a company for reduction of capital by distribution of the accumulated profits amongst the shareholders; Secondly, the company will file an application in the Court for an order confirming the reduction of capital; Thirdly, after it is confirmed, it will be registered by the Registrar of Joint Stock Companies; Fourthly, after the registration the company will issue notices to the shareholders inviting applications for refund of the share capital; and Fifthly, on receiving the applications the company will distribute the said profits either by crediting the proportionate share capital to each of the shareholders in their respective accounts or by paying the said amounts in cash. Out of the said five steps the first four are only necessary preliminary steps, which entitle the company to distribute the accumulated profits.

HELD: It is clear on a reading of section 2(22)(d ) that, on distribution, there will be an issue of dividend only to the extent to which the company possesses accumulated profits. The purpose of this section appears to be to bring within the net of taxation payments made by distribution of assets or moneys of the company which can be taken to have come from the accumulated profits. If there was no accumulated profit in the company, the fiction could not be attracted and if the accumulated profit in the company is less than the value of the assets or moneys distributed, the fiction will be applied only to the extent of the available accumulated profit.

The profits of the year of accounting which will be taxed in the assessment year, ‘till the date of distribution’ is also included in the term 'accumulated profits' as defined in section 2(22) by virtue of the Explanation thereto. Apart from the profits of the year on the date of distribution, accumulated profits can take in accumulated profits of the years previous to the previous year as long as the profits accrued before 1-4-1933, are not taken into account. Accumulated profits, therefore, is the amount which has been accumulated from the profits arising from the past performance of the company year by year. It is of course undistributed profit which is implied by the term ‘accumulated’. From the entries in a balance-sheet, it may not be possible at a glance to find out what exactly is the accumulated profit of the company at any given time. Even assuming that the general reserves of the company may reflect accumulated profits, whether the entirety of the general reserves would be accumulated profits cannot be discerned by merely looking at the balance-sheet of the company. In the absence of specific reserves for taxation or other liabilities of the company in relation to its performance in the past years, those liabilities may have to be met from the general reserves. To take the figures from the balance-sheet, therefore, with regard to the accumulated profits would not in all cases be a correct procedure, for the quantum of the general reserves need not represent the accumulated profits. If the liabilities that accrued from year to year had been taken into account year by year and the accumulated profits had been depleted year by year by writing down the accumulated profits and only the balance carried over, the total of the accumulated profits in any given year will be less than in cases where there has been no deduction made for accrued liabilities.

HEADNOTE: Section 2(22) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 2(6A) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922], read with section 78 of the Companies Act, 1956 - Deemed dividend - Assessment year 1954-55 - Assessee-company held preference shares in 'R' company which had in year 1945 issued share at a premium and kept share premiums so received under head 'capital reserve' - Out of said capital reserve, 'R' company paid a sum as dividend to assessee - For relevant assessment year, ITO taxed said sum in hands of assessee as dividend with section 2(6A) of 1922 Act - Tribunal as well as High Court upheld ITO's order - Whether if a distribution of accumulated profits, whether capitalised or not, entails release by company to its shareholder of all or any part of its assets, it is dividend - Held, yes - Whether since it could not be said that premiums received by 'R' company were not profits within Regulation 97 of Table A of 1913 Act, ITO, therefore, rightly taxed sum received by assessee as dividend - Held, yes

FACT: The assessee-company held preference shares in 'R' company, which had in the year 1945 issued shares at a premium and kept the shares premiums so received under the head 'Capital Reserve'. Out of the above capital reserve, the 'R' company paid a sum as dividend on the said preference shares to the assessee. For the assessment year 1954-55, the ITO taxed the said sum in the hands of the assessee as dividend within section 2(6A) of 1922 Act. On appeal, the AAC held that said dividend was not taxable. On appeal, the Tribunal, however, agreed with the ITO. On reference, the High Court upheld the order of the Tribunal.

On appeal to the Supreme Court :

HELD: It is evident from the definition of the word 'dividend' in section 2(6A) of 1922 Act that if a distribution of accumulated profits, whether capitalised or not, entails the release by the company to its shareholder of all or any part of its assets, it is dividend. It was not disputed that the distribution of dividend entailed the release of the assets of 'R' company. It could not be said that the premiums received by the 'R' company were not profits within regulation 97 of Table A of 1913 Act. Previous to the enactment of section 78 of 1956 Act, and the corresponding section in the English Companies Act, it was recognised that a company could distribute premiums received on the issue of shares as dividends.

A company which had issued shares at a premium before the commencement of 1956 Act would by virtue of section 78 of 1956 Act have to open a share premium account and transfer to it the premium so received. If before the commencement of 1956 Act the company had already dealt with the premium in such a way that they had ceased to remain as an identifiable part of the company's reserves, in that event the premiums so dealt with shall be disregarded in determining the sum to be included in the share premium account. If such premiums are to be disregarded for the creation of the share premium account, it means that they fall outside the purview of section 78 of 1956 Act. It has no application to them. If this is so, it is difficult to appreciate how the assessee could utilise this section for the purpose of showing that the premiums which had already been distributed became invested with the character of capital in the hands of the distributing company. It could not be said that for the purpose of income-tax any future application of the share-premium account in one of the ways mentioned in sub-section (2) will be treated as distribution of capital. No such question arose for determination in the instant case. But it was held that section 78 of 1956 Act does not in any way change the taxability of dividends declared out of premiums on shares received by a company before the Act of 1956 came into force. If it was taxable, apart from section 78, it remains so taxable.

In the result, the High Court was justified in disallowing assessee's claim. Hence, the appeal was dismissed.

Note : The case was decided in favour of the revenue.

It is a well settled rule of construction that entries in the legislative lists cannot be read in a narrow or restricted sense: they should be construed most liberally and in their widest amplitude. The Supreme Court in a number of decisions held that the expression 'income' in entry 54 of List I of the Seventh Schedule to the Government of India Act, 1935, and the corresponding entry 82 of List I of the Seventh Schedule to the Constitution of India, shall be widely and liberally construed so as to enable a legislature to provide by law for the prevention of evasion of income-tax.

While an entry delineating a legislative field must be widely and liberally construed, there must be a reasonable nexus between the item taxed and the field so delineated. The section 2(6A)(d) of the 1922 Act, deals with the distribution by a company on the reduction of its capital to the extent to which the company possesses accumulated profits. Accumulated profits of a company may be utilised in the following 3 ways: (1) for increasing the capital stock; (2) for distributing the same among the shareholders by way of dividends; and (3) for reducing the capital. Ordinarily, a company reduces the capital when there is loss or depreciation of assets; in that event there is no question of distribution of profits to the shareholders but the shares are only devaluated. But a company may, on the pretext of reducing its capital, utilise its accumulated profits to pay back to the shareholders the whole or part of the paid up amounts on the shares. A shareholder though in form gets back the whole or a part of the capital contributed by him, in effect he gets a share of the accumulated profits which, if a straightforward course was followed, he should have received as dividend. This is a division of profits under the guise of division of capital; a distribution of profits under the colour of reduction of capital. If this was permitted, there would be evasion of super-tax, the extent of the evasion depending upon the prevalence of the evil. The legislature, presumably in the interest of the exchequer, enlarged the definition of 'dividend' to catch the said payments within the net of taxation. By doing so, it is really taxing the profits in the hands of the shareholders, though they are receiving the said profits under the cloak of capital.

Under company law the question of reducing capital is a domestic one for the decision of the majority of shareholders. The court comes into the picture only to see that the reduction is fair and equitable and that the interests of the minority and the creditors do not suffer. It may not also be concerned with the motive of the general body in resolving to reduce the capital; but the income-tax law is concerned with tax evasion. Tax can be evaded by breaking the law, or avoided in terms of the law. When there is a factual avoidance of tax, in terms of law, the legislature steps into amend the income-tax law so that it can catch such an income within the net of taxation. There is, therefore, no inconsistency between a receipt being a capital one under the company law, and by fiction being treated as taxable income under the Income-tax Act.

Therefore, as section 2(6A)(d) of the 1922 Act, embodies a law to prevent evasion of tax, it falls within the ken of entry 54 of List I of Schedule VII to the Government of India Act, 1935.

'Dividend', which was distributed was not that which one ordinarily understand by that expression, but dividend by definition. Under section 2(6A)(d) of the 1922 Act it is one of the ingredients of the definition that it shall have been distributed by a company on reduction of the capital to the extent to which the company possesses accumulated profits. Under section 16(2) of the 1922 Act such a dividend shall be deemed to be an income of the previous year in which it is paid, credited or distributed. Unless such a distribution as is mentioned in clause (d) of section 2(6A) of the 1922 Act had taken place, it would not be a dividend. If it was not so distributed, section 16(2) of the 1922 Act would not be attracted. To put it in other words, if the accumulated profits were distributed, it would satisfy not only the definition of 'dividend' in clause (d) but also would fix the year in which it would be deemed to be income. What then is the meaning of the expression 'distribution'? The dictionary meaning of the expression 'distribution' is 'to give each a share, to give to several persons'. The expression 'distribution' connotes something actual and not notional. It can be physical; it can also be constructive. One may distribute amounts between different shareholders either by crediting the amount due to each one of them in their respective accounts or by actually paying to each one of them the amount due to him.

see may have made an actual loss by subscribing to the capital of a company and may have in distribution of assets in winding-up received much less than capital subscribed; but as per law in whatever form distribution may have been made, to extent to which that distribution is out of accumulated profits, it is a dividend and attracts tax as any ordinary dividend would under income-tax law [Vidyutrai Y. Desai v. CIT [1958] 33 ITR 510 (Bom.)]. The words 'attributable to the accumulated profits of the company immediately before its liquidation' cannot be read as equivalent to 'accumulated before its liquidation' in the sense that the company had gathered the amount in its hands before the date of liquidation. The phraseology would only seem to indicate that the company had kept, collected and did not distribute, disburse or make some other similar provision in respect of the amount [CIT v. Scindia Steam Navigation Co. Ltd. [1980] 125 ITR 118 (Bom.)].

Notional distribution not covered - Notional distribution of amounts not actually available with liquidator is not covered [K. N. Narayana Iyer v. CIT [1993] 202 ITR 774 (Ker.)].

'Accumulated profits', meaning of - Refund of tax to which company was entitled before its liquidation but which was received after liquidation formed part of 'accumulated profits' of company immediately before its liquidation and, on distribution, it would be deemed to be 'dividend' [CIT v. Scindia Steam Navigation Co. Ltd. [1980] 125 ITR 118 (Bom.)].

Where, on liquidation of company, assets are sold at a price less than actual cost, then profits assessable by virtue of fiction u/s 41(2) could not form part of the 'accumulated profits' [CIT v. Urmila Ramesh [1998] 96 Taxman 533 (SC)].

DISTRIBUTION ON REDUCTION OF COMPANY'S SHARE CAPITAL [SECTION 2(22)(d)]

Constitutional validity - Provision is constitutionally valid [Punjab Distilling Industries Ltd. v. CIT [1965] 57 ITR 1 (SC)].

Consists of two components - The amount distributed by a company on reduction of its share capital has two components, i.e., distribution attributable to accumulated profits and distribution attributable to capital (except capitalised profits) [CIT v. G. Narasimhan [1999] 102 Taxman 66 (SC)].

Date of resolution is relevant in ascertaining accumulated profits - The date of the resolution for the reduction of capital, and not the several dates of payments to the shareholders, is the date for ascertaining the quantum of accumulated profits [Punjab Distilling Industries Ltd. v. CIT [1965] 57 ITR 1 (SC)].

No deduction as to face value of shares - Entire amount received by shareholder on purchase by company of shares pursuant to scheme of reduction of capital would constitute 'divided' without deducting face value of shares [CIT v. Jai Hind Investment Industries (P.) Ltd. [1992] 62 Taxman 361 (Cal.)].

PAYMENT BY WAY OF LOAN/ADVANCE TO SPECIFIED BENEFICIAL SHAREHOLDERS OR TO ITS RELATED CONCERN [SECTION 2(22)(e)]

Constitutional validity - Provision of section 2(22)(e) is not beyond the legislative competence of the Legislature. It also does not contravene the rights conferred under Articles 19(1)(f) and 19(1)(g) of the Constitution of India [Navnit Lal C. Javeri v. K. K. Sen, Appellate Asstt. CIT [1965] 56 ITR 198 (SC)].

Provision to be strictly interpreted - The dividend, taken note of by this provision, is a deemed dividend and not a real dividend. Loan or payment made by the company to its shareholder is actually not a dividend. In fact, such a loan has to be returned by the shareholder to the company. It does not become income of the shareholder. Notwithstanding the same, for certain purposes, the Legislature has deemed such a loan or payment as dividend and made it taxable at the hands of the said shareholder. It is, therefore, not in dispute that such a provision which is a deemed provision and fictionally creates certain kinds of receipts as dividends, is to be given strict interpretation [Gopal & Sons (HUF) v. CIT [2017] 77 taxmann.com 71/245 Taxman 48 (SC)].

To the extent of accumulated profits, entire payment made by company and not merely proportionate to shareholdings of assessee shareholder should be deemed as dividend in hands of shareholder [CIT v. Mayur Madhukant Mehta [1972] 85 ITR 230 (Guj.)].

Regarding the provision for taxation included in debit balance of P&L account and existing tax liability raised by the IT authorities but disputed by the assessee and not provided in the books, the accumulated profits are to be construed as commercial profits for the purposes of section 2(22). In the absence of specific reserves for taxation created by the company those liabilities might have to be met from the general reserves. In such circumstances to take the figure of general reserve from the balance sheet for ascertaining the accumulated profits would not be a correct procedure for the quantum of the general reserves would not represent the accumulated profits. Having regard to the aforesaid reasons, deduction was liable to be made for ascertaining accumulated profits.

However, the accumulated profit worked out in this way being a negative figure, it could not be said that the company possessed accumulated profits and, hence, provisions of section 2(22) were not applicable.

As regards the issue of levy of capital gains, the Commissioner (Appeals) had held against levy of capital gains without discussing facts and issues involved and without indicating reasons in support of his finding in the impugned order.

The basic issue for the purposes of levy of capital gains is whether reduction of share capital by a company results in extinguishment of rights in shares held by shareholders covered by the expression ‘transfer’ as defined in section 2(47). When a company reduces its share capital by paying off a part of the capital thereby reducing the face value of the shares, the share remains but the right of the shareholder to dividend of his share capital and the right to share is extinguished proportionately to the extent of reduction in capital. In the instant case, the Assessing Officer had no occasion to consider the issue of levy of capital gains under section 45 as a result of reduction of share capital since he came to the conclusion that accumulated profits possessed by the company exceeded the distribution made to the shareholders on reduction of share capital. While reversing the conclusion of the Assessing Officer and deleting the addition on account of dividend under section 2(22)(a) the Commissioner (Appeals) did not apply his mind to the issue of levy of capital gains under section 45, particularly since the distribution made by the company on reduction of share capital had been treated as transfer by the Supreme Court in the various decisions. In the circumstances the issue of levy of capital gains was set aside to the file of the Assessing Officer with the direction that the issue of levy of capital gains might be re-examined by him.

The counsel for the assessee strongly put forth two arguments and contend that the provisions of Sec.2(22) are not attracted in the present case. According to the Ld.Counsel for the assessee, Sec.2(22) (a)/2(22) (d) requires distribution which would only imply distribution without any quid pro quo. Since, the scheme of purchase of own shares is made through offer and acceptance and therefore, this involves an element of quid pro quo, and therefore, there is no 'distribution'. He further argued that Sec.2(22)(d) requires distribution on the reduction of capital. Therefore, the reduction of share capital is to be coterminous with the distribution. In the present case, the reduction was only a consequence of the scheme owing to the stipulation in Sec.77 that a company cannot purchase its own shares. There has been no distribution on the reduction of share capital. We do not find any merit in the contention of the assessee, because, the word 'distribution' in Sec.2(6A) of the Income-tax Act, 1922, which is analogous to Sec.2(22) of the current Income-tax Act, 1961, was considered in Punjab Distilling Industries Ltd. (supra). The Hon'ble Supreme Court held that the meaning of the word 'distribution' means division/payment between/to several people. The only condition specified was that it must be actual and not notional. Therefore, the definition of the word 'distribution' does not contain any aspect of quid pro quo or lack thereof. In our considered view, the assessee trying to add to the ordinary meaning of the word 'distribution' as interpreted by the Supreme Court by adding conditions which do not otherwise exist. The pre-requisites for distribution is that there must be payment and the disbursal of the same must be made to more than one person. Further, capital reduction as per Sec.100 of the Companies Act, 1956, itself permits that it can be made in any manner. The second contention of the assessee is that there is no distribution on reduction of share capital. At the outset, it must be clarified that the definition of dividend in Sec.2(22) is an inclusive definition. The intent, as borne out from the case laws, is to cover all scenarios whereby a company distributes its accumulated profits without strictly coming within the term 'dividend' as understood in common commercial parlance. Therefore, a literal and hyper technical reading of the term on the 'reduction of share capital' would be contrary to the legislative intent. In simple words, key essentials that are required to be seen in order to attract provisions of Sec.2(22)(d) are that, there must be reduction of share capital and distribution of accumulated profits to the shareholders. Therefore, in our considered view, sec.2(22)(d) does not make a distinction as to whether reduction of share capital is the intended result of the resultant consequence to the scheme, as long as there is reduction of share capital. Further, a reading of the relevant clauses of the scheme documents would show that there has been distribution on reduction. The payment of consideration and transfer of title to goods gets complete on the effective date. Thereafter, as per clause 7.1 of the scheme, the extinguishment will happen after 15 days. Therefore, the contract is concluded, and title is transferred on the effective date of the scheme as per Sec.19 of the Sale of Goods Act, 1930. The mere fact that actual share certificates are extinguished only after 15 days will not have any bearing. Because, extinguishment is a mere ministerial function. In any event, assuming without conceding, that it cannot be treated as distribution on reduction of share capital, then it will automatically fall within the ambit of Sec.2(22)(a) of the Income-tax Act, 1961,as there is distribution of accumulated profits entailing release of assets to the shareholders.

On appeal to the Supreme Court:

Court’s power to sanction scheme

It is settled that in all such cases as the instant one, the Court does not exercise its appellate powers or review powers. It cannot sit in appeal over scheme of arrangement between the company, its members and creditors. Court in a way acts as a ‘Corporate Ombudsman’ to ensure that the scheme of arrangement/compromise among the company, its members and creditors is fair and just and does not subvert public interest or breach law. [Para 9]

The question that often confronts the Court is whether it can decline approval/sanction to a scheme of arrangement, even when the majority of members approved the scheme in the meeting convened pursuant to order of Court and all the creditors gave their consent for the scheme. There cannot be any doubt that even in such a case, the Court can refuse its approval if such scheme is found to contravene the law. The Court can reject sanction if the scheme is found to have been conceived with ulterior motive of playing fraud on public authorities. The Court can also withhold its imprimatur if it is found that in the long run, such scheme is not in the interest of its members, creditors, employees and subverts public interest. The Court can always throw out the scheme if it is intended to legitimize the lapses and illegalities that crept into the corporate governance for which persons at the helm of affairs of the company are alone responsible. Lastly, if the scheme of arrangement is an inchoate transaction affecting future, the Court can always refuse sanction. [Para 10]

Thus, the law providing for Court sanction for scheme is a safeguard against ultra vires corporate excesses and is intended to subserve public interest. Of late, the corporate world derives abundant sustained strength by State support which comes by way of direct/indirect financial participation, subsidized infrastructural facilities, continuous flow of supplies of human resources and sovereign guarantees where international finances are involved. Therefore, even though the Court ought to view the scheme of arrangement submitted for approval with deference to the wishes of proposers and members, nevertheless the Court should be cautious not to be swayed by approval of imposing majority. All decisions of majority at all times cannot be presumed to be legal or legitimate, and corporate leadership cannot always be presumed to be correct in absolute terms. The Court when called upon to examine a scheme for the purpose of according sanction, must therefore keep in view not only the subject matter before it but also look to effect of its decision on the future corporate arrangements. [Para 12]

Reduction of Share Capital vis-a-vis Capital Redemption Reserve

Capital includes ‘share capital’ which may again comprise equity share capital and preference share capital. In addition to this, the reserve account created by the company from out of its profits earned also forms a part of capital. A perusal of the provisions in Part IV Schedule I and Schedule VI would show that the capital of the company consists of mainly shareholders’ funds which include capital, reserves and surplus. When the share capital together with reserves/surplus is found to be in excess of requirements of the company, it would certainly be an unwise business proposition to carry on business with such surplus capital. Therefore, the company, if its memorandum and articles so authorize, can reduce its share capital. [Para 13]

The Companies Act primarily recognises three modes of reduction of share capital. Regulation 46 of the Regulations for management of a company limited by shares (Table A Schedule I) provides that a company may by special resolution reduce in any manner (i) its share capital; (ii) any capital redemption reserve account; or (iii) any share premium account. Section 100(1) indicates three ways of reducing its share capital. These are (i) by extinguishing or reducing liability in respect of unpaid share capital; (ii) by cancelling paid-up share capital which is lost or unrepresented by available assets; or (iii) by paying off any paid-up share capital which is in excess of wants of the company. Any resolution of the company to reduce share capital in any of the three ways needs confirmation of the Court which is required to follow the procedure contemplated in sections 100 to 104 and rules 46 to 65 of the Companies (Court) Rules. Capital Reserve can be Used to Set off Loss, with Company Court’s Approval

S. VENUGOPALAN

The author is a Company Secretary.

The author here deals with the issue as to when capital reserve can be used to set off losses. The highlights of the article are the definition of ‘capital reserve’, circumstances in which it is created and its utilisation. In this context, the author has analysed the judgment of the Delhi High Court in Allianz Capital & Management Services Ltd., In re [2005] 63 SCL 496 wherein it has been held that after obtaining the Government’s approval, capital profits can be used to set off loss, and submits that this decision is binding within jurisdiction of the Delhi High Court only.

What is capital reserve

1. Reserve is profit retained or ploughed back in the business and accumulated over the years. Reserves are of two kinds (1) Revenue reserve and (2) Capital reserve. A reserve created out of trading profits is revenue reserve.

A reserve which is created out of capital profits is a capital reserve. The Companies Act, 1956 does not directly define the term ‘capital reserve’. But according to Part III of Schedule VI of the Act, "the expression ‘capital reserve’ shall not include any amount regarded as free for distribution through the profit and loss account; and the expression ‘revenue reserve’ shall mean any reserve other than a capital reserve." In reality, the capital reserve is at time distributable as dividends among shareholders. But normally, it is not so distributed. The capital reserve is not created by transferring the profit through the appropriation account as is the case of the revenue or the general reserve. But, it is created out of the profits of a capital nature.

A reserve which is created out of capital profits is a capital reserve.

How a capital reserve is created

2. The capital reserve is created out of the capital profits. Some of the circumstances under which the capital reserve is created are as under:

(a) Premiums received on the issue of shares and debentures are capital profits. They are considered as the capital reserve.

(b) Balance to the credit of forfeited shares account after the re-issue of such forfeited shares is transferred to the capital reserve.

(c) Profit on the redemption of debentures at a discount is considered as a capital profit and is transferred to the capital reserve.

(d) When on purchase of a business the purchase price is less than the value of the net assets acquired, the difference is normally transferred to the capital reserve.

(e) Similarly the profits prior to the incorporation of the limited company are considered capital profits and are transferred to the capital reserve.

(f) Profits which are of an exceptional nature and which have not been earned during the regular course of business are at times considered as capital profits and are transferred to the capital reserve. But it is not so treated always.

(g) Where the company sells its fixed assets at an amount which is higher than their cost, the excess over cost is considered as a capital profit. This profit is not earned during the regular course of business. Hence, such profits are normally transferred to the capital reserve.

(h) Sometimes a company may revalue its fixed assets as a result of appreciation in their value. The amount of appreciation is normally transferred to the capital reserve. Revaluation of fixed assets is made by following the Accounting Standard-10 accounting for fixed assets. Revaluation of assets should be done of a class of assets and not individual assets.

(i) If directed by the articles of association, certain profits may not be available for distribution among shareholders. In other words, such profits are not free for distribution through the profit and loss account. Such profits are transferred to the capital reserve.

(j) Certain capital gains and other items of profits which are not regarded as available for distribution as dividend are transferred to the capital reserve. (Adapted from Auditing Principles and Practice by V.H Krishnadwala pg. 2.265)

Disclosure of capital reserve in the balance sheet

3. According to Part I of Schedule VI to the Act, the capital reserve should be shown as a separate item under the head ‘Reserves and surplus’. It should not be mixed up with the revenue reserves. The share premium account is a capital profit, but it is shown as a separate item in the balance sheet.

Utilisation of capital profits (and hence the capital reserve)

4. Capital profits can be utilised for writing off intangible assets like the preliminary expenses, share/debenture issue expenses, goodwill, etc.

The share premium account can be applied for the following purposes as directed by section 78 of the Companies Act, 1956 :

(a) in paying up unissued shares of the company to be issued to its shareholders as fully paid bonus shares,

(b) in writing off preliminary expenses,

When a company is prosperous and accumulates a large surplus, it converts that surplus into capital and divides the capital amongst the members in proportion to their rights. That is done by issuing fully paid-up shares representing the increased capital. The shareholders to whom the shares are allotted have to pay nothing. The purpose is to capitalize profits which may be available for division. Bonus shares go by the modern name of 'capitalization shares'. If the Articles of a company empower the company, it can capitalise profits or reserves and issue fully paid-up shares of nominal value, equal to the amount capitalized, to its shareholders. The idea behind the issue of bonus shares is to bring the nominal share capital into line with the excess of assets over liabilities. A company would like to have more working capital but it need not go into the market for obtaining fresh capital by issuing fresh shares. The necessary money is available with it and that money is converted into shares which really means that the undistributed profits have been ploughed back into the business and converted into share capital. Therefore, fully paid-up bonus shares are merely a distribution of capitalized undivided profit. It would be a misnomer to call the recipients of bonus shares as donees of shares from the company. As regards vires of section 2(6A)(d ) it was contended that a legislation under entry 54 of the Federal Legislative List-I of the Seventh Schedule of the Government of India Act, 1935 must confined itself to taxes on ‘income’ and section 2(6A)(d) in so far as it makes ‘capital’ taxable is ultra vires the Central Legislative. It is a well-settled principle that entries in legislative lists are given a broad and comprehensive interpretation; the cardinal rule of construction being, that words should be read in their natural and grammatical meaning subject to the rider that in construing the words in a constitutional enactment conferring legislative power the most liberal construction should be put upon the words so that the same may have effect in their widest amplitude. Moreover, the various entries in the Lists are not powers of legislation but fields of legislation. Thus, the legislative field is extensive and the items of legislation include not merely the main purposes but also all ancillary and subsidiary matters which can fairly and reasonably be said to fall within the scope of a particular entry.

According to section 2(6A)(d ) any distribution on the reduction of capital becomes dividend to the extent to which the company possessed accumulated profits. The effect of section 2(6A)(d) was that distribution by a company on the reduction of its capital to the extent of the amount which the company possessed as accumulated profits was being treated as dividend. The capital character of the distribution which was in excess of the accumulated profits was not being distributed and to that extent that sum was not being treated as dividend under section 2(6A)(d ). In the instant case, the company, on the reduction of its capital from Rs. 25 lakhs to Rs. 15 lakhs, had to distribute a sum of Rs. 10 lakhs. Out of this Rs. 10 lakhs, law treats the distribution of Rs. 4,69,244 as of accumulated profits and, therefore, as "dividend". The company could not by styling the entire amount for distribution as capital evade its liability to be taxed on Rs. 4,69,244, which, being accumulated profits, fell within the definition of "dividend". The amendment to section 2(6A) had succeeded in according the likehood of evasion by a company, by transferring its profits to the capital and then by reducing the capital proportionately and thereby distributing profits under the label of ‘capital reduction’ this is authority for the proportion that competent to legislate regard income-tax would include the power to legislate in order to check evasion [vide K.M.S. Lakshmana Aiyer v. Addl. ITO [1960] 40 ITR 469, 478 and S. Kumaraswami v. ITO [1961] 43 ITR 423, 426]. In view of the above the impugned provision of section 2(6A)(d) was within the legislative competence of the Central Legislature and was within the ambit of entry No. 54 of List I of the said Seventh Schedule not only in form but also in substance.

The Ld.Counsel for the assessee argued that the ratio on which the assessee seeks to rely on said judgment was it has distinguished purchase of own shares on the one hand and reduction of share capital on the other hand. We do not find any merit in the arguments of the Ld.Counsel for the assessee for simple reason that the observation of the Court or Tribunal should be read in conjunction with the facts. Even a passing references cannot be read in isolation with the issue before the Court or Tribunal. Therefore, the distinction sought to be made with reference to said observation of the Bench was only made with reference to buyback of shares referred to u/s.77A of the Companies Act, 1956, and in that context, it was held that Sec.46A of the Act is alone applicable. In the present case, the assessee itself clearly states that the scheme approved by the Hon'ble High Court is not a buyback u/s.77A of the Companies Act, 1956, and thus, referring to said decision and findings therein are not at all correct in the given facts and circumstances of the case. Therefore, we reject the case law relied upon by the Ld.Counsel for the assessee.

51. In this view of the matter and considering the facts and circumstances of the case, and also by considering various case laws, we are of the considered view that consideration paid by the assessee for purchase of its own shares in accordance with scheme sanctioned by the Hon'ble High Court of Madras in terms of provisions of Sec.391-393 of the Companies Act, 1956, amounts to distribution of accumulated profits which entails release of all or part of assets of a company on reduction of capital which attracts provisions of Sec.2(22) of the Income-tax Act, 1961. The Ld.CIT(A) has discussed the issue at length in light of plethora of judicial precedents and held the transaction of purchase of own shares by the appellant company is distribution of accumulated profits within the meaning of section 2(22) of the Income-tax Act, 1961. Therefore, we are of the considered view that there is no error in the reasons given by the Ld.CIT(A) to treat the transactions of the assessee as dividend u/s.2(22)(a)/2(22)(d) r.w.s.115-O of the Income-tax Act, 1961, and thus, we are inclined to uphold the findings of the Ld.CIT(A) and dismiss appeal filed by the assessee.

52. In the result, appeal filed by the assessee is dismissed.

The purpose of section 2(22 )(d) is to bring within the net of taxation payments made by distribution of assets or money of the company which can be taken to have come from the accumulated profits. This is so as the fiction contained in sub-clause is limited to the extent of the accumulated profits. Where there are no accumulated profits in the company, the fiction cannot be attracted.

Accumulated profits of the company may be utilised by the company for increasing the capital stock or for distributing the same among the share-holders by way of dividend and for reducing the capital. Ordinarily, a company reduces the capital when there is loss or depreciation of assets. In that event, there is no question of distribution of profits to the share-holders. In that eventuality, the shares are only devaluated. But a company may on the pretext of reducing its capital may utilise its accumulated profit to pay back to the shareholders the whole or part of the paid up amounts on the shares. A shareholder, though in form gets back the whole or a part of the capital contributed by him in effect he gets a share of the accumulated profit which, if a straight away course is followed, he should have received as dividend. This is a diversion of profit in the guise of division of capital - a distribution of profit under colour of reduction of capital. The Legislature. therefore, in the interest of the ex chequer, elongated the scope of the definition of "dividend" so as to catch the said payments within the net of taxation.

It is a well-settled principle that entries in legislative lists are given a broad and comprehensive interpretation; the cardinal rule of construction being, that words should be read in their natural and grammatical meaning subject to the rider that in construing the words in a constitutional enactment conferring legislative power the most liberal construction should be put upon the words so that the same may have effect in their widest amplitude. According to section 2(6A)(d ) any distribution on the reduction of capital becomes dividend to the extent to which the company possessed accumulated profits. The effect of section 2(6A)(d) was that distribution by a company on the reduction of its capital to the extent of the amount which the company possessed as accumulated profits was being treated as dividend. The capital character of the distribution which was in excess of the accumulated profits was not being distributed and to that extent that sum was not being treated as dividend under section 2(6A)(d ). When a company reduces its share capital by paying off a part of its share capital under section 100(1)(c ) of the Companies Act, the share remains but the right of the shareholder to dividends on his share capital and the right to share in the distribution of the net assets upon liquidation is extinguished proportionately to the extent of the reduction in capital. When there is an issue of bonus shares, money remains with company and nothing comes to shareholders as there is no transfer of property, and thus, provisions of section 56(2)(vii)(c) are not attracted. The issue which arises for consideration in this appeal is 'as to whether the fair market value of bonus shares computed as per Rule 11U and Rule 11UA of the Income-tax Rules can be considered as income from other sources as per section 56(2)(vii) of the Act. A careful scrutiny of section 56(2)(vii) of the Act contemplates two contingencies firstly, where the property is received without consideration and secondly, where it is received for consideration less than the fair market value. The issue of bonus shares by capitalization of reserves is merely a reallocation of the companies funds. There is no inflow of fresh funds or increase in the capital employed, which remains the same. The total funds available with the company remains the same and issue of bonus shares does not result in any change in respect of capital structure of the company. Thus, there is no addition or alteration to the profit making apparatus and the total funds available with the company remain the same. In substance, when a shareholder gets a bonus shares, the value of the original share held by him goes down and the market value as well as intrinsic value of two shares put together will be the same or nearly the same as per the value of original share before the issue of bonus shares. Thus, any profit derived by the assessee on account of receipt of bonus shares is adjusted by depreciation in the value of equity shares held by him. In the instant case, there is no material on record to infer that bonus shares have been transferred with an intention to evade tax, which is the object of the provision in question. Therefore, the CIT (Appeals) as well as the tribunal have rightly held that when there is an issue of bonus shares, the money remains with the company and nothing comes to the shareholders as there is no transfer of the property and the provisions of section under section 56(2)(vii)(c) of the Act are not attracted to the fact situation of the case. 7.5-6 Redemption of preference shares

In Anarkali Sarabhai v. CIT [1997] 224 ITR 422/90 Taxman 509 (SC), it was held that redemption of preference shares was sale of shares by the shareholder. Conversely, the redemption could be construed as purchase of shares by the issuing company. Hence, redemption of preference shares may also be covered by section 115QA. Will the redemption now enter the computation of capital gains so far as the shareholder is concerned?

Suppose the preference shares costing Rs. 100 were redeemed by the company for Rs. 100. Suppose the indexed cost of acquisition was Rs. 130. Before the amendment in section 115QA, there was a capital loss of Rs. 30 (Rs. 130 less Rs. 100) arising to the shareholder. Will there may be any such capital loss after the amendment to section 115QA?

According to one view, section 10(34A) provides that any income arising to a shareholder on account of buyback of shares by the company as referred to in section 115QA shall be exempt from tax. It has been held that for the purposes of section 10, income includes loss [CIT v. S. Thiagarajan [1981] 129 ITR 115 (Mad.); G. K. Ramamurthy v. Jt. CIT [2010] 37 SOT 345 (Mum)]. Now, it is now well settled that any income exempt from tax does not enter the computation of income under different heads of income as mentioned in section 14. Thus, the income, including loss, arising on redemption of preference shares would no longer enter the computation of income under the head capital gains.

Therefore, it could not be said that the view taken by the Assessing Officer was one of the impossible views. He had taken one of the possible views considering the facts of the case and the ratio laid down by the Supreme Court in its decisions which had been elaborately discussed by the Assessing Officer. The Commissioner wanted to take a different view on the basis of the same decision which might perhaps be a view favourable to the interest of the revenue. But that did not render the order of the Assessing Officer as erroneous. The Assessing Officer had only followed what, according to him, was the correct legal consequence of the decisions of the Apex Court. In such a situation, it could not be said that the order of the Assessing Officer was erroneous. It was, therefore, to be held that the order passed by the Commissioner under section 263 was the result of a change of opinion and all that the Commissioner acting under section 263 wanted was the substitution of his own opinion for that of the Assessing Officer which was clearly impermissible within the scope of section 263. [Para 11]

Accordingly, the order of the Commissioner under section 263 was vacated.

The observation made by the Regional Director is solely premised on the fact that the petitioner company is a profitable one. There is no principle of law which prohibits a profitable company from reducing its share capital and thus the fact that the petitioner company is a profitable one cannot possibly, in absence of any other material fact, lead to the conclusion that the reduction of capital is for a collateral purpose. The fact that the petitioner is a profitable company would only indicate that the company has in addition to its capital also generated further funds and the same would not negate the reason that the petitioner has capital in excess of its requirements. It is also relevant to note that the reduction of capital is not on proportionate basis. Therefore, the ratio of the entitlement of the shareholders to future profits by way of dividends would also stand altered by reason of reduction in capital as proposed. This would not be a feature where the sole intention of proposing reduction of capital was distribution of profits amongst shareholders. It stands to reason that if the company wanted to distribute dividend to its shareholders, the same would have been done proportionately. In this view it does not appear that the sole object of the company is to distribute dividends and not reduce the share capital. [Para 19]

In the present case, the petitioner has been treating the convertible preference shares as equity in conformity with the aforementioned RBI Guidelines. The reduction of capital in the present case cannot be treated as repayment of ECB. In view of the decisions of the Madras High Court in CIT v. India Co. (P.) Ltd. [1984] 149 ITR 548/ 18 Taxman 376 and Shantha Rangarajan v. CIT [1995] 215 ITR 104, it was to be heldin the instant case that there was transfer while there was distribution of shares in the form of assets by the assessee-company to its shareholders in order to discharge its liability to the shareholders on account of reduction of share capital.

As regards the Tribunal's finding that there was adequate consideration, it pointed out that when the paid-up capital is reduced, an equivalent amount is reduced by taking out certain assets and distributing the same to the shareholders at the book value; if the revenue wants that the value of the assets should be revised upwards to the extent of its market value, then it would require also upward revision of the value of the shares as such. Revaluing the shares in an upward manner was not possible in the instant case, since by a resolution the value was fixed for each share. In order to equalise the amount paid and the market value of the properties transferred, it could not be said that what was lost by the shareholders in the company was in the ratio of 21/100. When the company transferred properties worth more than Rs. 8,17,194, the revenue, by applying the provisions of section 4(1)(a), initiated the gift-tax proceedings. Under such circumstances, the assessee-company could not plead that if the value of the shares was valued in an upward manner, that would equalise the amount paid and the immovable property transferred to the shareholders. When the resolution passed by the General Body Meeting stated that what was payable by the company was only Rs. 790 per share, the shareholders were entitled to nothing more than that. It was not the case that what was transferred by the company to the shareholders was a portion of the share difference or the value of the shares. Hence, the Tribunal was not correct while stating that if the shares were valued in an upward manner, that would show that the consideration was adequate.

Further, the assessee had not submitted any valuation of the market value of the immovable property transferred. It was also not shown as to what would be the market value of the shares as on the date of transfer. No attempt was made on this aspect to show that the liquid cash paid Plus the market value of the immovable property transferred would be equal to the market value of the shares as on the date of transfer.

In CIT v. C.C. Subbarayudu [1988] 171 ITR 310 the Andhra Pradesh High Court pointed out that the Tribunal should have determined the market value upon relevant data, compared it with the sale consideration specified in the sale deed and then should have come to a proper conclusion as to whether there was inadequate consideration or adequate consideration, either for attracting or for not attracting the provisions of section 4(1)(a ). That was not done in the instant case.

In view of the foregoing reasons, it was concluded that the Tribunal was not correct in holding that there was no transfer in this case, and even if there was transfer, the transfer was for adequate consideration.

of the capital and once the law is such that certain payments must be deemed to be payments of dividend, for all purposes it has to be treated as dividend and the restriction that the payment of dividend should not be from capital will attach to such payment as well. Therefore, Tribunal was right in directing the advances being the deemed dividends assessed in the hand of the various shareholders in the past assessment years, should be deducted from the surplus while determining the ‘accumulated profits’ in the hands of the company. As regards the question of capital gains, there is a particular procedure prescribed by the 1956 Act for reduction of capital. If that procedure is gone through, there can be reduction of capital. In reduction of capital, there need not necessarily be a reduction in the number of shares held by the company. In the instant case too, there had been no such reduction in the number of shares. What had happened was only to reduce the face value of the shares. Consequent upon the reduction of the capital, the company deemed it fit to distribute some assets and some money to the shareholder. That naturally happens in all such cases of reduction for it may be found that it was not necessary to keep all the assets of the company and that it can be distributed to the shareholders. There may be other objects also in such reduction of capital. Perhaps it is to minimise the possibility of such distribution of amounts that the deeming provision in section 2(22)(d ) had been introduced by the statute by insisting that on such assets being distributed, tax should be paid deeming such assets as dividends issued by the company. A shareholder can transfer a share. He can also surrender the share to the company and when surrendering the share, there may be relinquishment of the share. There can also be cancellation of the shares. Apart from that, there can be no transactions vis-a-vis the company and the shareholders as regards the shares held by a shareholder. The shares as such are held by the shareholders and the only provision in the Companies Act which would have any representations between the company and the shareholder would be in the circumstances of surrender and cancellation of shares. There had been no surrender or cancellation of shares in the company. It could not be said that there had been any exchange on reduction of the shares or any part of the value of the shares. The shareholder had not transferred anything to the company. Therefore, section 45 was not attracted. All the rights of the shareholder as a shareholder in the company still remained. He continued to hold the same number of shares. Whether, on liquidation, he would get the amount which he would have received had a liquidation taken place at the time of the reduction of capital could not touch the question as to whether by the reduction of capital there had been any extinguishment. It was conceivable that he would receive less in the event of the winding up of the company after reduction of capital in view of the fact that there had been distribution of assets. But on the possibility of the company not prospering and not augmenting its assets, it is not possible to come to any conclusion that there had been any extinguishment of the rights of the shareholder. The shareholder's right to receive the assets of the company, can arise only in the event of winding up of the company and on liquidation taking effect. That event not having taken place, it could not postulate any extinguishment. Therefore, the Tribunal was right in holding that no capital gain was assessable in the hands of the assessee as there was no extinguishments of any right of the assessee and consequently there was no transfer within the meaning of section 2(47) by the assessee of any capital assets for the relevant assessment year.

It involves nominal capital whether issued or unissued, and motives behind the reduction of capital are irrelevant, according to the decision in Panruti Industrial Co. Equity Insurance Co. Ltd. [1948] 18 Comp. Cas. 309 (Oudh).

A company limited by shares had only deposits and none as capital; when the defect was pointed out by the Registrar it introduced a proper share capital: held it was not a reduction of capital - Srivilliputtur Permanent Fund Ltd., In re [1952] 22 Comp. Cas. 299 (Mad.).

An amount received by a company not as capital was shown as capital in the balance sheet wrongly, held that the provisions of sections 100 to 103 were not attracted - Rupak Ltd. v. Registrar of Companies [1984] 56 Comp. Cas. 206 (Pat.).

In a scheme of arrangement a company was dissolved without winding up and the preference shares were paid off held it was no reduction of capital - T. Durairajan v. Waterfall Estates Ltd. [1972] 42 Comp. Cas. 563 (Mad.).

A company in voluntary liquidation paid off its preference and ordinary share capital, and nextly it was revived by induction of fresh capital which was less than its original capital, held it was no reduction of capital - Mcleod & Co. v. S.K. Ganguly [1975] 45 Comp. Cas. 563 (Cal.).

The requirement of setting out the intention to move the resolution for reduction of share capital as a special resolution in a scheme of amalgamation cannot be said to be a mandatory requirement, though passing the resolution as a special resolution is mandatory - Sumitra Pharmaceuticals & Chemicals Ltd., In re [1997] 88 Comp. Cas. 619/14 SCL 8 (AP).

When the paid up capital is reduced by the cancellation of the required amount of paid up capital equal to the capital lost or unrepresented by available assets, it is not mandatory to follow the procedure set out in section 101(2) unless directed by the Court - Maneckchowk & Ahmedabad Mfg. Co. Ltd., In re [1970] 40 Comp. Cas. 819 (Guj.).

If a reduction of capital comes about as a consequence of the Court s order under section 402, the procedure set out in sections 100 to 104 need not be followed, Cosmosteels (P.) Ltd. v. Jairam Das Gupta [1978] 48 Comp. Cas. 312 (SC). In Asian Investments Ltd., In re [1992] 73 Comp. The assessee was a Public Limited Company. It had incurred a huge loss and was declared a relief undertaking under the Tamil Nadu Relief Undertaking (Special Provision) Act. With a view to revive the company, a scheme for reduction of share capital under section 101 of the Companies Act, as well as a compromise or arrangement under section 391 of the Companies Act was arrived at. The scheme was approved by the majority of the shareholders and the secured creditors and a Single Judge of instant High Court had also sanctioned the scheme. However, some of the unsecured creditors raised objections against the order granting sanction to the scheme and filed an appeal before a Division Bench. The Division Bench reversed the judgment of the Single Judge and remanded back the matter for rehearing. Against the judgment of the Division Bench, the respondent therein had filed a special leave petition before the Supreme Court and the Supreme Court had granted the leave and stay of operation of the judgment of the Division Bench. The Assessing Officer, on the basis of the scheme sanctioned by the Single Judge, invoked the provisions of section 41(1) and levied tax on the amounts sacrificed by the creditors and suppliers of the company. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) upheld the Assessing Officer’s order. On further appeal, the Tribunal considered the matter in the light of the judgment of Division Bench wherein order of the Single Judge granting sanction to said scheme was set aside. It was held that in view of the judgment of the Division Bench the scheme was not sanctioned and, therefore, no sacrifice was made by any of the creditors. The appeal filed by the assessee was, therefore, allowed.

The assessee created a development rebate fund to avail of the deduction under section 33. Section 34(3)( a) does not prohibit the assessee from using any amount credited to the fund for the purpose of its business but he cannot utilise the amount for eight years for 'distribution by way of dividends or profits'. If the ITO finds that the assessee has utilised any amount out of the reserve fund for distribution by way of dividends or profits, he can withdraw the allowance given under section 33 by proceeding under section 155.

In the instant case, there was no allegation that the assessee had distributed any dividend out of the amounts standing to the credit of the fund. But the assessee issued bonus shares and for that purpose transferred the amount standing to the credit of the fund to the share capital account. One view is that issue of bonus shares to the shareholders involves a dual operation by which an amount is released to the shareholders from a reserve fund but is retained by the company and applied in payment of the bonus shares which are issued as fully paid up. The shareholders are treated as having paid for the bonus shares and the supposed payments by the shareholders are taken to share capital account from the reserve fund of the Company. In effect, the shareholders have not paid the face value of the bonus shares. It is to all intents and purposes equivalent to distribution of accumulated profits in cash by the company.

The second view is that when bonus shares are issued, an amount equal to the face value of the shares cannot be regarded as having been received by the shareholders. The issuance of bonus shares is nothing but mere capitalisation of the profits of the company in respect of which certificates are issued to the shareholders entitling them to participate in the amount of the reserve but only as part of the capital.

The correct view could be that the profits made by the company may be distributed as dividends or retained by the company as its reserve which may be used for improvement of the company's works, buildings and machinery. That will enable the company to make larger profits. There cannot be any dispute that the shareholders will benefit from the improvements brought about in the profit-making apparatus of the company. Likewise, if the accumulated profits are capitalised and capital base of the company is enlarged, this may enable the company to do its business more profitably. The shareholders will also benefit if the share capital is increased. They may benefit immediately by issue of bonus shares. But neither in the case of improvement in the profit-making apparatus nor in the case of expansion of the share capital of the company, can it be said that the shareholders have received any money from the company. They may have benefited in both the cases. But this benefit cannot be treated as distribution of the amount standing to the credit of any reserve fund of the company to its shareholders.

In fact, the transfer of the amounts standing to the credit of development rebate reserve to the share capital account does not involve any disbursement of money by the company. Nothing comes out of the till of the company to the shareholder. The entire amount of money shown as development rebate reserve is retained by the company in another account. It cannot be said that by the issue of bonus shares, the company has distributed its reserve fund to the shareholders even though it has retained the entire amount with it in the share capital account.

When a shareholder gets a bonus share, the value of the original share held by him goes down. In effect, the shareholder gets two shares instead of the one share held by him and the market value as well as the intrinsic value of the two shares put together will be the same or nearly the same as the value of the original share before the bonus issue.

It appears from the various decisions that issuance of bonus shares does not amount to distribution of accumulated profit of a company. The shareholder derives some benefit by the process of capitalising of the accumulated profits but at the same time, the value of his original shareholding goes down.

Viewed from any angle, it could not be said that in this case the assessee-company had distributed any part of its development rebate reserve fund when it issued the bonus shares. The accumulated profit lying to the credit of the development rebate reserve had been retained by the company. The amount had been transferred to the share capital account. If that was not done, the intrinsic value of the shares held by the shareholders would have been more. After the issue of the bonus shares, the intrinsic value of the original shares had gone down rateably. The accumulated profits of the company had remained with the company in one account or another. In the instant case, neither in form nor in substance, had there been any distribution of profits by the company in making the bonus issue. If the substance and not the form of the transaction was looked to, the issue of bonus shares was in the language of Rowlatt J., 'a bare machinery' for capitalising profits and there was no distribution of profits to the shareholders.

It appears that the provision envisages positive distributed income. If the consideration paid by the company on buyback of shares is less than the amount received by the company for issue of such shares than the distributed income would be negative and in these circumstances, obviously there will not be any liability under section 115QA.

7.5-4 Reduction of capital Section 100 of the Companies Act, 1956 (corresponding to section 66(1)(b) of the Companies Act, 2013) provides that a company may reduce the share capital and may 'pay off' any paid up share capital which is in excess of the wants of the company. According to one view, purchase of share under section 77A of the Companies Act, 1956 (corresponding to section 68 of the Companies Act, 2013) and reduction of capital under section 100 pursuant to which shares are 'transferred' to the company are two distinct transactions and such reduction cannot be construed as purchase of shares by the company within the meaning of section 115QA. In Goldman Sachs (India) Securities (P.) Ltd. v. ITO [ITA No. 3726 of 2015, decided on 12-2-2016] (Mum. - Trib.), the Tribunal cited observations from SEBI v. Sterlite Industries (India) Ltd. [2003] 45 SCL 475 (Bom.) and held that the observations of the Court did not leave any doubt that buyback of shares could not be equated with reduction of capital.

Further, the term used in section 66 is 'pay-off', which has been defined in Random House Dictionary as "to pay (someone) everything that is due to that person; To pay (debt) in full." Thus, the term 'pay-off' suggests that there is a due to the shareholder to the extent of his interest in the company that is been paid-off. It appears that this cannot be equated with purchase of shares in which there is nothing due to the seller till the sale transaction takes place.

According to the other view, the payment upon reduction is also purchase of shares. Section 2(22)(d) provides that dividend includes any distribution to its shareholders by a company on reduction of capital. However, the definition also provides that dividend does not include any payment made by a company on purchase of its own shares in accordance with the provisions of section 77A of the Companies Act, 1956. The fact that there is a specific exclusion of payment upon purchase of shares shows that in the absence of such exclusion, purchase of shares under section 77A could have been regarded as reduction of capital. Conversely, reduction of capital should also be construed as purchase of shares by the company.

It appears that the better view is that reduction of capital under section 66 of the Companies Act, 2013 is not a purchase within the meaning of section 115QA, although as a consequence of this view, the shareholder could be liable to

28.19 Regulation 96 of Table A provides for capitalization of profits to say that the company in general meeting may, upon the recommendation of the Board, resolve to capitalize any part of the amount for the time being standing to the credit of any of the company’s reserve accounts, or to the credit of the profit and loss account, or otherwise available for distribution, in kind, amongst the members who would have been entitled to it if distributed by way of dividend and in same proportions, sections 78(2) and 80(5). Such amount is available to be applied either in or towards paying up any amount for the time being unpaid on any shares held by each such member, or paying up in full un-issued shares of the company to be allotted and distributed, credited as fully paid-up, to and amongst such members in their respective proportions, or partly in one way and partly the other. However, a share premium account or a capital redemption reserve account can be applied only in the paying up of un-issued shares to be issued to members of the company as fully paid bonus shares to the members according to their respective entitlements but not as a gift, CIT v. Chunilal Khusaldas [1974] 44 Comp. Cas. 90 (Guj.). This accords with the Proviso to section 205(3), saying that the requirement of the Act for payment of dividend in cash in no way prohibits the capitalization of profits or reserves of a company for the purpose of issuing fully paid-up bonus shares or paying up any amount for the time being unpaid on any shares held by the members of the company. The effect of issue of bonus shares from general reserves is to seal off the chances of the amounts being available for distribution as dividend permanently by conversion into share capital without contribution from the shareholders. According to the decision of Supreme Court in Shree Gopal Paper Mills Ltd. v. CIT AIR 1970 SC 1750, bonus shares become vested from the date of the resolution in general meeting and not from the date of subsequent allotment by the Board of directors. For issue of bonus shares, see discussion in Ch 20.

In general, if there is a provision in the articles corresponding to Regulations 96 and 97 of Table A - which only deal with capitalization of profits—any company limited by shares may capitalise profits available for distribution as dividend by issue of fully paid bonus shares and issue the same to the existing members pro rata. From the DCA Circular 9/1994 dated 6-9-1994 it would appear that the guidelines for issue of bonus shares issued by SEBI under the SEBI (DIP) Guidelines, 2000 for listed companies are applicable to all companies—that is to say, that bonus shares are to be issued out of free general reserves built out of genuine profits or share (securities?) premium account collected in cash, but not out of reserves created by revaluation of fixed assets. Issue of bonus shares has the effect of reducing the share value proportionately in the ratio of its issue, Chandrakant Mulraj v. Tata Engg. & Locomotive Co. Ltd. [1985] 58 Comp. Cas. 320 (Bom.); and the character of bonus shares in the hands of the shareholders is capital but not dividend : IRC v. Blott (1921) 2 AC 171 (HL).

Finance Act, 1999

Buy back of shares

5.1 Section 77A of the Companies Act, 1956 permits a company to buy back its own shares upon fulfilment of the prescribed conditions. It has tax implications and broadly, there were two views :

♦

As per one view, utilisation of accumulated profits for the buy back, entailing reduction of capital, could amount to dividend attracting tax @ 10% under section 115-O of the Act in the hands of the company.

♦

As per the other view, the company is not liable to dividend tax inasmuch as the purchase of its own shares does not amount to reduction in capital and only the shareholders are liable to pay tax on the gains, if any.

To set the controversy at rest, the Finance Act, 1999 has made the following provisions :

(a)

The payment made by a company for purchase of share would not constitute dividend [vide section 2(22)(iv)]; and

(b)

Shareholders would be chargeable to capital gains tax (by inserting section 46A).

5.1-1 Dividend - Section 2(22) of the Act defines dividend inclusively. After listing the distribution or payment amounting to dividend, it lists certain distribution or payment not constituting dividend. In that list, the payment made by a company on purchase of its own shares from shareholder in terms of section 77A of the Companies Act, 1956 has been added [vide, sub-clause (iv)] meaning that such payment would not constitute dividend. Accordingly, the provisions of section 115-O of the Act would not apply.

However, this provision would not apply in respect of buy back of any shares or other securities by the company under any other provisions of the Companies Act, 1956 (i.e., other than section 77A) under any scheme of arrangement (e.g. an order under section 402 of the Companies Act, 1956) or otherwise. Accordingly, any payment made by the company in such a case for such purchase may constitute dividend within the meaning of section 2(22) of the Act.

5.1-2 Section 46A - The section provides as follows :

♦

When a shareholder or holder of other specified securities receives any consideration from a company,

♦

Upon purchase of its own shares or securities by the company,

♦

The difference between cost of acquisition and purchase price of shares or securities paid by the company would constitute capital gains,

♦

In computing the capital gains, section 48 should be given effect to,

♦

The gain would be chargeable to tax in the year of purchase and

♦

For the purpose, the other securities have the same meaning as assigned in Explanation to section 77A of the Companies Act, 1956.

5.1-2a NECESSITY - Shares or securities do constitute capital asset. It is settled law that upon purchase by the company, there is a transfer of shares [Anarkali Sarabhai v. CIT [1997] 224 ITR 422 (SC)]. Accordingly, any gain arising therefrom is chargeable to tax as capital gains or otherwise. Further, there was no controversy that a shareholder was liable to capital gains tax. Also, the question of reducing accumulated profit considered as dividend in computing the capital gain would not arise in view of the amendment made in section 2(22). In the circumstances, the need for a separate provision was not there. Also, the need for including other specified securities in the provision is also not clear.

5.1-2b MEANING OF 'SHAREHOLDER' OR 'HOLDER' - The Supreme Court in Howrah Trading Co. Ltd. v. CIT [1959] 36 ITR 215, 219-220] held that a shareholder or holder, means, a member, i.e., a person whose name is entered in the register of members. Accordingly, a beneficial owner of shares, say, a firm who holds shares through its partners, would not be considered as a shareholder. Similarly, the holder of specified security would mean the person whose name is entered in the register or record maintained by the company and not the beneficial owner.

Prima facie in such a case, (i.e., a beneficial owner), the provisions of section 46A may not apply, unless, a view is taken that in the context of section 46A, the shareholder could mean a person who receives the price for the buy back from the company. Apart from that, assuming for a moment section 46A cannot apply in case of a beneficial owner, taxation of gain on buy back cannot be ruled out under section 45. This is because where the special provision does not apply, the general provision can always apply.
