Prior to the amendments by Finance Act, 2016

(a)

distributed income was defined to mean the consideration paid by the company on buy back of shares as reduced by the amount which was received by the company for issue of such shares;

(b)

buyback had been defined to mean the purchase by a company of its own shares in accordance with the provisions of section 77A of the Companies Act, 1956. Thus the definition of buyback did not cover buybacks undertaken by a company under other provisions of the Companies Act, 1956 or the Companies Act, 2013.

Again there could be situations where shares may have been issued by the company in tranches, for different considerations, at different point of time or may have been issued in lieu of existing shares of another company under amalgamation, merger or demerger. In all these cases there was lack of clarity in determination of consideration received by the company at the time of issue of shares being bought back by the company (as per Explanatory Memorandum to Finance Bill, 2016).

In Capgemini India (P.) Ltd., In re [2016] 67 taxmann.com 1 (Bom.) it was held that the Indian company law, as it stood then, permitted a company to buy-back its shares either without Court approval (by adopting procedure of buy-back regulations) or with the Court's approval. If the law permitted a company to follow one of the two methods, it could not be compelled to follow only that method that results in higher tax liability. The Court held that the purchase of shares under section 391 of the Companies Act, 1956 (now section 230 of the Companies Act, 2013) was not covered by section 115QA.

In view of the above, section 115QA has been amended with effect from 1-6-2016 to provide that

(a)

Buyback will mean purchase by a company of its own shares in accordance with the provisions of any law for the time being in force relating to companies [Explanation (i) to section 115QA(1)].

(b)

Distributed income means the consideration paid by the company on buyback of shares as reduced by the amount, which was received by the company for issue of such shares, determined in the manner as may be prescribed [Explanation (ii) to section 115QA(1)].

7.5-1 'Purchase' of shares is a precondition

Even after the amendment in Explanation (i), 'purchase' of shares by a company is a precondition for applicability of section 115QA. If a particular transaction does not result in 'purchase' by the company, then section 115QA is not triggered.

Thus, section 115QA will now apply to buy backs under

(a)

sections 391 to 394 of the Companies Act, 1956 (corresponding to sections 230 to 232 of the Companies Act, 2013);

(b)

section 395 of the Companies Act, 1956 (corresponding to section 235 of the Companies Act, 2013);

(c)

section 402 of the Companies Act, 1956 (corresponding to section 242(2)(b) of the Companies Act, 2013).

7.5-2 Unlisted share is a precondition

Even after the amendment, section 115QA applies only in respect of purchase of unlisted shares. The term 'shares' will include all types of shares including preference shares and convertible preference shares. However, listed shares or convertible debentures are not covered.

7.5-3 Positive distributed income

It appears that the provision envisages positive distributed income. If the consideration paid by the company on buyback of shares is less than the amount received by the company for issue of such shares than the distributed income would be negative and in these circumstances, obviously there will not be any liability under section 115QA.

7.5-4 Reduction of capital

Section 100 of the Companies Act, 1956 (corresponding to section 66(1)(b) of the Companies Act, 2013) provides that a company may reduce the share capital and may 'pay off' any paid up share capital which is in excess of the wants of the company. According to one view, purchase of share under section 77A of the Companies Act, 1956 (corresponding to section 68 of the Companies Act, 2013) and reduction of capital under section 100 pursuant to which shares are 'transferred' to the company are two distinct transactions and such reduction cannot be construed as purchase of shares by the company within the meaning of section 115QA. In Goldman Sachs (India) Securities (P.) Ltd. v. ITO [ITA No. 3726 of 2015, decided on 12-2-2016] (Mum. - Trib.), the Tribunal cited observations from SEBI v. Sterlite Industries (India) Ltd. COVERAGE OF SECTION 46(2)

Section 46 deals with capital gains on distribution of assets by companies on liquidation. Section 46(1) provides that notwithstanding anything contained in section 45, where the assets of a company are distributed to its shareholders on its liquidation, such distribution shall not be regarded as a transfer by the company for the purposes of section 45. The company hence need not pay tax on any capital gain by making computation on such distribution.

Section 46(2) says that where a shareholder on the liquidation of a company receives any money or other assets from the company, he shall be chargeable to income-tax under the head 'Capital gains', in respect of the money so received or the market value of the other assets on the date of distribution, as reduced by the amount assessed as dividend under section 2(22)(c) and the sum so arrived at shall be deemed to be the full value of consideration for the purpose of section 48.

HELD: Reduction of share capital of company is permissible under the Companies Act by following a specific procedure as laid down therein. This decision is taken after affording the individual shareholder to participate in the decision making process wherein they are free to give their views and the majority view or opinion prevails. If the decision to reduce share capital is approved the consequences follows obviously by following the statutory formalities. In the instant case the reduction of share capital in the plaintiff-company has taken place not by such process but as a part of a rehabilitation scheme sanctioned by AAIFR in the process of reviving the plaintiff-company. The sole object while sanctioning or approving a scheme on a company being referred to under SICA is to rehabilitate and if possible to revive the company from the stage for which the company had to be referred to BIFR under SICA. The individual shareholder though had a right to participate in the proceedings before BIFR or AAIFR and express their views but the same was in a limited score unlike their participation to reduce share capital under the Companies Act, 1956 being the act prevalent at the time when reduction of share capital in the plaintiff-company was allowed. A rehabilitation scheme like the one introduced in the plaintiff-company is sanctioned under the provisions of section 18(2)(f) and section 18(4). The scheme becomes binding on an individual shareholder for the purpose of reviving the company till the scheme is successfully worked out or implemented. The scheme is always open to modification to accommodate the difficulties faced in course of implementing the scheme. Any provision including the step approved for reduction of share capital like that in case of the plaintiff remains open till the scheme is successfully worked out. It may so happen that the scheme fails and the company is directed to be wound up. The act of reduction of share capital under a scheme like that in the plaintiff is a contingent act, which fructifies on the successful implementation of the scheme. The reduction of share capital allowed under the scheme, therefore, cannot be said to have achieved finality during the implementation of the scheme. This act of reduction of share capital in the plaintiff-company pursuant to the scheme will crystallize only on the scheme being successfully worked out. [Para 16]

In the instant case the reduction of share capital was brought by way of a Rehabilitation Scheme framed under section 18(2)(f) and section 18(4) and not by following the procedure available under the Companies Act. The BIFR and the AAIFR under the provisions of section 18(2)(f) and section 18(4) are competent to formulate a composite scheme permitting reduction of share capital for rehabilitation of the company. This fact is not in dispute. In such factual background the reduction in share capital permitted under the Rehabilitation Scheme shall continue to hold good till the scheme is in operation or in such time it is successfully implemented. The situation will be different if the implementation is not successful and an order of winding up of the plaintiff-company is ultimately directed. It is also possible that the Rehabilitation Scheme permitting reduction of share capital may be further modified during the course of implementation which may have an effect over the portion of the scheme which permits reduction of share capital. It can, therefore, be said that still the scheme has been successfully implemented, the reduction of share capital permitted under the said scheme does not achieve finality and is subject to being further modified. [Para 20]

Power of the sanctioning court in the Scheme of Arrangement was again discussed in the recent case of Jt. CIT v. Reliance Jio Infocomm Ltd. [2019] 112 taxmann.com 275 (NCL-AT). In the light of the recent decision, an academic analyses is made on authority/jurisdiction of the sanctioning court in an application for approving the scheme of arrangement.

The term 'sanctioning court' and Tribunal has been used in the article interchangeably.

Facts of the case

'Reliance Jio Infocomm Limited'- Demerged/ Transferor Company, 'Jio Digital Fibre Private Limited'- Resulting Company and 'Reliance Jio Infratel Private Limited'- Transferee Company moved a joint petition under Sections 230-232 of the Companies Act, 2013, seeking sanction of the Composite Scheme of Arrangement amongst themselves and their respective shareholders and Creditors.

Hon'ble National Company Law Tribunal (NCLT) vide order dated 11th January 2019 directed the Regional Director, North Western Region to make a representation under Section 230(5) of the Companies Act, 2013 and the Income Tax Department to file representation.

Aggrieved by the impugned order which was pronounced on 20th March 2019 sanctioning the Scheme, the Joint Commissioner of Income Tax (OSD), Circle (3)(3)-1, Mumbai and the income Tax Officer, Ward 3(3)-1, Mumbai has preferred an appeal before the Hon'ble National Company Law Appellate Tribunal (NCLAT).

Composite scheme of arrangement in brief

'Reliance Jio Infocomm Limited' had issued 1,300 preference shares of Rs. 10 each at a premium of Rs. 40 each to its holding company, 'Reliance Industries Ltd.' (RIL), aggregating to Rs. 65,000 crore. These funds were inter alia utilized for investment in the optic fiber and tower infrastructure undertakings.

Under the Scheme, amongst other, the preference share capital and corresponding share premium would be cancelled and converted into an equivalent amount of loans from 'Reliance Industries Ltd.' to 'Reliance Jio Infocomm Limited' (Rs. 7,822 crore), 'Jio Digital Fibre Private Limited' (Rs. 45,342 crore) and 'Reliance Jio Infratel Private Limited' (Rs.11,836 crore).

In brief, preference share capital including its premium amount was converted to equivalent amount of loans though composite scheme of arrangement.

Legal Issues before the Tribunal

A plain reading the instant case of Reliance Jio bring to the mind the following aspects –

(i)

Power of the sanctioning court.

(ii)

Whether preference shares including its premium can be cancelled and converted into loans.

(iii)

Whether Income Tax department can raise objection that scheme was used as a tool to evade and avoid tax.

(iv)

Whether evasion/avoidance of tax can be a ground of objection in an application for approving Scheme of Arrangement.

In the instant case, preference shares including premium amount was worth Rs.65,000 crore was converted into loans through composite scheme of arrangement.

Power of the Court/Tribunal

In order to reduce the burden of the High Courts, the Companies Act, 2013 has rightfully shifted the power to approve the scheme arrangement to Tribunal.

A plain reading of Section 230 inter alia reveals that where majority of persons representing three-fourths in value of the creditors/class of creditors or members/class of members agree to any compromise or arrangement and if it is sanctioned by the Tribunal by an order, the same shall be binding on the Company, members and creditors, as the case may be.

Arguments against the Scheme

In the appeal filed by the Income-tax Department, it was amongst others submitted that -

(i)

Tribunal has not dealt with specific objection that conversion of preference shares by cancelling them and converting them into loan, it would substantially reduce the profitability of Demerged Company/ 'Reliance Jio Infocomm Limited' which would act as a tool to avoid and evade taxes.

(ii)

The proposed composite scheme of arrangement amounts to reduction in profitability would also bring down the payment of dividend distribution tax which is again a way to avoid payment of taxes. The structure of proposed composite scheme was a permissible method of tax planning or is a tool to avoid and evade payment of taxes.

(iii)

By scheme of arrangement, the transferor company has sought to convert the redeemable preference shares into loans i.e. conversion of equity into debt which is not only contrary to the well settled principles of company law as well as Section 55 of the Companies Act, 2013 but also would reduce the profitability or the net total income of the transferor company causing a huge loss of revenue to the Income Tax Department.

1.23.11 Applicability to Court sanctioned schemes A question that arises is whether the provisions of Chapter XA would apply to a transaction or a scheme approved by a Court. To illustrate, an amalgamation or demerger is effective only upon the order of the High Court under section 394 of the Companies Act, 1956. Can such Court approved scheme be declared as an IAA? According to one view, this is permissible:

(a) the definition of arrangement is very wide and includes schemes; hence, on a literal reading, even a Court approved Scheme could be considered as an arrangement.

(b) the following cases show that a Court approved scheme could be challenged on the ground of tax avoidance:

(i) Marshall Sons & Co. (India) Ltd. v. ITO [1996] 89 Taxman 619/[1997] 223 ITR 809 (SC)

"We, however, make it clear that we have not expressed any opinion on the plea of learned counsel for the Revenue that the amalgamation itself is a device designed to evade the taxes legitimately payable by the subsidiary company. If the income-tax authorities think that they are entitled to raise this question in the proceedings under the Income-tax Act, it is open to them to do so by way of a separate proceeding according to law."

(ii) A. J. Shetty & Co. (P) Ltd. v. Asstt. CIT [ITA No. 2392/Bang./04] (Source : Lexsite, LexDoc ID : 333155)

In the context of spin off prior to introduction of demerger provisions with effect from assessment year 2000-01, the Tribunal observed that if the transaction is for the purposes of avoiding any tax, then the Capital Gain may be liable.

(c) The Ministry of Finance has also clarified as follows :

"The approval of High Court or Supreme Court is with specific objective and may not take into account tax avoidance issues and circumstances which are relevant at the time of GAAR" (para 15.31 of the SC Report)

According to the other view, a duly approved scheme cannot be challenged subsequently on the ground that it was effected as a tax planning device.

(a) See Asstt. CIT v. Gautam Sarabhai Trust No. 23 [2002] 81 ITD 677 (Ahd. - Trib.)

"Various amalgamations and mergers have been duly approved by the High Court and after such amalgamations have been sanctioned as made in conformity with the requirements under the Companies Act, no such allegation of tax planning or tax evasion can be levelled by the Revenue against the assessee. While according sanction the High Court has duly considered that the scheme of amalgamation is in public interest which essentially implies that the amalgamation is not motivated by consideration of capital gains tax."

(b) It is now well-settled that a scheme under section 394 will not be approved by a Court unless it is in public interest. Tax avoidance is certainly not in public interest, [Wood Polymer Ltd., In re [1977] 109 ITR 177 (Guj.)]; hence, if a Court has approved a scheme, it would mean that tax avoidance which is detrimental to public interest was not its main purpose and GAAR cannot be invoked.

(c) The position could be even more appropriate in a case where the Court has issued notice to the Income Tax Department and the Court has considered the objections of the Income tax department or where the income tax department has not responded at all to a Court notice.

(d) In Wood Polymer Ltd., In re [1977] 109 ITR 177 (Guj.), the Court did not approve a scheme of amalgamation which was primarily for tax avoidance. In Vodafone Essar Gujarat Ltd., In re [2012] 342 ITR 135 (Guj), it was held that if a transaction is intended solely to avoid income-tax, stamp duty and VAT, the scheme cannot be sanctioned under sections 391 to 394 of the Companies Act.

These judgments suggest that consideration of tax avoidance is within the realm of powers of a Court.

The matter is not free from doubt. One may also need to see whether the Court approved scheme can be assailed as aggressive tax planning or satisfying the intent behind the introduction of GAAR as specified in the Finance Minister's Speech/Explanatory Memorandum (see para 1.2).

1.23.12 Specific Anti Avoidance Regulations (SAAR) v. General Anti Avoidance Regulations (GAAR)

At various places, the Act has specific anti-avoidance provisions. To illustrate, section 2(22)(e) provides for taxation of loans and advances to specified shareholders as dividend income.

On a plain reading, it appears that Chapter XA could apply to such SAAR also. This is because:

(i) Section 95 provides that GAAR will apply notwithstanding anything contained in the Act.

1.23.11 Applicability to Court sanctioned schemes A question that arises is whether the provisions of Chapter XA would apply to a transaction or a scheme approved by a Court. To illustrate, an amalgamation or demerger is effective only upon the order of the High Court under section 394 of the Companies Act, 1956. Can such Court approved scheme be declared as an IAA? According to one view, this is permissible:

(a) the definition of arrangement is very wide and includes schemes; hence, on a literal reading, even a Court approved Scheme could be considered as an arrangement.

(b) the following cases show that a Court approved scheme could be challenged on the ground of tax avoidance:

(i) Marshall Sons & Co. (India) Ltd. v. ITO [1996] 89 Taxman 619/[1997] 223 ITR 809 (SC)

"We, however, make it clear that we have not expressed any opinion on the plea of learned counsel for the Revenue that the amalgamation itself is a device designed to evade the taxes legitimately payable by the subsidiary company. If the income-tax authorities think that they are entitled to raise this question in the proceedings under the Income-tax Act, it is open to them to do so by way of a separate proceeding according to law."

(ii) A. J. Shetty & Co. (P) Ltd. v. Asstt. CIT [ITA No. 2392/Bang./04] (Source : Lexsite, LexDoc ID : 333155)

In the context of spin off prior to introduction of demerger provisions with effect from assessment year 2000-01, the Tribunal observed that if the transaction is for the purposes of avoiding any tax, then the Capital Gain may be liable.

(c) The Ministry of Finance has also clarified as follows :

"The approval of High Court or Supreme Court is with specific objective and may not take into account tax avoidance issues and circumstances which are relevant at the time of GAAR" (para 15.31 of the SC Report)

According to the other view, a duly approved scheme cannot be challenged subsequently on the ground that it was effected as a tax planning device.

(a) See Asstt. CIT v. Gautam Sarabhai Trust No. 23 [2002] 81 ITD 677 (Ahd. - Trib.)

"Various amalgamations and mergers have been duly approved by the High Court and after such amalgamations have been sanctioned as made in conformity with the requirements under the Companies Act, no such allegation of tax planning or tax evasion can be levelled by the Revenue against the assessee. While according sanction the High Court has duly considered that the scheme of amalgamation is in public interest which essentially implies that the amalgamation is not motivated by consideration of capital gains tax."

(b) It is now well-settled that a scheme under section 394 will not be approved by a Court unless it is in public interest. Tax avoidance is certainly not in public interest, [Wood Polymer Ltd., In re [1977] 109 ITR 177 (Guj.)]; hence, if a Court has approved a scheme, it would mean that tax avoidance which is detrimental to public interest was not its main purpose and GAAR cannot be invoked.

(c) The position could be even more appropriate in a case where the Court has issued notice to the Income Tax Department and the Court has considered the objections of the Income tax department or where the income tax department has not responded at all to a Court notice.

(d) In Wood Polymer Ltd., In re [1977] 109 ITR 177 (Guj.), the Court did not approve a scheme of amalgamation which was primarily for tax avoidance. In Vodafone Essar Gujarat Ltd., In re [2012] 342 ITR 135 (Guj), it was held that if a transaction is intended solely to avoid income-tax, stamp duty and VAT, the scheme cannot be sanctioned under sections 391 to 394 of the Companies Act.

These judgments suggest that consideration of tax avoidance is within the realm of powers of a Court.

The matter is not free from doubt. One may also need to see whether the Court approved scheme can be assailed as aggressive tax planning or satisfying the intent behind the introduction of GAAR as specified in the Finance Minister's Speech/Explanatory Memorandum (see para 1.2).

The petitioner-company's banking business was nationalised on 19-7-1969. Pursuant to the acquisition, the company, by a circular, gave option to its shareholders, to sell to it shares held by them in it. Before issuing the circular, the company had obtained legal opinion of a former Chief Justice of India, to the effect that the amount payable by the company, for the purchase of its own shares could not be considered as 'deemed dividend' within the meaning of section 2(22)(d). Furthermore, to put the matter beyond doubt, the company had addressed a letter to the Central Board of Direct Taxes (CBDT), seeking their confirmation that the impugned payment sought to be made would not be 'deemed dividend'. The Board, however, refused to give any decision in the matter, on the ground that there was no provision for any 'advance ruling' on a reference. Meanwhile, the Life Insurance Corporation of India (LIC), which was among the major shareholders of the company, expressed the opinion that the company need not treat the difference between the sale price and the face value of the shares as 'dividend' and, therefore, it had no right to deduct tax on such payment at source.

Thereafter, the shares of face value of Rs. 10, were purchased by the company, by the device of reduction of its capital, for Rs. 50 per share, but the shareholders were paid on the basis of Rs. 33.10 per share, and the balance of Rs. 6.90 per share was retained by the petitioner, on the specific condition and undertaking that the company, would be entitled to treat it as 'tax deducted at source' in case it was ultimately held to be subject to tax, failing which, the retained amount would be paid to the erstwhile shareholders. In this situation, the LIC and the petitioner, filed a suit under Order XXXVI, rule 1, of the Code of Civil Procedure, to the High Court for a decision of the question as to whether the impugned payment could be considered deemed dividend or not. Notice of the suit was also issued to the revenue. The suit was, however, adjourned sine die on the objection of the revenue that the question could only be deciding in proceeding under the Income-tax Act and not in any suit.

The ITO, thereafter, issued a notice under section 201 to the petitioner and rejecting its contention, in reply, that the impugned payment could not be termed as 'deemed dividend' within the meaning of section 2(22)(d) as the amount was the purchase price and no amount by way of dividend was paid on the reduction of share capital, held that the company was in default under section 201 for not depositing the tax as found due by him. On appeal, the AAC partly allowed the appeal of the company. Before the Tribunal, the order of the AAC was challenged both by the company, as well as by the revenue. The Tribunal accepted the company's appeal and set aside the order of the ITO and of the AAC, on the ground that the proceedings against the company were barred by limitation. The Tribunal also rejected the revenue's application for reference. The High Court, also rejected the revenue's application for calling a reference. Thereupon, the revenue claimed to have filed a petition for special leave in the Supreme Court but it was still to come up for preliminary hearing.

Meanwhile, three different Benches of the abovementioned Tribunal, by their orders, arising out of independent proceedings in the assessment of income of three different shareholders, who had received the amount pursuant to the sale of their shares, held that amounts received by them could not be treated as 'deemed dividend' but were taxable in their hands as 'capital gains' on the sale of the shares. These orders were not challenged by the revenue and had, therefore, become final, since the limitation for a challenge had, by then, expired.

The sole issue involved in this case is, whether the addition can be made in the book profit under section 115JB on account of shares sold by the assessee, which was held as 'capital reserve', which the Assessing Officer and Commissioner (Appeals) have treated on account of amount standing in revalued reserve relating to revaluation of assets in terms of clause (j) of Explanation 1 of section 115JB. Two subsidiary companies of the assessee, PREPL and PPPL were amalgamated with the assessee company being holding company, vide judgment and order of High court, wherein the Court has sanctioned the scheme of amalgamation. First of all it would be quite pertinent to note the relevant clauses of scheme of amalgamation which are important for the purpose of adjudication of present controversy. The relevant clauses dealing with accounting standard and purchase method adopted for valuing the assets and liabilities at a fair market value and how any excess on such transfer of assets and liabilities has to be treated as part of the capital reserve, which reads as that on the scheme becoming effective and with effect from the appointed date, transferee company shall account for amalgamation of transferor company no. 1 and transferor company no. 2 in its books of account as per the 'purchase Method' specified under the Accounting Standard 14 - 'Accounting for Amalgamation'. All the assets and liabilities of transferor company No. 1 and transferor company No. 2 shall be transferred to and vested in transferee company pursuant to this scheme and shall be recorded at their respective fair values. Any excess arising on transfer of assets and liabilities of transferor company no. 1 and transferor company no. 2 would be considered to form part of the "capital reserve" of transferee company. Such capital reserve shall be a reserve which arises pursuant to this scheme and shall not be, for any purpose, be considered to be a reserve created by transferee company. Any deficit shall be considered to form part of goodwill. [Para 13]

Aforesaid scheme thus clearly provides that, firstly, the 'purchase method' as prescribed in AS-14 was adopted stating that the transferee company shall account for amalgamation of transferor companies in its books of account; secondly, all assets and liabilities of the transferor companies shall be transferred and would be recorded in the respective fair values; and lastly, any excess arising on transfer of assets and liabilities of the transferor companies would be considered to form part of the "capital reserves" of the transferee company and such capital reserve shall not be for any purpose be considered to be a reserve created by the transferee company. Ergo, and if there is an excess on account of valuation on purchase method determining the fair market value was to form part of the capital reserve and no other mandate was given to the transferee company. The shares of IHFL was held by the amalgamating companies which has been transferred to the assessee-company and thus, it was akin to acquisition of an asset which as per the mandate of amalgamation scheme has to be treated as part of the capital reserve. Now, this scheme has been duly approved by High Court. In the conclusion of the said order, Court has specifically observed that any person interested shall be at liberty to apply to the court in the above matter for any directions that may be necessary. The said order of High Court sanctioning the entire amalgamation scheme had become final. It is further seen that vide General Circular No. 1 of 2014 issued by Ministry of Corporate Affairs to all Regional Directions and Registrars of Companies and all stake holders and notices were issued to all the concerned parties including the Income Tax Department. [Para 14]

Thereafter, High Court had also issued notices to the Income Tax Department through Assessing Officer which was received in the office of the Assessing Officer. The Assessing Officer/ Department nowhere had objected to said Scheme at any point of time, neither in pursuance of circular issued by Ministry of Corporate Affairs nor when the notice was issued by the High Court. Thus, scheme of amalgamation sanction by High court had become final. Such an order has a binding effect upon all. Once the amalgamation scheme has been approved and sanctioned by the Court, it has a statutory force and is binding on the company and all the stake holders.Thus, when amalgamation scheme has been approved by the Court, it is not open for the Assessing Officer and Commissioner (Appeals) to hold that amalgamation has been used by the assessee-company as a tool for tax evasion. The amalgamation order passed by the High Court is a judicial order and has statutory force and in case, the department had any objection, then same should have been given before the High Court for which sufficient time was allowed. Now, the department cannot clamour that such an amalgamation have been used by the assessee as a tool for tax evasion or as colourable device. [Para 15]

The calculation of capital gains under this provision shall be done as per section 72 (corresponding to Section 48 of the ITA 1961), which provides as follows: For the taxability under this provision, the trigger points will be:

(a)

There is a buyback [see Para 6.2-4a].

(b)

Such a buyback is of shares or specified securities [see Para 6.2-4b].

(c)

Such a buyback is done by a company [see Para 6.2-4c].

(d)

Consideration is received by a shareholder or holder of securities [see Para 6.2-4d].

6.2-4a Meaning of the 'buyback' - The provision does not specify any condition under which the company should buy back shares. Thus, a buyback by a domestic company under sections 68, 230 to 232, or 242 of the Companies Act, 2013, or by a foreign company, will be taxable under this provision.

However, any reduction of capital by the company under section 66(1)(b) of the Companies Act, 2013, could not be equated to share buyback4 and thus will not be taxable under this provision. Therefore, any distribution to its shareholders by a company on reduction of its capital to the extent to which the company possesses accumulated profits is deemed to be a dividend under section 2(40)(d) [corresponding to section 2(22)(d) of the ITA 1961].

6.2-4b Buyback of shares or securities - To trigger liability under this provision, the buyback by the company should be of its own shares or specified securities.

As per section 2(84) of the Companies Act, 2013, "share" means a share in the share capital of a company and includes stock. Thus, the "shares" can be listed or unlisted, equity or preference shares, and their buyback will be taxable under this provision. Even redemption of preference shares will be taxable under this provision5.

The specified securities shall mean as defined in Explanation I to section 68 of the Companies Act, 2013, which includes employees' stock option or other securities as may be notified by the Central Government from time to time.

6.2-4c Applicable to a company - Under the provisions, the taxability arises from payments made by a Company, as defined in Section 2(28) of the ITA 2025 (corresponding to Section 2(17) of the ITA 1961). Based on the definition of the company under section 2(28), it could be said that the capital gains will arise on the buyback of shares by the following entities:

(a)

A company (private or public) incorporated and registered in India;

(b)

A company incorporated and registered outside India (foreign company);

(c)

A corporation established by or under a Central, State or Provincial Act;

(d)

Any institution, association or body declared by CBDT to be a company under section 2(17);

(e)

Any other entity declared by the Board to be a company, as assessed as a company under the Act or the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922.

6.2-4d Taxability at the time of the payment of consideration - There are three stages in the buyback of shares:

(a)

Pre-buyback activities

(b)

Buyback activities

(c)

Post buyback activities

The pre-buyback activities include passing the resolution, announcing the offer, filing the letter of offer and solvency, dispatching the letter of offer, etc. In buyback activities, the company verifies and accepts the offer within 15 days of the offer's closure date and pays consideration to the shareholders. The post-buyback activities include extinguishing the shares bought back, filing Form SH-11 with the ROC, and maintaining a register of buybacks in Form SH-10.

No taxable event shall arise during the pre-buyback activities. It should happen when the company finishes the buyback activities, which include verification, acceptance of the shareholders' offer to sell shares for buyback, and payment to the shareholders.

This was resisted by the company on which the bankers of the company received a notice under section 226(3) of the Act to the effect that the aforesaid amount was due from the company and required the bankers to pay the ITO concerned forthwith, out of any amount held in any of the accounts of the company. The ITO thereafter called upon the company to show cause why the entire amount paid to the shareholders be not treated as 'deemed dividend' in terms of section 2(22)(d) and why the company should not be treated in default for failing to deposit the tax deducted at source from the amount paid to the shareholders. The company sent its reply to the notice, inter alia, contending that the payment of the amount could not be termed as 'deemed dividend' as the amount was the purchase price and no amount by way of dividend was paid on the reduction of share capital. Certain other contentions were also raised. The ITO, however, turned down the plea of the company and by an order made on 25-9-1975 held that the payment made for the purchase of shares to some of the erstwhile shareholders was 'deemed dividend' and the company was in default under section 201 for not depositing the tax, as found due by him. The order was challenged by the company in appeal before the AAC. The AAC partly allowed the appeal and the appellate order was challenged by the company as well as the revenue, before the Tribunal. The Tribunal by its order of 27-3-1979 accepted the appeal of the company and set aside the orders of the ITO and the appellate order of the AAC on the ground that the proceedings against the company were barred by limitation. The appeal of the revenue was dismissed. The Tribunal also rejected the revenue's application for stating a case and referring certain questions of law to this Court. This Court also rejected the revenue's application for calling a reference on 4-1-1982. The order of the Tribunal has, therefore, become final unless it was taken in appeal to the Supreme Court by a petition for Special Leave. The counsel for the respondent claimed that a petition for Special Leave had been filed in the Supreme Court but it was still to come up for preliminary hearing. In the context of spin off prior to introduction of demerger provisions with effect from assessment year 2000-01, the Tribunal observed that if the transaction is for the purposes of avoiding any tax, then the Capital Gain may be liable.

(c)

The Ministry of Finance has also clarified as follows :

"The approval of High Court or Supreme Court is with specific objective and may not take into account tax avoidance issues and circumstances which are relevant at the time of GAAR" (para 15.31 of the SC Report)

According to the other view, a duly approved scheme cannot be challenged subsequently on the ground that it was effected as a tax planning device.

(a)

See Asstt. CIT v. Gautam Sarabhai Trust No. 23 [2002] 81 ITD 677 (Ahd. - Trib.)

"Various amalgamations and mergers have been duly approved by the High Court and after such amalgamations have been sanctioned as made in conformity with the requirements under the Companies Act, no such allegation of tax planning or tax evasion can be levelled by the Revenue against the assessee. While according sanction the High Court has duly considered that the scheme of amalgamation is in public interest which essentially implies that the amalgamation is not motivated by consideration of capital gains tax."

(b)

It is now well-settled that a scheme under section 394 will not be approved by a Court unless it is in public interest. Tax avoidance is certainly not in public interest, [Wood Polymer Ltd., In re [1977] 109 ITR 177 (Guj.)]; hence, if a Court has approved a scheme, it would mean that tax avoidance which is detrimental to public interest was not its main purpose and GAAR cannot be invoked.

(c)

The position could be even more appropriate in a case where the Court has issued notice to the Income Tax Department and the Court has considered the objections of the Income tax department or where the income tax department has not responded at all to a Court notice.

(d)

In Wood Polymer Ltd., In re [1977] 109 ITR 177 (Guj.), the Court did not approve a scheme of amalgamation which was primarily for tax avoidance. In Vodafone Essar Gujarat Ltd., In re [2012] 342 ITR 135 (Guj), it was held that if a transaction is intended solely to avoid income-tax, stamp duty and VAT, the scheme cannot be sanctioned under sections 391 to 394 of the Companies Act.

These judgments suggest that consideration of tax avoidance is within the realm of powers of a Court.

The matter is not free from doubt. One may also need to see whether the Court approved scheme can be assailed as aggressive tax planning or satisfying the intent behind the introduction of GAAR as specified in the Finance Minister's Speech/Explanatory Memorandum (seepara 1.2).

1.23.12 Specific Anti Avoidance Regulations (SAAR) v. General Anti Avoidance Regulations (GAAR)

At various places, the Act has specific anti-avoidance provisions. To illustrate, section 2(22)(e) provides for taxation of loans and advances to specified shareholders as dividend income.

On a plain reading, it appears that Chapter XA could apply to such SAAR also. This is because:

(i)

Section 95 provides that GAAR will apply notwithstanding anything contained in the Act.

(ii)

Section 100 provides that the provisions of Chapter XA shall apply in addition to, or in lieu of any other basis for determination of tax liability.

(iii)

The Explanatory Memorandum also provides that these provisions can be used in addition to or in conjunction with other anti avoidance provisions or provisions for determination of tax liability, which are provided in the taxation law.

In view of the above the impugned provision of section 2(6A)(d) was within the legislative competence of the Central Legislature and was within the ambit of entry No. 54 of List I of the said Seventh Schedule not only in form but also in substance. As regards the assessability of "distribution of dividend" in the assessment year 1956-57; the controversy linged upon the meaning of the word "distribution" as used in section 2(6A)(d). The word "distribution" connotes "to deal out or bestow in portions or shares among many; to allot or apportion as one’s share." "Distribution" is not merely an act of dividing or apportioning but also dispensing or dealing out. The act of "distribution" has to be actual and not notional; physical and not mental. A resolution or decision to distribute is not "distribution" as there is no giving out, dispensing or disbursement involved. "Distribution" connotes two acts a "division" and "delivery". The word ‘distributed’ occurs in section 16(2). In that section three words are used: "paid, credited or distributed" and, according to well-known canons of statutory interpretation, each expression is to be given a distinct meaning. The word "credited" is used when an entry on the credit side of an account is made. It does not signify actual dealing out. A thing is said to be "paid" when something is given which need not be first apportioned and then disbursed. The word "distributed" is used in the sense of division and delivery. The expression which follows the word "distributed", namely, "deemed to have been . . . distributed" is significant. "Deemed" in this context means "supposed". When a thing is deemed to be distributed, it means that though in fact it is not distributed yet it will be considered or treated as if it had been distributed. If the word "distribute" were to signify a mental decision, or even a book entry, the use of the word "deemed" would perhaps be superfluous. The use of the word "distributed" in section 16(2) suggests that it refers to actual distribution or delivery. In other words, distribution is being considered in the factual and not in the notional sense, and distribution is the sequence of reduction of capital. In the phrase occurring in section 2(6A)(d) "any distribution by a company on the reduction of its capital", the preposition "on" means "after". As the act of distribution is not notional, reduction of capital does not imply contemporaneous distribution. It is a subsequent process after reduction of capital for purpose of contention of the word ‘distribution’ occurring in section 2(6A)(d ), the provisions of section 13 cannot be of any guide. In the instant case, the company sent a circular notice on 5-11-1954, to its shareholders requesting them to send their shares certificates to the company at an early date for necessary endorsement and refund of share capital. They were also informed that the share transfer register of the company would remain closed from 16-11-1954 to 30-11-1954 (inclusive). It may be mentioned that no entry regarding distribution was made in the accounting year which ended on 30-11-1954. In the balance sheet for the period ended 30-11-1954, the directors, in their report to the shareholders, made the following recommendation as to the payment of dividend. "to pay dividend or the year at 7¼% per annum Rs. 1,81,250". Against the words "capital issued, subscribed and paid up", the figure was Rs. 25,00,000 and not Rs. 15,00,000. A personal of this balance sheet did not give any indication either of the reduction of the capital or the consequent distribution of Rs. 15,00,000. Thus, the position shown in the company’s own account books was that the paid-up capital for the period which ended on 30-11-1954, was still Rs. 25,00,000 and this would not have been the case if any steps had been taken to distribute the money on reduction of capital. The fact, however, was that no distribution had taken place even up to 5-6-1955. From this, it was to be concluded that the accumulated profits as dividend were deemed to have been distributed in the assessment year 1956-57, because the debits of refunds were actually made in the accounts of the shareholders and the refunds were actually granted to the shareholders during the accounting period of the assessment year 1956-57. The contention of the assessee-company that the dividend was deemed to have been distributed in the accounting year to 1954-55, corresponding to the assessment year 1955-56, could not prevail and was, therefore, to be rejected notwithstanding the accounts of company being maintained on mercantile basis.

Note : The case was decided against the assessee.

The assessee-company did distribute, by way of dividends, more than 60 per cent of its assessable income for the previous years, corresponding to the assessment years in question 1953-54 and 1954-55. The department, however, felt that the proviso to sub-section (1) of section 23A applied and 100 per cent of its assessable income in both the years should have been distributed. The assessee's capital was Rs. 5 lakhs. The reserves however as per department was more than Rs. 5 lakhs constituting general reserve, reserve for taxation and reserve for dividends.

So far as the 'general reserve' was concerned, there was no dispute that it would constitute a reserve representing accumulation of past profits within the meaning of the proviso. As regards the item of 'reserve for taxation', the ITO held that the whole amount should be treated as a reserve within the meaning of the proviso to section 23A(1), but the AAC took the view that only the difference between the amount set apart to provide for taxation less the actual tax payable would be the amount which could be said to be the 'reserve'. Accordingly he held that only Rs. 35,686 for the assessment year 1953-54 and Rs. 29,863 for the assessment year 1954-55 could be taken as reserve for taxation. This view was confirmed by the Tribunal in its order. Therefore, the actual figures which had to be taken towards reserves under the proviso so far as the 'reserve for taxation' was concerned, were Rs. 35,686 and Rs. 29,863 for the two respective years. The dividend reserve was the same figure, namely, Rs. 2,25,000 for the first year and Rs. 1,75,000 for the second year. The figure of the amount in the profit and loss account according to the department was Rs. 2,98,676 for the first year and Rs. 4,26,248 for the second year.

The ITO held as regards both the years that the figures mentioned in profit and loss account amounted to a reserve. He held that the assessee was showing a relatively large amount as profit and loss account balance and was definitely making 'an attempt to avoid application of the proviso to section 23A(1)'. The AAC held that the balance in the profit and loss account would amount to a reserve but after deduction of such amounts as were deemed to be dividends under section 23A(1). He, therefore, held that the amounts of dividends under section 23A of Rs. 1,23,183 in each of the two years should be deducted from the figure mentioned in the profit and loss account and the balance should be held to be a reserve representing accumulations of past profits within the meaning of the proviso.

When the matter came before the Tribunal they held that the entire amount mentioned in the profit and loss account was nothing more than undistributed profits which had not been 'crystallised' in the sense that these profits had not been appropriated to any reserve fund by the company and, therefore, they could not be said to be 'reserves' at all.

2. IS SHARE INFUSION AN 'INTERNATIONAL TRANSACTION'?

Section 922 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 (the Act) requires that any income, allowance for any expenses (including allocations) and allowance for any interest, arising out of international transactions should be computed having regard to the arm's length price.

The question is whether share infusion falls within the definition of the term 'international transaction' under section 92B of the Act. It may be mentioned that the term 'international transaction' as originally defined covered a wide gamut of transactions (including transactions having a bearing on assets) entered into between two associated enterprises (out of which, at least one should be a non-resident). By the Finance Act, 2010, an explanation was added to further extend the scope of this term. This extended definition was made retrospectively effective from the day the Indian Transfer Pricing Regulations were introduced i.e. April 1, 2001.

This extended definition includes a clause, which reads as follows:

'(e) a transaction of business restructuring or reorganisation, entered into by an enterprise with an associated enterprise, irrespective of the fact that it has bearing on the profit, income, losses or assets of such enterprises at the time of the transaction or at any future date'

The term 'business restructuring' or 'reorganisation' have not been defined in the Act and hence prone to a wider interpretation. It is possible that the tax department may seek to infer that these terms cover any change in shareholding, including share infusion. Even without resorting to the extension of the definition, a view is possible that 'share' is a form of an 'assets' and hence, any change in the value of shares, would impact the assets of a taxpayer. Therefore, it can be said that share infusion stands covered by the original definition of the term international transaction.

While examining taxation of any transaction, normally, a two-stepped approach is adopted. The first step is to examine whether the transaction is giving rise to 'income' under the applicable tax laws and whether that income is liable to taxation in that particular jurisdiction. If the answer to these questions is yes, then the income needs to be characterized in accordance with the tax law, as there may be differences in approach of taxing different types of income. The second step concerns valuation/quantification of the transaction under consideration. If the parties to the transaction are associated enterprises, then the quantification of income has to be in accordance with the transfer pricing regulations. Recently, this basic approach of taxation has been a subject matter of intense discussion in India, for the reason that the tax department took a position that shares infused at a price lower than the arm's length price (as determined by the tax department), would give rise to income taxable in India.

The prime contention of the tax department is that the difference between the arm's length price of shares (so determined) and the price at which shares were issued by an Indian company to the associated enterprise (AE), is income liable to taxation in India. In some cases, the said shortfall (i.e. difference between the issue price and the arm's length price so determined) was also considered as an amount outstanding with the AE i.e. loan recoverable from the AE, requiring additional payment of interest to the Indian company.

Expectedly, the additions made by the tax authorities has drawn loud protest from the business community, particularly foreign investors interested in investing in India. It is argued that infusion of shares is an investment and cannot be held to be income neither as per international understanding, nor as per the Indian taxation law. This issue is yet to be decided by an Income Tax Appellate Tribunal (ITAT) or higher judicial bodies. In this Article, the authors have analyzed various aspects of this controversy.

1. ISSUE BEFORE THE BOMBAY HIGH COURT

The question of taxability of share infusion was recently raised before the Bombay High Court in the case of Vodafone India Services Private Limited (VISPL) by way of a Writ Petition1. The brief facts of the case were that, VISPL, a wholly owned subsidiary of Vodafone Tele Services (India) Holdings Limited, Mauritius, during Financial Year 2008-09, issued 2,89,224 equity shares to the latter. The price charged per share was INR 8,601 (INR 10 being the face value plus a premium of INR 8,591per share), which was determined in accordance with the method prescribed by the Capital Issues Control Act, 1947. The total consideration for this issue of shares thus recorded in the books of account of VISPL was INR 2,463.8 Million.

This transaction of issue of shares was disclosed to the tax department by VISPL in the Accountants Report (i.e. Form No. 3CEB) by way of a note, which stated that issue of shares having no bearing on the income is being reported only as a matter of abundant caution.

During the course of audit proceedings, the Assessing Officer (AO) referred the determination of arm's length price of the aforesaid transaction to the Transfer Pricing Officer (TPO). The TPO opined that the valuation of shares needs to be carried out on Net Asset Value basis, after considering the transfer pricing adjustments in preceding years.

Accordingly, the TPO computed the arm's length price of each share at INR 53,775, resulting in shortfall of INR 13,089.1 Million appurtenant to the issue price of shares. The amalgamation order passed by the High Court is a judicial order and has statutory force and in case, the department had any objection, then same should have been given before the High Court for which sufficient time was allowed. Now, the department cannot clamour that such an amalgamation have been used by the assessee as a tool for tax evasion or as colourable device. [Para 15] Here in this case, by transferring the excess fair market value of the assets/shares to capital reserve could not be treated as a tax evasion practice. The difference between the fair market value of assets and liabilities taken over as per the book values, which has resulted in 'capital reserve', was recorded in the books. As per said scheme itself, such capital reserve was prohibited for any purpose by the transferee company, thus, such a creation of capital reserve cannot be questioned by the Assessing Officer or Commissioner (Appeals) or perceive it as any kind of tax evasion practice. Here in this case, the assets transferred to the assessee company from transferor companies pursuant to scheme of amalgamation, included 1,06,39,926 shares of IHFL. The fair market value of the said shares on the date of amalgamation was Rs. 456.47 per share which aggregated to Rs. 485.68 crores. Post amalgamation, the assessee company had sold 20,42,053 shares of IHFL out of 1,06,39,926 shares acquired on amalgamation, which was sold for consideration of Rs.453.88 per share resulting into a short term capital loss of Rs. 52.69 lakhs. Said loss has been included in the profit and loss account. The Assessing Officer has alleged that this reserve which has been created is on account of revaluation of assets and since during the relevant previous year such revalued assets has been disposed of and such amount which is standing as reserve was not credited in the profit and loss account. [Para 16]

Such a premise of the Assessing Officer cannot be approved for the reason that; firstly, this reserve has not been created on revaluation of asset albeit same has been acquired through amalgamation and the shares have been valued as per the purchase method for a certain price. Secondly, it is not revaluation of any asset held by the assessee, because no such reserve has been created by the assessee on revaluation of shares and revaluation of assets takes place only when the assessee decides to revalue the asset existing in the balance sheet. Lastly, in this case all the assets belonged to amalgamating companies, that is, the shares of IHFL originally belonged to PREPL and PPPL and appeared in their balance sheet; and these assets entered in the books of assessee by virtue of amalgamation valued on fair market value as mandated by the order of High Court. Thus, it would be wrong to say that there was any kind of revaluation of assets. Therefore, there could not be any question of invoking clause (j) of Explanation to section 115JB for calculation of book profit under section 115JB. Here in this case, nowhere it has been disputed that the profit and loss account has not been prepared in compliance of requirement of Part-I and Part-II of the Companies Act, 2013 and as per accounting standard. The profit and loss account has been approved by the statutory auditors and also laid before the Members in the AGM, which is sacrosanct for computing the book profit under section 115JB. Thus, once the accounts have been prepared in accordance with the Companies Act duly certified by statutory auditors and approved by Company AGM, then same cannot be disturbed. Here the Assessing Officer cannot tinker with such profit and loss account or treat the part of capital reserve by holding that it should have been routed through regular profit and loss account. [Para 17]

Thus, in this case the provisions of clause (j) of Explanation 1 to section 115JB would not be applicable at all as, there is no disposal of asset from the amount standing in revaluation reserve relating to revalued asset as per the reasoning given above; and accordingly, the addition made by the Assessing Officer and sustained by the Commissioner (Appeals) is directed to be deleted. [Para 19]

The Court has power to sanction all matters which for their effectuation require a special procedure to be followed under the Act. The only exception to this is the special procedure to be followed under section 101 for reduction of capital since rule 85 of the Court Rules specifically enjoins the following of a special procedure prescribed for reduction of share capital. [Para 19] The opening words of section 77A, viz., "notwithstanding anything, contained in this Act, but subject to the provisions of sub-section (2) of this section and section 77B, a company may purchase its own shares or other specified securities...." show that section 77A is a facilitating provision which enables the companies to buy-back their shares without having to approach the Court under section 391 and sections 100 to 104 subject to compliance with the provisions of sub-sections (2), (3) and (4). Prior to the introduction of section 77A, the only manner in which a company could buy-back its shares was by following the procedure set out under sections 100 to 104 and section 391 which required the calling of separate meetings of each class of shareholders and creditors as well as (if required by the Court) the drawing up of a list of creditors of the company and obtaining of their consent to the scheme for reduction. The legislative intention behind the introduction of section 77A is to provide an alternative method by which a company may buy-back up to 25 per cent of its total paid-up equity capital in any financial year subject to compliance with sub- sections (2), (3) and (4). It does not supplant or take away any part of the pre-existing jurisdiction of the Company Court to sanction a scheme for such reduction under sections 100 to 104 and section 391. [Para 22]

The non obstante clause in section 77A, namely ‘notwithstanding anything contained in this Act....’ only means that notwithstanding the provisions of section 77 and sections 100 to 104, the company can buy-back its shares subject to compliance with the conditions mentioned in that section without approaching the Court under sections 100 to 104 or section 391. There is nothing in the provision of section 77A to indicate that the jurisdiction of the Court under section 391 or 394 has been taken away or substituted. It is well-settled that the exclusion of the jurisdiction of the Court should not readily be inferred; such exclusion should be explicitly or clearly implied. There is nothing in the language of section 77 that gives rise to such an inference. Therefore, section 77A is merely an enabling provision and the Court’s powers under sections 100 to 104 and section 391 are not in any way affected. The conditions provided in section 77A are applicable only to buy-back of shares under section 77A. The conditions applicable to sections 100 to 104 and section 391 cannot be imported into or made applicable to a buy-back under section 77A. Similarly the conditions for a buy-back under section 77A cannot be applied to a scheme under sections 100 to 104 and section 391. The two operate in independent fields. [Para 23]

It is not disputed that reduction in the capital can be effected under section 77 read with sections 100 to 104 and 391 even in the case of buy-back of shares. Even in cases where capital is reduced by optional sale reduction results after the option is exercised to the extent of the shares cancelled. This is as equally a reduction of capital as in the case of compulsory cancellation of shares. There is no distinction between the two on the aspect of the reduction. The word ‘arrangement’ is of wide import and is not restricted to a compulsory purchase or acquisition of shares there is no reason as to why a cancellation of shares and the consequent reduction of capital cannot be covered by section 391 read with section 100 merely because a shareholder is given an option to cancel or to retain his shares. In view of the foregoing discussion, the objection of the appellants based on section 77A must be rejected. [Para 24]

Any interest tax. 1.9-2 Reserves adjustment under Explanation (b)/(i) - One of the adjustments required to be made relates to amounts carried to any reserve by whatever name called. The user of the phrase 'by whatever name called' signifies that the nomenclature given to an amount is of no importance or relevance. If the amount set apart represents a reserve within the meaning of the Schedule, it has to be added back to the net profit.

To illustrate, a company may follow a practice of providing doubtful debts on ad hoc basis and it may be named as 'provision for doubtful debts'. In fact, there may not be any doubtful debts. In other words, the sundry debtors may be realisable at the value stated. In such a case, such setting apart does not constitute a provision within the meaning assigned to it by the Schedule; but, in fact constitutes a reserve as defined in the Schedule. Thus, though it is called a provision, it is a reserve. Therefore, irrespective of the nomenclature, the amount so set apart has to be added back to the profits in terms of Explanation defining book profits.

1.9-2a RESERVES ADJUSTMENT UNDER EXPLANATION (i) - Explanation (i) requires reduction of amount withdrawn from any reserve or provision, if it is credited to profit and loss account.

Such reduction can be made in respect of any reserves or provisions created in respect of any year relevant to assessment year 1997-98 and thereafter only when the amount of such reserves or provision was added back under Explanation (b).

Accordingly, if any reserve has been created in any earlier year and if that is credited to profit and loss account, the adjustment, by way of reduction, under, this Explanation can be made.

1.9-2b CREDIT TO CAPITAL RESERVE - The Special bench of the Tribunal (Calcutta) in Sutlej Cotton Mills Ltd. v. ACIT [1993] 45 ITD 22 was concerned with an adjustment not specifically permitted by section 115J of the Act. The company in that case had revalued its fixed assets in earlier years. In the subsequent year, it revalued all its quoted investments at market value. The difference on revaluation of these shares was credited to capital reserve account. In the next year, relevant to assessment year 1988-89, it sold certain shares. The sale proceeds were not credited to profit and loss account; but were adjusted in the asset account and/or capital reserve account. In the assessment proceedings, the Assessing Officer took a View that the objective of revaluation was to defraud revenue and avoidance of tax under section 115J by changing method of valuation. In the appellate proceedings, the Appellate Authority held that the treatment was not in accordance with para 3(xii)(a)of the Schedule which read as follows:

"Profits or losses on investments showing distinctly the extent of the profits or losses earned or incurred on account of membership of a partnership firm to the extent not adjusted from any previous provision or reserve." [Emphasis supplied]

On the aforesaid facts, the Tribunal held as follows :

The requirement of the Schedule show that it is concerned with the result of the working of the company. Thus, it cannot be directly concerned with changes in capital structure. Profit on realisation of capital assets will not be an item of income.

Company had followed a consistent practice in relation to revaluation of capital assets. The practice adopted was in accordance with para 3(xii)(a) referred above, as a credit to Profit & Loss Account was required to be taken to the extent not adjusted, as provided therein. The practice followed by the company was a sound accounting practice as the profit was not available for distribution. Accordingly, the profit realised cannot form part of book profit.

As per Explanation below section 115J(1A) providing for adjustments, only the permitted adjustments can be made. Beyond that, book profit cannot be adjusted. For the purpose, even section 145 cannot be applied. Accordingly, the Assessing Officer was bound to proceed with computation of book profit as shown in the Profit and Loss Account.

As far as valuation of assets, etc., is concerned, really it cannot be compared with the method of valuation in relation to stock in trade. In any case, section 145 does not apply to revaluation of fixed assets.

The Assessing Officer cannot disturb reserve, which has been adjusted in accordance with requirement of the Schedule and as per the para referred above.

This was not a device for avoidance of tax.

Provisions of section 45, deeming capital gains as income, cannot apply to book profit under section 115J on account of non obstante clause. This is because a deemed income cannot be included as part of book profit.

In the instant case the legal fiction had been created by section 23A for the purpose of taxing in the hands of individual shareholders income which had not been distributed by way of dividends by the company, but which was deemed to have been distributed by the company under the circumstances set out in the said section 23A. This fiction could not be carried in every respect to its logical conclusion. This fiction would not enable the shareholders to demand from the company payment by way of dividends of that which had been deemed to have been distributed under the provisions contained in section 23A. The object of the legislature in enacting section 23A is to tax the shareholder. The head-note to the section indicates the drift of the section.

It could not be denied on the facts of the instant case that the company had in fact distributed amounts in excess of six per cent of its paid-up capital. The company had purported to do so by way of dividends. The distribution had been made out of profits of various previous years. But merely because the distribution had taken place out of the profits of previous years, it could not be said that distribution had not been made during the relevant accounting year 1955.

Merely because an amount is deemed to have been notionally distributed, it could not be said that such amount is therefore incapable of being subsequently distributed as dividend. The fiction created by section 23A which is intended for taxing income in the hands of shareholders could not be extended when taxing the income of a company. The distribution that had been made in the instant case fell within the plain, natural and grammatical meaning of the words used in clause 1(b) of the second proviso to paragraph D of Part II of the schedule to the Finance Act, 1956. There is no reason why when a distribution falls within the language of a provision, one should hold that it does not fall within it.

In the instant case, the year of account was 1955 and the four amounts referred had been distributed during that year. Merely because they happened to be distributed out of the profits of various previous years, it could not be said that the distribution had not been made during the year in which the said amounts have been distributed.

Therefore, the action of the ITO in reducing the rebate allowable to the assessee company under clause (ii) of proviso 1 to paragraph D of Part II of the Schedule to the Finance Act, 1956, in terms of clause 1(b) of proviso 2 of the same paragraph was legal and, the distribution of the dividend during the previous year 1955 was not saved by the orders of the ITO under section 23A in respect of the profits of the previous years 1947, 1948 and 1949 directing that the dividends should be deemed to have been distributed on the respective dates of the annual general meetings falling prior to the previous year 1955.

19. Excess share premium not taxable in hands of closely held co. if its shareholders are relatives: ITAT

[Vaani Estates (P.) Ltd. v. ITO [2018] 98 taxmann.com 92 (Chennai - Trib.)] The assessee-company had only two shareholders 'S' and her husband. On passing away of husband, his shares devolved on their daughter 'V'. The assessee proposed to acquire an immovable property at approximately Rs. 23.09 crores. 'S' brought in money into the company in lieu of allotment of fresh 10,100 shares with a share premium of Rs. 23.31 crores.

The Assessing Officer opined that company had received excess price/share premium for the shares allotted to 'S' over and above the face value of shares. Accordingly, he brought Rs. 23.31 crores to tax in the hands of the company under Section 56(2)(viib).

The ITAT held in favour of assessee as under:

When 'S' introduced money into the company for allotment of shares at an exorbitant premium in contrast to its intrinsic value of just Rs. 10 per share, the benefit of such investment had only passed on to her daughter because there were only two shareholders in the company at that point of time. Had 'S' gifted the money to her daughter 'V' and thereafter if daughter had brought the same into the company for allotment of equity shares at face value, question of invoking of the provisions of section 56(2)(viib) would not have arisen.

Provisions of section 56(2)(viib) couldn't be invoked in the case of the assessee-co. because by virtue of introducing cash in the company by 'S' for allotment of equity shares with unrealistic premium the benefit had only passed on to her daughter 'V' and there was no scope in the Act to tax when cash or asset was transferred by a mother to her daughter.

20. No concealment penalty if assessee has bona fide belief that notional income isn't taxable: ITAT

[DCIT v. Shah Rukh Khan [2018] 93 taxmann.com 320 (Mumbai - Trib.)]

The assessee, Mr. Shah Rukh Khan, had received a villa at Dubai as gift and offered an amount of Rs. 14 lakhs as the notional income of the villa for tax in his return of income for the year under consideration. During the course of assessment proceedings, assessee claimed that Article 6 of India-UAE tax treaty doesn't expressly recognize the right of the resident State to tax the income from immovable property situated in the source State. Therefore, the notional income of the villa owned by him in Dubai could not be subjected to tax in India.

The ITAT held that claim raised by the assessee being clearly backed up by a bonafide belief on his part that the notional income of the villa was not liable to be taxed in India, no penalty for concealment of income could be validly imposed on the assessee.

21. Australia has taxing rights under Australia-India DTAA even if there is no provision in its domestic law: Australian Court

[Satyam Computer Services Ltd. (Now Tech Mahindra Limited) v. Commissioner of Taxation [2018] 98 taxmann.com 358 (FC-Australia)]

The Applicant, Tech Mahindra, had offices in Sydney and Melbourne through which it provided software products and information technology services to entities in Australia. Payments received by applicant for the services provided in Australia by the employees located in India were treated as 'Royalties' as per Article 12(3)(g) of the Australia-India DTAA .

Applicant argued that, though Australia was allocated the right to tax the 'Royalties' by the Indian Agreement but it could only exercise that right if it had the right to impose tax on those amounts under Australia's domestic law. As of now, the domestic law does not give any right to Australia to tax such income.

The Federal Court of Australia held as under:

The language of Article 23 should be given effect to according to its terms and the context. Article 23 provides that that income derived by a resident of one contracting States may be deemed to be income from sources in other contracting state for purpose of law of that other State. Therefore, royalty income was to be included in the applicant's assessable income because it was income from an Australian source by reason of Article 23 of the Australia-India DTAA. The Court rejected the argument that the tax treaties can only be used as shields not swords. It held that the tax treaties also provide standalone taxing power and independent imposing of tax to a particular income.

Javeri v. K.K. Sen3, the validity of section 12(1B) of the 1922 Act, was questioned. Section 12(1B) provided that a loan made to a shareholder by private-controlled company is taxable as dividend. It was recognized that merely because the loan is taxed as a dividend in the hands of a shareholder, the loan may not cease to be a loan, and that it would be open to the company to recover the loan by resorting to law. The petitioner’s argument was that what is not income is being taxed as ‘income’ and, therefore, it is beyond the legislative competence of the Parliament. (The impugned provision was introduced by the Finance Act, 1955.) The argument was rejected in the following words :

“In dealing with this point, it is necessary to consider what exactly is the connotation of the word ‘income’ used in the relevant entry. It is hardly necessary to emphasize that the entries in the Lists cannot be read in a narrow or restricted sense, and as observed by Gwyer, CJ. in the United Provinces v. Atiqa Begum1, each general word should be held to extend to all ancillary or subsidiary matters which can fairly and reasonably be said to be comprehended in it. What the entries in the Lists purport to do is to confer legislative powers on the respective Legislatures in respect of areas or fields covered by the said entries; and it is an elementary rule of construction that the widest possible construction must be put upon their words. This doctrine does not, however, mean that Parliament can choose to tax as income an item which in no rational sense can be regarded as a citizen’s income. The item taxed should rationally be capable of being considered as the income of a citizen. But in considering the question as to whether a particular item in the hands of a citizen can be regarded as his income or not, it would be inappropriate to apply the tests traditionally prescribed by the Income-tax Act as such...” (p. 1379)

The Court reaffirmed the principles enunciated in Navinchandra Mafatlal’s case (supra), Baldeo Singh’s case (supra) and Balaji’s case (supra).

It is equally relevant to notice that in Baldeo Singh’s case (supra), the validity of section 23A of the 1922 Act was questioned. Section 23A provided that where the ITO is satisfied that in respect of any previous year the profits and gains distributed as dividend by any company within twelve months immediately following the expiry of that previous year are less than 60 per cent of the total income of the company of that previous year [as reduced by the amounts specified in clauses (a), (b) and (c) of sub-section (1)], the ITO shall, unless he is satisfied that having regard to losses incurred by the company in earlier years, or to the smallness of the profits made in the previous year, the payment of a dividend, or a larger dividend than that declared, would be unreasonable, make an order in writing that the company shall, apart from the sum determined as payable by it on the basis of the assessment under section 23 of the 1922 Act, be liable to pay super-tax at the rate specified by sub-section (1) of section 23A. This section was enacted to prevent avoidance of super-tax by shareholders of a company in which the public are not substantially interested. The assessee’s argument was that since the company and shareholders are distinct entities, taxing the shareholders on dividends not distributed by the company, and not received by them, cannot be justified as a tax on income received by shareholders. This argument was repelled on the ground that the obvious intention of section 23A was to prevent evasion of tax, and that Entry 54 in List I of the Seventh Schedule should be read not only as authorising the imposition of a tax, but also as authorising an enactment which prevents the tax imposed being evaded. It was also observed that section 23A dealt with a situation where shareholders did not deliberately distribute the accumulated profits as dividend among themselves and, therefore, provided that these accumulated profits will be deemed to have been distributed to shareholders and tax levied on that basis.

Section 56(2)(viib) of the Act is another provision which deals with issue of shares. The purpose of introducing this provision was explained in the Memorandum explaining the Finance Bill as follows:

'Section 56(2) provides for the specific category of incomes that shall be chargeable to income-tax under the head Income from other sources.

It is proposed to insert a new clause in section 56(2). The new clause will apply where a company, not being a company in which the public are substantially interested, receives, in any previous year, from any person being a resident, any consideration for issue of shares. In such a case if the consideration received for issue of shares exceeds the face value of such shares, the aggregate consideration received for such shares as exceeds the fair market value of the shares shall be chargeable to Income-tax under the head "Income from other sources. However, this provision shall not apply where the consideration for issue of shares is received by a venture capital undertaking from a venture capital company or a venture capital fund.'

In summary, the object of section 56(2)(viib) of the Act is to tax the excess premium received by a company on account of issue of shares. This provision seeks to cover situations, where a company receives from a 'resident' any consideration in excess of the fair market value of shares. Obviously, this will not be applicable to the situation where shares are issued by an Indian company to a non-resident at a price lower than fair market value.
