It was not disputed that the assessee intended to spin off its Panasonic Division to company M and as required under the Companies Act, 1956 it moved an application under section 391 for seeking sanction of the High Court. The High Court as per requirement of section 391 directed the assessee to convene a general meeting of the shareholders, creditors secured and unsecured and after going through the scheme of arrangement and hearing the necessary parties, accorded the approval. The very purpose of issuance of such notice was that the Central Government shall also watch its interest and file its objection if any of the provisions of the scheme of arrangement was prejudicial to the interest of the Central Government. It had not come on record that Central Government had filed any objection about the same. After the scheme of arrangement was approved by the High Court, it acquired statutory recognition. The fact remained that scheme of arrangement once approved was binding on all the parties. It was undisputed fact that clause 12 of the scheme of arrangement prescribed that each shareholder in possession of one share of Rs. 10 each would be given two shares of equal amount by the buyer company and total amount of shares so given to the shareholders was Rs. 17.64 crores.

The phrase ‘full value of consideration received or accruing as a result of the transfer of the capital asset’ is crucial for disposal of the issue involved. Admittedly, the full value of the consideration was Rs. 50.12 crores which was not disputed by either party. The issue did not end there as the words ‘full value of consideration’ are qualified by the words ‘received’ or ‘accruing’ and these two words are important, and for that it had to be seen as to whether the assessee had received whole of the amount of Rs. 50.12 crores or it accrued to the assessee.

The amount which had been given to shareholders never reached the assessee. As scheme of arrangement was duly sanctioned by the High Court and acquired statutory binding effect, the amount to be given to the shareholders was diversion of the amount of Rs. 17.64 crores at the very source and it could not be said to be application of income because the assessee did not receive that amount at all. It was not like that the amount given to shareholders did reach the assessee first and later on it was applied by the assessee by paying the shares of company M to shareholders.

The provisions of the Companies Act are quite specific as the High Court is supposed to direct the company to convene an extraordinary general meeting of shareholders, creditors, secured and unsecured as well as other concerned parties for seeking their approval to the scheme of arrangement. This scheme of arrangement is to be approved by more than 75 per cent of the strength and in case shareholders are not agreeable to the scheme of arrangement, the same cannot be though and the High Court will have to refuse the necessary approval. It meant that shareholders were having their say in the approval of the scheme of arrangement and if the board of directors of the assessee and the company M chalked out the proposition that shareholders might also be given their respective shares out of this spin off of Panasonic Division from the assessee to the company M, then it could not be said that it was with any ulterior motive.

Not only that, clause 12 of scheme of arrangement was quite specific as each shareholder was entitled as a right to claim and receive from the company M an allotment of two equity shares of Rs. 10 each credited as fully paid. That clause was specific and created a right in favour of each shareholder and that entitlement had existing right. It is also under the provisions of the Companies Act that the High Court which accords the permission, is to see that scheme of arrangement is enforced as per the provision of section 392 of the Companies Act. The section is specific on the point and it gives powers to the High Court to enforce the terms of arrangement.

If a right was created in shareholders to get two shares of Rs. 10 each, that right was enforceable under the scheme of arrangement and the High Court would have stepped in if there was any violation. Accordingly, the shareholders were entitled to get the amount as a matter of right given to them under scheme of arrangement and the same stood duly approved by the High Court.

The obligation to give the amount of Rs. 17.64 crores to shareholders was under scheme of arrangement which had got statutory binding effect and, thus, the amount so given to shareholders could not be said to be part of income of the assessee as it stood diverted at the source.

Interplay of Transfer Pricing and Taxation of Receipt of Shares by a Company [Section 56(2)(viia)]

Freddy R Daruwala * 1. The lines quoted above by the legendary jurist N A Palkhiwala hit the nail on the head in this situation created by the interplay of transfer pricing provisions and the insertion of section 56(2)(viia) by the Finance Act, 2010.

The administrators of the law in their usual fashion adopted a harsh and adverse interpretation so as to tax even genuine receipts without consideration and extort taxes thereon.

The confusion has been even more confounded on cross-border receipts without consideration or at less than fair market value due to several factors like reorganizations and restructurings due to the warp and weft of DTAA provisions, the regular income-tax provisions and the special transfer pricing provisions (TPP) embodied in sections 92 to 92F (and relevant rules) of the Domestic Income-tax Act. A further complication in the matter is that most double taxation treaties are silent on the issue of gifts and club them with other income, which is generally taxed in either the source or residence country.

This amendment in section 56(2)(viia) of the Act seeks to tax shares received by a firm or company in which the ‘public are not substantially interested’ as per section 2(18) of the Act. This amendment takes effect from June 1, 2010 and throws up the following issues from a cross-border tax perspective:

u How far would deeming provisions introduced in the assessment year 2010-11 for receipt of shares by an unlisted company in section 56(2)(viia) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 apply in cases of such cross-border receipts of securities deemed as ‘gifts’?

u What would be the course of action when the receipt is classified in a different manner in the two jurisdictions of the donor and receiver?

u What is the remedy when the residential status of the receiver is different under the two jurisdictions (e.g. US law takes the situs of the shareholder as residential jurisdiction while Indian law treats the situs of incorporation of the company as residential jurisdictions)?

u Does the market value of a gift (essentially without consideration) have to be tested on the anvil of ‘arms length price’ to determine its taxability?

u Whether withholding tax would apply on such receipts?

These are only some of the issues in this new and nascent area of the law and the only thing that may be said with certainty is that there will be many more uncertainties as the law meanders through the banks of judicial decisions.

Interplay with newly introduced section 56(2)(viia ) with DTAA and TPP

2. An important point to note in this context is that the TPP are procedural and methodology driven (best method, comparisons, tested party, FAR analysis) while the provisions embodied under section 56(1)(viia) are ‘consideration driven’ (i.e., take the fair market value as the starting point of the computation of income). Another difference to note is that the TPP generally apply to business income while the section 56 provisions apply to income from other sources.

Thus, such a company receiving shares (by any method except for the exempted methods laid out in Act) will be taxed on the difference between the consideration and the ‘fair market value’ of the shares. Such difference will be taxed under the head ‘income from other sources’. It is worth noting that the Finance Minister in his budget speech used the term ‘transfer of shares’ while the amendment in the Finance Act, 2010 uses the term ‘receives’, thereby lending credence to the old adage that ‘there is many a slip bewixt the cup and the lip’. This amendment applies to residents and non-residents alike.

This intended amendment creates conflict and confusion particularly in the area of cross-border taxation in the following areas :

u The TPP will now be made applicable to such receipt of shares, even on a foreign business reorganization or bankruptcy proceedings since the difference between consideration (even though not ascertainable) and fair market value will be taxable. This overrules the rulings of the AAR in three cases, namely, Dana Corporation (shares received subject to chap 11 proceedings in USA) and STAR AAR/Amaintit AAR (shares received subject to a business reorganization in a foreign country). These rulings are dealt with in a little detail in the subsequent paragraphs.

u If a company receives shares and is taxed under the head ’Income from other sources’, tax credits under the corresponding head of the relevant treaty which India has with the home jurisdiction of such company may not be easily availed of.

u Valuation in relation to cross-border receipts is an important issue and brings one back to the bogey of ‘arms length’ and, thus, virtually guaranteeing a backdoor application of the TPP.

3.1 The Shell controversy - The controversy fundamentally revolves around taxation on the undervaluation of shares issued by Shell India to its overseas group entity, more specifically under the extant Indian TP regulations and seeks to tax Shell India on alleged issuance of shares at a discounted rate. Shell India, having diversified businesses in India, was issued with TP notices from the tax authority alleging that the Company had undervalued its shares while raising money from the Shell group entity during the financial year 2008-09. Shell India issued 870 million equity shares at INR 10 each (which was the par value) to Shell Gas BV. During TP audit, the TPO asked Shell India to justify the pricing of the equity shares issued to Shell Gas BV. In response, Shell India justified the price of the equity shares based on discounted cash flow ("DCF"), as provided under the Indian foreign exchange regulations and the value per share was determined at INR 6.93.

The TPO re-computed the price per share, using DCF method, but at INR 183.44 and held that Shell India had transferred its equity shares to its overseas group entity at a price below their fair market value. The difference in valuation so arrived by TPO was branded as a 'loan' advanced by Shell India to its overseas group entity. While doing so, the TPO also alleged that Shell India ought to have charged interest on the same, thereby resulting in an overall adjustment to the tune of INR 152bn (equivalent to USD 2.8bn). Consequently, the TPO imposed tax on the short receipt of share capital as well as a notional return calculated on such short receipt.

To challenge the constitutional, jurisdictional, legality, validity and judicial propriety of the TP order, Shell India filed a writ petition before the Hon'ble Bombay High Court. In its grounds of appeal, Shell India mentioned that the action of the tax authority was based on misrepresentation of the fact and hence, was confiscatory in nature. It further stated that the adjustment on account of re-characterization of transaction was not permitted in Indian TP regulations and such an action showed arbitrariness and was unfair besides being illegal and had disregarded the fact that as per the corporate and regulatory framework and laws, the alleged shortfall (i.e., so called share premium) could never be received by Shell India as the shares were issued at par value.

This matter is yet to be adjudicated by the Hon'ble High Court and would not be apt to comment on the righteousness of the case or any facts thereto.

3.2 The Vodafone's case - In 2009, Vodafone India issued shares to its AE, Vodafone Teleservices Mauritius. The revenue authority issued an order to Vodafone India alleging that the Indian company had underpriced its shares issued to the Mauritian Company by around INR 13bn.

On the lines of Shell India, Vodafone India also filed a writ petition before the Hon'ble Bombay High Court in relation to the under valuation of shares.

3.3 These controversies add another perspective to TP regime - The reference to these cases gains importance owing to couple of reasons. First, is the amount involved on account of TP adjustment made by the revenue authority and second, which is more significant, is the aggressive position taken by revenue authority to look beyond the certified valuations for capital transactions and, thus, imposing tax on virtual shift in the values and tax the amounts which are not considered to impact income of any of the parties.

Traditionally, the line of argument adopted by taxpayers has been that TP provisions are not applicable to issue of shares, being capital transactions not having a direct bearing on profits or rather lack any income element. This view has also been supported by the Hyderabad Income Tax Appellate Tribunal ("ITAT") in the recent case of Vijai Electricals Ltd. [IT Appeal No. 842 (Hyd.) of 2012]. The ITAT in the ruling in this case held that investment in foreign subsidiaries was not an international transaction. The ITAT ruled that TP provisions were not applicable as there was no income. Though the transaction in Vijai's case (supra) was of Indian company investing in foreign subsidiaries and not vice versa (as in Shell or Vodafone's case), the crux of the issue was applicability of TP provisions to such transactions, which did not impact income. It was however, pertinent to highlight that while deciding this case, the ITAT did not consider the amendments made by the Finance Act, 2012 widening the definition of 'international transaction' with retrospective effect from April, 2002.

the shares held in the demerged company, as per the agreed exchange ratio, the resulting company issues its shares to the shareholders of the resulting company;

♦ pursuant to the order of the court and filing thereof, all the properties, assets etc. of the undertaking of the demerged company vest in the resulting company;

♦ accordingly, it can be said that the demerged company is divided and the undertaking divided merges into the resulting company.

In the above circumstances, it can be said that: ♦ The undertaking of the amalgamating company or the demerged company, along with all its assets and liabilities, pass to the amalgamated company or the resulting company (being transferor)

♦ the shareholders of the amalgamating company or the demerged company, in respect of the shares held by them in the said company are allotted the shares in the amalgamated company or the resulting company.

For the purposes of taxation, with a view to provide tax neutral reorganisation or restructuring of businesses, exemption is provided by the Act. While referring to the transaction, some of the provisions of the Act suggest that in consideration of the vesting of the undertaking and/or its assets and liabilities, shares are issued to the shareholders of the amalgamating company or the demerged company.

In case of amalgamated company or the resulting company, the undertaking passes to it and it issues the shares, which, as such, does not result in to any profit or gain and, therefore, presently, no provision is made in the Act in that behalf. For the purposes of calculation of cost of the assets of the undertaking, suitable provisions are made in the Act.

In relation to the applicability of the clause to the amalgamated company or the resulting company, there could be two possible views when shares are issued pursuant to amalgamation or demerger of a resident amalgamating/demerged company, respectively.

As per one view, the clause would apply, inter alia, for the following reasons:

♦ Under the scheme of amalgamation or demerger, the amalgamated company or the resulting company issues shares to the shareholders of the amalgamating company or the demerged company, in consideration for vesting of the undertaking [apart from the applicable provisions of the Act, like, definition of demerger, exemption to the shareholders etc., a reference may be made to a decision of Supreme Court in Hindustan Lever v. State of Maharashtra [2003] 117 Comp. Cas. 758, where it was observed that once the shareholders of the transferee company receive the consideration it would be deemed as if the owner has received the consideration (page 774)].

♦ Further, as held by Supreme Court in Hindustan Lever v. State of Maharashtra [2003] 117 Comp. Cas. 758, the amalgamation is a compromise or arrangement between the parties, which, inter alia, includes the amalgamated company issuing the shares and the shareholders of the amalgamating company, which is supervised by the court, in terms of the provisions of the Companies Act, 1956. In other words, there is an agreement or arrangement, inter alia, by and between the amalgamated company issuing the shares and the shareholders of the amalgamating company. The Clause contemplates the issue of shares and the receipt of consideration from a resident person and it is fulfilled in case of amalgamation.

♦ The Clause applies to any consideration, whether in cash or in kind or whether at the instance of the company or otherwise.

♦ The Clause applies to any consideration whether received from the person to whom the shares are issued or otherwise.

♦ The events attracting tax are present, namely, receipt of consideration and issue of shares.

♦ Whether the issue triggers consideration or otherwise is of no relevance.

As per the other view, the clause cannot apply, inter alia, for the following reasons:

♦ The objective of insertion of the provision is relevant for determining the true scope and ambit of the provision.

♦ The objective is to tax 'conversion of unaccounted' money and accordingly include within its scope only such transactions, which facilitate such conversion.

♦ The issue of shares is not to invite subscription by the persons to whom an offer is made. The issue of shares is to give effect to the amalgamation or the demerger, as per the mutual agreement and the Court order. In other words, the issue of shares does not trigger any consideration; in fact, the obligation to give consideration, triggers the issue of shares.

♦ The clause contemplates 'receipt' of the consideration for the shares from a resident person. In other words, it contemplates a transaction between a resident person and the company issuing the shares. In case of an amalgamation or a demerger, the consideration, which would be the undertaking along with all its assets and liabilities is in the form of vesting by the amalgamating or the demerged company; whereas, the shares are issued to its shareholders. Thus, it is a tripartite arrangement not contemplated by the Clause.

It is clear that this payment of dividend is in kind and not by way of cash. Payment of dividend in kind is expressly prohibited by section 123(5). Therefore, the gifting of the shares of TAAL by the petitioner company to its shareholders will be in violation of section 123(5) of the 2013 Act. [Para 25] The submission of the petitioner that a company can distribute its assets under the provisions of sections 100-104 of the 1956 Act and that accordingly no fault can be found with the scheme is unacceptable. First and foremost, as is clear from the clause 5 of the scheme itself, the reduction of the SPA is merely an accounting treatment in the books of the petitioner company. Further this reduction is a consequence of the gifting of the shares of TAAL by the petitioner company to its shareholders and this is clear from the opening words of clause 5. Even otherwise it is clear that the main purpose and object of the scheme is the gifting of shares of TAAL by the petitioner company to its shareholders. Moreover, even a reduction of capital under the Companies Act must not be in violation of the other provisions of the Companies Act. The gift of the shares of TAAL by the petitioner company to its shareholders will therefore necessarily have to comply with the provisions of section 123 of the 2013 Act, particularly in view of the finding that the said gift amounts to distribution of dividend. In the circumstances the provisions of sections 100 to 104 of the 1956 Act and section 52 of the 2013 Act are of no assistance to the petitioner company and will not save the scheme. [Para 26]

It is clear from section 281 of 1961 Act that the gift of any asset by an assessee to any person during the pendency of any proceedings under the Income-tax Act will be void as against any claim in respect of any tax or any other sum payable by the assessee as a result of the completion of such proceedings or otherwise. In the instant case it is an undisputed position that the assessment proceedings in respect of assessment year 2013-14, outstanding demands in respect of assessment years 2006-07 and 2007-08 respectively and penalty proceedings in respect of assessment years 2006-07 to 2012-13 under the Income-tax Act are pending against the petitioner company. Despite the pendency of these proceedings, by the scheme the petitioner proposes to gift its shares in TAAL to its shareholders. Such a gift would therefore clearly be hit by the provisions of section 281(1) and would be void as against the claims of the Income-tax Department resulting from the proceedings mentioned above. It is pertinent to note that it is not the case of the petitioner that the gift of the shares of TAAL would not be void on account of the proviso to section 281(1). In the circumstances there can be no doubt that the proposed gift of the shares of TAAL by the petitioner to its shareholders will defeat the provisions of section 281(1). [Para 31]

Even if the contention of the petitioner that it has more than sufficient assets to discharge the tax liability in the event that the same crystallizes upon the petitioner, the same does not alter the position with regard to the applicability of section 281(1). Section 281(1) does not carve out any exception on the basis of sufficiency or otherwise of the assets of the assessee. The petitioner therefore cannot avoid the applicability of the provisions of section 281(1) on the ground that it may have sufficient assets to discharge the tax liability as and when the same accrues. [Para 32]

As noticed above, there are assessment proceedings, outstanding demands and penalty proceedings under the Income-tax Act pending against the petitioner company. These proceedings may very well result in taxes or other sums being payable by the petitioner company to the Income-tax Department. The gift of the shares of TAAL by the petitioner company to its shareholders will be void as against the claim or claims of the Income-tax Department in respect of the aforesaid taxes and sums, in view of section 281(1). The Income-tax Department would therefore be entitled to recover its dues by attachment and sale of the said shares of TAAL. If these shares are today permitted to be gifted under the scheme to the shareholders of the petitioner company, the same may not be available at the time when the claim of the Income-tax Department is crystallized, since there may be further sales of these shares by the shareholders receiving the same. It must be kept in mind that TAAL is a Public Limited Listed Company whose shares can be traded on the Stock Exchange. In this manner this asset of the petitioner company will be lost to the Income-tax Department. This will defeat the purpose and object of section 281(1). Accordingly it will not be proper to permit the petitioner company to gift its shares in TAAL to its shareholders as envisaged under the scheme. The Court will not put its imprimatur on such a scheme. [Para 33]

There is no doubt that the petitioner can arrange its affairs in a manner so as to avoid payment of tax. However, this does not entitle the petitioner to dispose of its assets in a manner so as to defeat the provisions of section 281(1). [Para 34]

Without going to the record and without placing any evidence or substantiate the allegation by appearing before the Tribunal, it was not open to the Income-tax Department to hold that the Composite Scheme of Arrangement amongst the petitioner companies and their respective shareholders and creditors is giving undue favour to the shareholders of the company and also the overall scheme of arrangement results into tax avoidance. The Income-Tax Department, which sought for liberty, while accepted by the petitioner companies (respondents) and the Tribunal while approving the Composite Scheme of Arrangement has granted liberty. Such liberty to the Income-Tax Department to enquire into the matter, if any part of the Composite Scheme of Arrangement amounts to tax avoidance or is against the provisions of the Income-tax and is to let it take appropriate steps if so required. Mere fact that a Scheme may result in reduction of tax liability does not furnish a basis for challenging the validity of the same. [Para 38]

IASC started issuing revised standards a couple of years ago. The revised standards do not permit alternative accounting treatments and instead zero in on one treatment as the ideal and best. The IAS-18 referred to above is one such reversed standard, which is all the more reason why it should be looked upon as an authority. The standards evolved by the ICAI, while following the broad pattern of the IASC, are tempered to suit Indian laws and practices.

Need of review of Supreme Court's decision 7. It is, therefore, humbly urged that the Supreme Court may review its judgment in Vijaya Bank Ltd.'s case (supra) in the light of the accounting authorities cited and discussed above. The Accounting Standard-13 of the ICAI has tremendous force when it says that interest/dividend relatable to the pre-acqitisition period must not be viewed as income but has recovery of cost and, therefore, should be viewed as a capital receipt. And capital receipts are not taxable for the simple reason that they do not constitute income. The Supreme Court rightly held where a bank purchased securities at a price with reference to their actual value as well as the interest accrued thereon till the date of purchase, the entire price paid would be in the nature of capital outlay. As a corollary, it follows that when this cost is recovered by way of interest, such recovery, far from being income, is an abatement against the cost originally incurred and should be reduced from the cost of purchase. It is this aspect urged in this article and buttressed by the accounting authorities that craves for reconsideration by the Supreme Court. The Supreme Court held the assessee (Vijaya Bank) to be liable for the entire interest including for the broken period, i.e., the pre-acquisition period. It is submitted that this is not correct. The broken period interest, it is reiterated, is a capital receipt and should be rightly reduced from the cost of securities. This accounting treatment is nothing new. Those familiar with preparing consolidated accounts of the holding company with the accounts of its subsidiary, would know that the proportionate part of pre-acquisition profits of the subsidiary relatable to the holding company's holding in the subsidiary is always reduced from the cost of investment and is never shown as part of reserves and surplus. This analogy should be sufficient to remove the mental block or the mind-set of those who are unable to come round to the view-point that broken period interest is a capital receipt.

Implications for shares

8. The Accounting Standard-13 applies to shares as much as it does to interest-bearing securities. In case of shares, the treatment propounded is likely to be even less palatable to tax administration because it will have the effect of converting dividend into capital gains, and if the holding period is more than 12 months, the investor is going to get away with a host of benefits that come with long-term capital gains - to be specific, a flat rate of 20 per cent tax irrespective of the quantum of gains and section 54F benefit which exempts long-term capital gains from tax if they are ploughed back in a residential house.

Implications for stock-in-trade

9. A dealer in securities is not going to be affected one way or the other, whether he is required to follow the law laid down by the Supreme Court in Vijaya Bank Ltd.'s case (supra) or the one propounded by the accounting standards and endorsed in this article. For, in any case, the entire transaction is revenue in nature. The cost of interest-bearing securities is going to be debited to the profit and loss account and the carrying amount at the end of the financial year, cost or market value, whichever is less, is going to be credited to such account. In the event, interest relating to the broken-period is not an issue at all in his case. It must be made clear that in Vijaya Bank Ltd. 's case (supra), the Supreme Court did not say that in case of a bank purchase of interest-bearing securities will invariably constitute investments. Nor did it say that they will invariably constitute stock-in-trade. This classification will, therefore, be governed by the RBI norms and other accounting considerations which are outside the scope of this article. What is relevant is the Supreme Court's verdict in Vijaya Bank Ltd.'s case (supra) has grave portents for investors.

5. ARGUMENTS BEFORE THE HIGH COURT 6. HIGH COURT'S VERDICT

The Bombay High Court held that on the facts of the present case, issue of shares at a premium by VISL to its non-resident AE does not give rise to any income from an admitted international transaction and thus, Indian Transfer Pricing provisions are not applicable for the following reasons:

Income arising from an international transaction is a pre-condition for application of Transfer Pricing provisions. Further, the Act defines the term income in an inclusive manner. Income, in its normal meaning, will not include capital receipts unless specifically provided. The amounts received on issue of share capital including the premium are on capital account. In this case, what is being sought to be taxed is capital forgone i.e. not received from a non-resident in the form of short premium. Therefore, absent express legislation, an amount received, accrued or arising on capital account transactions cannot be subjected to tax as income.

The High Court further held that the transaction on capital account or on account of restructuring would become taxable to the extent it impacts income i.e., under-reporting of interest received/over reporting of interest paid or claiming of depreciation. It is that income (and not the capital receipt) which is to be determined having regard to the ALP under the Transfer Pricing provisions.

The Transfer Pricing provisions are brought into statute books to ensure that the transaction is taxed only on the income computed as per the ALP of the transaction and to ensure that there is no manipulation of prices/consideration between AEs.

In any case, the entire exercise of taxing the amounts allegedly not received as share premium fails, as no tax is charged on the amount received as share premium.

Neither the capital receipts received by VISL on issue of equity shares to its AE nor the shortfall between the alleged FMV of its equity shares and the issue price of the equity shares can be considered as income within the meaning of the expression as defined in the Act and hence not subject to Transfer Pricing provisions in India.

The reasoning that if the ALP were received, the Taxpayer would be able to invest the same and earn income, proceeds on a mere surmise/assumption and that this cannot be the basis of taxation.

The Tax Authorities relied on this section to argue that differences between the ALP and the price charged for issue of shares is the benefit conferred upon the holding company.

Relying on section 92(2) of the Act is misplaced. Section 92(2) of the Act, which deals with a situation where two or more AEs enter into an arrangement whereby they are to receive any benefit, service or facility then the allocation, apportionment or contribution of the corresponding cost or expenditure is to be determined for each AE based on ALP, is meant to cover cases of cost sharing arrangements and/or cost contribution arrangements. Section 92(2) would have no application in cases like the present one, where there is no occasion to allocate, apportion or contribute any cost and/or expenses between the Taxpayer and its AE. Ignoring words in a statute to achieve a predetermined objective is not permissible and the same would amount to re-drafting the legislation, which is beyond the jurisdiction of the Courts.

The contention of the Tax Authorities that in view of the Transfer Pricing provisions, notional income is to be taxed and real income is not relevant is unacceptable. The entire exercise of determining the ALP is only to arrive at the real income earned.

Even income arising from international transactions between AEs must satisfy the test of income per se under the Act and must find its home under one of the charging provisions. It is a re-computation exercise to be carried out only when income arises in case of an international transaction between AEs. It does not warrant recomputation of a consideration received/given on capital account except in cases of interest paid/received on loans taken/given, depreciation taken on machinery, etc. Therefore, in the absence of a charging provision to tax issue of shares at a premium to a non-resident, the occasion to invoke the computational Transfer Pricing provisions does not arise.

Further, in view of inclusion of issue of shares, by a company to another resident, at a price in excess of FMV in the definition of income under the Act, there is conscious intention of the Parliament to not tax amounts received from a non-resident for issue of shares, as it would discourage capital inflow from abroad.

7. CONCLUSION

In the backdrop of the present Government's initiative to bring in foreign investment, this decision from the Bombay High Court's is a landmark. The High Court has been rightly able to distinguish between the 'income' per se and the capital which is primarily the source to earn income. One important take away from the decision is the High Court's acknowledgement that mere reporting of an international transaction out of abundant caution would not make the same taxable if there is no income arising from such international transaction.

Current Judicial Trends

3. There are a few advance rulings and judicial decisions on the subject. However, due to the inherent infirmity of advance rulings, these may only be relied upon in a persuasive manner rather than a binding capacity. Further, the insertion of section 56(1)(viia ) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 from the assessment year 2010-11 also overturns most established judge made law in one fell swoop.

Nevertheless, let us examine the major decisions to determine the line of judicial thinking on this issue.

(a) Amiantit International Holding Ltd. In re [2010] 189 Taxman 149 (AAR - New Delhi)

This is so far the only the AAR dealing directly with the issue. The crux of the matter is that a Bahrain based company transferred shares of its Indian based subsidiary to its cyprus associate enterprise without any consideration pursuant to a corporate restructuring. Since the situs of incorporation of the company whose shares are transferred is India, the Indian revenue authorities have the jurisdiction to tax the transaction.

The main issue decided by the AAR is whether in case of shares transferred to an associated enterprise, the Indian TPP would apply.

The AAR in a well-reasoned judgment ruled that since the transfer is without consideration, there is no question of applying the touch stone of the ‘arms length price’ to determine a capital gain which could not be computed and, hence, ruled that the authorities could not ram the TPP down the assessee’s throat and tax an income which is not there. The Supreme Court’s decision in CIT v. B.C. Srinivasa Shetty [1981] 128 ITR 294/5 Taxman 1 which has laid down that in case the computation provision fails the charging section also fails seems to have been applied by the AAR notwithstanding the fact that the giver and recipient of the shares are associated enterprises.

However, it needs to be borne in mind that the Finance Act, 2010 has inserted section 56(2)(viia) which taxes receipt of shares at the difference between the fair market value and consideration in the hands of the recipient as ‘income from other sources’. The fair market value determination may certainly involve the principle of ‘arms length’ valuation and, hence, imply a backdoor application of the TPP in a modified form.

(b) Dana Corporation, In re [2010] 186 Taxman 187 (AAR - New Delhi)

This is another ruling which deals with a similar issue. In this case, the US parent entity files for bankruptcy under Chapter 11 and as a result of the bankruptcy proceedings an independent private equity player infuses capital in exchange for an integral package of assets and liabilities which involves shares of a merged US entity. As a result, indirect control and ownership of Indian subsidiaries is transferred to the private equity player.

The question before the AAR is whether such transfer of indirect control would constitute a gain in the hands of the private equity player and, hence, application of the arms length provisions to determine the costs of acquisition.

The AAR in this case also ruled that since the shares are transferred indirectly and also as part of a package where it is argued that the liabilities are more than the assets, no direct cost could be attributable to them. Hence, once again the computation provisions fail and, hence, the charging section would also fail and the TPP would not have any application.

Having said this, it is pertinent to note that the current vodafone controversy also has at its core the capital gains on indirect control and transfer of shares of an Indian subsidiary company and the AAR seems to have disregarded this aspect in its ruling.

(c) Star Television Entertainment Ltd., In re [2010] 188 Taxman 206 (AAR - New Delhi)

The Star Ruling also has similar facts but shares of an Indian company are transferred indirectly by virtue of corporate reorganization, here too the AAR rules that no tax is leviable since the computation provisions have failed and that the TPP are held not applicable.

profits and gains of such business and in that connection the second proviso to section 10(2)(vii) of the 1922 Act provides that the excess over written down value received by the assessee on the sale of a capital asset shall be deemed to be the profit of the assessee in the previous year in which the sale took place so that such excess may be included in the computation of the profits and gains of the assessee and may be brought to tax in his hands. The legal fiction in other words is created in order to enable the revenue to take back that it had given by way of depreciation allowance in preceding years since what was given in preceding years was in excess of that which ought to have been given. Unless this were done, the result would be to recoup the assessee an amount in excess of the real operating cost of the capital asset and, therefore, in order to take back what, had been wrongly allowed in the earlier years, the true character of the receipt is masked and by the legal fiction the receipt is treated as if it were profit for the purpose of computation of the assessable income of the assessee so that it would be brought to tax as such in the hands of the assessee. This being the purpose of the enactment of the legal fiction, the legal fiction must be limited to the field of that purpose; of course, within the framework of that purpose the legal fiction must be given full effect and must be carried to its logical consequence but it cannot be availed of for a different purpose. Having been enacted for the purpose of enabling the revenue to tax the receipt of excess over written down value, as soon as such receipt is taxed the fiction would be exhausted and would not operate in any other field unconnected or unrelated to the purpose for which the fiction is created. It was, therefore, clear that the fiction must be limited to the purpose of computation of the assessable income of the assessee under section 10 of the 1922 Act and it cannot be extended to other provisions such as section 2(6A)(c) of the 1922 Act which are unconnected with the assessment of the assessee and, therefore, unconnected with the purpose for which the fiction is created. It could not therefore by said that the words 'accumulated profits' in section 2(6A)(c) of the 1922 Act include receipt of excess over written down value on sale of capital assets which, though not profit in the accepted connotation of the word, is deemed to be profit by the legal fiction enacted in the second proviso to section 10(2)(vii) of the 1922 Act.

In a taxing statute one has to look merely at what is clearly said. There is no room for any intendment. There is no equity about a tax, there is no presumption as to a tax. Nothing is to be read in, nothing is to be implied. One can only fairly looked at the language used and if we do so, the conclusion to which we have arrived was the only conclusion which can be reached. Therefore, the distribution of Rs. 1,570 per share was not a distribution out of accumulated profits of the company so as to be liable to be regarded as dividend within the meaning of section 2(6A)(c) of the 1922 Act.

Issuing bonus shares out of revaluation reserve 6.1 Existing prohibition - Section M of the SEBI Guidelines for Disclosure and Investor Protection does not allow issue of bonus shares out of the Revaluation reserve. This prohibition is applicable to listed companies. The Department of Company Affairs vide its Circular No. 9/94 (Circular Letter No. 17/32/93 - CL V dated September 6,1994) has also prohibited issue of bonus shares out of revaluation reserve by the existing private/ closely-held and unlisted companies.

The Guidance note on availability of revaluation reserve for issue of bonus shares issued by the ICAI (Published in November 1994 issue of the Chartered Accountant) argues that the excess of the revalued amount over the net book value of fixed assets, which is credited to revaluation reserve, is created as a result of book adjustment only. The revaluation reserve does not result from an arm's length transaction; it represents an expert's perception of value. The revaluation reserve thus does not represent realised gain.

The ICAI Guidance Note also states that share capital represents money or money's worth received from the owners and capitalisation of earned profits or other gains arising out of arm's length transactions. It is a cardinal principle that only such profits as are earned or the relevant capital receipts (e.g. share premium) as are realised, can be capitalised.

6.2 Expert's value perception - So long as the expert's perception of the fair value of a fixed asset is judicious, there is nothing wrong in depending on such valuation, in case the upper limit of revaluation is restricted to the net recoverable amount. Substitution of historical cost becomes necessary when it materially differs from the fair value of the fixed assets. A going concern may not think of disposing of a particular asset, still the increase in value of the asset, although unrealised, cannot be denied. Since the revaluation reserve forms part of the shareholders' funds, it should be treated as a free reserve.

6.3 Arm's length transactions and business income -The concept of arm's length relationship is altogether irrelevant in this context. The reported net profit of an entity is not necessarily the result of arm's length transactions. Also it is not necessary for the purpose of a bonus issue to consider to what extent the accumulated surplus of the entity has resulted from arm's length transactions.

6.4 Unrealised gain - Of course, the revaluation reserve represents unrealised gain. But it represents real gain and cannot be treated as a fictitious gain. Accordingly, the shareholders should not be denied the right to utilise any such real gain in the manner they want. It is not unknown to the shareholders that such a bonus issue, if any, results from unrealised gain.

6.5 Accounting effect of bonus issue - Presently, many companies take a transfer from the revaluation reserve to the extent of additional depreciation. To that extent profit is inflated every year and the revaluation reserve is converted into the so called 'earned profit'. It is just a matter of time to convert revaluation reserve into 'earned profit' and as soon as the conversion is complete there is no bar on utilising such 'earned profit' for issuing bonus shares.

In case the revaluation reserve is utilised for a bonus issue, the company would have no choice but to charge additional depreciation out of profit.

6.6 Corporate freedom - One of the basic tenets of economic liberalisation is reduction/elimination of bureaucratic interference on the activities of private entrepreneurs. Corporate management should be given freedom to adopt a suitable financial management policy. A bonus issue out of the revaluation reserve will not generally be supported by increase in the earning capacity. However, the management will not find difficulty in maintaining the dividend rate in real terms. A decline in post-equity pricewill have no effect in real terms, since this book adjustment has no effect on the earnings of the entity.

6.2 Buy-back of shares will be taxable as capital gains [Section 69 of ITA 2025 (corresponding to Section 46A of ITA 1961)]

The Finance Act, 2026 has made several amendments to the provisions of the ITA 2025 regarding the taxation of buy-back of shares. Under the amended provisions, the sum paid by a domestic company to the shareholders under a buyback shall be treated as capital gains in the hands of the shareholders.

6.2-1 Introduction

Corporate action to buyback shares can serve multiple strategic purposes. Primarily, it's used to increase earnings per share by reducing the number of outstanding shares, often leading to a higher stock price. Additionally, buybacks are a method to return excess cash to shareholders, an alternative to dividend payouts. Companies might also repurchase shares if they believe their stock is undervalued, signalling confidence in the future. Moreover, buybacks can deter hostile takeovers by increasing the company's ownership percentage.

Section 68 of the Companies Act, 2013 gives the company the power to purchase its own securities. It defines a buyback as the purchase of its own shares or other specified securities (i.e., Employee Stock Options or Sweat Equity) by the Company itself.

6.2-2 History of tax on buyback of shares as per the ITA 1961

Before the assessment year 2000-01, the Income Tax Act did not include a special provision for taxing share buybacks. There were two views on the buyback of shares: either it could attract dividend distribution tax, or shareholders would be liable to pay tax on any gains.

To set the controversy at rest, the Finance Act, 1999 inserted section 46A with effect from assessment year 2000-01, which stated that shareholders would be charged to tax on the capital gains arising from the buyback of shares. A corresponding amendment was also made to section 2(22) by inserting clause (iv), which provides that a payment for the purchase of shares does not constitute a dividend. Therefore, the consideration received by a shareholder on the buyback of shares by the company in accordance with section 77A of the Companies Act, 19561 (corresponding to Section 68 of the Companies Act, 2013) was not treated as a dividend. The same was taxed under Section 46A of the Act as capital gains.

Subsequently, the unlisted companies, as part of the tax avoidance scheme, were found resorting to buyback of shares instead of payment of dividends in order to avoid payment of tax by way of DDT, particularly where the capital gains arising to the shareholders were either not chargeable to tax or were taxable at a lower rate under respective Double Taxation Avoidance Agreements. In A Mauritius, In re [2012] 20 taxmann.com 52, the AAR held that only a genuine buyback is excluded from the definition of 'dividend' under section 2(22)(iv) and exempt from DDT under section 115-O. A colourable buyback will attract DDT. In that case, the buyback was held to be a colourable device for tax avoidance, as dividends were distributed in the guise of a buyback to avoid DDT.

Taking a cue from the above decision of the AAR, the Finance Act, 2013 inserted a new Chapter XII-DA, 'Special Provisions relating to tax on distributed income of domestic company for buyback of shares,' consisting of sections 115QA to 115QC, with effect from 1-6-2013. The Finance (No. 2) Act, 2019 extended the levy of tax on the buy-back of shares listed on a recognised stock exchange on or after 5 July 2019 by amending section 115QA.

In November 2022, the Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI) released a consultation paper on a review of the SEBI (Buyback of Securities) Regulations, 2018, proposing various changes to existing buyback norms. One of the proposed changes is to shift the tax burden of buybacks from the company to the shareholders. This proposal was based on the fact that promoters tendered more shares than their pre-buyback holdings, resulting in the company paying taxes not only on shares tendered by the promoters but also on the additional shares tendered by them. These taxes were paid from the company's reserves on behalf of the existing shareholders and promoters at the expense of continuing shareholders. Therefore, it was suggested that the tax burden on buybacks should be shifted to shareholders, as it is with dividend distributions.

The assessee-company was engaged in owning and operating container freight services, (CFS) at various places and warehousing services. The assessee filed its original return of income declaring total income at Rs.50.37 crores. Subsequently, the assessee filed its revised return of income declaring total income at Rs.49.85 crores. During the course of assessment proceedings, the Assessing Officer noticed that a sum of Rs.73.99 crores had been debited to the profit & Loss Account, being 'Exceptional Items' on account of investments, written off, in certain companies.

■

The Assessing Officer noticed that in the calculation of taxable income, such amount of exceptional items had been added back, while calculating income under the regular provisions of the Act. However, such amount was not added back in computation of the tax payable under the provisions of section 115JB. As per clause (i) of Explanation 1 to sub-section 2 of section 115JB, the 'book profit' shall further be increased by the amount or amounts set aside, as provisions for diminution in the value of any asset. However, as stated above, such adjustment to the book profit had not been made, while working it, as per the provisions of section 115JB.

■

As per the facts of the case, such reduction in investment in share tantamount to diminution in the value of assets and accordingly required to be added back, while working the 'Book profit' under the provisions of section 115JB. Accordingly, the 'Book profit' was required to be altered to that extent. The assessee was, therefore, requested to explain, as to why such sum of Rs.7399.28 lakhs, should not be added back while working the 'Book profit' under the provisions of section 115JB.

■

The assessee submitted that 'write off' of Rs.7399.28 lacs, was on account of capital reduction of investment in equity shares and preference shares in the group companies. This capital reduction was carried out under section 100 to 104 of the Companies Act, 1956. The assessee submitted that the capital reduction was duly approved by the Bombay High Court. The assessee submitted that when the balances of the assets at the end of the year are reflected at a reduced value, then amount of such reduction shall be treated as 'actual write off' and not 'provision'.

■

Hence, once the amount of diminution in the value of investments was written off against the asset, there could be no use of any amount having been set-aside for diminution in the value of assets. Based on these facts, the assessee submitted that the fundamental premise of existence of asset to treat the amount under clause (i) of Explanation 1 of Section 115JB(2) was lacking, and hence no addition should be made in the hands of the assessee.

■

However, the Assessing Officer rejected the above contention of assessee and observed that assessee had done these transactions under a larger scheme of planning to avoid taxes. Therefore, Assessing Officer did not accept the plea of the assessee that such reduction in value of investment cannot be added back, while computing the book profit under section 115JB.

■

That is, Assessing Officer held that such reduction in value of investment was a part of clause (i) of Explanation 1 of section 115JB(2), and it should be added while computing the book profit under section 115JB. Accordingly, the book profit, as per the provisions of section 115JB, was worked out by the Assessing Officer to the tune of Rs.7399.28 lakhs and added as per clause (i) of Explanation 1 to section 115JB(2).

■

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) confirmed the addition made by the Assessing Officer.

Annual accounts under the Companies Act 3. The Companies Act, 1956 ('the Act') imposes a duty (a) on the auditors to audit the accounts and to make a report thereon to the shareholders, and (b) on the Board of directors of the company to lay the annual accounts duly audited before get them adopted by the shareholders and at an annual general meeting (A.G.M.).

Section 211 of the Act dealing with the form and contents of the balance-sheet and profits and loss account provides that the balance-sheet and the profit and loss account shall give a true and fair view of the state of affairs of the company at the end of the financial year and of the profit or loss of the company for the financial year. The true and fair view contemplates that the reasonable expectations of readers of accounts are duly met. Accounting standards create a prima facie presumption that accounts which do not comply with them are not true and fair. Financial statements should not give any misleading impression or picture. Non-compliance with the provisions of the said section is an offence punishable under it. Thus, the balance-sheet and the profit and loss account, once they are audited by the company's auditor and adopted by the shareholders at the A.G.M., are given high sanctity. Failure to give a true and fair view in respect thereof amounts to breach of trust to shareholders, creditors and others relying on these documents and leads to penal consequences as mentioned above.

Failure to make provision for tax on distributed profits

4. It is noticed that some companies, not being fully conversant with the provisions of section 115-O and its effect, fail to make any provision for tax on distributed profits in their annual accounts for the Financial year 1996-97. The department of Company Affairs (the department) has ex-pressed the view that failure to make provision for taxation and proposed dividends would not disclose true and fair view of the state of affairs of the Company-Department's Letter No. 3/124/75-CL-VI dated July9, 1975. Accounts placed before the shareholders without making any provision for tax as aforesaid cannot be said to give a true and fair view of the state of affairs or profit (or loss) of the company for the said year as required by section 211, and this would attract the penalty as mentioned in the said section. Ways and means will have to be found out to overcome the difficulty which have arisen in the matter.

Revision of annual accounts - When permissible

5. The Act does not contain any provision regarding the reopening and revision of the annual accounts. The working group on the Companies Act has not also made any suggestion on the subject.

The department as well as the Institute of Chartered Accountants of India (ICAI), the professional body dealing with chartered accountants, has consistently expressed the view that it is open to the Board of directors of a company to revise the annual accounts and to re-submit the same to the auditor for his report thereon, so long as the original accounts have not been placed before and adopted by the shareholders at the A.G.M. Auditor's report on the revised accounts will be in substitution of his earlier report on the original accounts.

The department has also expressed the view that a company cannot reopen and revise its accounts after their adoption at the A.G.M. ICAI has also 'decided that the re-opening or rectification of accounts after they have been adopted at the annual general meeting should not be permitted under any circumstances'. In other words, once the accounts are adopted at the A.G.M. they are treated as sacrosanct and unalterable in any case. It is considered that there seems to be no warrant to take such a rigid view of the matter.

Department's clarification

6. In 1987 in partial modification of its aforesaid view the Department clarified that a company could re-open and revise its accounts even after their adoption in the annual general meeting in order to comply with technical requirements of taxation laws [Department's letter to ICAI dated August 19, 1987]. In such an event the revised annual accounts would be required to be adopted at the subsequent A.G.M. and thereafter filed with the Registrar of Companies as required by the Companies Act.

Probably the query raised by the department related to technical requirements of taxation laws and, hence, the department expressed the view in the matter as aforesaid. There seems to be no justification to take such a restricted view that a company can revise and re-open its accounts only for the limited purpose aforesaid. It is considered that re-opening and revision of accounts is permissible in all cases where directors discover that accounts presented by them are defective and they should be corrected. Appropriate rules or regulations made by the department on the subject would clarify the position in the matter.

Current Judicial Trends

3. There are a few advance rulings and judicial decisions on the subject. However, due to the inherent infirmity of advance rulings, these may only be relied upon in a persuasive manner rather than a binding capacity. Further, the insertion of section 56(1)(viia) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 from the assessment year 2010-11 also overturns most established judge made law in one fell swoop.

Nevertheless, let us examine the major decisions to determine the line of judicial thinking on this issue.

(a) Amiantit International Holding Ltd., In re [2010] 189 Taxman 149 (AAR - New Delhi)

This is so far the only the AAR dealing directly with the issue. The crux of the matter is that a Bahrain based company transferred shares of its Indian based subsidiary to its Cyprus associate enterprise without any consideration pursuant to a corporate restructuring. Since the situs of incorporation of the company whose shares are transferred is in India, the Indian revenue authorities have the jurisdiction to tax the transaction.

The main issue decided by the AAR is whether in case of shares transferred to an associated enterprise, the Indian TPP would apply.

The AAR in a well-reasoned judgment ruled that since the transfer is without consideration, there is no question of applying the touch stone of the ‘arm’s length price’ to determine a capital gain which could not be computed and, hence, ruled that the authorities could not ram the TPP down the assessee’s throat and tax an income which is not there. The Supreme Court’s decision in CIT v. B.C. Srinivasa Shetty [1981] 128 ITR 294/5 Taxman 1 which has laid down that in case the computation provision fails the charging section also fails seems to have been applied by the AAR notwithstanding the fact that the giver and recipient of the shares are associated enterprises.

However, it needs to be borne in mind that the Finance Act, 2010 has inserted section 56(2)(viia) which taxes receipt of shares at the difference between the fair market value and consideration in the hands of the recipient as ‘income from other sources’. The fair market value determination may certainly involve the principle of ‘arm’s length’ valuation and, hence, imply a backdoor application of the TPP in a modified form.

(b) Dana Corporation, In re [2010] 186 Taxman 187 (AAR - New Delhi).

This is another ruling which deals with a similar issue. In this case, the US parent entity files for bankruptcy under Chapter 11 and as a result of the bankruptcy proceedings an independent private equity player infuses capital in exchange for an integral package of assets and liabilities which involves shares of a merged US entity. As a result, indirect control and ownership of Indian subsidiaries is transferred to the private equity player.

The question before the AAR is whether such transfer of indirect control would constitute a gain in the hands of the private equity player and, hence, application of the arm’s length provisions to determine the costs of acquisition.

The AAR in this case also ruled that since the shares are transferred indirectly and also as part of a package where it is argued that the liabilities are more than the assets, no direct cost could be attributable to them. Hence, once again the computation provisions fail and, hence, the charging section would also fail and the TPP would not have any application.

Having said this, it is pertinent to note that the current vodafone controversy also has at its core the capital gains on indirect control and transfer of shares of an Indian subsidiary company and the AAR seems to have disregarded this aspect in its ruling.

(c) Star Television Entertainment Ltd., In re [2010] 188 Taxman 206 (AAR - New Delhi)

The Star Ruling also has similar facts but shares of an Indian company are transferred indirectly by virtue of corporate reorganization, here too the AAR rules that no tax is leviable since the computation provisions have failed and that the TPP are held not applicable.

The Company Court exercises jurisdiction which was founded on fairness. While exercising its jurisdiction, the Court was competent to examine the bona fides or fairness of the valuation of shares or the exchange ratio and whether the proposal conforms to commercial morality. It was held that having regard to the litigation history in the transferee company involving the objector and other related developments and also having regard to the financial status of the transferor company as discussed above, objection raised by the objector and by the Central Government through the Regional Director regarding the exchange ratio of shares between the two companies could not be brushed aside. Accordingly, the Registrar of Companies was directed to work out the exchange ratio in a fair manner through independent experts keeping in view the discussions made and were asked to submit the same to the Court in two months time. Thereafter Court might sanction the scheme with modifications.

2. Heritage Housing Finance Ltd., Inre [2013] 40 taxmann.com 103/[2014] 124 SCL 319 (Cal.)

Similar to the case discussed above was the case of "Heritage Housing Finance Ltd" wherein the Central Government raised an objection that the share exchange ratio as proposed in the said scheme was not fair and reasonable. The petitioner filed petition contending that the Central Government could not raise aforesaid objection when in the shareholders' meeting the entire scheme had been approved unanimously. It was held that the plain reading of the provisions did not postulate the nature of the objection required to be raised by the Central Government but what it provided was that the Court before passing any order ,must take into consideration the representations and/or objections raised by the Central Government. It was held that the Central Government was certainly within their competence to raise the objection as they were required to see that no unfairness and/or unreasonableness to be shown either to the creditors or the class of creditors and/or members or the class of members and public interest, which certainly imbibed itself with the power to question the said share exchange ratio. Therefore, there was no force in the submission of the petitioner that the Central Government could not raise objection to the share exchange ratio. It was therefore directed to the official liquidator to engage a Chartered Accountant from its panel, who should submit the report before the court relating to fairness of the share exchange ratio.

Option to substitute fair market value Under section 55(2)(b)(i), the option to substitute fair market value is available only if the shares in the resulting company were allotted to the shareholder in demerged company before 1-4-1981. According to the literal interpretation of section 55(2)(b), if the shares in resulting company are allotted on or after 1-4-1981, then despite the fact the shares in demerged company were acquired before 1-4-1981, the shareholder does not have an option to substitute the fair market value of these shares on 1-4-1981 while computing capital gains on sale of shares on 1-4-1981 in resulting company. This is because section 55(2)(b)(ii) allows the substitution of fair market value for the cost of acquisition only if the capital asset becomes the property of the assessee in the circumstances specified in section 49(1) and a case of demerger is not covered by section 49(1). In the context of amalgamation, the aforesaid literal interpretation has, however not been upheld by the Special Bench of the Tribunal in the case of H.F. Craig Harway v. Third ITO (supra).

Applying the arguments in the aforesaid decision, a shareholder in the resulting company gets an option to substitute the FMV of shares in demerged company as on 1-4-1981.

17. Reopening of cases of Rahul Gandhi and Sonia Gandhi is valid as they failed to disclose shares allotted in excess of FMV: HC

[Sonia Gandhi v. ACIT [2018] 97 taxmann.com 150 (Delhi)]

The assessees, Mr. Rahul Gandhi and Mrs. Sonia Gandhi, extended a loan to the National Herald to write off the accumulated debts and recommence the newspaper publication. The said loan was assigned by the assessee to a newly incorporated non-profit company 'Young India' (YI) and in lieu of that they were allotted shares of YI. However, in Income-tax returns, they failed to pay tax on the shares allotted by Young India. The assessees argued that the allotment of shares did not trigger any taxing event. It was also argued that since they were shareholders of a non-profit and charitable company, they were under no obligation to disclose the value of shares.

The High Court held in favour of revenue that sub-clause (ii) of clause (c) of Section 56(2) provides that if certain shares or property are acquired at a price which is less than its aggregate fair market value by an amount exceeding Rs. 50,000, the fair market value as reduced by the considered paid shall be charged to tax. In the instant case, the assessee bought the shares at Rs. 100 per share which could not be deemed as its fair market value. The assesse had nowhere disclosed the fair market value of such shares and had not recorded the facts relating to above taxing event. Further, it couldn't be held that the individual was exempted altogether from disclosing her or his interest in the acquisition of shares merely because shares were of not-for-profit Company. Therefore, the AO was justified in reopening the cases.

Income from other sources is a residuary head of income and sweeps in all taxable incomes that fall outside the other four heads of income. The provisions relating to the taxability of residuary income are contained in Section 92 of the ITA 2025 [Corresponds to Section 56 of the ITA 1961]. The relevant provisions read as follows:

"Income from other sources 92 (1) Income of every kind which is not to be excluded from the total income under this Act, shall be chargeable to income-tax under the head "Income from other sources", if it is not chargeable to income-tax under any of the heads specified in section 13(a) to (d).

(2) In particular, and without prejudice to the generality of the provisions of sub-section (1), the following incomes shall be chargeable to income-tax under the head "Income from other sources":—

(a)

any dividend;

(b)

…………………………..;

(c)

…………………………..;

(d)

…………………………..;

(e)

income by way of interest on securities, if the income is not chargeable to income-tax under the head "Profits and gains of business or profession";

(f)

to (m)………………………………."

Clauses (a) to (m) of Section 96(2) provide for the chargeability of various incomes under the head of other sources. Clause (a) explicitly specifies that dividend shall be taxed under the head of 'income from other sources'. However, for several other items of income specified in Clauses (b) to (m), the provision is qualified by the phrase 'if such income is not chargeable to income-tax under the head' Profits and gains of business or profession'.

For instance, as per clause (e), interest on securities is chargeable to tax under the head of other sources only when it is not chargeable to income-tax under the head "Profits and gains of business or profession". The exclusion of the said phrase from clause (a) suggests that the dividend income can never be taxed as business income and must always be taxed under the head of 'income from other sources'.

However, the taxability of dividend income under the head' business or profession' when it is connected to the business carried on by the assessee (for example, dividend received in respect of shares held as stock-in-trade) has always been a matter of turf war.

The Delhi High Court, in the case of CIT v. Excellent Commercial Enterprises & Investments Ltd. [2005] 147 Taxman 558 (Delhi), held that where shares are held by the assessee as a stock-in-trade, then it could not be said that the dividend income would fall as an income from other sources as contemplated under section 56. The Supreme Court, in the case of Brooke Bond & Co. Ltd. v. CIT [1986] 28 Taxman 426 (SC), held that the nature of the dividend income must be determined having regard to the true nature and character of the income.

It is recommended that like other clauses, dividend income should be taxable under the head of 'income from other sources' if it is not chargeable to income-tax under the head 'Profits and gains of business or profession'. Section 92(2)(a) should be read as under:

(2) In particular, and without prejudice to the generality of the provisions of sub-section (1), the following incomes, shall be chargeable to income-tax under the head "Income from other sources" :—

(a) dividends [, if such income is not chargeable to income-tax under the head "Profits and gains of business or profession"];

9. Exemption to be given on transfer of shares held as stock-in-trade in the scheme of amalgamation

As per Section 70(1)(f) of the ITA 2025 [Corresponds to Section 47(vii) of the ITA 1961], any transfer of a capital asset, such as shares held by a shareholder in the amalgamating company (transferor), under a scheme of amalgamation is not regarded as a transfer, provided the specified conditions are satisfied. Thus, no tax implication arises in the hands of the shareholder at the time of allotment of shares of the amalgamated company (transferee) in lieu of shares held as a capital asset in the amalgamating company (transferor).

The above exemption is available only when the shareholders hold the shares as capital assets. If such shares are held as stock-in-trade, no exemption is provided, and profits and gains arising from the transfer of shares will be chargeable to tax under the head 'profits and gains from business and profession'.

This differential tax treatment, based solely on the nature of the investment made by shareholders, is arbitrary. Thus, it is recommended that the government bring parity and amend Section 70(1)(f) to extend the exemption to shares held as stock-in-trade.

work. But to what extent and in what manner, delegation should be, is always a matter of great concern. Section 119 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 and section 37B of the Central Excise Act, 1944 also provide delegation by the Parliament to the Central Board of Direct Taxes (herein after called CBDT) and the Central Board of Excise and Custom (herein after called CBEC); but the scope of this power has always been in controversy. The journey regarding scope of circular issued by the CBDT was practically started from the five Judges’ Bench ruling in case of Navnit Lal C. Javeri v. K. K. Sen, Appellate Assistant CIT [1964] 56 ITR 198 in the year 1964. In that case, a Constitution Bench of the Supreme Court was examining the constitutional validity of sections 2(6A)(e) and 12(1B) inserted in the Indian Income-tax Act of 1922 by the Finance Act of 1955. These sections provided that any payment made by a closely held company to its shareholder by way of advance or loan to the extent to which the company possessed accumulated profits should be treated as dividend taxable under the Act and this would include any loan or advance made in the relevant year prior to the assessment year 1955-56, if such loan or advance remained outstanding on the first day of the previous year, relevant to the assessment year 1955-56. In order to mitigate the rigour of the provision to some extent and to fulfil the assurance of the Hon’ble Minister for Revenue and Civil Expenditure, the Central Board of Revenue issued a circular under section 5(8) of the Act to the effect that if any such outstanding loans or advances of past years were repaid on or before June 30, 1955, they would not be taken into account in determining the tax liability of the shareholders who received such loans or advances. The decision was "circular of the kind which was issued by the Board would be binding on all officers and persons employed in the execution of the Act". In case of Ellerman Lines Ltd. v. CIT [1964] 56 ITR 198 and K. P. Varghese v. ITO [1981] 7 Taxman 13/[1964] 56 ITR 198 ratio of Navnit Lal C. Javeri is got generalized in the following words’ "The directions given in that circular clearly deviated from the provisions of the Act, yet this court ( in Navnit Lal C. Javeri’s case (supra)) held that the circular was binding on the Income-tax Officer". This may be due to the fact that, though the provisions are applicable from 1.04.1955, yet by issue of circular, these are made applicable from 1.07.1955. So the circular clearly was against the provisions. This may be the fact for which the Court gave more weight in the two later rulings. In Keshavji Ravji & Co. v. CIT [1964] 56 ITR 198/[1990] 49 Taxman 87, a Bench of three Judges of the Supreme Court has also taken the view that circulars beneficial to the assessee which tone down the rigor of the law and are issued in exercise of the statutory powers under section 119 are binding on the authorities in the administration of the Act. The benefit of such circulars is admissible to the assessee, even though the circulars might have departed from the strict tenor of the statutory provision and mitigated the rigour of the law. The Court, however, clarified that the Board cannot pre-empt a judicial interpretation of the scope and ambit of a provision of the Act. Also a circular cannot impose on the taxpayer a burden higher than what the Act itself, on a true interpretation, envisages. The task of interpretation of the laws is the exclusive domain of the Courts. 9. (1) Under the provisions of the Income-tax Act, income by way of dividend on shares will be taxed at the rate of 10 per cent. The issuing company shall transfer the dividend payments net after deduct tax at source to the Overseas Depositary Bank.

(2) On receipt of these payments of dividend after taxation, the Overseas Depositary Bank shall distribute them to the non-resident investors proportionate to their holdings of Global Depositary Receipts evidencing the relevant shares. The holders of the Depositary Receipts may take credit of the tax deducted at source on the basis of the certification by the Overseas Depositary Bank, if permitted by the country of their residence.

(3) All transactions of trading of the Global Depositary Receipts outside India, among non-resident investors, will be free from any liability to income-tax in India on capital gains therefrom.

(4) If any capital gains arise on the transfer of the aforesaid shares in India to the non-resident investor, he will be liable to income-tax under the provisions of the Income-tax Act. If the aforesaid shares are held by the non-resident investor for a period of more than twelve months from the date of advice of their redemption by the Overseas Depositary Bank, the capital gains arising on the sale thereof will be treated as long-term capital gains and will be subject to income-tax at the rate of 10 per cent under the provisions of section 115AC of the Income-tax Act. If such shares are held for a period of less than twelve months from the date of redemption advice, the capital gains arising on the sale thereof will be treated as short-term capital gains and will be subject to tax at the normal rates of income-tax applicable to non-residents under the provisions of the Income-tax Act.

(5) After redemption of the Depositary Receipts into underlying shares, during the period, if any, which these shares are held by the redeeming non-resident foreign investor who has paid for these shares in foreign exchange at the time of purchase of the Global Depositary Receipt, the rate of taxation of income by way of dividends on these shares would continue to be at the rate of 10 per cent, in accordance with section 115AC(1) of the Income-tax Act. The long-term capital gains on the sale of these redeemed underlying shares held by non-resident investors in the domestic market shall also be charged to tax at the rate of 10 per cent, in accordance with the provisions of section 115AC(1).

(6) When the redeemed shares are sold on the Indian Stock Exchanges against payment in rupees, these shares shall go out of the purview of section 115AC of the Income-tax Act and income therefrom shall not be eligible for the concessional tax treatment provided thereunder. After the transfer of shares where consideration is in terms of rupees payment, the normal tax rates would apply to the income arising or accruing on these shares.

(7) Deduction of tax at source on the amount of capital gains accruing on transfer of the shares would be made in accordance with sections 195 and 196C of the Income-tax Act.
