[Para 129] Once it was held that on payment of the amount under the bank guarantee, the HDFC Bank had become the lender of money and under the scheme of demerger, all assets and liabilities of the Sachana unit would vest in ‘N’, then there was no scope to say that HDFC, though a lender, would be entitled to say that particular amount be kept outside the scheme. It would absolutely be correct to say that the compromise and demerger scheme was a package deal and when a party was agreeable to the compromise in a package deal, then such party would be entitled to all the benefits flowing from the scheme. It was also true to say that the statutory liabilities and other liabilities, known or unknown, real or contingent, would have to be suffered by ‘N’ and at that stage, it was not possible to define with reasonable certainty and exact calculation as to what would be the sum total of such liabilities. At the relevant time the amount under the bank guarantee had been paid for or on behalf of Core and if that amount ultimately was to be refunded, then the benefit must go to the party entitled to it under the scheme. It would also be correct to say that if ‘N’ fulfilled the export obligations, then their right to recover the money from the Customs Department would be a right flowing from the scheme and, in fact, the amount to be paid to N would not be an amount, which was to go back to the HDFC Bank. In case, there was no scheme and petitioner fulfilled the export obligations, then Core would be entitled to the refund and HDFC, even at that time, could not say that the money should be paid to them directly. Under the circumstances, the objection raised by HDFC did not merit consideration. [Para 131]

The members of the company, in a general meeting, can approve reduction of the share capital by a special resolution, if the same is passed by statutory majority and while approving the scheme, the members simultaneously approve reduction of the share capital by a special resolution. In the instant case, the procedure prescribed in sections 100 and 101 had been carried out by the company and section 102 would not be attracted. In view of the settled law, the objection raised by the objector did not survive. [Para 134]

So far as the objection of the objector that the scheme was invalid because it amounted to fraud on the revenue as the scheme provided for benefit of set off with carry forward losses and depreciation of the Sachana undertaking of Core in the hands of N was concerned, it was to be seen that section 72A(4) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 itself provides that such carried forward losses or unabsorbed depreciation of demerged undertaking would be carried forward and set off in the hands of the resulting company. If the statutory benefit was available to N and they were entitled to take advantage of such set off, then the objectors could not be allowed to say that the scheme would be a fraud on the revenue. It would be correct to say that what was permissible under the law could never be regarded as contrary to the public policy or fraud on the revenue. [Para 135]

In relation to the objection regarding the share exchange ratio, the petitioners had submitted that none of the objectors-banks were shareholders of the petitioners and, therefore, they were not entitled to raise such objection. From the submissions made by the petitioners, it would clearly appear that the exchange ratio was fixed on the basis of the report of the chartered accountants. According to them, the report was placed at the meeting of the shareholders and the lenders and no objection whatsoever was raised in any of the meetings as to fixation of the said ratio. If by allotment of shares of N to the shareholders of Core, the said shareholders were to be benefited, then the objectors could not have any objection. In the case of sale of the assets and winding up of the company, the shareholders of Core would not get anything. If under the scheme, such shareholders were to receive some benefits, then conferral of such benefits upon such shareholders was not going to affect the rights of the objectors. It was also to be noted that the shareholders of Core would continue to hold their shares and additional benefit would be conferred upon them. Conferral of that benefit upon the shareholders would also have to be appreciated from the viewpoint of the shareholders, who were to get something against nothing and that was persuading them to accept the scheme. In any case, the objectors were not entitled to challenge the scheme on the ground of share exchange ratio. [Para 136]

The assessee was the wife of one ‘K’ who was partner in a firm and was also a member of an HUF. She owned a substantial number of shares in the ‘H’ company and the remaining shares of that company, although it was a public limited company, were all held by members of the family, including the ladies. ‘H’ was the managing agent of the ‘J’ company and among its directors, two were relatives of the assessee. ‘H’ company held 62,000 shares of the ‘J’ company and on 27-5-1940, it sold out 48,000 of those shares to the assessee and such other ladies for a total consideration of Rs. 5,28,000. The shares were sold at the rate of Rs. 11 per share, although the market price at the time was about Rs. 16. It was decided that this sale of the 48,000 shares was not a bona fide transaction, but a device designed to reduce the excess profits tax liability of the company. The sale to the eight ladies was on blank transfer forms and the transfers were not registered till 1943. Upto 1943, the dividends paid on these shares were taxed in the hands of the ‘H’, because the income-tax department declined to recognise the transfers till they were registered. Ultimately, in February and March, 1945, all the 48,000 shares were sold away by the ladies. The assessee sold her 4,300 shares for Rs. 1,44,788 thus making a profit of Rs. 97,488. The ITO included that profit in the assessable income of the assessee on the ground that the amounts concerned constituted income from an adventure in the nature of trade. On appeal, the AAC held that they were capital receipts and so not taxable. The Tribunal reversed the order of the AAC and agreed with the ITO.

The balance sheet of the assessee-company as at 31-3-1986 indicated that the fixed assets had been revalued. The assessee had investments in shares and these consisted of both quoted and unquoted shares. These shares were not revalued in the year ended 31-3-1986 along with the other assets. However, in the next year in the balance sheet as at 31-3-1987 the assessee revalued all the quoted shares at the market value. The difference in revaluation of these shares was taken to capital reserve account. The assessee had sold certain quoted shares on 13-5- 1987 and 21-9-1987. In the balance sheet as at 31-3-1987, the value of the remaining quoted investments was recorded at book value which was as revalued in the earlier year. The amount fetched by sale of shares sold was fully invested in units of the Unit Trust of India, and showed as part of investments held by the assessee. Thus, the sale proceeds of investment in shares were not credited to profit and loss account nor the loss was debited to it but was carried to the capital reserve account.

While completing the assessment for the assessment year 1988-89 the Assessing Officer held that the shares had been revalued with the sole intention of defrauding the revenue and avoiding of payment of tax due under the provisions of section 115J, and that the change in the method of valuation of quoted shares was adopted only for one year and not followed consistently thereafter. Following the principles laid down by the Supreme Court in the case of McDowell & Co. Ltd. v. CTO [1985] 154 ITR 148/22 Taxman 11, the ITO computed the book profit for the purpose of section 115J. On appeal the Commissioner (Appeals) held that under clause 3(xii)( a) of Part II to Schedule VI of the Companies Act, the profit on investment had to be shown in the profit and loss account and that would include also the capital profit. It was held that the book profit taxable under section 115J was not just as shown by the assessee but as should be shown in accordance with the provisions of the Companies Act and that the assessee had tailored its accounts in order to escape the mischief of section 115J.

Mode and manner of treatment of ESOPs by a company in its books of account

4. A company has to amortize the differential share price of Rs. X per share for total shares of XYZ over a period of stipulated period (say 24 months) on a straightline basis over the vesting period. The company debits this amount of Rs. XXX which is amortized for the period relevant to the accounting year, to its profit and loss account under the head ‘Administration and other expenses’ or any other relevant head under ESOS/ESOP. Having, thus, amortized the employees stock option compensation expenses as per guidelines issued by SEBI, a company shall have to reduce the same from its share premium account, if any, available. This kind of accounting treatment is normally given effect to by every company and the same is well in accordance with the Income-tax law as well as in consonance with the provisions of section 78 of the Companies Act, 1956. Sub-section (2) of section 78 permits a company to appropriate its share premium amount only to certain specific purposes including issuing shares at discount. In other words, the amount of discount that shall be granted by a company may be recouped from out of the share premium amount or from out of its free reserves, if available.

Therefore, a company treats in its books of account the amortized-employees ESOS compensation expenses to the extent of Rs. XXX, which is relevant to the period of accounting, as allowable business expenditure from out of its income under the law.

discussion was made as to what was considered to be 'majority' as far as passing resolution was considered.

Held: It was held that it was impossible to say which of several available valuation models were 'best' or most appropriate. No valuation was to be disregarded merely because it had used one or other of various methods; it must be shown that chosen method of valuation was such as has resulted in an artificially depressed or contrived valuation well below what a fair-minded person may consider reasonable. Further it was held in that, at the simplest level, "majority" would mean majority of all shareholders of the Company across all classes. However that was not the correct test in the matter. There were admittedly two classes, the promoter shareholders and the non-promoter shareholders. The promoter shareholders far outnumbered the non-promoter shareholders. For the time being even if concentration was done only on responses of the minority i.e the non-promoter shareholders, within the minority itself again there were two divisions, those who voted in favour of the proposed resolution at the General Meeting and those voted against. Among the non promoters, those in favour outnumbered those against, and these must constitute the relavent "majority" for the present purpose. Thus, a peculiar situation was there: overall, the majority shareholders (Including the promoter-shareholders) voted for the scheme and at the same time, bulk of non-promoter shareholders (i.e., a majority of the minority) had also voted in favour of the scheme. Hence it was held that in the proposed Scheme valuation of shares was done by Court appointed valuer and was accepted by overwhelming majority including the bulk of non-promoter minority, hence scheme was to be sanctioned.

Azadi Bachao Andolan [2003] 263 ITR 706/ 132 Taxman 373 (SC) The Apex Court clearly held that legitimate tax planning cannot be challenged merely on the basis of assumed underlying intentions of tax evasion. The Court, commenting on the McDowell’s decision whilst referring to various other judgments, agreed that not every action or inaction on the part of the taxpayer, which results in reduction of tax liability, must be viewed with suspicion. Taxpayers are free to carry out any trade/activity or plan their affairs with circumspection, within the framework of law, unless the same falls in the category of a colourable device without substance. So principally, the right of taxpayer to ‘plan’ his transactions to mitigate tax liability cannot be questioned only because it is ‘tax advantage’ provided ‘economic substance’ is demonstrated in the same. However, if the motive of the tax avoidance is seen to outweigh the purpose of the transaction evidenced and evaluated with factual aspects, the Courts in India more likely than not will tread the path of assuming that ‘substance over form’ should prevail and the transaction should be challenged.

Conclusion

6. In the case of Walfort Share & Stock Brokers (P.) Ltd. (supra ), the Supreme Court of India has reiterated that tax planning is perfectly valid, since it is within the four corners of law. However, the revenue department has time and again attemp-ted to tax legally permissible transactions as tax avoidance mechanism. The Government of India is in the process to introduce the Direct Taxes Code. The Direct Taxes Code proposes to introduce a General Anti Avoidance Rule (‘GAAR’), which could empower tax authorities to re-characterize a transaction entered into by a taxpayer and the income therefrom. The GAAR provisions are proposed to override the other provisions of the DTC. Currently tax planning is considered as legal in light of the Azadi Bachao Andolan’s case (supra). CIT [2008] 302 ITR 255/171 Taxman 390 (Delhi) is an authority for the proposition that even when an assessee becomes entitled to an undefined and undivided share in a property, through an agreement, which he later relinquishes, the gain has to be assessed as income from capital gain, and not as income from other sources." It was finally submitted on behalf of the assessee that the Tribunal clearly fell into error by not appreciating the fact that the provisions of Section 17(3)(iii) of the Act were clearly not attracted in this case since the amount received by the assessee had no nexus or correlation with the cessation of his employment with TTPL and further that the Assessing Officer as well as the Tribunal had clearly misconstrued the scope and ambit of Section 17(3)(iii) of the Act.

The High Court took into consideration the arguments put forth on behalf of both sides and answered the principal question whether the Tribunal was justified in bifurcating the settlement consideration between salary and capital gains in the negative by noting that a bifurcation of the consideration amount between salary and capital gains was one which was never advocated by the respondents (Revenue). The High Court went on to observe that "it thus clearly appears to represent an exercise which the Tribunal undertook of its own volition."

The High Court allowed the appeal of the assessee by setting aside the order passed by the Tribunal on the following grounds—

(a)

TTPL had never doubted the fact that the assessee did possess share certificates of the 50,000 sweat equity shares which had been allotted to it. This aspect should also be viewed in light of the well settled position in law of a share certificate being prima facie evidence of valid title. The litigation before the CLB had ensued only because of a refusal on the part of TTPL to record the name of the assessee in the Register of Members. It was in the aforesaid context that the assessee had addressed a prayer for specific performance before the CLB.

(b)

From various clauses of the Settlement Agreement the consideration was concerned with an unconditional and irrevocable relinquishment of the right of the assessee to seek and enforce the registration of the shares held by him. It was the relinquishment of the aforesaid right which formed the basis for the assessee being compensated by TTPL.

(c)

As the assessee undertook not to take any steps to enforce any right, title or interest in the shares in question, the consideration thus would appear to be undeniably connected with the relinquishment of all claims which could have been raised by the assessee in respect of sweat equity.

(d)

The Tribunal lost sight of the difference between a 'perquisite' and 'profits in lieu of salary' and both of whom have been dealt with separately in Section 17 of the Act. This subtle difference was appreciated by the High Court by explaining that "Section 17 of the Act, while seeking to define the expression 'salary', includes perquisites' in terms of sub-section (2) and sweat equity being a constituent of perquisites by virtue of clause (vi) thereof. Sub-section (3) to Section 17, on the other hand, deals with 'profits in lieu of salary.'"

'Profits in lieu of salary', spoken of in Section 17(3), would deal with compensation received by an assessee from his employer or former employer in connection with the termination of his employment or on a modification of terms and conditions of service. Clause (iii) of Section 17(3) should be construed bearing in mind the subjects covered in the preceding parts of that sub-section. Consequently, the lump sum amount spoken of in clause (iii) would also have to draw colour and meaning from compensation received in connection with termination of employment or modification of terms and conditions of service and which are the principal subjects of 'profits in lieu of salary'. In the instant case, as already stated above, termination of employment took place as early as 24th August, 2010 and

(h)

All that the Tribunal was called upon to examine was whether the settlement consideration was liable to be construed as capital gains or taxed as 'profits in lieu of salary'. The RBI and CBDT valuations, being derived from different bases (DCF value as per the issuing company and the taxman respectively), will not converge. The starting point of the divergence is the issue of shares to the non-resident which will be based on the RBI guidelines. Thereafter the taxman enters the picture, determines that the shares have been undervalued when they were issued and seeks to tax the alleged discount. Both RBI and the CBDT, being apex bodies of the Government – and indeed of the same Ministry of Finance – there should not be such a divergence between the valuations of these two bodies. The valuations can at most vary by 10-20% but more than that means one of the apex bodies are not doing their job correctly and causing loss to the nation, either by giving up foreign exchange or taxes due to the country. A variation of 1850% in the Shell India/Netherlands case indicates a very basic disconnect between two apex government bodies to whom the share issuer and the non-resident share allottee are subject. Issuers of shares to non-residents and their allottees should not be made victims of separate valuation methodologies of different arms of the Government. This calls for serious and urgent review at the highest levels of the Government.

"Two departments of the Government cannot in law adopt contrary or inconsistent contentions or act at a cross purposes. To use the famous word of Lord Denning in that case, 'The right hand of the Government cannot pretend to be unaware of what the left hand is doing'"

The Supreme Court also in M G Abrol, Additional Collector of Customs v Shanti Lal Chhotalal & Co. AIR 1966 SC 197, decision which was referred to in Mobile Communication India (P.) Ltd. What is the rationale for issuing shares at a discount to the overseas parent?

Where the taxman alleges that an Indian company has issued shares to its 100% overseas parent at a discount, a fundamental question arises as to why the subsidiary should attempt to do so? A 100% parent can control the subsidiary by the fact of its shareholding percentage and would not be bothered about the number of shares it holds in the subsidiary. If shares are undervalued and issued, more number of shares are issued, compared to a situation where lesser number of shares are issued when the shares are priced higher. In both situations, the shareholding still remains 100% in the subsidiary. What is therefore to be gained by issuing shares at a discount, when the shares are meant to be permanently held by the parent as part of its group structure and not meant to be disposed of soon after allotment? To take the Shell India/Netherlands example, Shell India could have, instead of inviting any tax scrutiny/liability by issuing 87 crore shares at an undervalued price of Rs. 10 each i.e. Rs. 870 crores, have easily issued 4.7 crore shares (of Rs. 10 par value) at an issue price of Rs. 185 and collected the same amount of Rs. 870 crores that it required for its operations. If Shell Netherlands was the sole parent company controlling Shell India, this control could have been equally exercised in the same manner with 4.7 crore shares as with 87 crore shares. Hence, the motive for seeking to undervalue the issue of shares by Shell India to Shell Netherlands needs to be fundamentally established by the taxman, before seeking to establish the quantum of undervaluation. If no motive can be established, the attempts to tax the undervaluation lacks substance and would amount to taking advantage of a technicality.

Share buybacks raise a characterisation issue under the DTAAs. The central issue is whether the gain or income arising in the hands of the shareholder should be treated as a dividend, a capital gain, or other income. This characterisation is critical because it determines which article of the DTAA applies and, consequently, which country retains the right to tax such income. The OECD Model Convention defines "dividends" under Article 10(3) to mean income from shares, jouissance shares or jouissance rights, mining shares, founders' shares or other rights that are not debt-claims but participate in profits, as well as income from other corporate rights which is subjected to the same taxation treatment as income from shares by the laws of the state of which the company making the distribution is a resident. This definition is broad and explicitly connects the characterisation of dividend income to the domestic law of the source state. Paragraph 28 of the OECD Commentary on Article 10 addresses situations involving redemption, liquidation, and disguised distributions of profits, and notes that where the domestic law of the source state treats the amounts paid to a shareholder on buyback as a distribution of profits, such amounts fall within the definition of dividends under Article 10.

Para 31 of the OCED Model Commentary on Article 13 provides that if shares are alienated by a shareholder in connection with the liquidation of the issuing company or the redemption of shares or reduction of paid-up capital of that company, the difference between the proceeds obtained by the shareholder and the par value of the shares may be treated in the State of which the company is a resident as a distribution of accumulated profits and not as a capital gain. The Article does not prevent the State of residence of the company from taxing such distributions at the rates provided for in Article 10. Where the domestic law of the source country does not treat the buyback proceeds as dividend income but instead characterises the transaction as a sale or transfer of a capital asset, Article 13 of the treaty on Capital Gains would apply.

In simple terms, the treatment of share buybacks under a DTAA is not governed by a single universal rule but depends critically on the characterisation of the proceeds under the domestic law of the source state, the specific treaty language, and the model convention on which the bilateral treaty is based. Where domestic law treats buyback proceeds as a deemed dividend or distribution of profits, Article 10 applies, and the source state retains the tax rights. Where domestic law treats income from share buybacks as capital gains, the classification should be the same under the DTAA unless a treaty provides otherwise. Regardless of characterisation, taxpayers must remain mindful of anti-avoidance provisions such as the PPT, which may override treaty benefits where arrangements lack sufficient commercial substance.

6.2-5h Taxable in the hands of the shareholder - The capital gains computed under section 69 shall be taxable in the hands of the shareholder. The term 'shareholder' is not specifically defined in either the Income-tax Act or the Companies Act. However, section 2(55) of the Companies Act, 2013 defines 'member' as a person whose name is entered in the register of members of the company. Additionally, a person who holds shares in a company and whose name is recorded as a beneficial owner in the depository's records is considered a member.

For income tax purposes, the term 'shareholder' generally refers to a registered shareholder. A beneficial owner whose name does not appear in the register of shareholders is not considered a 'shareholder'11.

According to the Prohibition of Benami Property Transactions Act, 1988 ("Benami Act"), it is not permissible for a person to be a shareholder when the beneficial owner of those shares is some other person. However, section 2(9) of the Benami Act provides certain exceptions where the shareholder may be a different person from the beneficial owner, subject to specific conditions:

A shareholder who is the Karta of an HUF, with the beneficial owner being the HUF itself.

A shareholder acting in a fiduciary capacity, such as a trustee, executor, partner, director, depository, or depository participant, with the beneficial owner being the Trust, estate, partnership firm, company, or demat account holder.

A shareholder who is an individual, with the beneficial owner being his or her spouse or child.

A shareholder who is an individual, with the beneficial owner being his or her brother, sister, or lineal ascendant or descendant, as joint owners.

The Supreme Court, in Howrah Trading Co. Ltd. v. CIT [1959] 36 ITR 215 (SC), held that a shareholder means a person whose name is entered in the register of members. Thus, a beneficial owner, such as a firm holding shares through its partners, is not considered a shareholder. Consequently, if shares are held in a fiduciary capacity for another person, the taxability lies with the person who holds the shares as the registered shareholder. However, this principle shall not apply when a depository or depository participant holds shares in a fiduciary capacity for a demat account holder, as the demat account holder is considered the member in relation to the company, not the depository.

A shareholder who is the Karta of an HUF, with the beneficial owner being the HUF itself.

A shareholder acting in a fiduciary capacity, such as a trustee, executor, partner, director, depository, or depository participant, with the beneficial owner being the Trust, estate, partnership firm, company, or demat account holder.

A shareholder who is an individual, with the beneficial owner being his or her spouse or child.

A shareholder who is an individual, with the beneficial owner being his or her brother, sister, or lineal ascendant or descendant, as joint owners.

The Supreme Court, in Howrah Trading Co. Ltd. v. CIT [1959] 36 ITR 215 (SC), held that a shareholder means a person whose name is entered in the register of members. Thus, a beneficial owner, such as a firm holding shares through its partners, is not considered a shareholder. Consequently, if shares are held in a fiduciary capacity for another person, the taxability lies with the person who holds the shares as the registered shareholder. However, this principle shall not apply when a depository or depository participant holds shares in a fiduciary capacity for a demat account holder, as the demat account holder is considered the member in relation to the company, not the depository.

It subsequently, sold said shares. Since there was no difference between the sale price and revalued price at which the shares were shown in the books of account, the assessee did not show any profit on sale of shares in its profit and loss account prepared under the Companies Act, 1956. The accounts, thus prepared, were duly certified by the statutory auditors of the assessee-company and filed along with its return for the purposes of section 115JA. The assessee claimed that the capital gain on sale of the said shares was exempted under section 54EA and, therefore, no capital gains tax was chargeable for the following reasons: one, there was no profit on sale of shares as the shares were sold at the valued price; two, there was no capital gain on the sale of shares as the sale proceeds stood invested in specified securities under section 54EA. The Assessing Officer, by referring to the Accounting Standards notified by the Institute of Chartered Accountants of India, held that the capital gain, which is deemed to be its income under section 45, was liable to be included in the book profit as shown in the profit and loss account for the purposes of section 115J. Thus, holding so, he added Rs. 25,25,800 being profit on sale of investments to the book profit of Rs. 2,02,24,954 shown in the profit and loss account certified by the statutory auditors of the assessee-company, and brought the same to tax under section 115JA after making some adjustments.

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) reversed the order of the Assessing Officer and deleted the capital gains from the book profit.

Doctrine of Unjust Enrichment

8. The resolution plan cannot provide for extinguishment of the liability of the corporate debtor in respect of amounts deducted or collected as fiduciary of the statutory authorities. One example is tax deducted at source; other common example is indirect tax.

Such an amount cannot be said to be forming a part of the estate of the corporate debtor. The resolution applicant who submits resolution plan intends to acquire the corporate debtor at the best (read, lowest) possible price. However, extinguishment of amounts as aforesaid will lead to what is commonly referred to as "unjust enrichment" of the shareholders of the acquirer, that too at the cost of the persons who suffered taxes.

Concluding Remarks

9. As is evident from the discussion so far, plans or schemes approved under statutes have been given overriding effect, so as to be called "a statutory magic"; however, a pre-condition is that the same shall "legitimately" bind those who dissented to the scheme/plan. A statutory creditor who was not even provided an opportunity to be there in the meeting of creditors for approval and rejection of the resolution plan cannot be excluded in entirety and denied the right to be repaid. A plan framed under one statute cannot prevail over another statute.It may also be noted here that the conflict here is between two classes of creditors. A class of creditors cannot extinguish the rights of other class of creditors.

Therefore, the following may be concluded as regards statutory dues –

(i)

Statutory dues cannot be reduced or extinguished without seeking consent of the concerned authority. The authority shall be given a right to object to the provisions of the resolution plan affecting its right to receive statutory dues. It is opined that a public notice shall be issued by the resolution applicant asking for objections against the resolution plan.

(ii)

The above holds true even if statutory dues are deferred or scheduled to paid in tranches.

(iii)

The resolution plan shall, at bare minimum, provide for payment of liquidation value due towards statutory dues. The plan cannot go beyond such minimum level. See "Guide to Liquidation Value under the Insolvency Code"7, by Sikha Bansal.

(iv)

In case of statutory arrears, the retention of which leads to unjust enrichment of the corporate debtor, waiver/extinguishment is not possible.

The Delhi Tribunal in SAIL v. DCIT (1991) 38 ITD 193, under the provisions of section 115J held that for the purposes of working out permissible adjustment of the lower of depreciation or loss, profits made in the earlier year cannot be ignored. The losses or the depreciation must be set off against earlier years' profits. In Geetanjali Woollens Pvt. Ltd. v. ACIT [1994] 50 ITD 558 the Ahmedabad Tribunal took a view that in determining, amount of loss or depreciation, to be set off, the amount already not set off in the past can only be considered.

The Chandigarh Bench of Income-tax Appellate Tribunal in ITO v. Parbhat Forging Pvt. Ltd [1991] 38 ITD 319 held that unprovided depreciation in respect of the past cannot be adjusted. While holding so, it also considered provisions similar to section 205 which were incorporated in section 115J of the Act.

Section 115JA does not have a similar provision. Now, what is permissible is reduction of the lower of brought forward loss or unabsorbed depreciation, as per books of account. This does imply that the loss or the depreciation must have been reflected in the books of account. In case of a company, which was incurring loss, depreciation may not have been provided at all.

Accordingly, in the year of profit, if it also provides for depreciation in respect of earlier years, then in computing the book profit, whether any adjustment can be made in respect of unprovided depreciation of earlier years ?

Having regard to the provisions, under the Explanation below section 115JA(2)no such adjustment can be made.

However, it may be pointed out that, as discussed earlier, a bench of Tribunal has taken a different view. Possibly, the different view could be contested on the ground that the provision for depreciation is a legal requirement, before declaring any dividends, and therefore in terms of the statute, the provision was made and therefore should not be a subject matter of adjustment.

The Cochin Bench of the Tribunal in Apollo Tyres Ltd v. DCIT [1992] 43 ITD 464 was concerned with a case where assessee provided for extra shift depreciation an its accounts, pursuant to insertion of Schedule XIV to the said Act. It was observed by the Tribunal that in view of the statutory amendment, the assessee was legally bound to provide for arrears of such extra shift depreciation. Further, this was in accordance with the provisions of the Schedule. Apart from that there was no earmarked adjustment for the provision. Accordingly, in computing book profit, an adjustment in respect thereof cannot be made.

In Bombay Tyres International Ltd v. DCIT[1994] 51 ITD 339, the company had changed the method of depreciation from straight line to WDV method based on technical or other evaluation and provided for the same in the accounts. The Bombay Tribunal took a view that change was bona fide based on recommendation of financial and technical personnel; it was a valid change and as per legal or accounting requirement as inferred, it was appropriate and not a colourable device. It took a view that the arrears pertained to a provision of an ascertained and known liability and therefore did not constitute reserve. Having regard to decision of Special Bench in Sutlej case (supra), the adjustment made by the department was not permitted.

In Beta Napthol Pvt. Ltd. v. DCIT [1994] 50 TTJ 375, Indore Bench of the Tribunal with reference to change in method of depreciation and section 115J has taken a view that an assessee is entitled to change method of depreciation and also entitled to claim extra depreciation as arrears of past.

One of the grounds discussed for taking such a view was that it affects capital structure of a company and does not affect working results and as per the Schedule cannot form part of book profit.

In Indo Marine Agencies (Kerala) Pvt. Ltd. v. ACIT [1995] 51 TTJ 18, the Cochin Bench of Tribunal has taken a view that profit on sale of capital asset shown in Profit and Loss Account should be reckoned for computing book profit.

The assessee-company sold certain shares at the rate less than the face value thereof. The ITO was of the view that the said shares had been sold at an unusually low price to a great advantage to the vendee and, therefore, he proceeded to ascertain their break-up value and brought the surplus to tax.

On appeal the AAC determined the value of the shares, taking the mean of the break-up value and the market price of those shares. On second appeal, the Tribunal held that the break-up value of the said shares did not indicate their market value on the date of sale on account of the low return on the basis of average maintainable commercial profits, and further that the value at which the said shares had been sold, that is, at little less than the per value, was very reasonable, and thus the assessee did not make any capital gain but suffered a loss.

Further, the ITO had also refused to allow development rebate in respect of certain capital items like coal tubs, cast iron pipes, etc. The Tribunal allowed the development rebate subject to the assessee complying with the provisions of the reserve.
